translit: intirarum nāraṇarum eṇṇil piramarkaḷum vantiṟaiñcum veḷḷi malaiyāṉē - tantiṭunal
translation: O Lord of the sky-reaching silver mountain. Indra, Narayana, and countless Brahmas come and bow before you.
commentary: Indra (the king of heaven), Narayana, and countless creator gods all come to bow before the Lord of the silver mountain. He stands far above the greatest gods of tradition.

translit: tāykkuṅ kiṭaiyāta taṇṇaruḷkoṇ ṭaṉparuḷam vāykkuṅ kayilai malaiyāṉē - tūykkumaraṉ
translation: O Lord of Mount Kailash who abides in the hearts of devotees. You possess a cool grace not found even in a good, giving mother.
commentary: Mount Kailash is a famous sacred peak, but the Lord's true home is the devotee's heart. His grace is a cool, comforting mercy that runs deeper than even a devoted mother's love.

translit: tantaiyē eṉṉarumait tantaiyē tāyēyeṉ cintaiyē kōyilkoṇṭa tīrttaṉē - cantamikum
translation: O father, my precious father. O mother. O pure one who made my mind your temple. Possessing abundant beauty,
commentary: Vallalar loves God as both mother and father, and says the divine has chosen his own mind as its temple.

translit: eṇṭō ḷuṭaiyāy eṉaiyuṭaiyāy mārpakattil vaṇṭō liṭuṅkoṉṟai mālaiyāy - toṇṭarviḻi
translation: you have eight shoulders. You possess me. You wear on your chest a konrai garland where bees buzz. To the eyes of your devotees,
commentary: Siva appears in his traditional form, eight-shouldered, with the golden konrai garland on his chest. In the middle of all that grandeur sits one plain statement of belonging: Vallalar is owned completely by God.

translit: uṇṇaṟ keḷiyāy uruttiraṉmā lātiyartaṅ kaṇṇiṟ kaṉaviṉiluṅ kāṇpariyāy - maṇṇulakil
translation: you are easy to drink in. Yet you are difficult to see even in the dreams of Rudra, Vishnu, and the other gods. In this earthly world,
commentary: True devotion makes God easy for the seeker to drink in. The same truth stays hidden even from the greatest gods, Vishnu and Rudra among them, who cannot see him even in dreams.

translit: eṉpōṉ ṟavarkkum iruḷnīkki iṉputavum poṉpōṉṟa mēṉip purātaṉaṉē - miṉpōṉṟa
translation: you remove the darkness and grant bliss even to people like me. O ancient one with a golden form. With your lightning-like
commentary: Grace reaches down to ordinary people in this physical world, people like Vallalar. It clears away the darkness of ignorance and puts pure joy in its place.

translit: ceñcaṭaiyāy mūvarukkum tēvarukku miyāvarukkum añcaṭaiyā vaṇṇam aḷippōṉē - viñculakil
translation: red matted hair, you grant protection to the three primal gods, the celestials, and all beings so that fear never touches them. In the supreme world,
commentary: God is the sanctuary of every form of life. His grace keeps fear away from everyone, from the highest ruling gods down to the simplest living creatures.

translit: ellārkku nallavaṉē ellāñcey vallavaṉē ellārkkum oṉṟā yiruppōṉē - tollūḻi
translation: O one who is good to all. O one capable of doing all things. O one who exists as the single reality for everyone. Through ancient eons...
commentary: One reality unites every living being. It is good to all of them and able to do anything at all.

translit: ārnta carācaraṅka ḷellā maṭiniḻalil cērntoṭuṅka mānaṭaṉañ ceyvōṉē - cārntulakil
translation: O one who performs the great cosmic dance so that all abundant moving and unmoving things gather and dissolve in the shadow of your feet. Manifesting in the world...
commentary: Tamil tradition sorts the world into moving creatures and unmoving things like plants and stones. The Lord's great dance brings the whole cosmos into being, and every one of these forms finally comes to rest in the shelter of his feet.

translit: ettēvar meyttēva reṉṟuraikkap paṭṭavarkaḷ attēvark kellāmuṉ ṉāṉōṉē - cattāṉa
translation: Whichever gods are declared to be true gods, you are the one who existed before all those gods. Taking on the true...
commentary: People declare many different deities to be the one true god. The ultimate divine reality exists long before all these named gods and serves as the single source for them all.

translit: veṇmaimutal aivaṇamu mēvi-aintu tēvarkaḷāyt tiṇmaipeṟum aintoḻiluñ ceyvōṉē - maṇmutalām
translation: Taking on the five colors beginning with white, manifesting as the five deities, O one who performs the firm fivefold cosmic acts. Beginning with the earth...
commentary: Tradition names five deities for five cosmic duties: creation, protection, destruction, hiding the truth, and granting grace. The supreme divine is the real power behind them all, taking on these five forms and their symbolic colors to run the universe.

translit: aintā yirucuṭarā yāṉmāvāy nātamuṭaṉ vintā kiyeṅkum virintōṉē - antaṇaveṇ
translation: As the five elements, as the two great luminaries, as the soul, and as the primal sound and primal light, O one who expands everywhere. Taking the form of the pure...
commentary: The one divine presence spreads out to become everything. It forms the elements of the world, the sun and the moon, every soul, and the primal sound (nādam) and primal energy (vindu) that first set the universe moving.

translit: nīṟuṭaiyā yāṟuṭaiya nīṇmuṭiyāy nēṭariya vīṟuṭaiyāy niṉṟaṉakkōr viṇṇappam - māṟupaṭa
translation: O Lord adorned with sacred ash! O Lord with a tall crown bearing the river! O Lord possessing unsearchable greatness! I have a petition for you.
commentary: The formal appeal opens with familiar images of Siva wearing sacred ash and carrying the river Ganges on his head. Then Vallalar comes to God with a direct, personal plea.

translit: eḷḷa laṭiyēṉ eṉakkuḷ oḷiyāmal uḷḷa paṭiyē yuraikkiṉṟēṉ - viḷḷuṟumiyāṉ
translation: I, a lowly servant worthy of scorn, speak exactly as it is, hiding nothing contrarily within myself. I who declare this...
commentary: Before the petition itself, Vallalar promises to hide nothing. He drops all spiritual pride and vows to confess his flaws exactly as they are.

translit: vaṉco luṭaṉaṉṟi vaḷḷaluṉa taṉpartamak kiṉco luṭaṉpaṇintoṉ ṟīntatilai - puṉcoleṉum
translation: O generous Lord! I have never respectfully spoken sweet words and offered anything to your devotees. I have only spoken with harsh words.
commentary: The confession starts with everyday kindness. Vallalar admits he met the Lord's devotees with harsh words and never once offered them gentle speech or a gift.

translit: poyyuraikka veṉṟāṟ puṭaiyeḻuvēṉ aṉṟiyoru meyyuraikka veṉṟum viḻaintatilai - vaiyakattil
translation: If it is to speak lies, which are vile words, I spring up eagerly. I have never desired to speak a single truth.
commentary: Lies come to him eagerly, Vallalar admits, almost by nature. Truth he never even wanted to speak.

translit: pollā viratattaip pōṟṟiyuvan tuṇpatallāl kollā viratattaik koṇṭatilai - allātār
translation: In this world, I have never adopted the vow of non-killing. I have only praised wicked vows and eaten gladly.
commentary: The deepest failing he confesses is the failure of compassion. Vallalar admits to eating food obtained through harm instead of keeping the vow of non-killing. For Vallalar, Jeevakarunyam (compassion for all living beings) is the absolute foundation of spiritual life. The vows he once praised without it, he now calls wicked.

translit: vaṉpukaḻaik kēṭka maṉaṅkoṇṭa tallāmal niṉpukaḻaik kēṭka niṉaintatilai - vaṉpukoṇṭē
translation: I set my mind on hearing empty worldly praise. I never thought to hear your praise.
commentary: Vallalar ran after the world's shallow flattery and never cared to hear of the Lord's greatness. Most of us know this failing well.

translit: iṉṉaṭikku nuṇṇiṭaiyārk kēvalpurin tēṉalatuṉ poṉṉaṭikkut toṇṭu purintatilai - paṉṉukiṉṟa
translation: With a harsh heart I served women with sweet steps and slender waists. I never performed service for your golden feet.
commentary: Vallalar owns up to chasing desire. His energy went into pleasing women, and none of it into serving the Lord's golden feet.

translit: cekkuṟṟa eḷḷeṉavē cintainacin tēṉalatu mukkuṟṟan taṉṉai muṟittatilai - tukkamikun
translation: My mind was crushed like sesame seeds caught in an oil press. I never destroyed the three well-known faults.
commentary: Worldly life grinds the mind like sesame seeds in a heavy stone oil press. Vallalar laments that he let it crush him and never once tried to conquer the three faults of desire, anger, and delusion.

translit: tāvil valaṅkoṇṭu cañcarittēṉ allatuniṉ kōvilvalaṅ koḷḷak kuṟittanilai - pūvulakil
translation: Overcome by great sorrow, I wandered in vain. I never set my mind on circumambulating your temple.
commentary: Vallalar sets his restless wandering beside the simple act of walking around a temple. He covered endless miles in worldly sorrow but never took the few steps needed to circle the divine presence in worship.

translit: vaṉṉitiyōr muṉkūppi vāḻttiṉēṉ aṉṟiyuṉṟaṉ caṉṉitiyiṟ kaikūppit tāḻntatilai - puṉṉeṟicēr
translation: In this earthly world, I stood before the cruel rich and praised them. I never folded my hands and bowed down in your presence.
commentary: People often lower themselves to win favor from the wealthy and powerful. Vallalar confesses he stood begging before cruel rich men and praising them falsely, yet never folded his hands in reverence before God.

translit: miṇṭaroṭu kūṭi viyantatallā laiyāniṉ toṇṭa roṭuṅkūṭic cūḻntatilai - kaṇṭavaraik
translation: O Lord! I gathered with the arrogant and admired them. I never gathered with your devotees to stand around you.
commentary: We are easily drawn to worldly people who boast of their pride. Vallalar confesses he chose the company of the arrogant over the quiet presence of true devotees, and he knows how dangerous bad company is.

translit: kaṉṟumukaṅ koṇṭu kaṭukaṭuttup pārppatallāl eṉṟu mukamalarcci yēṟṟatilai - naṉṟupeṟu
translation: Whenever I saw people, I only looked at them with a harsh face and glared at them bitterly. I never greeted anyone with a blossoming smile.
commentary: A spiritual life begins with how we treat others in ordinary moments. Vallalar admits he met people with bitterness when a welcoming smile would have cost him nothing. Grace asks for a warm, open face toward everyone we meet.

translit: naṉṉeñca ruṉcīr navila vatukēṭṭuk kaṉṉeñcaic caṟṟuṅ karaittatilai - piṉṉeñcāp
translation: When those who possess goodness and a pure heart spoke of your glories, I listened, but I never softened my stony heart even slightly.
commentary: Hearing about God is useless if the heart stays hard. Vallalar listened while good people praised the Lord, and he felt nothing. Until the inner self softens, the teaching never gets in.

translit: paṇṇīrmai koṇṭatamiḻp pāmālai yāṟṟutittuk kaṇṇīrkoṇ ṭuṉpāṟ kaṉintatilai - taṇṇīrpōl
translation: I never praised you with unfailing, melodic garlands of Tamil verse. I never ripened in devotion toward you with tears filling my eyes.
commentary: Devotion is meant to pour out through the body as much as the heart. Vallalar speaks of maturity as ripening, where love overflows as tears. He never sang sweet songs of praise or wept with longing, so his heart stayed unripe.

translit: neñcam uruki niṉaikkumaṉpar pōleṉainī añcaleṉa niṉṟāḷ aṭuttanilai - viñculakar
translation: Yet you approached and ruled me, saying "Fear not," treating me like your true devotees who think of you with hearts melting like water.
commentary: After all that harshness and the closed heart, the Lord still comes near and says, "Fear not." Grace arrives when we have done nothing to earn it. The supreme light gives the flawed soul the same love it gives the most devoted saint.

translit: meyyaṭiya ṉeṉṟuraikka vittakaniṉ poṉṉaṭikkup poyyaṭimai vēṭaṅkaḷ pūṇṭatuṇṭu - naiyamiku
translation: O wise Lord, just to be called a true devotee, I put on false disguises of servitude to your golden feet.
commentary: Vallalar confesses to religious hypocrisy. He put on the outward costume of a holy man to win praise from others, while true devotion to God was missing underneath.

translit: maiyal viṉaikkuvanta mātar puṇarcciyeṉum veyya viṉaikkuḻiyil vīḻntatuṇṭu - tuyyartamai
translation: Languishing greatly, I fell into the cruel karmic pit called union with women, driven by the karma of lust.
commentary: Sensual desire is a trap for the soul. Vallalar laments falling into the pit of lust, which binds a person to worldly suffering and pulls attention away from spiritual growth.

translit: eṉṉoṉṟu millā tiyalpākap piṉṉoṉṟu muṉṉoṉṟu māka moḻintatuṇṭu - maṉṉukiṉṟa
translation: Regarding the pure ones, I acted without any integrity, speaking one thing to their faces and another thing behind their backs.
commentary: Deceit eats away at integrity. Vallalar owns the shame of being two-faced, speaking sweetly to the pure-hearted and saying the opposite behind their backs.

translit: māṉañ ceyātu maṉanon tirappōrkkut tāṉañcey vārait taṭuttatuṇṭu - īṉamilā
translation: When people begged with aching hearts, I failed to treat them with abiding dignity, and I even stopped those who stepped forward to give them charity.
commentary: Jeevakarunyam (compassion for all living beings) is the foundation of spiritual life, and this is the failure Vallalar confesses. He ignored the suffering of those who begged. Worse, he stopped others from giving them charity.

translit: vāramurai yātu vaḻakki ṉiṭaiyōra vāra muraittē malaintatuṇṭu - īramilā
translation: In the middle of disputes, rather than speaking with flawless impartiality, I spoke with bias and caused strife.
commentary: Justice means speaking the truth without favoritism. Vallalar regrets taking sides in disputes, using biased words that stirred up conflict when he could have brought peace.

translit: neñca ruṭaṉkūṭi nēcañcey tummaṭiyē tañcameṉat tāḻātu tāḻntatuṇṭu - eñcalilāt
translation: I have joined with deceitful people and shown them affection. I have degraded myself instead of bowing to your feet as my true refuge.
commentary: Worldly attachments lead people away from their true refuge. Vallalar wasted his affection on deceitful companions and lowered his own character, while safety at the feet of God went unsought.

translit: tāyaṉaiyā yuṉṟaṉatu cannitinēr vantumoru nēyamumil lātotipōl niṉṟatuṇṭu - tīyaviṉai
translation: O flawless mother, even when coming directly into your presence, I have stood completely devoid of love like a lifeless tree.
commentary: Standing close to the divine does not open the heart by itself. Calling God a flawless mother, Vallalar admits he stood in that sacred presence with no love at all, like a dry, lifeless tree.

translit: māḷāk koṭiya maṉaccelvar vāyiliṟpōyk kēḷāc civanintai kēṭṭatuṇṭu - mīḷāta
translation: I have gone to the doors of the cruel-hearted wealthy who are burdened by endless evil deeds, and I have listened to unspeakable blasphemy against Siva.
commentary: Seeking favors from cruel people harms the soul. Vallalar waited at the doors of the arrogant rich and sat quietly while they insulted Siva.

translit: pollāp pulaiyaraippōṟ puṇṇiyarai vaṉmatattāl collā vacaiyellāñ coṉṉatuṇṭu - nallōraip
translation: Driven by intense arrogance, I have hurled every unspeakable insult at virtuous people, acting like the wicked and base.
commentary: Arrogance poisons the mind against good people. Vallalar is deeply sorry for the times his ego drove him to hurl terrible insults at the virtuous and holy.

translit: pōṟṟātu poyyuṭampaip pōṟṟic civapūcai āṟṟātu cōṟṟuk kalaintatuṇṭu - tēṟṟāmal
translation: Failing to revere good people, nurturing only this false body, and neglecting the worship of Siva, I have wandered aimlessly just for the sake of food.
commentary: Obsession with physical survival crowds out the spirit. Vallalar fell into that trap, wandering about just to feed a temporary body while he neglected the worship of Siva entirely.

translit: īpattā eṉṟiṅ kirappōr tamaikkaṇṭu kōpattāl nāypōṟ kuraittatuṇṭu - pāpattāl
translation: Seeing beggars crying for alms, I have barked at them like an angry dog.
commentary: Jeevakarunyam (compassion for all living beings) is the absolute foundation of Vallalar's path, so this is no small confession. Taking on the voice of an ordinary person, he admits to meeting the hungry with anger where mercy belonged.

translit: cintaiyoṉṟu vākkoṉṟu ceykaiyoṉṟāyp pōkaviṭṭē entainiṉai yēttā tiruntatuṇṭu - puntiyinta
translation: Driven by sin, I let my mind think one thing, my words speak another, and my actions do something else entirely, and I have lived without praising you, my Father.
commentary: Thought, word and deed have to line up. Vallalar admits to a life of hypocrisy, and a scattered, deceitful mind like that never makes any real connection with the divine.

translit: collaikkal leṉṟunallōr coṉṉaputti kēḷāmal ellaikkal lottē yiruntatuṇṭu - tollaiviṉai
translation: Ignoring the good people who told my mind to learn the sacred words, I have stood stubbornly like a lifeless boundary stone.
commentary: A boundary stone marks a fixed limit and never grows or moves. That is how Vallalar pictures his refusal of spiritual wisdom, standing deaf to the guidance of the wise.

translit: āḻttā mayavulaki laṟpa makiḻcciyiṉāl vāḻttāma luṉṉai maṟantatuṇṭu - tāḻttāmaṟ
translation: Sunk by ancient karma into this illusory world, I reveled in trivial pleasures, forgot you, and failed to praise you.
commentary: Fleeting, trivial joys trap the soul in the material world. Vallalar grieves at how easily they make a person forget God.

translit: pūṇā velumpaṇiyāyp pūṇṭōyniṉ poṉvaṭivaṅ kāṇātu vīḻnāḷ kaḻittatuṇṭu - māṇāta
translation: O Lord who unhesitatingly wears a garland of bones that no one else would wear, I have wasted my days without ever seeing your golden form.
commentary: In traditional imagery, Siva wears a garland of bones to show his mastery over death and the dissolution of the universe. Vallalar looks back with regret on a lifetime spent in ignorance, never once seeing that radiant golden form.

translit: kāṭupōṉ ñālak kaṭunaṭaiyi lēyirukāṉ māṭupōl niṉṟuḻaittu vāḻntatuṇṭu - nāṭakaṉṟa
translation: I have lived toiling like a two-legged beast of burden in the harsh paths of this forest-like world.
commentary: A purely material life wears a person out and leaves them empty. Vallalar sees himself as a beast of burden, working endlessly just to survive in a harsh world with no higher purpose.

translit: kaḷḷivā yōṅkuperuṅ kāmak kaṭuṅkāṭṭiṟ koḷḷivāyp pēypōṟ kutittatuṇṭu - oḷḷiyarāl
translation: Leaving the civilized paths, I have leapt about like a fire-mouthed demon in the harsh, vast forest of lust overgrown with tall cacti.
commentary: Unchecked desire turns a person into something destructive. Picture a fire-mouthed demon leaping through a cactus forest: that is lust and worldly craving burning the mind and leading people away from compassionate living.

translit: eḷḷuṇṭa māyā iyalpuṟupuṉ kalviyelāṅ kaḷḷuṇṭa pittaṉaippōṟ kaṟṟatuṇṭu - naḷḷulakil
translation: Like a drunken madman, I have learned all the petty, illusory worldly knowledge mocked by the wise.
commentary: Worldly education often distracts from spiritual truth. Vallalar confesses that he gathered useless, ego-driven knowledge like a drunkard, wasting time on subjects the truly wise recognize as illusion.

translit: cīrācai yeṅkuñcoṟ ceṉṟiṭavē vēṇṭumeṉum pērācaip pēytāṉ piṭittatuṇṭu - tīrāveṉ
translation: The demon of immense greed possessed me in the midst of the world, making me crave fame and demand that my word reach everywhere.
commentary: Craving fame and influence is its own kind of demonic possession. Vallalar admits to wanting everyone to hear his words and praise his name, a greed that feeds the ego and blocks spiritual growth.

translit: cātakamō tīviṉaiyiṉ cātaṉaiyō nāṉaṟiyēṉ pātakameṉ ṟāleṉakkup pāṟcōṟu - tītakaṉṟa
translation: I do not know if this is my unceasing destiny or the culmination of my evil deeds. To me, a heinous sin is as sweet as milk-rice.
commentary: Vallalar confesses total moral blindness. He is so used to doing wrong that a terrible sin feels as sweet and comforting as milk-rice, and he cannot tell whether his own past actions have cursed him.

translit: tūymainaṉṟā meṉkiṉṟa toṉmaiyiṉār vāykkiṉiya vāymaiyeṉṟāl eṉṉuṭaiya vāykumaṭṭuṅ - kāymaitarum
translation: If I am asked to speak the sweet truth of the ancients who declare that purity is good, my mouth feels nauseated. It brings me bitter disgust.
commentary: Speaking the wholesome truth of the wise makes Vallalar feel physically sick, he says. An aversion to goodness that extreme shows the spiritual sickness afflicting humanity until divine grace heals it.

translit: kaṟku nikarāṅ kaṭuñcolaṉṟi naṉmaturac coṟkum eṉakkumveku tūraṅkāṇ - poṟpumika
translation: Apart from harsh words that strike like stones, good and sweet words remain very far from me.
commentary: Vallalar admits his words are as hard and damaging as stones. Cruelty comes easily to him. Speaking gently and kindly to others feels completely foreign.

translit: naṇṇiyuṉaip pōṟṟukiṉṟa nallōrk kiṉiyaciva puṇṇiyameṉ ṟāleṉakkup pōrāṭṭam - aṇṇaluṉai
translation: If asked to perform the sweet holy acts of Siva cherished by the good people who draw near and praise you with great grace, it is a struggle for me.
commentary: Siva punniyam means holy or virtuous actions dedicated to God. True devotees find joy in these acts, Vallalar says, while for him doing good is an exhausting battle.

translit: nāḷuraiyā tēttukiṉṟa nallōrmēl illāta kōḷuraiyeṉ ṟāleṉakkuk koṇṭāṭṭam - nīḷaniṉai
translation: O Lord, if given the chance to speak false slander against the good people who daily praise you beyond words, it is a celebration for me.
commentary: Vallalar admits he finds real joy in spreading false rumors about sincere devotees. It is the ego at its darkest, raising itself by pulling down those who are genuinely devoted to God.

translit: nēcikku nalla neṟiyāñ civākamanūl vācikka veṉṟāleṉ vāynōkuṅ - kācikku
translation: If asked to read the Sivagama scriptures that reveal the good path to love you deeply, my mouth aches.
commentary: The Sivagamas are foundational scriptures that guide the worship of Siva. Merely trying to read them gives Vallalar a physical ache, a vivid picture of complete inner resistance to spiritual discipline.

translit: nīṭikki lāṉālu nērntaṟiva tallatuvīṇ vēṭikkai yeṉṟāl viṭuvatilai - nāṭayalil
translation: Even if it is fleeting, I experience it directly, and I never abandon vain amusement. If in a neighboring land...
commentary: Vallalar speaks in the voice of an ordinary, flawed person confessing to God. He admits he clings to empty worldly amusements and will not give them up, brief and meaningless as they are.

translit: vīṟā muṉatu viḻācceyiṉum avviṭantāṉ āṟā yiraṅkāta māṅkaṇṭāy - māṟāṉa
translation: ...your magnificent festival is celebrated, that place appears to be six thousand leagues away. You see this. If someone mentions contrary...
commentary: The worldly mind has no appetite for God. If a festival in His honor is held close by, it makes excuses, and a short walk turns into an impossible distance of thousands of miles.

translit: pōkameṉṟā luḷḷamikap pūrikkum aṉṟiciva yōkameṉṟā leṉṉuṭaiya uṇṇaṭuṅkum - cōkamuṭaṉ
translation: ...worldly pleasures, my heart swells with immense joy. But if they mention Siva yoga, my inner being trembles with sorrow.
commentary: Worldly indulgence fills him with joy, while the thought of spiritual discipline fills him with dread. Siva yoga means the practice of uniting the soul with the Divine. To a mind caught in material desire, the effort that union asks feels like a terrible burden.

translit: tuḷḷaloḻin teṉṉeñcañ cōrntaḻiyuṅ kālattiṟ kaḷḷameṉṟā luḷḷē kaḷitteḻumpum - aḷḷaṉeṟi
translation: When my heart ceases its leaping and wastes away in exhaustion, if someone speaks of deceit, it leaps up with inner delight. If told to walk the path of mire...
commentary: Bad habits run deep. With body and heart worn out, the mere mention of deceit or mischief still sends a sudden, glad burst of energy through him.

translit: celleṉṟāl aṉṟic civacivā veṉṟorukāl colleṉṟāl eṉṟaṉakkut tukkamvarum - nallaneṟi
translation: ...I will go. But if told to say "Siva Siva" even once, sorrow overcomes me.
commentary: His heart runs backward. He will gladly walk into the mud of base worldly life, yet being asked to say God's name even once makes him truly miserable.

translit: vāmpalaṉkoṇ ṭōrkaḷ maṟantum peṟākkoṭiya cōmpaleṉpa teṉṉuṭaiya contaṅkāṇ - ēmpaluṭaṉ
translation: See, cruel laziness, which the virtuous never experience even in their forgetfulness, is my true possession.
commentary: Laziness, he confesses, is the one thing that is really his. Those who practice virtue never fall into it even by forgetting, and he owns it outright, a cruel, paralyzing sloth.

translit: eṟṟō irakkameṉpa teṉṟaṉaikkaṇ ṭañciyeṉai uṟṟō raiyumuṭaṉviṭ ṭōṭuṅkāṇ - caṟṟēṉum
translation: In distress I cry, alas! Compassion sees me, becomes terrified, and runs away, abandoning even those close to me.
commentary: Here is a heart with no compassion left in it. Compassion takes one look at his cruelty, grows frightened, and flees, carrying its blessings away from everyone around him too.

translit: ākkamē cērā taṟatturattu kiṉṟaveṟun tūkkamē yeṉṟaṉakkuc cōpaṉaṅkāṇ - ūkkamikum
translation: See, mere empty sleep, which chases away virtue and brings not even a little prosperity, is my only joy.
commentary: He sleeps his life away instead of waking to spiritual truth or doing good. That heavy, useless sleep is his only pleasure, though it drains away everything he might have become.

translit: ēṟuṭaiyāy nīṟaṇiyā īṉarmaṉai yāyiṉumveṇ cōṟukiṭait tālatuvē corkkaṅkāṇ - vīṟukiṉṟa
translation: O Lord who rides the mighty bull! Even if it is the home of base people who do not wear the sacred ash, if I get white rice there, that itself is heaven to me.
commentary: God is traditionally depicted riding a bull in Hindu scripture, and Vallalar addresses Him that way before confessing plain gluttony. He cares nothing for spiritual purity. He will happily eat in the homes of base people who do not wear sacred ash (a physical mark of devotion), and any place that feeds him a simple meal of white rice is the only heaven he wants.

translit: vāḻvuraikku nalla maṉattartamai yeññāṉṟun tāḻvuraittal eṉṉuṭaiya cātakaṅkāṇ - vēḷviceyun
translation: See, my constant habit is to speak ill of good-hearted people who teach the path to a glorious life.
commentary: Now he admits to mocking the very people who try to help others. Good-hearted teachers show the way to a better life, and his constant habit is to insult them and tear them down.

translit: toṇṭar tamaittutiyāt tuṭṭaraippō leppoḻutuñ caṇṭaiyeṉpa teṉṟaṉakkut tāytantai - koṇṭa-eḻu
translation: Like the wicked who never praise your devotees, constant quarreling is a mother and father to me.
commentary: Speaking as a flawed person, Vallalar makes the need for grace plain. Instead of respecting devoted people he cherishes conflict. Anger and argument are his family, mother and father both.

translit: tātāṭa ōṅkit talaiyāṭa vañcaroṭu vātāṭa eṉṟāleṉ vāytuṭikkuṅ - kōtāṭac
translation: If told to argue with deceitful people, with my energy flaring and my head tossed high, my mouth quivers with eagerness.
commentary: Even his body is eager for a petty fight. Offer him a pointless debate with deceitful people and he feels the rush of energy and pride, the very opposite of inner peace.

translit: cintai tirintuḻalun tīyaraippōl naṟṟaruma nintaiyeṉpa teṉpaḻaiya nēcaṅkāṇ - muntaniṉai
translation: Like evil people who wander with twisted minds, scorning true virtue is my old beloved habit.
commentary: Sneering at good deeds and moral living is a common trap of the worldly mind. Vallalar laments that mocking true virtue has become an old, familiar comfort, and he ranks his own mindset with that of the deeply wicked.

translit: eṇṇeṉṟāl aṉṟi yiṭarcey tiṭuṅkoṭiya peṇṇeṉṟāl tūkkam piṭiyātu - peṇkaḷuṭaṉ
translation: If told to think of you first, I refuse. But if the topic is cruel women who bring trouble, sleep completely abandons me.
commentary: Asked to fix his mind on the Divine first, he refuses. Let the talk turn to women and worldly lust, and the thought alone keeps him wide awake all night.

translit: pulleṉṟāl tēkam puḷakikkum aṉṟiviṭṭu nilleṉṟāl eṉkaṇṇi ṉīrarumpum - pullareṉṟa
translation: If told to embrace women, my body thrills with joy. But if told to leave them and stand apart, tears well up in my eyes.
commentary: The senses can overpower the spirit completely. Told to embrace women, his body thrills with joy. Told to leave them and stand apart in detachment, he weeps.

translit: pērkkumvirup peytāta peṇpēykaḷ veyyaciṟu nīrkkuḻiyē yāṉkuḷikku nīrppoykai - cīrkkaraiyiṉ
translation: The hot puddle of urine from demonic women with unyielding lust is the very pond where I bathe.
commentary: Vallalar is disgusted with his own obsession with lust. He compares his physical desires to bathing in a foul puddle of bodily waste. The harsh image carries his shame at choosing a passing physical attraction over the divine.

translit: ēṟāppeṇ māta riṭaikku ḷaḷinteṉṟum āṟāppuṇ ṇukkē yaṭimaināṉ - tēṟāta
translation: Never reaching the good shore, I yield to the waists of women and remain a slave forever to that unhealing wound.
commentary: He sees himself trapped by lust. Calling the object of his desire an unhealing wound shows that sensory pleasure only brings pain. He is stranded on the wrong shore of life, a slave to the body when he should be moving toward spiritual freedom.

translit: veñcalañcey māyā vikāratti ṉālvarumvīṇ cañcalamellā meṉatu campantam - añceḻuttai
translation: All the vain sorrows born from the confused, cruel, and deceitful distortions of illusion are my only relationships.
commentary: Worldly attachments are cruel illusions (māyā). Vallalar says his only companions are the sorrows and confusion this false reality produces. Where divine relationships should be, he finds empty anxiety.

translit: nērntārk karuḷpuriyu niṉṉaṭiyar tāmēyuñ cārntā latuperiya caṅkaṭṭam - ārntiṭumāṉ
translation: Even if your devotees, who bestow grace upon those devoted to the five letters, approach me, I feel only great distress.
commentary: Vallalar feels so degraded that the presence of holy people fills him with shame. These devotees chant the sacred five syllables (añceḻuttu, the mantra Na-Ma-Si-Va-Ya) and bring grace to others. His guilt makes him shrink from their purifying company.

translit: kāntum viḻippuliyaik kaṇṭatupōl nallakuṇa cānta meṉaik kaṇṭāl talaicāykkum - āntakaiyōr
translation: Just as a startled deer reacts upon seeing a tiger with burning eyes, good character and tranquility hang their heads and turn away when they see me.
commentary: Goodness and peace run from Vallalar the way a deer flees a tiger. Virtues like tranquility turn their heads away in fear when they see him. With this image his confession of unworthiness is complete.

translit: cēra maṉattiṟ ceṟivit tiṭumpuruṭa tīrameṉaik kaṇṭāṟ cirikkuṅkāṇ - kōramataik
translation: True courage fully gathered in the mind will laugh if it sees me. Look at that horror.
commentary: Courage itself would laugh at him. He feels empty of the mental strength the spiritual path demands.

translit: kāṇi lulakiṟ karuttuṭaiyōr koḷḷukiṉṟa nāṇa meṉaikkaṇṭu nāṇuṅkāṇ - ēṇulakil
translation: If thoughtful people in the world see it, the very shame they possess will feel ashamed upon seeing me. Look, in this esteemed world,
commentary: His flaws run so deep that shame itself would be embarrassed by him. It is a poetic way of confessing complete unworthiness.

translit: ñāṉaṅ koḷāveṉatu nāmamurait tālumapi māṉam payaṅkoṇṭu māyntuviṭum - āṉavuṉṟaṉ
translation: even if my foolish name is uttered, dignity will perish out of fear. Therefore, I am
commentary: Dignity and self-respect flee in fear at the mere mention of his name.

translit: kēṇmaik kulattoṇṭar kīrtti peṟakkoṇṭa āṇmaikku nāṉeṉṟā lākātu - vāṇmaipeṟum
translation: no match for the strength of character possessed by the glorious lineage of your close devotees. O radiant
commentary: True devotees have a glorious strength of character. Vallalar confesses he has none of it and cannot begin to compare himself with them.

translit: aiyaniṉṟāṭ pūcikku maṉparuḷḷat taṉpiṟkum poyya ṉeṉakkum poruttamilai - vaiyakattōr
translation: Lord, there is no match between me, a liar, and the love in the hearts of devotees who worship your feet. People of the earth...
commentary: The pure love in the hearts of real worshippers is missing in Vallalar. He calls himself a liar and measures the wide gap between their sincere devotion and his own spiritual poverty.

translit: illeṉiṉuñ cummānī yīkiṉṟē ṉeṉṟorucol colleṉiṉuñ collat tuṇivukoḷēṉ - nallaiyemak
translation: Even if I possess nothing, I lack the resolve to simply say the word "I will give" when someone asks me.
commentary: Someone in the grip of selfishness cannot even offer an empty promise of charity to a person in need. Speaking in the voice of such a character, Vallalar shows us the exact opposite of Jeevakarunyam (compassion for all living beings). His heart is so closed that the thought of giving cannot form.

translit: kīyeṉpā raṉṟiyaṉṉai yeṉpayattā ṉiṉcōṟṟil īyeṉpa taṟku micaiyāḷkāṇ - īyeṉpārk
translation: When people say, "You are good to us, give," I refuse. Out of fear of me, even my mother will not dare to tell me to give away a mere fly from my rice.
commentary: His hostility to sharing frightens even his own family. A mother would normally teach her child to be generous. This one is too afraid of his anger to ask him to part with something as worthless as a fly.

translit: keṇṇuñ cilarmaṇ ṇiṭuvā reṉakkanta maṇṇuṅ koṭukkamaṉam vārātu - aṇṇuṟumeṉ
translation: To those who ask for alms, some people might at least consider throwing some dirt. I do not have the heart to give them even that dirt.
commentary: Cruel people may mock a beggar by throwing dirt instead of food. Vallalar admits a greed so complete that he cannot part with even the dirt on the ground.

translit: illai yaṭaintē yirappavaruk keppōtum illaiyeṉpa teṉvāyk kiyalpukāṇ - tollulakai
translation: When beggars draw near and approach my house, it is the ingrained nature of my mouth to always tell them I have nothing.
commentary: Turning away the poor has become a reflex. His mouth forms the refusal out of sheer habit, before he has given a thought to the suffering of the person standing at his door.

translit: āṇṭālu maṉṟi ayalārpuṉ kīraimaṇip pūṇṭālu meṉkaṇ poṟukkātu - nīṇṭa-eḻu
translation: Whether others rule the ancient world or my neighbors wear a tiny jewel as small as a spinach seed, my eyes cannot bear to see it.
commentary: Greed breeds envy. Vallalar is tormented by the good fortune of others, whether a stranger rules the world or a neighbor wears a jewel the size of a seed. Such bitter jealousy poisons the mind and leaves no room for love toward fellow living beings.

translit: tīpa muṟuvōr ticaiyōrmaṟ ṟiyāvarkkuṅ kōpa matunāṉ koṭukkiluṇṭu - āpattil
translation: I have enough anger to distribute to those dwelling on islands, to those in all directions, and to everyone else. In times of distress,
commentary: The ego, as Vallalar paints it, is a bottomless well of anger. Speaking as an ordinary sinner, he says he has enough rage to hand out in every direction and to every distant island. That is how anger floods the unrefined mind.

translit: vīcaṅ koṭutteṭṭu vīca meṉappiṟarai mōcañ ceyanāṉ mutaṟpātam - pācamuḷōr
translation: I give others a single fraction of a coin and deceive them by claiming it is eight fractions. I am foremost in such fraud. For the hands of those with worldly attachments,
commentary: A vīcam is an old fractional Tamil coin. Vallalar admits to lending a tiny amount and fraudulently demanding eight times as much in return. Greed like this feeds on people in distress, and taking advantage of them is a deep failure of compassion.

translit: kaikkuṭaiya vēyeḻutik kaṭṭivaitta ivvulakap poykkataiyē yāṉpaṭikkum puttakaṅkaḷ - meyppaṭuniṉ
translation: people have written and bound the false stories of this world, and these are the only books I read. I possess a mouth that does not chant Your true
commentary: The mind drifts toward what is familiar. Vallalar admits he spends his time on the false stories of this world, books written by and for people caught in worldly attachments. Reading them keeps the reader trapped in the same illusions.

translit: mantirattai uccariyā vāyuṭaiyēṉ eṉpōlat tantirattil kaitērn tavarillai - entai-iṉi
translation: mantra. No one is as skilled in cunning tricks as I am. My Father, what more
commentary: The mouth that should be repeating God's true mantra stays silent. Yet in worldly cunning and manipulation Vallalar calls himself an expert without equal. That is where human intelligence so often goes: into selfish survival, far from God.

translit: ēteṉ ṟuraippē ṉiruṅkaṭalcūḻ vaiyakattil cūteṉpa tellāmeṉ cuṟṟaṅkāṇ - ōtukiṉṟa
translation: shall I say now? In this world surrounded by the vast dark ocean, all that is known as deceit is my own kin.
commentary: Deceit is so ingrained in him that he calls it his own kin. In a world ringed by the vast ocean, he stands alone in a web of lies. His confession of spiritual bankruptcy is now complete, and nothing is left to lean on but God's grace.

translit: nañcamelāṅ kūṭṭi naviṉṟiṭiṉum ovvāta vañcamelā meṉkai vacaṅkaṇṭāy - añcavarum
translation: See, I hold within my grasp every form of deceit. Even if you gathered all the poisons together, they could not equal my treachery.
commentary: Vallalar confesses a deep spiritual sickness. Deceit in the human heart, he says, is worse than every poison gathered together. Blaming oneself this hard is a traditional way for a seeker to strip off all pride before asking God for help.

translit: vīṇavamām vañca viṉaikkumuta lākiniṉṟa āṇavamē eṉkāṇi āṭciyatām - māṇiṟainta
translation: Arrogance itself is my inherited domain. It stands as the root cause of terrifying, vain, and deceitful actions.
commentary: The root of all this deceit is arrogance (āṇavam). Vallalar calls this ego his inherited property, a piece of land he owns outright. Pride lies under every useless and harmful act.

translit: nallaṟivē eṉṉaineṭu nāṭpakaitta taṉṟimaṟṟaip pullaṟivē eṉṉuṭ poruḷkaṇṭāy - collavoṇā
translation: Glorious true knowledge has harbored enmity toward me for a long time. Petty ignorance is the actual substance within me.
commentary: True wisdom, Vallalar admits, has been his enemy for a long time. What fills him instead is petty ignorance. He is frank about how stubbornly the human mind resists divine light.

translit: vēṭarukkuṅ kiṭṭāta veṅkuṇattā liṅkuḻalum mūṭarukkuḷ yāṉē mutalvaṉkāṇ - vīṭaṭutta
translation: I wander here possessing cruel qualities unmatched even by unspeakable savages. See, I am the absolute foremost among such fools.
commentary: Vallalar claims a cruelty worse than that of the most savage people, and names himself the very worst of fools. Humility pushed this far is a deliberate spiritual practice. It tears the ego down so that grace might enter.

translit: mētaiyarkaḷ vēṇṭā vilaṅkāyt tirikiṉṟa pētaiyeṉpa teṉṉurimaip pērkaṇṭāy - pētamuṟa
translation: The wise who have approached liberation reject me. I wander like an unwanted beast. See, fool is my rightful name.
commentary: Those who have reached spiritual freedom turn him away, and he wanders like an untamed animal. Fool, he says, is his rightful name. Living without wisdom or compassion reduces a person to a mere beast.

translit: ōtuvateṉ paṟpalavāy uṟṟatavat tōrnītta tītukaḷel lāmeṉatu celvaṅkāṇ - ātaliṉāl
translation: Why say many things? All the evils discarded by great ascetics are my wealth.
commentary: Vallalar is blunt about his spiritual poverty. The flaws and worldly attachments that holy people throw away are the only treasure he hoards.

translit: pēyiṉaiyot tivvulakil pittāki niṉṟavinta nāyiṉainī āṇṭiṭutal naṉkaṉṟē - āyiṉumuṉ
translation: Therefore, it is not good for you to rule over this dog who stands mad in this world like a ghost.
commentary: With all these flaws he feels wholly unworthy of grace. He compares his confused, wandering mind to a ghost and a mad dog, and suggests that a pure divine master should not take on so wretched a servant.

translit: maṇṇā ruyirkaḷukkum vāṉavarkkun tāṉiraṅki uṇṇāk koṭuviṭamum uṇṭaṉaiyē - eṇṇāmal
translation: Even so, in the past, taking pity on the souls of the earth and the celestials, you drank the deadly poison that no one should consume.
commentary: Then the turn. Unworthy as he is, Vallalar remembers how vast God's compassion is. In the ancient story the Lord drank the world-destroying poison to save both the souls of earth and the celestials. Mercy that large can save anyone in desperate peril.

translit: vēyttavaḷa veṟpeṭutta veyya-arak kaṉtaṉakkum vāyttavara mellām vaḻaṅkiṉaiyē - cāyttamaṉa
translation: Without hesitation, you granted all fitting boons to the cruel demon who lifted the bamboo-filled white mountain.
commentary: Grace reaches even the arrogant and cruel. A powerful demon king once tried in his pride to uproot the divine mountain, and when he finally offered praise, God still granted him every fitting boon. If that demon could be forgiven, there is hope for Vallalar.

translit: vīmpuṭaiya vaṉmuṉivar vēḷviceytu viṭṭakoṭum pāmpaiyel lāntōḷiṟ parittaṉaiyē - nāmperiyar
translation: You wore on your shoulders all the cruel snakes sent by the harsh sages with arrogant, deviant minds who performed the sacrifice, thinking, "We are great."
commentary: Arrogant sages once tried to destroy God by sending deadly snakes out of their sacrificial fire. Instead of striking back at them, God took the snakes and wore them on his shoulders as ornaments. The divine can take the worst hostility or impurity and change it completely.

translit: eñcēmeṉ ṟāṇavattā lēṟṟa iruvaraiyum añcēleṉ ṟāṭkoṇ ṭaruḷiṉaiyē - tuñcupaṉṟit
translation: You graced the two who clashed out of ego, declaring "We will not yield." You told them "Fear not" and took them under Your rule. When a pig died...
commentary: Brahma and Vishnu, Hindu mythology tells us, once fought a bitter war over which of them was supreme, each refusing to yield. Grace stepped in, ended the fighting, and broke even that great pride. Those who surrendered were given safety.

translit: tōyāk kuruḷaikaḷiṉ tuṉpam poṟātaṉṟu tāyāy mulaippālun tantaṉaiyē - vāyicaikkup
translation: ...unable to bear the sorrow of its unweaned piglets, You became a mother that day and fed them breast milk. For the song...
commentary: A famous sacred story from Madurai tells how the Lord took the form of a mother pig to nurse a litter of orphaned piglets. God's compassion belongs to every creature equally, whatever body it wears.

translit: pāṇṭiyaṉmuṉ collivanta pāṇaṉ poruṭṭaṭimai vēṇṭi viṟakeṭuttu viṟṟaṉaiyē - āṇṭorunāḷ
translation: ...of the bard who sang before the Pandiyan king, You willingly took the form of a servant, gathered firewood, and sold it. And one day...
commentary: Panabhadran, a devoted musician, had to win a contest at the royal court. The Lord dressed as a poor woodcutter and sang in the streets with flawless beauty, humbling the proud competitor on His devotee's behalf.

translit: vāymuṭiyāt tuṉpukoṇṭa vantikkō rāḷākit tūymuṭimēl maṇṇuñ cumantaṉaiyē - āytuyara
translation: ...You became a hired laborer for Vanti, who suffered untold distress, and You carried earth upon Your pure head. For Manikkavasagar...
commentary: When the Vaigai river flooded, the king ordered everyone to help build a dam. Vanthi was an old, destitute woman. God came as her hired laborer and carried the earth on His own head. The divine serves the poorest and most vulnerable directly.

translit: māvakañcēr māṇikka vācakaruk kāykkutiraic cēvakaṉpōl vītitaṉil ceṉṟaṉaiyē - māvicayaṉ
translation: ...whose great heart was steeped in deep sorrow, You rode through the streets as a cavalryman. The great Arjuna...
commentary: Manikkavasagar spent the king's money building a temple instead of buying war horses. To save His devotee from punishment over the missing funds, the Lord turned foxes into magnificent horses and rode them into the city Himself.

translit: villaṭikku neñcam virumpiyatal lāleṟinta kallaṭikkum uḷḷaṅ kaḷittaṉaiyē - mallaluṟum
translation: Your heart welcomed the strike of the bow, and your mind rejoiced at the strike of the thrown stone.
commentary: God accepts devotion in whatever form it comes if the heart is pure. Arjuna, named at the close of the previous line, struck the Lord with his bow during a test of strength. Another devotee threw stones at the sacred image every day as his own ritual of love. God rejoiced at both, seeing only the devotion behind the blows.

translit: vilvak kiḷaiyutirtta veyya mucukkalaiyaic celvat turaimakaṉāyc ceytaṉaiyē - collakaliṉ
translation: You transformed the fierce monkey that dropped the vilva branch into a wealthy royal prince.
commentary: A monkey knocked a branch out of a tree, and a sacred vilva leaf fell onto the deity below. It was a tiny act, and not even intended. For it, God let the animal be reborn as a wealthy prince. That is how freely grace gives.

translit: nīḷukiṉṟa neyyarunta nēreliyai mūvulakum āḷukiṉṟa maṉṉavaṉāy ākkiṉaiyē - kōḷakala
translation: You made the rat that approached to drink the spreading ghee into a king who rules the three worlds.
commentary: A temple rat went after the leftover ghee in a dying lamp. Pulling on the wick to reach the fat, it made the flame burn brighter and lit up the shrine by accident. For that small gift of light, God raised the creature to be a great king.

translit: vāyccaṅku nūliḻaitta vāyccilampi taṉṉai-uyar kōcceṅkaṭ cōḻaṉeṉak kūṭṭiṉaiyē - ēccaṟunal
translation: You elevated the spider that wove a web from its mouth into the noble king Kocengat Chola.
commentary: A spider wove its web over a sacred image to shield it from falling leaves. God saw even that. The tiny creature was reborn as Kocengat Chola, a famous king known for building great temples.

translit: āṟaṭuttavākīcark kāmpaciyaik kaṇṭukaṭṭuc cōṟeṭuttup piṉṉē cumantaṉaiyē - kūṟukiṉṟa
translation: Seeing the hunger of Vagisar as he walked the path, you took packed rice and carried it behind him.
commentary: Vagisar, a great saint, grew exhausted and hungry on a long walk. God took the form of an ordinary man and walked behind him carrying packed rice, ready to feed him when he needed it most. The Lord will be a humble servant to those devoted to Him.

translit: toṉmaiperuñ cuntararkkut tōḻaṉeṉṟu peṇparavai naṉmaṉaikkut tūtu naṭantaṉaiyē - naṉmaipeṟa
translation: Claiming to be the friend of the great and ancient Sundarar, you walked as a messenger to the fine house of the lady Paravai to bring about a good outcome.
commentary: Sundarar's bond with God was so intimate that the Lord, calling Himself the saint's friend, walked through the streets as a messenger to appease his wife, Paravai. No errand is too humble for Him when a true devotee needs it.

translit: iṟṟeṉṟa iṟṟeṉṉā ettaṉaiyō pērkaḷceyta kuṟṟaṅ kuṇamākak koṇṭaṉaiyē - paṟṟulakil
translation: In this world of attachments, you accepted the faults committed by countless people as virtues without judging them one way or another.
commentary: God's forgiveness is absolute and keeps no ledger of human mistakes. People bound by attachments commit countless faults, and He treats them with such grace that they are accepted as virtues.

translit: aṉpuṭaiya tāyarkaḷō rāyirampē rāṉālum aṉpuṭaiyāy niṉṉaippō lāvārō - iṉpamuṭaṉ
translation: Even if a thousand loving mothers were to gather, O loving Lord, could they joyfully equal you?
commentary: Gather the tenderness of a thousand earthly mothers and it still cannot match the pure, joyful love God holds for living beings.

translit: īṇṭavarum tantaiyarkaḷ eṇṇilarē āyiṉumeṉ āṇṭavaṉē niṉṉaippō lāvārō - pūṇṭakaikoḷ
translation: Even if countless fathers gather here, my Lord, could they equal you who hold adorned hands?
commentary: Fathers fall short too. However many guard and guide us, their care cannot equal the Lord's, which holds all earthly parental love and goes far beyond it.

translit: ēṇuṭaiya niṉṉaiyaṉṟi entai pirāṉē-uṉ āṇai-eṉak kuṟṟatuṇai yārumillai - nāṇamuḷaṉ
translation: My Father and Lord who possesses greatness, I swear upon you, I have no true companion other than you. I am filled with shame.
commentary: God is the soul's only true companion. Seeing how vast and unconditional that love is, Vallalar feels humbled and ashamed, completely inadequate before such grace.

translit: āṉēṉ piḻaika ḷaṉaittiṉaiyu maiyānī tāṉē poṟukkat takuṅkaṇṭāy - mēlnōṟṟa
translation: O Lord, I have committed all these faults. It is fitting that You alone forgive them.
commentary: Vallalar throws himself entirely on divine mercy. His faults have piled up, and he trusts that only boundless grace can wash them away.

translit: māṟṟaṉukku meṭṭā malarkkaḻalōy nīyeṉṉaik kūṟṟaṉukkuk kāṭṭik koṭukkaṟka - pāṟṟavaḷa
translation: O Lord whose lotus feet are unreachable even by rivals who perform supreme penance! Do not hand me over to the god of death.
commentary: Vallalar asks plainly to be kept from death. Harsh physical penance cannot force the divine presence, even for those who perform the highest austerities. Only grace grants it.

translit: nantak kaṭaṟpuviyil nāṉiṉṉum vaṉpiṟavip pantak kaṭalaḻuntap paṇṇaṟka - muntaineṟi
translation: On this earth surrounded by the milky white ocean, do not make me sink further into the ocean of the cruel bonds of birth.
commentary: Repeated birth is a cruel ocean that binds. Vallalar asks God to pull him out of it so he stops returning, life after earthly life.

translit: niṉṟēyuṉ poṟṟāḷ niṉaiyātār pāḻmaṉaiyil ceṉṟē uṭalōmpac ceyyaṟka - naṉṟēniṉ
translation: Do not make me go to the desolate homes of those who abandon the ancient path and never think of Your golden feet, merely to sustain my body.
commentary: Hunger drives people to the doors of those who never think of God. Vallalar asks to be spared that, to never keep his body alive by begging at such homes.

translit: ṟōṅku neṟiyōr uḷattamarntōy eṉṟaṉṉait tīṅku neṟiyil celuttaṟka - vīṅkaṭaṅki
translation: O Lord who resides in the hearts of those on the highly exalted path of goodness! Do not direct me onto evil paths.
commentary: God makes a home in the hearts of those who walk the path of pure goodness. Vallalar asks for grace to stay firmly on that path and never be steered toward harm.

translit: vāḻi yeṉattāṉ vaḻuttiṉumeṉ coṟkaṭaṅkā ēḻai maṉattā liḷaikkiṉṟēṉ - vāḻumarak
translation: Even when I praise you saying "Long live," my poor mind does not obey my words, and I grow weak. Like a living tree's...
commentary: Even in prayer the mind will not settle. Vallalar says "Long live" with his lips while his thoughts rebel and go their own way, and the struggle wears him down.

translit: kōṭēṟum pollāk kuraṅkeṉavē poyyulakak kāṭēṟu neñcāṟ kalaṅkukiṉṟēṉ - pāṭēṟum
translation: ...branch-climbing wicked monkey, my heart leaps into the forest of this false world, and I am bewildered. Overcome by the suffering-increasing...
commentary: Picture a monkey leaping wildly from branch to branch. The restless mind jumps the same way into the tangled forest of worldly distraction, leaving the seeker confused and lost.

translit: uḷḷaṟiyā māyaiyeṉu muṭpakaiyār kāmameṉuṅ kaḷḷaṟiyā tuṇṭu kavalkiṉṟēṉ - teḷḷuṟumeṉ
translation: ...subtle inner enemy called illusion, I unknowingly drink the intoxicating liquor of lust and grieve. O Lord who are like my clear...
commentary: Worldly illusion is an enemy hiding inside the mind. It tricks the soul into drinking the intoxicating liquor of physical desire, and all that comes of it is grief.

translit: kaṇṇaṉaiyāy niṉtāḷ kamalaṅ kaḷaivaḻuttā maṇṇaṉaiyār pāṟpōy mayaṅkukiṉṟēṉ - tiṇṇamilāk
translation: ...eyes, I approach those who are like mere dirt, people who do not praise your lotus feet, and I am deluded. Lacking firm...
commentary: Vallalar calls the Lord his own clear eyes, and those who ignore Him mere dirt. Going to such people for guidance or support is a trap. He sees the foolishness of it and still finds himself deluded.

translit: kātaravān tuṉpak kavalaik kaṭalvīḻntē ātaravoṉ ṟiṉṟi alaikiṉṟēṉ - ōtumaṟai
translation: ...resolve, I fall into the fearful ocean of sorrow and worry. I wander without a single support. The chanted Vedas...
commentary: Without a firm spiritual anchor, the soul drowns in anxiety and grief. Vallalar feels entirely alone, tossed about by worldly troubles with nothing to hold onto.

translit: ātta reṉumuṉ aṭiyār tamaikkaṇṭu nāttikañcol vārkku naṭuṅkukiṉṟēṉ - pāttuṇṭē
translation: I tremble at those who speak blasphemy when they see your faithful devotees.
commentary: When people mock true devotees, a sensitive heart is shaken. Vallalar trembles at the harsh, cynical words spoken against those who love God.

translit: uyva taṟiyā uḷattiṉē ṉuyyumvakai ceyva taṟiyēṉ tikaikkiṉṟēṉ - caivaneṟi
translation: My heart does not know how to share with others and find salvation. I do not know what I must do to be saved, and I stand bewildered.
commentary: Spiritual safety lies in sharing what we have with others. Vallalar feels he has failed at this basic act of compassion, and so he stands bewildered, not knowing how to reach God.

translit: uṇṇirampu niṉkaruṇai uṇṭō ilaiyō-eṉ ṟeṇṇiyeṇṇi uḷḷam iḷaikkiṉṟēṉ - maṇṇiṉiṭaik
translation: I wonder again and again whether the inner-filling grace of your Saiva path exists for me or not, and my heart grows weary.
commentary: Longing for grace brings its own moments of doubt. Again and again Vallalar wonders whether he is truly worthy of God's compassion and inner light, and the worrying wears his heart out.

translit: koṉceykai koṇṭakoṭuṅ kūṟṟaṉ kuṟukilataṟ keṉceyvō meṉṟeṇṇi eykkiṉṟēṉ - muṉceyviṉai
translation: If the cruel god of death with his murderous deeds approaches me in this world, what will I do? Thinking of this, I grow exhausted.
commentary: For someone who feels spiritually unprepared, the fear of death is a heavy burden. Without the certainty of grace, the thought of life ending abruptly brings exhaustion and despair.

translit: āmaṟaiyā nōyā lakamelivuṟ ṟaiyōnāṉ tāmaraiyi ṉīrpōl tayaṅkukiṉṟēṉ - tāmamuṭi
translation: Wasted away within by an incurable disease caused by my past deeds, alas, I tremble like a drop of water on a lotus leaf.
commentary: Past deeds weigh on Vallalar like an incurable sickness within. Life in that state is fragile, trembling like a drop of water on a lotus leaf.

translit: vaḷḷal aruḷkoṭukka vantilaṉē iṉṉumeṉa uḷḷamatu nīrā yurukukiṉṟēṉ - eḷḷaluṟu
translation: Thinking the benevolent Lord has not yet come to bestow His grace, my heart melts into water.
commentary: Spiritual longing takes a heavy toll on the body. Waiting for the Lord to come with His grace, Vallalar grieves until his heart loses its solid form and melts like water.

translit: mālaipāyn tiṉṉumeṉṉa vantiṭumō eṉṟuneñcam ālaipāyn tuḷḷam aḻikiṉṟēṉ - ñālamicaik
translation: The mocking evening descends. Wondering what more will befall me now, my mind is crushed in a sugarcane press and my heart perishes.
commentary: In Tamil love poetry, evening is the hour when separation hurts most. As night falls, worry grinds the mind down. Vallalar compares that agony to a hard sugarcane stalk crushed flat in a heavy press.

translit: kōṭpāra vāḻkkaik koṭuñciṟaiyi ṉiṉṟeṉṉai mīṭpā rilātu viḻikkiṉṟēṉ - mīṭpākum
translation: Staring in despair, I find no one to rescue me from the cruel prison of burdened life in this world.
commentary: Ordinary life, with its heavy and endless burdens, can become a cruel prison. Vallalar looks around in despair and sees that no human being can pull him out.

translit: āṟṟi lorukālum aṭaṅkāc camucārac cēṟṟiloru kālumvaittut tēykiṉṟēṉ - tōṟṟumayaṟ
translation: Keeping one foot in the river of rescue and one foot in the unyielding mud of worldly existence, I waste away.
commentary: The seeker is caught between two worlds. One foot stands in the clean river of rescue, and the other is stuck deep in the mud of worldly existence. Unable to step fully into the water, he wastes away from the strain.

translit: pākamuṟu vāḻkkaiyeṉum pālaivaṉat tuṉṉaruḷnīrt tākamatu koṇṭē tavikkiṉṟēṉ - mōkamatil
translation: In the desert of worldly life born of arising delusion, I suffer with a burning thirst for the water of Your grace.
commentary: Worldly life is a barren desert built on delusion, with nothing in it to sustain the soul. The only hope is the water of God's grace, and the soul burns with thirst for it.

translit: pōyppaṭumōr pañcap poṟikaḷāl vempāmpiṉ vāyppaṭumōr tēraiyaippōl vāṭukiṉṟēṉ - māyppavaru
translation: Tormented by the five fleeting senses, I wither like a toad caught in the mouth of a fierce snake.
commentary: A toad caught in a snake's mouth is slowly and helplessly consumed. Vallalar feels just as helpless against the overwhelming pull of the five senses.

translit: mīṉpōlu mātar viḻiyāl valaippaṭṭa māṉpōluñ cōrntu maṭaṅkukiṉṟēṉ - kāṉpōla
translation: Ensnared by the fish-like eyes of ruinous women, I grow exhausted and collapse like a deer trapped in a net.
commentary: Physical attraction is a trap that drains a seeker's spiritual strength. Vallalar sees himself as a netted deer, worn out and unable to break free.

translit: vīṟṟu mulaka vikārap piraḷayattil tōṟṟuñ cuḻiyuṭ cuḻalkiṉṟēṉ - āṟṟavunāṉ
translation: I swirl in the whirlpool that forms in the deluge of worldly delusions spreading out like a vast wilderness.
commentary: Worldly life is a chaotic flood of illusions. Vallalar spins in its whirlpool of attachments and finds no solid ground anywhere.

translit: ippāril uṉmēlaṉ pilleṉiṉum aṉpaṉeṉa oppāri yēṉum uṭaiyēṉkāṇ - tappāynta
translation: Even if I lack profound love for you in this world, see that I at least bear the outward appearance of a loving devotee.
commentary: A moment of raw honesty. Vallalar admits his love for God may lack depth, and he asks to be accepted anyway, because at least he tries to live outwardly as a devotee.

translit: maṭṭuviṭēṉ uṉtāḷ maṟakkiṉumveṇṇīṟṟuneṟi viṭṭuviṭēṉ eṉṟaṉaikkai viṭṭuviṭēl - tuṭṭaṉeṉa
translation: I will not overstep my boundaries. Even if I forget your feet, I will not forsake the path of the sacred white ash. Do not abandon me.
commentary: Sacred white ash marks a life given to spiritual discipline. Vallalar promises to keep this basic practice even when his mind forgets the Lord's feet. He begs never to be abandoned, flaws and all.

translit: mālun ticaimukaṉum vāṉavarum vantutaṭut tāluñ ciṟiyēṉait taḷḷiviṭēl- cālulaka
translation: Even if Vishnu, Brahma, and the celestials come to obstruct you, do not push this lowly one away.
commentary: Vallalar begs to be kept close to the Lord. The bond matters so much that even if Vishnu, Brahma and the celestials come to object, he asks that this lowly one never be pushed away.

translit: vātaṉaikoṇ ṭōṉeṉṟu maṟṟevarā ṉālumvantu pōtaṉaicey tālumeṉaip pōkkiviṭēl - nītayavu
translation: Even if anyone else comes and counsels you that I am possessed by abundant worldly habits, do not cast me aside.
commentary: Others may point to Vallalar's flaws and worldly habits. He prays that God will ignore their counsel and keep him safe anyway. His hope rests entirely on divine mercy.

translit: cūḻntiṭuka eṉṉaiyuniṉ toṇṭaruṭaṉ cērttaruḷka vāḻntiṭuka niṉtāḷ malar.
translation: May your compassion surround me. Graciously unite me with your devotees. May your flower-like feet flourish.
commentary: The plea ends in simple surrender to compassion. Vallalar asks to be gathered into the company of true devotees and to find his eternal home at the Lord's feet.

note: Editor's note: the 1896 edition numbers the two opening couplets (the invocation) 1 and 2 and then starts the kalivenba again at 1. This book numbers straight on, so the print's couplet n is couplet n + 2 here. The 1896 footnotes point to several couplets that echo the Thirukkural (Kural 151, 302, 305, 332, 336 and 339).
translit: cīrcāṉṟa mukkaṭ civakaḷiṟṟaic cērntiṭilām pērcāṉṟa iṉpam peritu.
translation: If we reach the glorious three-eyed Siva elephant, the renowned bliss we attain is immense.
commentary: A traditional opening invocation to Vinayakar, the elephant-headed deity who removes obstacles. By calling him the "three-eyed Siva elephant", Vallalar ties the son directly to the supreme nature of his father, Siva. Reach this presence and the joy keeps widening.

translit: āṟu mukattāṉ aruḷaṭaiyiṉ āmellāp pēṟu mikattāṉ peritu.
translation: If we attain the grace of the six-faced Lord, all the blessings we receive are exceedingly great.
commentary: Next comes Murugan, the six-faced god of Tamil tradition. Seek his grace first, and every other spiritual gift rests on it. These two opening prayers set a tone of humility and devotion before the main teaching begins.

translit: poṉṉār malaipōl polivuṟ ṟacaiyāmal ennāḷum vāḻiyanī eṉṉeñcē - piṉṉāṉa
translation: O my heart, may you live forever, shining and unshakable like the golden mountain.
commentary: Now Vallalar speaks directly to his own heart. He wants his mind as stable and radiant as Mount Meru, the legendary golden mountain of Indian cosmology. Without a steady mind, no real spiritual progress happens.

translit: ippiṟappi ṉōṭiṅ keḻupiṟappum aṉṟiyeṉai eppiṟappum viṭṭakalā eṉṉeñcē - ceppamuṭaṉ
translation: O my heart, you never leave my side in this later birth, in the seven births to come, or in any birth whatsoever.
commentary: The heart is the soul's closest and most lasting companion. It travels with the soul through countless cycles of birth and death, sharing every experience along the way. That long shared history makes it the perfect student for what Vallalar is about to teach.

translit: cevvorucār niṉṟu ciṟiyēṉ kiḷakkiṉṟa ivvorucol kēṭṭiṭuka eṉṉeñcē - evvev
translation: O my heart, stand attentively by my side and listen to this single word spoken by this humble one.
commentary: Vallalar asks his mind to stand close and pay attention. He is readying his own heart for a single spiritual truth, and he offers it gently, the way a friend would.

translit: ulakum paravum orumutalāy eṅkum ilakum civamāy iṟaiyāy - vilakum
translation: You are the one primal source praised by the world. You are Sivam shining everywhere. You are the Lord. You stand distinct.
commentary: God is the single origin of everything in the world, shining everywhere as Sivam (the supreme reality of grace). Present in all things, the Lord still stands completely distinct, never confined by creation.

translit: uruvāy uruvil uruvāy uruvuḷ aruvāy aruvil aruvāy - uru-aruvāy
translation: You are form. You are form within form. You are the formless within form. You are the formless within the formless. You are both form and formless.
commentary: The divine exists in every possible state of being. God is the physical shape of things, the hidden essence inside those shapes, and the wholly invisible reality beyond them. The supreme light holds form and formlessness at once.

translit: nittiyamāy nirkkuṇamāy niṟcalamāy niṉmalamāyc cattiyamāyc cattuvamāyt tattuvamāy - muttiyaruḷ
translation: You are eternal. You are without attributes. You are motionless. You are immaculate. You are truth. You are purity. You are the ultimate reality. You grant liberation.
commentary: This reality has no physical qualities and no limits. It is pure, motionless and eternal. And it is this absolute truth that grants the soul liberation.

translit: oṉṟāyp palavāy uyirāy uyirkkuyirāy naṉṟāy navamāy naṭunilaiyāy - niṉṟōṅkum
translation: You are the One. You are the many. You are the soul. You are the soul of the soul. You are goodness. You are ever new. You are the impartial center. You stand exalted.
commentary: God is both the single source and the countless forms of life. Deep inside our own soul, the divine sits as the soul of that soul. Always fresh and perfectly balanced, this reality stands exalted above everything else.

translit: vētamāy vētānta vittāy viḷaṅkupara nātamāy nātānta nāyakamāy - ōtum
translation: You are the Vedas. You are the seed of Vedanta. You are the radiant supreme sound. You are the Lord beyond the supreme sound. You are praised in recitation.
commentary: God is the truth hidden inside all sacred knowledge. The Vedas (ancient scriptures) and Vedanta (the philosophy drawn from them) sprout from that divine seed. The Lord is the supreme cosmic sound of creation, and also the master who lives entirely beyond it.

translit: ceṟivāyt tiramāyc citākāca māyccol aṟivāy aṟivuḷ aṟivāy - neṟimēvu
translation: You are the fullness, the firmness, and the space of pure consciousness. You are the articulated wisdom and the profound knowledge within knowledge. You abide in the path.
commentary: The divine is the vast space of pure consciousness (citākācam) and also the deepest layer of our own knowing. The wisdom we speak aloud comes from it. So does the quiet, hidden intelligence that makes any understanding possible.

translit: kālamāyk kālam kaṭanta karuttāynaṟ cīlamāyc ciṟparamāyc ciṉmayamāy - ñālam
translation: You are time and the true intent that transcends time. You are noble virtue, the supreme consciousness, and the embodiment of pure awareness.
commentary: God is the flow of time we live through, and also the eternal purpose standing outside it. Vallalar calls the divine supreme consciousness (ciṟparam) and pure awareness (ciṉmayam). In the world, it shows itself through noble character.

translit: poruntāp poruḷāyp poruntum poruḷāyp peruntā rakamcūḻnta pēṟāyt - tiruntāta
translation: In this world you are the reality that escapes our grasp and the reality that intimately unites with us. You are the great blessing encompassed by supreme support.
commentary: A paradox of divine presence. The ultimate reality escapes our worldly grasp, yet it unites with us intimately from within. It is the great blessing that upholds all things.

translit: pōkkum varattumilāp pūraṇamāyp puṇṇiyarkaḷ nōkkum tiṟatteḻunta nuṇṇuṇarvāy - nīkkamilā
translation: You are the perfection completely free from the flawed cycle of coming and going. You are the subtle awareness that blossoms in the vision of the virtuous.
commentary: Most living beings are caught in an endless cycle of birth and death. The divine is unbroken perfection, free from that flawed coming and going. This perfection is a subtle awareness, and it wakes only in those who live virtuous lives.

translit: ātiyāy ātinaṭu antamāy āṅkakaṉṟa cōtiyāyc cōtiyāc coṟpayaṉāy - nītiyāy
translation: You are inseparable. You are the origin. You are the beginning, the middle, and the end. You are the expansive Jothi. You are the supreme fruit of unfathomable words. You are justice.
commentary: The divine spans the entire timeline of existence: the origin, the middle and the final end. God is the vast Jothi (light) that fills all space. Human words keep trying to capture this truth, and in the world it acts as perfect justice.

translit: āṅkāra nīkkum akāra ukāramatāy ōṅkāra māyavaṟṟiṉ uṭporuḷāyp - pāṅkāṉa
translation: He is the syllables A and U that dispel the ego. He is the syllable Om and the inner meaning of these sounds. He is the beautiful
commentary: A, U and Om are old sounds of meditation, used to quiet the mind and dissolve the ego. Vallalar says God is these sacred sounds and also the truth hidden inside them.

translit: cittamāyc cittānta tēcāyt tikamparamāyc cattamāyc cutta catānilaiyāy - vittamāy
translation: consciousness, the light of Siddhanta, the vast sky, the primal sound, and the pure eternal state. He is the seed.
commentary: He is the seed from which all reality grows. Pure awareness, the infinite sky, the first sound and the guiding light of Siddhanta, an ancient school of philosophy, are all names for that one source.

translit: aṇṭamāy aṇṭat taṇuvāy aruḷakaṇṭā kaṇṭamāy āṉantā kāramatāy - aṇṭattiṉ
translation: He is the universe. He is the atom within the universe. He is the undivided and divided space of grace. He is the form of bliss. Of the universe,
commentary: From the whole universe down to its smallest atom, God is present at every scale. He is the space of grace itself, and that grace takes the form of pure joy.

translit: appālāy ippālāy aṇmaiyāyc cēymaiyatāy eppālāy eppālum illatumāyc - ceppālum
translation: He is what lies beyond and what lies on this side. He is near and He is far. He is on every side, yet He is absent from every side. He is a state
commentary: You cannot pin God to one place. He is near and far, on every side at once, and still free of the limits of physical space.

translit: neñcālum kāya nilaiyālum annilaikkuḷ añcāluṅ kāṇṭaṟ karumpatamāy - eñcāp
translation: impossible to perceive through words, through the heart, through the condition of the body, or through the five senses within that condition. He is the unfailing
commentary: Our faculties are too small for this. Spoken words, feelings, the body and its five senses all fall short of Him.

translit: paramāyp pakāpporuḷāyp pālāyc cuvaiyiṉ taramāyp parappiramam tāṉāy-varamāya
translation: Being the supreme, the indivisible reality, the milk, the essence of taste, and the Supreme Absolute itself.
commentary: Vast and intimate at once. God is the undivided reality of the universe, and yet as nourishing and directly known as milk, as the very essence of taste.

translit: oṉpāṉ vaṭivāy oḷiyeṇ kuṇakkaṭalāy aṉpāy akanilaiyāy aṟputamāy - iṉpāy
translation: Being the blessed nine forms, the radiant ocean of eight qualities, love, the inner reality, a wonder, and bliss.
commentary: God takes on all the sacred forms and holds an ocean of perfect qualities. Vallalar names these traditional categories and then goes further. The divine is met directly as love, inner truth, wonder and bliss.

translit: akamāyp puṟamāy akampuṟamāy nīṅkum cakamāyc cakamāyai tāṉāy - cakamāyai
translation: Being the inner, the outer, both inner and outer, the passing world, and the illusion of the world itself.
commentary: Nothing is left out. God is our inner self, the outer universe and the physical world around us, and even the fleeting, illusory nature of that world.

translit: illātāy eṉṟum iruppatāy yātoṉṟum kollātārk kiṉpam koṭuppatāy - ellārkkum
translation: Being free of worldly illusion, existing eternally, and granting bliss to those who never kill any living being.
commentary: God encompasses the world, yet stays free of its illusions. Vallalar states plainly that God grants eternal bliss specifically to those who refuse to kill any living being. This shows that Jeevakarunyam (compassion for all life) is the absolute foundation for receiving grace.

translit: naṇṇuvatāy naṇṇātāy nalviṉaiyāy alviṉaiyāy eṇṇuvatāy eṇṇiṉ iyalātāy - eṇṇukiṉṟa
translation: Being accessible to all and yet inaccessible, being good actions and bad actions, being the object of thought and yet remaining beyond the reach of thought.
commentary: Paradox after paradox. God is present in all things, even in the good and bad actions of the world. Anyone can approach Him, and still the mind cannot grasp or understand Him.

translit: vāṉāy nilaṉāy vaḷiyāy aṉalāynīr tāṉāy vaḻipaṭunāṉ tāṉtāṉāy - vāṉāti
translation: Beginning with the sky, it becomes earth, wind, fire, and water. It becomes the worshipping self and the absolute Self.
commentary: The divine light is the substance of the physical universe, making up sky, earth, wind, fire and water. It also bridges the gap between human and divine. Vallalar says the light is both the one who prays and the truth prayed to.

translit: oṉṟiṭattum oṉṟātāy oṉṟuvatāy āṉantam maṉṟiṭattil eṉṟum vativatāy - oṉṟiyatōr
translation: It remains unattached to any single element yet unites with everything. It dwells forever in the hall of bliss.
commentary: The light becomes everything in the universe, yet no physical thing traps or limits it. It touches all and stays free. Vallalar calls its home the hall of bliss, a state of pure joy where it dwells forever.

translit: ainniṟamāy anniṟattiṉ āmoḷiyāy avvoḷikkuḷ enniṟamum vēṇṭā iyaṉiṟamāy - munniṟattil
translation: It becomes the five unique colors and the light of those colors. Within that light, it becomes the natural radiance that requires no other hue.
commentary: The five elements of the world are often linked to five distinct colors. The divine light is the source of all these forms, yet in itself it is a pure and natural radiance. It shines on its own and needs no color or worldly trait to complete it.

translit: pūppatuvāyk kāppatuvāyp pōkkuvatāyt tēkkuvatāy nīppatuvāyt taṉṉuḷ niṟuttuvatāyp - pūppatiṉṟi
translation: It blossoms to create, protects, dissolves, fills, and grants release, establishing all things within itself.
commentary: Many traditions divide God's work into separate roles like creation, protection and destruction. Vallalar gives all of it to the single divine light. It brings the universe into being, sustains it, absorbs it and grants spiritual freedom, holding all of existence within itself.

translit: vāḷā tiruppatuvāy vātaṉā tītamāy nīḷātu nīṇṭa nilaiyiṉatāy - mīḷāp
translation: It remains in perfect stillness without manifesting. It stands beyond all mental impressions, possessing an infinite state that defies measurement.
commentary: Behind all the activity of the universe, the reality itself stays still and silent. The mental habits and lingering impressions that bind human beings never touch it. Vallalar describes an endless, unmeasurable peace beyond the reach of the mind.

translit: peritāyc ciṟitāyp peritum ciṟitum aritāy aritil aritāyt - turiya
translation: It is the large. It is the small. It is the rare state beyond the large and the small. It is the rarest of the rare. It is the transcendent.
commentary: The Divine holds both the vastest thing imaginable and the tiniest. It is also the transcendent reality (turiya), lying wholly beyond any physical measure.

translit: veḷiyāyp paraveḷiyāy mēvupara vintiṉ oḷiyāyc civāṉanta ūṟṟāyt - teḷiyāti
translation: It is the open space. It is the supreme space. It is the light of the supreme source. It is the spring of divine bliss. It is the clear primal beginning.
commentary: Past every physical limit lies the boundless spiritual space of the Divine. That reality is the first light and the source of everything. It is also a deep spring of joy (civāṉanta), so whoever reaches this light reaches real happiness.

translit: kaṟpakamāyk kāṇuñcaṅ kaṟpa vikaṟpamāy niṟpatā kāra niruvikaṟpāyp - poṟpuṭaiya
translation: It is the wish-fulfilling tree. It is the perceived certainty and doubt. It stands as the immutable reality beyond all form. It is beautiful.
commentary: Vallalar likens the Divine to the wish-fulfilling tree of Indian tradition (kaṟpakam), which supplies every need. It lives inside our very thoughts, behind our certainties and our doubts alike. Under those shifting forms of the mind it stays unchanging, formless and beautiful.

translit: muccuṭarāy muccuṭarkkum muṉṉoḷiyāyp piṉṉoḷiyāy eccuṭarum pōtā iyaṟcuṭarāy - accil
translation: It is the three flames. It is the light before and the light after those three flames. It is the natural flame unmatched by any other flame.
commentary: The three flames are the sun, the moon and fire. The Divine is the source that lit them and the light that outlasts them, a natural flame no physical fire can match.

translit: niṟaivāyk kuṟaivāy niṟaikuṟai villātāy maṟaivāy veḷiyāy maṉuvāy - maṟaiyāta
translation: Found at the core, it is fullness. It is deficiency. It is the state possessing neither fullness nor deficiency. It is the hidden. It is the revealed. It is the sacred mantra. It is the unvanishing.
commentary: This truth defies ordinary logic, so Vallalar presses opposites together. The Divine is complete fullness and total emptiness, the hidden secret and the plain truth. It is also the sacred word (maṉu), a presence that never fades.

translit: caccitā ṉantamatāyt taṉṉikaroṉ ṟillātāy viccaiyāl ellām virippatuvāy - meccukiṉṟa
translation: Being existence, consciousness, and bliss, possessing no equal, expanding all things through divine skill, and becoming the praiseworthy
commentary: Pure existence, consciousness and bliss (caccitāṉantam): that is how Vallalar names the Divine. This peerless reality unfolds the whole universe out of itself by its own divine skill.

translit: yōkamāy yōkiyar yōkat teḻuntaciva pōkamāyp pōkiyāyp pōkamaruḷ - ēkamāyk
translation: yoga, becoming the divine bliss that arises in the yoga of yogis, becoming the enjoyer, granting enjoyment, becoming the One,
commentary: God is the practice of yoga and also the bliss that rises from it. The same reality is the enjoyment, the giver of it and the enjoyer, all gathered into one presence.

translit: kēvalamāyc cutta cakalamāyk kīḻccakala kēvalaṅkaḷ caṟṟum kiṭaiyātāy - māvalattil
translation: becoming the supreme solitary state and the pure all-encompassing state, remaining completely untouched by the lower states of action and inertia, and in great power
commentary: God rests in a supreme, solitary stillness (kēvalam) and also fills the world as a pure, all-embracing presence (cutta cakalam). Yet the lower states that trap ordinary souls, busy action and dark inertia, never touch the Divine.

translit: kāṭciyāyk kāṇpāṉāyk kāṇap paṭuporuḷāyc cūṭciyāyc cūṭciyāl tōyvaritāy - māṭcipeṟac
translation: becoming the sight, the seer, and the object seen, becoming the subtle reality that is hard to reach even through subtle means, and to attain glory
commentary: We usually take ourselves to be observers looking at a world apart from us. Vallalar erases that line, for the Divine is the seer, the seeing and the thing seen. Even a refined mind finds this subtle truth hard to grasp.

translit: ceypavaṉāyc ceytoḻilāyc ceyporuḷāyc ceytoḻilāl uypavaṉāy uyvikkum uttamaṉāy - moykoḷ
translation: becoming the doer, the action, and the object of action, becoming the one saved through action, becoming the supreme Lord who grants salvation, and possessing abundant
commentary: As with seeing, so with doing. God is the one who acts, the work done and the material worked on. God is also the soul saved through that action and the supreme Lord who grants the saving.

translit: atuvāy avaḷāy avaṉāy avaiyum katuvātu niṉṟa kaṇippāyk - katuvāmal
translation: Becoming that, becoming her, becoming him, and becoming all things, they stand as the immeasurable reality untouched by any of these.
commentary: Realized beings see the Divine in every form of life, male, female or inanimate. They become one with everything, yet these passing shapes never touch them.

translit: aiyam tiripō ṭaṟiyāmai viṭṭakaṟṟip poyyeṉpa toṉṟum poruntārāyc - ceyyeṉṟa
translation: They cast away doubt, delusion, and ignorance, and they never associate with anything false.
commentary: A clear, steady mind is where spiritual life begins. Having thrown off doubt, confusion and ignorance, these pure souls keep no company with anything false and side wholly with the truth.

translit: ōrviṉaiyil iṉpamumaṟ ṟōrviṉaiyil tuṉpamumām cārviṉaiviṭ ṭōṅkum takaiyiṉarāyp - pārviṉaiyil
translation: They rise to greatness by abandoning the binding karma that brings pleasure in one action and pain in another.
commentary: Ordinary life runs on karma, actions that bring pleasure for a while and pain after it, over and over. Greatness comes from stepping out of that binding cycle altogether.

translit: ōrpāl veṟuppumaṟṟai ōrpāl viruppumuṟum cārpāl mayaṅkāt takaiyiṉarāyc - cārpāya
translation: They remain unconfused by the attachments of the world, which cause aversion on one side and desire on the other.
commentary: The world keeps pulling people toward some things and away from others. The spiritually mature stay level, and these passing likes and dislikes never cloud them.
