translit: ōriṭattil taṇmaiyumaṟ ṟōriṭattil veñciṉamum pāriṭattil koḷḷāp pariciṉarāy - nīriṭattil
translation: They possess a nature that does not show calm favor in one place and fierce anger in another in this world.
commentary: Maturity shows in how a person treats others. These holy people are not gentle with some and fierce with others. Everyone they meet gets the same steady grace.

translit: taṇmainika rāteṉṟum cāntam paḻuttuyarnta oṇmaiyuṭaṉ oṉṟai uṇarntavarāy - veṇmaiyilā
translation: They have realized the One with elevated radiance, ripening in unparalleled and eternal tranquility.
commentary: The highest realization brings a peace that is total and lasting. You can recognize true wisdom by this radiant calm, the soul resting in the one divine truth.

translit: oṉṟum aṟiviṉ utayāti īṟaḷavum eṉṟum iraṇṭeṉpa tillavarāy - maṉṟavoḷir
translation: With an intelligence free from ignorance, they never speak of duality from the beginning to the end.
commentary: True wisdom sees no separation between the soul and God. Such people live in unity from start to finish, free of the ignorance that chops the world into separate things.

translit: ammūṉṟi ṉuḷḷē aṭukkivarum oṉṟakaṉṟa mummūṉṟiṉ mūṉṟum muṉintavarāyt - tammūṉṟi
translation: Rooting themselves firmly, they have rejected the three, and the three threes less one that multiply within those three.
commentary: Vallalar is using the old numerical riddles to name what blocks the way. The 'three' are the soul's core impurities: ego, past actions, and illusion. The realized root themselves in truth and throw off these deep bindings.

translit: vīṭātu niṉṟum virintum vikaṟpanaṭai nāṭātu nāṉkum nacittavarāy - ūṭāka
translation: They have destroyed the four, never seeking the path of differences that ceaselessly stands and expands.
commentary: The 'four' are the inner workings of the mind: intellect, ego, active thought, and memory. Left restless, the mind keeps making divisions and differences. Whoever seeks the highest truth has to silence all four.

translit: eñcāmal añciṉ iṭamāy naṭamāṭum añcāti añcum aṟuttavarāy - eñcāmal
translation: They have completely cut off the five fives that dance endlessly as the domain of the five.
commentary: The 'five fives' are the twenty-five basic building blocks of the physical and mental universe, among them the five elements and the five senses. Realized souls break clean out of their distracting dance.

translit: īṇṭāṇ ṭaruḷum iṟaiyōr tamaiyāṟil āṇṭāṇṭu kaṇṭā ṟakaṉṟavarāy - īṇṭātu
translation: The divine lords who rule and bestow grace here see the Supreme in the six centers and transcend those six realms. Without gathering here,
commentary: Even the gods who govern the universe seek the Supreme. They meditate on the six spiritual centers in the body, and they too must move past them to reach the truth.

translit: vāḻiyuṟṟa vāṉōrum vantu tamakkiraṇṭō ṭēḻiyaṟṟa ēḻum ikantavarāy - ūḻiyaṟṟak
translation: the prosperous celestial beings arrive and transcend the fourteen worlds. Passing beyond the endless eons,
commentary: The heavenly beings have to go beyond their own worlds as well. Reaching the Supreme means passing the fourteen worlds of the old cosmology and stepping outside time itself.

translit: kaṭṭiniṉṟuṭ cōtiyoṉṟu kāṇat toṭaṅkukiṉṟōr eṭṭukiṉṟa eṭṭiṉmēl eytiṉarāyk kaṭṭukiṉṟa
translation: those who stand steadfast and begin to see the one inner Jothi reach the state above the eight attainable realms. Mingling with the binding,
commentary: Real seekers turn wholly inward to see the inner Jothi, the divine light. Holding that focus steady, they rise above every traditional state of spiritual attainment.

translit: tēṉtōy karuṇaic civaṅkalantu tēkkukiṉṟa cāṉṟōrtam uḷḷam taṇavātāy - māṉṟamalat
translation: honey-steeped grace of Sivam, the Supreme never leaves the hearts of the wise who brim with it. The attack of the deluding impurity
commentary: Sivam is the Supreme Reality. Its grace fills the hearts of the wise like honey, and once it settles there it never leaves, guarding them against the darkness of ignorance.

translit: tākkoḻintu tattuvattiṉ cārpām - taṉuvoḻintu vākkoḻintu māṇā maṉamoḻintu - ēkkamuṟa
translation: is destroyed, along with the body that relies on the elements. Speech is lost, the unredeemed mind is lost, and as longing grows,
commentary: Deep union with the divine breaks the grip of the physical world. The body's limits fall away, ordinary speech goes, the restless mind goes. What remains is an intense longing for God.

translit: vāykkum cukamoḻintu maṇṇoḻintu viṇṇoḻintu cāykkum irāppakalum tāṉoḻintu - nīkkoḻintu
translation: When accessible pleasures cease, when earth ceases, when heaven ceases, when alternating night and day cease, when the self ceases, when separation ceases,
commentary: Everything temporary fades here. Physical pleasures go, earth and heaven go, the day and night that measure time go, and even the sense of a separate self comes to an end. With it goes all separation between the soul and the divine.

translit: nāṉumoḻi yātoḻintu ñāṉamoḻi yātoḻintu tāṉum oḻiyāmaṟ ṟāṉoḻintu - mōṉanilai
translation: when the 'I' completely ceases, when knowledge completely ceases, and when 'He' ceases without ceasing in the state of silence,
commentary: In the deepest silence (mōṉanilai), the idea of an independent "I" disappears. Even the pursuit of knowledge fades, since no gap is left between knower and known. At this height, seeing God as a separate "He" dissolves into perfect, silent union.

translit: niṟkum pirama niraticayā ṉantamatāy niṟkum parama niruttaṉevaṉ - taṟparamāy
translation: who is the supreme dancer who stands as that abiding, boundless bliss of Brahman? Who stood as the supreme absolute?
commentary: He is the supreme dancer who reigns in this absolute stillness, embodying the boundless bliss of the absolute reality (Brahman). This dancing Lord stands as the truth beyond every limit.

translit: niṉṟāṉ evaṉaṉpar nēyamaṉat tēviraintu ceṉṟāṉ evaṉcarva tīrttaṉevaṉ - vaṉtīmai
translation: Who rushed swiftly into the loving hearts of devotees? Who is the embodiment of all holy waters? Who is utterly free from cruel evil?
commentary: God dwells in high, silent bliss, yet he is fiercely quick to answer human love. The Lord rushes into the hearts of true devotees. He is the source of purity, holding the cleansing power of all holy waters, and nothing cruel or evil touches him.

translit: illāṉ evaṉyārkkum īcaṉ evaṉyāvum vallāṉ evaṉanti vaṇṇaṉevaṉ - kallālil
translation: Who is the Lord to everyone? Who is capable of all things? Who has the hue of evening twilight? Under the banyan tree...
commentary: The Lord holds all power over creation and is master of everyone. Vallalar draws on traditional images here: the deep reddish glow of evening twilight, and the banyan tree under which the Lord sits as the supreme teacher of ancient wisdom.

translit: cuṭṭakaṉṟa ñāṉa cukātītam kāṭṭimuṟṟum viṭṭakaṉṟa yōka viṉōtaṉevaṉ - maṭṭakaṉṟa
translation: Who is the wondrous yogi who revealed the supreme bliss of wisdom that transcends all designation and then completely withdrew?
commentary: A divine master shows the soul a joy of wisdom that no word can name. Then he steps back, so the soul can rest in that pure experience on its own.

translit: aṇṭaṅkaḷ ellām aṇuvil aṭaittaruḷit tiṇṭaṅku māṟiruttum cittaṉevaṉ - paṇṭaṅku
translation: Who is the Siddha who gracefully packed all the boundless universes into a single atom and firmly established them there?
commentary: A Siddha is a perfected being with extraordinary mystic powers, and here the word points to the Supreme Divine. Vallalar marvels at God's command over scale and space. Universes without end are folded into the tiniest particle.

translit: vīyāc ciṟupeṇ viḷaiyāṭṭuḷ aṇṭamelām tēyātu kūṭṭuvikkum cittaṉevaṉ - yāyātum
translation: Who is the Siddha who unites all the universes without them diminishing in the ancient and eternal play of a young girl?
commentary: Holding all creation together costs the divine no effort. Vallalar compares it to the easy, joyful games of a young girl. The universes stay in perfect balance and lose nothing of their vastness.

translit: vēṇṭāmai vēṇṭuvatu mēvāta cittartamait tīṇṭātu tīṇṭukiṉṟa cittaṉevaṉ - īṇṭōtu
translation: Who is the Siddha who touches without touching those Siddhas who are completely free from desiring or rejecting anything?
commentary: Some seekers reach a state where they neither chase after things nor push them away. The supreme master stays close to such beings, a presence that touches them without ever imposing a heavy hand.

translit: paṟṟuruvāyp paṟṟāp paravaṇuviṉ uḷviḷaṅkum ciṟṟuruvāy uḷḷoḷikkum cittaṉevaṉ - maṟṟuruviṉ
translation: Who is the Siddha who hides within as the subtle form shining inside the supreme atom, appearing attached here yet remaining unattached?
commentary: The divine hides deep inside the smallest atom of existence. Because it is the glowing heart of everything, it seems bound to the physical world. Yet it stays free, untouched by any material limit.

translit: vaiyātu vaittulakai māvin tiracālam ceyyātu ceyvikkum cittaṉevaṉ - naiyāmal
translation: Who is the Siddha who establishes the world without establishing it, and enacts the great magic without enacting it?
commentary: God works like a master magician, bringing the universe into being with no visible effort and no physical foundation. The Supreme creates everything while doing nothing at all. He moves the cosmos and stays perfectly still.

translit: appiṭaivaip pāmulakil āruyirai māyaiyeṉum ceppiṭaivait tāṭṭukiṉṟa cittaṉevaṉ - oppuṟavē
translation: Who is the Siddha who places precious souls into the box of illusion and makes them dance unwearied within this world surrounded by waters?
commentary: The world of matter is a magic box of illusion (maya). The ultimate Siddha (a perfected, fully realized divine being) places souls inside this earthly theater and keeps them moving. Their dance is the endless, exhausting activity of worldly life.

translit: nillāta kāṟṟai nilaiyāk kaṭattaṭaittuc cellātu vaikkiṉṟa cittaṉevaṉ - pollāta
translation: Who is the Siddha who fittingly traps the restless wind inside this unstable pot of a body and keeps it from escaping?
commentary: The body is a fragile clay pot that cannot stay whole for long. Breath is restless air. The mystery of life is that the divine binds that air inside so delicate a container and keeps it there to sustain us.

translit: vempāmpai mēlaṇintōr vempuṟṟiṉ uḷḷiruntē cempāmpai āṭṭukiṉṟa cittaṉevaṉ - tampāṅkar
translation: Who is the Siddha who wears a vicious, fierce snake upon his body, sits inside a hot anthill, and makes the red snake dance?
commentary: The imagery comes from traditional yoga and the hidden energies of the body. The hot anthill is the physical form, and the dancing red snake is the life force or spiritual energy stirring inside it. The divine master directs this inner awakening.

translit: oṇkayiṟṟāṉ oṉṟiṉṟi uṇṇiṉ ṟuyirkaḷaiyūḻt tiṇkayiṟṟāṉ āṭṭukiṉṟa cittaṉevaṉ - vaṇkaiyuṭait
translation: Who is the generous Siddha who stands within and makes souls dance with the strong rope of karma, without using a single visible bright rope by his side?
commentary: We feel we act entirely on our own, yet an unseen force guides every move. Karma (the accumulated result of our past actions) is the invisible rope pulling the strings. The divine stands hidden within and runs the puppet show of life without a single physical cord.

translit: tāṉacaintāl maṟṟaic cakamacaiyum eṉṟumaṟai tēṉacaiyac collukiṉṟa cittaṉevaṉ - ūṉamiṉṟip
translation: Who is the Siddhar proclaimed by the Vedas in sweet honeyed words, declaring that if He moves, the entire universe moves?
commentary: The ancient scriptures declare that God is the prime mover of all existence. If the divine will stirs even slightly, the entire universe is set in motion.

translit: pērttuyirka ḷellāmōr peṇpiḷḷai yiṉvacamāyc cērttu varuvikkum cittaṉevaṉ - pōrttumika
translation: Who is the Siddhar who flawlessly gathers all souls and brings them forth under the sway of a woman?
commentary: Every human life enters this world through a mother. Vallalar marvels at the divine power that guides countless souls, without fail, into physical existence through womanhood.

translit: alviravuṅ kālai akilamelām taṉpatattōr cilviralil cērkkiṉṟa cittaṉevaṉ - palvakaiyāyk
translation: Who is the Siddhar who gathers the entire universe into a few toes of His foot when thick darkness covers everything?
commentary: At the end of a cosmic cycle, total darkness covers everything. In that dissolution the divine draws the whole universe back into itself and holds it as lightly as a speck resting on a toe.

translit: kaikalanta vaṇmaik karuppā cayappaiyuḷ ceykaruvuk kūṭṭuvikkum cittaṉevaṉ - uykaruvai
translation: Who is the Siddhar who unites and nourishes the embryo within the fertile womb formed by diverse physical unions?
commentary: How a child forms in the womb is a deep mystery. An unseen divine hand weaves matter together to nourish and protect the fragile embryo.

translit: meyvaitta vērvaiyiṉum vīḻnilattum aṇṭattum ceyvittaṅ kūṭṭuvikkum cittaṉevaṉ - uyvikkum
translation: Who is the Siddhar who creates and fosters living forms in the sweat on the body, in the earth, and in the egg?
commentary: Traditional thought groups living creatures by how they are born: from sweat, from the earth, from eggs, or from wombs. God creates and cares for every one of them.

translit: vittoṉṟum iṉṟi viḷaivit taruḷaḷikkum citteṉṟum vallavoru cittaṉevaṉ - cattuṭaṉē
translation: Who is the Siddhar of eternal conscious power who truly brings forth a harvest without a single seed and grants grace?
commentary: Every harvest needs a seed, except this one. God brings the universe out of nothing, and Vallalar names Him a Siddhar (a perfected master of spiritual power), whose pure consciousness brings all things into being and then gives grace besides.

translit: uṟpatti yāyulakil oṉpatuvāyp pāvaikaḷcey ciṟpat toḻilvalla cittaṉevaṉ - paṟpalavām
translation: Who is the Siddhar capable of the sculptural art of creating the many nine-gated puppets born into the world?
commentary: The body is a puppet with nine openings, and a temporary one. Those nine gates are the eyes, ears, nostrils, mouth and the lower organs. Vallalar marvels at the master sculptor who shapes such living forms and sends them into the world.

translit: kārā ḻikaḷaik karaiyiṉṟi ellaiyilāc cērūḻi niṟkavaitta cittaṉevaṉ - pērāta
translation: Who is the Siddhar who made the shoreless dark oceans stand contained and unmoving for boundless ages?
commentary: Look at the sea. Nothing walls it in, yet for countless ages it has stayed where it is and never swallowed the earth. Vallalar asks who but God, master of nature's huge and chaotic forces, could hold it there.

translit: nīrmēl neruppai nilaiyuṟavait tevvulakum cīrmē vuṟacceyyum cittaṉevaṉ - pārāti
translation: Who is the Siddhar who places fire securely upon the water and makes all worlds, from the earth onwards, flourish in excellence?
commentary: Fire and water should destroy each other. God rests one safely on the other, and that exact balance of opposites is what lets the earth and every other world thrive.

translit: aintilaintu nāṉkorumūṉ ṟāmiraṇṭoṉ ṟāymuṟaiyē cintaiyuṟa niṉṟaruḷum cittaṉevaṉ - pantamuṟa
translation: Who is the Siddhar who stands within the mind and grants grace in orderly progression as five within five, four, a unique three, two, and one, forming worldly bonds?
commentary: The numbers name the building blocks of existence as tradition counts them: the five elements, the five senses, the four inner faculties of mind, the three qualities of nature, the two kinds of action (good and bad karma), and the one soul. God arranges these inside us like a hidden architect. Our worldly experience comes from that arrangement, and through it He guides us from within.

translit: āṇpeṇṇāyp peṇṇāṇāy aṇmai taṉaivāṉiṉ cēṇpaṇṇa vallavoru cittaṉevaṉ - māṇpaṇṇāp
translation: Who is the Siddha capable of turning a male into a female, a female into a male, and making what is near as distant as the sky?
commentary: Male into female, female into male, the nearest thing pushed out as far as the sky. Vallalar calls the power that can do this a Siddha, the same perfected master as before. It holds the body and the laws of space in its hand.

translit: pēṭāṇāyp peṇṇāyap peṇṇāṇ perumpēṭāyc cēṭākac ceyyavalla cittaṉevaṉ - cēṭāya
translation: Who is the Siddha capable of transforming the genderless into a male or a female, and a male or a female into the genderless?
commentary: The body's sex can be reshaped in any direction. The genderless can be made male or female, and male or female made genderless again, so the material body turns out to be fluid and wholly subject to divine will.

translit: veṇmai kiḻamāy viruttamanta veṇmaiyatāyt tiṇmai peṟacceyyum cittaṉevaṉ - oṇmaiyilā
translation: Who is the Siddha who firmly transforms youth into old age, and old age into youth?
commentary: Time answers to this master too. Youth can be stripped away into sudden old age, and old age turned back until youth is fully restored.

translit: ōṭṭiṉaiccem poṉṉā yuyarcempoṉ ōṭākac cēṭṭaiyaṟac ceykiṉṟa cittaṉevaṉ - kāṭṭiluṟu
translation: Who is the Siddha who effortlessly turns a clay potsherd into pure gold, and exalted pure gold into a clay potsherd?
commentary: A broken bit of clay becomes pure gold, and gold goes back to being worthless clay, with no effort at all. The value of matter is entirely under divine command, so wealth has no fixed reality of its own.

translit: kāñcirattaik kaṟpakamāyk kaṟpakattaik kāñciramāyt tēñcivaṇac ceykiṉṟa cittaṉevaṉ - vāñcaiyuṟa
translation: Who is the Siddha who transforms the bitter poison-nut tree into the heavenly wish-fulfilling tree, and the heavenly wish-fulfilling tree into the bitter poison-nut tree?
commentary: The Karpakam is the heavenly tree of Indian tradition that grants any wish. Set against it is the bitter poison-nut tree. Grace can change the inner nature of a living thing so completely that one becomes the other, and the miracle can run backward just as well.

translit: nāraṇaṉcēy nāṉmukaṉāy nāṉmukaṉcēy nāraṇaṉāyc cīraṇavac ceyyavalla cittaṉevaṉ - pēraṇavak
translation: Who is the Siddha capable of flawlessly making Narayana the son of the four-faced Brahma, and making Brahma the son of Narayana?
commentary: The myths say Brahma, the creator, was born from Narayana, the preserver. Vallalar's Siddha can turn that around without effort, making the father the son and the son the father. The supreme Lord is bound by no rule of myth or nature.

translit: kommai peṟuṅkōṭā kōṭiyaṇṭam ellāmōr cemmayirkkāl uṭpukuttum cittaṉevaṉ - cemmaiyilā
translation: Who is the Siddha who can fit billions of vast universes into a single red hair follicle?
commentary: Billions of vast universes, tucked inside a single red hair follicle. Scale means nothing to the supreme Siddha, whose reality works entirely outside the physical limits we know.

translit: vempuliyai veṇpāl viḷaipacuvāy appacuvaic cempuliyāc ceyyavalla cittaṉevaṉ - ampuliyai
translation: Who is the Siddha capable of turning a cruel tiger into a cow yielding white milk, and turning that cow into a fierce red tiger?
commentary: A fierce tiger becomes a gentle cow giving white milk, and the cow turns back into a tiger just as easily. God commands the inner nature of every creature, and instincts that run deep mean nothing before Him.

translit: aṅkatiroṇ ceṅkatirāy ampuliyāyp pampukiṉṟa ceṅkatiraic ceyyavalla cittaṉevaṉ - tuṅkamuṟā
translation: Who is the Siddha capable of turning the beautiful moon into the bright red sun, and turning the spreading red sun into the moon?
commentary: Sun and moon trade places at His command. In the hands of the Supreme, cool moonlight and burning sun are interchangeable.

translit: ōraṇuvōr māmalaiyāy ōrmā malaiyatuvōr cīraṇuvāyc ceyyavalla cittaṉevaṉ - vīramuṭaṉ
translation: Who is the Siddha capable of turning a single atom into a massive mountain, and turning a massive mountain into a tiny atom?
commentary: An atom too small to see swells into a towering mountain, and a mountain shrinks to a speck. Mass, the most solid-seeming thing we know, is fixed in neither direction. Only the Lord's power is permanent.

translit: muṉṉakaiyā niṉṟatoru muppurattai aṉṟorukāl ciṉṉakaiyāl tīmaṭutta cittaṉevaṉ - muṉṉayaṉmāl
translation: Who is the Siddhar who once set fire with a slight smile to the three flying cities that stood mocking? Brahma, Vishnu,
commentary: Arrogance falls to the Supreme with no effort at all. Vallalar recalls the old story of three demonic flying cities that stood mocking, and the divine burned them with nothing more than a smile. Siddhar means a perfected mystic or master, and here the word names God. Such a master needs no weapon to bring down what stands in the way.

translit: maṟṟirunta vāṉavarum vāyntacaikkā vaṇṇamoru ciṟṟurumpaināṭṭiniṉṟa cittaṉevaṉ - maṟṟavarpōl
translation: and the rest of the celestials could not stir it. Who is the Siddhar who planted a tiny piece of straw? Unlike them,
commentary: Even the greatest gods have no power of their own. In the old story the supreme divine sets a tiny blade of straw before the celestials, and with all their strength together they cannot make it tremble. Every bit of power in the universe belongs to this one Siddhar.

translit: allā ayaṉum ariyum uruttiraṉum cellā neṟiniṉṟa cittaṉevaṉ - ollāta
translation: Brahma, Vishnu, and Rudra cannot tread there. Who is the Siddhar who stands on that inaccessible path? Into unyielding
commentary: The supreme Siddhar stands on a level far above the traditional Hindu trinity. Vallalar says plainly that Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver, and Rudra the destroyer cannot even reach the path where the true Divine exists.

translit: kalliṟ cuvaiyāyk kaṉiyiṟ cuvaiyilatāyc cellap paṇikkavalla cittaṉevaṉ - allalaṟap
translation: stone he commands taste, and removes taste from a fruit. Who is this capable Siddhar? To eradicate all sorrow,
commentary: Nature's laws sit in his hand. He can tell a hard stone to taste sweet and take the flavor out of a ripe fruit.

translit: pārkkiṉṟa yāvarkaṭkum pāvaṉā tītaṉeṉac cīrkkiṉṟa meyññāṉac cittaṉevaṉ - mārkkaṅkaḷ
translation: he remains beyond the imagination of everyone who looks upon him. Who is this Siddhar of excellent true wisdom? The paths...
commentary: No one can picture the true Divine. Even those who look straight at this master cannot hold him in a thought or a mental image. True wisdom is knowing that our ideas about the Supreme cannot limit it.

translit: oṉṟeṉṟa mēlavarai oṉṟeṉ ṟuraittavarpāl ceṉṟoṉṟi niṟkiṉṟa cittaṉevaṉ - aṉṟorunāḷ
translation: Who is the Siddhar who goes and unites with those who praise the Supreme as the One? On a day in the past,
commentary: Recognize the divine as one undivided truth, and God comes and unites with you closely. Vallalar asks who this perfected being (Siddhar) is, praising how near he stays to true seekers.

translit: kallāṉai tiṉṉak karumpaḷittup pāṇṭiyaṉvīṇ cellā taḷittamakā cittaṉevaṉ - collāta
translation: who is the great Siddhar who fed sugarcane to the stone elephant and gracefully saved the Pandya king from ruin? Among those who speak of the indescribable
commentary: A beloved old legend lies behind these lines. God came as a wandering master and made a stone elephant eat sugarcane, and so saved the Pandya king from ruin. For Vallalar the story shows how easily divine power bends physical law to protect people.

translit: oṉṟē iraṇṭēmēl oṉṟiraṇṭē eṉpavaṟṟuḷ ceṉṟē naṭuniṉṟa cittaṉevaṉ - ceṉṟēṟum
translation: as One, as Two, and as One and Two, who is the Siddhar who goes and stands squarely in the center? Turning a soaring
commentary: Scholars argue without end over whether God and the soul are wholly one, wholly separate, or some mix of the two. The divine presence simply stands squarely in the center of all things, untouched by these limiting intellectual categories.

translit: attirattai meṉmalarāy ammalarai attiramāyc cittirattaip pēcuvikkum cittaṉevaṉ - ettalattum
translation: weapon into a soft flower and that flower into a weapon, who is the Siddhar who makes a painted image speak? In every realm,
commentary: Vallalar marvels at a power that reverses the very nature of things. He turns a deadly weapon into a soft flower and the flower back into a weapon, and he gives a flat painting a voice. Physical reality answers completely to the divine will.

translit: caṅkamatētāparamāyt tāparamē caṅkamatāyc ceṅkaiyiṭā tāṟṟavalla cittaṉevaṉ - taṅkukiṉṟa
translation: who is the Siddhar capable of making the moving unmoving and the unmoving moving without even touching them with his fair red hands? The abiding
commentary: The world holds creatures that move and forms fixed in place. This master freezes the moving and sets the still in motion, without so much as a touch of his hands.

translit: cattellām ākic cayampuvāy āṉantac cittellām vallaciva cittaṉevaṉ - tattellām
translation: Who is the Siva-Siddhar capable of all blissful consciousness, who becomes all existence and remains self-existent? All those restless thoughts...
commentary: Siva-Siddhar means a perfected being of supreme divine consciousness. He is self-existent, he becomes all that exists, and all blissful awareness is his to command. To reach him, a seeker first has to quiet the endless wandering of thought.

translit: nīṭṭātu neñcam nilaittavarkkum taṉṉuṇmai kāṭṭātu kāṭṭiniṟkum kaḷvaṉevaṉ - pāṭṭōṭu
translation: ...they do not prolong. Even to those whose hearts remain steadfast, who is the thief who reveals and yet conceals his true nature? With songs...
commentary: God plays the thief with his devotees. Even when a heart is steady and focused, he shows himself and then slips out of sight. This quiet hide-and-seek keeps drawing the seeker into deeper longing.

translit: vaṇṭāluṅ koṉṟai malarōy eṉamaṟaikaḷ kaṇṭālum kāṇāta kaḷvaṉevaṉ - toṇṭāka
translation: ...humming bees swarm your Kondrai flowers, declare the Vedas. Yet though they see him thus, who is the thief they do not truly see? In true service...
commentary: The ancient scriptures praise God with traditional poetry, describing him wearing a garland of Kondrai flowers swarming with bees. Vallalar says the scriptures only capture this outward image and miss his deepest reality. God remains a thief who hides his absolute truth from even the highest religious texts.

translit: aḷḷam ceṟiyārkkē aṉṟi aṟivārkkuk kaḷḷam ceṟiyāta kaḷvaṉevaṉ - eḷḷalaṟak
translation: ...except for those mired in ignorance, who is the thief who shows no deceit to the wise? Flawlessly...
commentary: His trickery confuses only those still bound by worldly ignorance. With the wise he is completely open and shows no deceit, and a pure mind sees him clearly.

translit: koṇṭavelān taṉpāl koṭukkumavar tammiṭattil kaṇṭavelām koḷḷaikoḷuṅ kaḷvaṉevaṉ - koṇṭuḷattil
translation: ...from those who give him all they possess, who is the thief who plunders everything he sees? Taking into the heart...
commentary: Give God everything you own and he answers by looting whatever attachments you still hold. This thief empties the devotee of ego and personal desire. He takes the whole person, and only divine grace is left behind.

translit: taṉṉaiyoḷik kiṉṟōrkaḷ tammuḷoḷit tuḷḷavelām kaṉṉamiṭak kaivanta kaḷvaṉevaṉ - maṇṇulakaic
translation: Who is the thief adept at breaking in, hiding within those who hide themselves and stealing everything inside?
commentary: Vallalar calls God a master thief. Try to hide your thoughts or pull away from him, and you find he is already waiting deep inside you, ready to carry off the ego and attachments you were guarding.

translit: caṟpaṉaicey kiṉṟatirō tāṉameṉum cattiyiṉāl kaṟpaṉaicey tēmayakkum kaḷvaṉevaṉ - muṟpaṭumit
translation: Who is the thief who deludes the earthly world, fabricating illusions through the power of concealment?
commentary: The power of concealment (tirotana) is a divine force that hides the ultimate truth. God works like an illusionist, throwing a veil of worldly confusion over the mind so that souls are pushed to seek real clarity.

translit: toṇṭulakil uḷḷa-uyir tōṟumoḷit tāṟṟalelām kaṇṭulavu kiṉṟatoru kaḷvaṉevaṉ - viṇṭakalā
translation: Who is the unique thief who hides within every living soul in this ancient world of service, watching all their actions as he wanders?
commentary: He is a silent witness hidden in every living being. Everything we do and everywhere we go, he watches closely. And he stays unseen the whole time.

translit: maṇmayakkum poṉmayakkum mātar mayakkumeṉum kaṇmayakkam kāṭṭiniṟkum kaḷvaṉevaṉ - uṇmayakku
translation: Who is the thief who reveals the inseparable visual delusions of the lust for land, the lust for gold, and the lust for women?
commentary: Land, wealth and physical pleasure are the three classic traps of worldly life. God tests souls by setting these powerful illusions right before their eyes.

translit: mācu paṟikkum matiyuṭaiyōr tammuṭaiya kācu paṟikkiṉṟa kaḷvaṉevaṉ - ācakaṉṟa
translation: Who is the thief who snatches the wealth of the wise who pluck away the stains of inner delusion?
commentary: Even the wisest seekers get robbed by this thief. The moment they clear away their own inner confusion, God steps in and takes what remains of their separate self, absorbing them entirely.

translit: peṇṇāl evaiyum piṟappittu maṟṟainutaṟ kaṇṇāl aḻikkiṉṟa kaḷvaṉevaṉ - eṇṇātu
translation: Who is the thief who creates all things through the Goddess and destroys them with the eye on his forehead?
commentary: God creates the universe through the feminine divine energy and dissolves it through the power symbolized by Siva's third eye. Vallalar playfully calls him a thief because he directs these vast cosmic acts while staying completely hidden from us.

translit: nāṉeṉṟu niṟkiṉ naṭuvēyan nāṉāṇat tāṉeṉṟu niṟkum caturaṉevaṉ - māṉeṉṟa
translation: If one thoughtlessly stands asserting "I", who is the capable one who stands within as "Himself", making that "I" feel ashamed?
commentary: We often act out of ego, proudly asserting our own importance. God is the real power acting from within. Once a person sees that inner presence, the arrogant "I" shrinks away in shame.

translit: māyaitaṉaik kāṭṭi maṟaippittam māyaiyiṟṟaṉ cāyaitaṉaik kāṭṭum caturaṉevaṉ - nēyamuṭaṉ
translation: Who is the capable one who projects the illusion of the deer to obscure the truth, and then reveals his own reflection within that very illusion?
commentary: The physical world distracts the mind, a covering of māyai (illusion) that hides the truth. Yet God is so capable that he uses that same illusion to reflect his own light, and through it he guides the soul back to reality.

translit: nāṉmaṟaiyum nāṉmukaṉum nāraṇaṉum nāṭutoṟum tāṉmaṟaiyum mēṉmaic caturaṉevaṉ - vāṉmaṟaiyām
translation: As the four Vedas, the four-faced Brahma, and Narayana seek him everywhere with love, who is the supreme capable one who hides himself from them?
commentary: Not even the greatest gods or the oldest scriptures can grasp the supreme reality. Brahma the creator, Narayana the preserver and the Vedas search for him everywhere. The supreme light stays hidden from them all.

translit: muṉṉai maṟaikkum muṭipporuḷeṉ ṟāypavarkkum taṉṉai maṟaikkum caturaṉevaṉ - uṉṉukiṉṟōr
translation: Who is the capable one who hides himself even from those who investigate him as the ultimate reality of the ancient heavenly Vedas?
commentary: Intellectual study alone can never reach God. Scholars may spend their lives investigating the ancient scriptures for the ultimate reality, and still the divine hides from their logic and analysis.

translit: cittattiṟ cutta citākācam eṉṟoruciṟ cattattiṟ kāṭṭum caturaṉevaṉ - muttareṉa
translation: Who is the capable one who reveals the pure space of consciousness within the mind through a single sound of supreme consciousness?
commentary: God can open a vast, pure space of awareness right inside the human mind. A single sound of supreme consciousness is enough to awaken that boundless inner sky, and Vallalar marvels at the master who can do it.

translit: yāvar iruntār avarkāṇa vīṟṟirukkum tēvar pukaḻtalaimait tēvaṉevaṉ - yāvarkaḷum
translation: He sits in majesty so that whoever exists as liberated beings may see him. Who is the supreme God praised by the celestial beings?
commentary: The highest presence shows itself fully to those who have won true spiritual freedom. Even the celestial gods look up to him and praise him. Vallalar asks who this God is, seated in glory above all the traditional deities.

translit: ivvaṇattaṉ ivviṭattaṉ ivviyalaṉ eṉṟaṟiyāc cevvaṇattaṉ āmtalaimait tēvaṉevaṉ - meyvaṇattōr
translation: No one can ever define him by saying he is of this color, this place, or this nature. Who is the supreme God of perfect form?
commentary: We keep trying to pin God down with a shape, a color, a place. He is beyond all such limits. His perfection will never fit the ordinary categories we use for the world.

translit: tāmvāḻa aṇṭa carācaraṅkaḷ tāmvāḻa nāmvāḻat taṉṉuraiyām nāṉmaṟaikaḷ - tāmvāḻac
translation: He acts so that those of true nature may flourish, so that the universe and all moving and unmoving things may flourish, so that we may flourish, and so that the four Vedas which are his own words may flourish.
commentary: His power is the life force that lets everything exist and grow. He sustains the whole universe of moving creatures and still things, the lives of good people, and the scriptures themselves.

translit: cāruruviṉ nallaruḷē cattiyāy meyyaṟiviṉ cīruruvē ōruruvām tēvaṉevaṉ - īruruvum
translation: Who is the God whose beautiful form of good grace acts as his divine power, and whose excellent form of true knowledge serves as his singular form?
commentary: Most people imagine gods with bodies, weapons or ornaments. The supreme God has no body of matter. His only form is pure grace and perfect knowledge, and his power is simply his compassion at work in the world.

translit: oṉṟeṉ ṟuṇara uṇartti aṭiyaruḷam ceṉṟaṅ kamarntaruḷum tēvaṉevaṉ - eṉṟeṉṟum
translation: Who is the God who makes us realize the One, and enters and abides gracefully in the hearts of His devotees forever?
commentary: God teaches us to see that there is only One. Once a devotee truly knows this, He enters that heart and stays there for good.

translit: taṟcakacam eṉṟē camayam camaracamām ciṟcapaiyil vāḻkiṉṟa tēvaṉevaṉ - piṟpaṭumōr
translation: Declaring it His natural state, who is the God who lives in the Hall of Consciousness where all religions harmonize? Leaving behind an inferior
commentary: God's natural home is the Hall of Consciousness (Cir Capai). In this space of pure awareness, all the conflicting claims of different religions finally dissolve into peace and harmony.

translit: poyviṭṭu meynneṟiyaip pōṟṟittaṟ pōtattaik kaiviṭ ṭuṇarvē kaṭaippiṭittu - neyviṭṭa
translation: falsehood, praising the true path, abandoning self-conceit, and holding firmly to true awareness alone. Like a fire fed with ghee,
commentary: Walking the true path means dropping falsehood and letting go of self-conceit. Real awareness only takes hold once self-centered thinking is left behind entirely.

translit: tīppōṟ kaṉalum cerukkaṟavē ceṅkamalap pūppōlum taṉtāḷ puṇaipaṟṟik - kāppāya
translation: arrogance blazes. To destroy it completely, grasping His red lotus-like feet as a raft. As protection,
commentary: Arrogance burns like a fire fed with ghee. The only way to put it out is to cling to His red lotus feet, holding on the way a drowning person holds a raft in a rough sea.

translit: veṇṇī ṟaṇintu vitirvitirttu meypoṭippak kaṇṇīr aruvi kalantāṭi- uṇṇīrmai
translation: wearing the white ash, trembling, the body thrilling, bathing in a waterfall of tears, with inner nature...
commentary: Real devotion shows in the body. Wearing the white ash, the devotee trembles, the skin thrills, and tears pour down like a waterfall out of sheer love.

translit: eṉpuruki uḷḷuruki iṉpār uyiruruki aṉpuruki aṉpuruvam ākippiṉ - vaṉpakaṉṟu
translation: Bones melting, the heart melting, the joyful soul melting, and love itself melting, one becomes the very form of love. Then all hardness departs.
commentary: A love this deep softens bones, heart and soul until the seeker becomes love itself. Once that happens, all inner hardness is gone.

translit: puṇṇiyā tiṅkaṭ puricaṭaiyāy poṉṉitaḻik kaṇṇiyā eṅkaḷ kaḷaikaṇṇē - eṇṇiyāṅ
translation: O embodiment of virtue! You wear the moon in your braided hair. You wear the garland of golden konrai flowers. You are our refuge! Just as they think of you,
commentary: Vallalar praises Siva with His familiar images, the crescent moon and golden konrai (Indian laburnum) flowers in His braided hair. He is our refuge. He answers the very moment a devotee reaches out.

translit: kaṉpark karuḷum aracē amutēpē riṉpak kaṭalē ematuṟavē - maṉpeṟṟu
translation: you bestow grace upon your devotees. O King! O Nectar! O ocean of great bliss! You are our true kin! Gaining lasting glory,
commentary: An ocean of bliss, and our truest kin. Grace comes at once to anyone who seeks Him that closely.

translit: māṟṟuraiyāp poṉṉē maṇiyē-em kaṇmaṇiyē ēṟṟuvanta meypporuḷē eṉṟunitam - pōṟṟiniṉṟāl
translation: O unalloyed pure gold! O precious gem! O pupil of our eyes! O exalted true reality! If one stands praising you daily in these words,
commentary: Unalloyed gold, a precious gem, the pupil of our own eye. God is the most precious treasure there is, flawless as pure gold, and as close and vital to us as the eye we see with.

translit: uḷḷūṟi uḷḷat tuṇarvūṟi avvuṇarviṉ aḷḷūṟi aṇṇit tamutūṟit - teḷḷūṟum
translation: sweetness wells up within. Awareness wells up in the heart. Within that awareness, abundant joy wells up. Tasting so sweet, nectar wells up and clear essence overflows.
commentary: Keep praising Him daily and this is what follows. Awareness wells up in the heart, and within it a joy as sweet as nectar, until the whole being overflows.

translit: vāṉpōl paravi matipōl kuḷirntuyarkōl tēṉpōl maturikkum tēvaṉevaṉ - vāṉpōṉār
translation: Who is the God who expands like the sky, cools like the moon, and tastes sweet like honey from a high branch? The celestial beings...
commentary: Vast like the sky, cooling like the moon, sweet like honey from a high branch. God is boundless, comforting, and a joy to experience.

translit: māṇkoṭukkum teyva maṭantaiyarkku maṅkalappoṉ nāṇkoṭukka nañcuvanta nātaṉevaṉ - nāṇmalarpey
translation: ...grant glory. To ensure their divine women kept their auspicious golden marriage threads, who is the Lord who joyfully consumed the poison? Showering fresh flowers...
commentary: When the cosmic ocean was churned, a deadly poison rose from it. The Lord drank it gladly to save the celestial gods, so that their wives would never become widows and lose their golden marriage threads. That is the measure of His compassion and sacrifice to protect life.

translit: tārttiyāyt tēvar arakaraveṉ ṟētta-aṭṭa mūrttiyāy niṉṟa mutalvaṉevaṉ - cīrttipeṟa
translation: ...woven into garlands, the gods praise him chanting Hara Hara. Who is the primal Lord who stands as the eightfold form? To attain glory...
commentary: The gods worship Him with fresh garlands and chant "Hara Hara," a traditional word of praise. Vallalar calls Him the primal Lord who stands as the eightfold form (aṭṭa mūrtti). In Tamil tradition this means the Divine is visibly present in the five elements, the sun, the moon and the soul, making up the entire universe.

translit: īṇṭaṟ putavaṭivāy ettēva rēṉuniṉṟu kāṇṭaṟ karitām kaṇēcaṉevaṉ - vēṇṭuṟṟup
translation: ...assuming an intensely wondrous form here, who is the Lord of hosts whom any god finds difficult to behold? With deep desire...
commentary: The Lord takes a wondrous form, yet even the highest celestial beings find Him hard to behold. His true nature is too immense for any ordinary mind or lesser god to grasp or see clearly.

translit: pūmiyeṅkum vāḻttip pukaḻvār virumpumiṭṭa kāmiyaṅkaḷ īyum kaṇēcaṉevaṉ - nāmiyaṅka
translation: ...they praise and glorify him everywhere on earth. Who is the Lord of hosts who grants the boons they wish for? So that we may move...
commentary: Beyond our full grasp, yet always listening. Whoever praises Him anywhere on earth receives the heartfelt wishes they ask for.

translit: ēṇa varumiṭaiyū ṟellām akaṟṟiyaruḷ kāṇa emakkīyum kaṇēcaṉevaṉ - māṇavaru
translation: Who is Lord Vinayakar who removes all arising obstacles and grants us the vision of grace?
commentary: Vinayakar, the elephant-headed one, is traditionally invoked first so that difficulties clear away. Vallalar asks who it really is that removes the obstacles in our path and opens our eyes to grace.

translit: munta maṟaiyiṉ muḻupporuḷai nāṉmukaṟkut tanta aruṭkaṭalām cāmiyevaṉ - tantamakkām
translation: Who is the Lord, the ocean of grace, who imparted the complete meaning of the ancient Vedas to the four-faced Brahma?
commentary: Brahma, the four-faced creator, is traditionally held to be the source of the Vedas. Yet someone taught him their complete meaning. Vallalar asks who that teacher is, the ocean of grace who instructed the creator himself.

translit: vātakaṟṟi uṇmai marapaḷittu vañcamalak kōtakaṟṟum neñcak kukēcaṉevaṉ - tītakaṟṟit
translation: Who is Lord Guha dwelling in the heart, who dispels futile arguments, bestows the true tradition, and removes the flaw of deceitful impurity?
commentary: Guha is another name for Murugan, the presence said to dwell hidden in the cave of the heart. Vallalar asks who this true inner guide is. He silences endless intellectual debate and clears away the deep impurities that deceive the mind.

translit: taṅkum ulakaṅkaḷ cāyāmaṟ ceñcaṭaimēl kaṅkaitaṉaic cērtta kaṭavuḷevaṉ - eṅkuṟiṉum
translation: Who is the God who gathered the river Ganges upon his red matted hair so that the enduring worlds would not be destroyed?
commentary: The old story says the falling Ganges came with such force it would have crushed the earth, so Siva caught it in his matted hair. Vallalar asks who this protector truly is, the one who saves the worlds from destruction.

translit: kūmpā nilaimaik kuṇattōr toḻukiṉṟa pāmpā paraṇap paramaṉevaṉ - kūmpātu
translation: Who is the Supreme Lord adorned with a serpent, worshiped by people of unwavering virtue?
commentary: In the traditional stories the supreme Lord wears a coiled serpent as an ornament. Vallalar asks who this highest reality truly is, worshiped by people of steady and flawless character.

translit: pōṟṟuraittu niṟkum puṉitaṉmēl vantakoṭuṅ kūṟṟutaitta centāḷ kuḻakaṉevaṉ - āṟṟaluṟu
translation: Who is the beautiful Lord whose red foot kicked cruel Death when he came for the pure devotee standing in praise?
commentary: In a famous sacred story Siva kicked Yama (the god of death) to protect the young devotee Markandeya. That red foot is supreme power conquering death to save a pure, devoted heart.

translit: vaiyam tutikkum makāliṅka mūrttimutal aiyaintu mūrttiyeṉum aiyaṉevaṉ - aiyantīr
translation: Who is the Lord appearing as the twenty-five forms beginning with the Mahalinga murthi praised by the powerful world?
commentary: The twenty-five forms (murthis) refer to the traditional physical manifestations of Siva in the Saiva religion, starting with the Mahalinga (the great pillar of light). The poem points to the single supreme Lord who assumes all these sacred shapes worshipped by the world.

translit: vallārcol vaṇṇamenta vaṇṇamanta vaṇṇaṅkaḷ ellām uṭaiya vitattaṉevaṉ - ellārkkum
translation: Whatever nature the flawless sages declare him to possess, who is the one manifesting in all those natures?
commentary: No single shape or description can hold the Divine. Whatever attributes or forms the realized sages name, the supreme reality is vast enough to be all of them.

translit: tāmtalaiva rākattam tāḷtoḻumet tēvarkkum āntalaimai īntapara mārttaṉevaṉ - pōntuyirkaḷ
translation: Who is the supreme reality serving as the leader for all, granting leadership to whatever gods bow at his feet?
commentary: People worship many gods in many traditions. Those lesser gods hold their authority only because they too bow to one supreme leader, and Vallalar points past them to him.

translit: eṅkeṅ kiruntumaṉat tiyātu viḻaintālum aṅkaṅ kiruntaḷikkum aṇṇalevaṉ - puṅkamikum
translation: Wherever souls may be and whatever they desire in their minds, who is the exalted Lord who grants it to them right there?
commentary: Wherever a soul is and whatever it prays for, the Lord hears it from within and gives what is needed in that very place. He is that close to every living being.

translit: aṇṇal tirumalarkkai āḻipeṟak kaṇṇiṭanta kaṇṇaṟ karuḷiyamuk kaṇṇaṉevaṉ - maṇṇiṭattil
translation: Who is the three-eyed Lord who bestowed grace upon Kannan when he plucked out his own eye to obtain the discus for his divine lotus hand? On this earth,
commentary: Vishnu (Kannan) wanted a powerful weapon, the discus, so he worshiped Siva with a thousand lotus flowers. Finding himself one flower short, he plucked out his own eye to complete the offering. Siva rewarded him for that extreme devotion.

translit: ōyātu cūlmutirnta ōrpeṇ taṉakkākat tāyāki vanta tayāḷaṉevaṉ - cēyāka
translation: who is the compassionate one who came as a mother for a woman heavily burdened with advanced pregnancy? Like the divine son,
commentary: God's compassion reaches people at their most vulnerable. In this legend a pregnant woman was stranded by floods while her own mother was still on the way to help with the birth. The Divine took the exact form of her mother and safely delivered the child.

translit: vēlpiṭitta kaṇṇappaṉ mēvumeccil vēṇṭumitat tāṟpocittu nērnta tayāḷaṉevaṉ - pāṟkuṭattait
translation: who is the compassionate one who lovingly desired and ate the tasted offering brought by Kannappan who held a spear? When the milk pots
commentary: Devotion matters more than ritual purity. Kannappan was a hunter who knew none of the formal rules of worship, so he tasted his food to be sure it was good before offering it. Because it was given with pure love, God accepted that tasted offering eagerly.

translit: tāṉtantai eṉṟeṟintōṉ tāḷeṟinta taṇṭikkut tāṉtantai āṉa tayāḷaṉevaṉ - tāṉkoṇṭu
translation: were kicked by a man claiming to be his father, who is the compassionate one who became a father to Sandi after Sandi severed that man's legs? Taking
commentary: Devotion sometimes overrides worldly family ties. Young Sandi was pouring milk in worship when his angry father arrived and kicked the pots over. Sandi struck his father's legs to protect the sacred act. In return, God declared himself the boy's true father.

translit: campu naṟuṅkaṉiyiṉ taṉvitaiyait tāḷpaṇinta campu muṉikkīyum tayāḷaṉevaṉ - ampuviyil
translation: the seed of the fragrant rose apple fruit, who is the compassionate one who gave it to the sage Jambu who bowed at his feet? On this beautiful earth,
commentary: Here is the origin of a famous sacred grove. A sage named Jambu worshiped intensely, and God rewarded him with a rare fruit seed. He swallowed it, and a sacred rose apple tree grew from his head, uniting his body for good with the divine presence.

translit: āṇṭavaṉeṉ ṟēttappoṉ ṉampalattil āṉantat tāṇṭavamcey kiṉṟa tayāḷaṉevaṉ - kāṇtakaiya
translation: Who is the compassionate one performing the dance of bliss in the golden hall, praised by all as the Lord?
commentary: The sequence opens with a question. Vallalar has in mind the traditional form of the Divine dancing the dance of bliss in the golden hall of Chidambaram, pouring compassion on the world.

translit: muttuccivikaiyiṉmēl muṉkāḻi ōṅkumuḻu muttait taṉivaitta muttaṉevaṉ - pattipeṟu
translation: Who is the liberated one who placed the flawless pearl of ancient Kazhi upon the beautiful pearl palanquin?
commentary: The pearl of Kazhi is Gnanasambandar, the child saint born in that town. Vallalar asks who gave this young devotee a palanquin of pearls so he could travel and sing his hymns. The question celebrates how tenderly the Divine cares for those who love Him.

translit: nāvoṉṟaracarkku nāmtaruvēm nallūril vā-eṉṟu vāymalarnta vaḷḷalevaṉ - pūvoṉṟu
translation: Who is the benefactor who spoke the gracious words, "Come to Nallur, and we shall grant our grace to the devoted king of speech"?
commentary: Appar was called the king of speech for his poetry. Vallalar asks who invited him to Nallur to bless him there. The Divine reaches out first, to lift the devoted seeker.

translit: naṉṟoṇṭar cuntararai nāmtaṭukka vantamaiyāl vaṉṟoṇṭaṉ nī-eṉṟa vaḷḷalevaṉ - naṉṟoṇṭiṉ
translation: Who is the benefactor who came to intercept the fine devotee Sundarar, who is like a rare flower, and named him the fierce devotee?
commentary: Traditional stories say the Lord came in disguise to stop Sundarar's wedding, claimed him as a lifelong servant, and named him the fierce devotee. Vallalar asks who did this sudden, forceful act of grace that pulled a soul out of ordinary worldly life.

translit: kāṇikkai yākak karuttaḷittār tammoḻiyai māṇikkam eṉṟuraitta vaḷḷalevaṉ - tāṇiṟkum
translation: Who is the benefactor who declared the words of the one who offered his mind as a tribute of good service to be a precious ruby?
commentary: Manikkavasagar offered his whole mind to God through his poetry. Vallalar asks who prized those words of complete surrender and called them as precious as rubies. A pure, surrendered heart is the greatest treasure a person can offer.

translit: taṉṉaṉpar tāmvaruntil caṟṟun tariyātu maṉṉaṉ paruḷaḷikkum vaḷḷalevaṉ - muṉṉaṉpil
translation: Who is the benevolent Lord who cannot bear it for a moment when His devotees suffer, and who grants them His enduring loving grace?
commentary: Here is a God whose compassion is immediate. When those who love Him suffer, He cannot bear it for even a moment, and His grace pours out at once to comfort them.

translit: cālpuṭaiya nallōrkkut taṇṇaruḷtan tāṭkoḷavōr mālviṭaimēl vantaruḷum vaḷḷalevaṉ - māṉmutalōr
translation: Who is the benevolent Lord who comes upon a great bull to grant His cool grace and claim the good people filled with ancient love?
commentary: The image comes from the old stories of Siva. He rides His great bull, Nandi, and comes in person to claim and bless the faithful whose love for Him runs deep.

translit: tāmalaiyā vaṇṇam takaiyaruḷi ōṅkuveḷḷi māmalaivāḻ kiṉṟa-aruḷ vaḷḷalevaṉ - āmavaṉē
translation: Who is the benevolent Lord of grace who dwells on the towering great silver mountain, and who granted fitting grace so that Vishnu and the other gods would not wander in distress?
commentary: The silver mountain is Mount Kailash, the traditional home of Siva. From there He gives refuge and grace to Vishnu and the other gods when they are troubled and lost.

translit: nammaip paṇikoṇṭu nāraṇaṉum nāṭaritām cemmaik katiyaruḷnam teyvaṅkāṇ - emmaiyiṉum
translation: He is indeed our God who takes us into His service and grants us the perfect state that is difficult even for Narayana to seek. Behold Him!
commentary: Now the questions get their answer. This supreme Lord is our own God. He takes ordinary people into His loving service and gives them a perfect state that even the greatest deities struggle to reach.

translit: nāṭak kiṭaittal namakkaṉṟi nāṉmukaṟkum tēṭak kiṭaiyānam teyvaṅkāṇ - nīṭaccīr
translation: He is our God who is available for us to seek in any birth, yet impossible even for the four-faced Brahma to find by searching. Behold Him!
commentary: In the old story, Brahma the creator searched endlessly for the Lord's crown and failed. Yet the same God lets ordinary people find Him when they seek with love, in any lifetime.

translit: nalvan taṉaiceyyum nampōlvārk kōrñāṉac celvan tarunamatu teyvamkāṇ - colvanta
translation: See, He is our God who grants the wealth of wisdom to people like us who offer good worship.
commentary: Sincere worship brings the highest reward. The Lord answers it with spiritual wisdom, the only true wealth.

translit: eṇmaipeṟum nāmulakil eṉṟum piṟantiṟavāt tiṇmai aḷittaruḷnam teyvamkāṇ - vaṇmaiyuṟa
translation: See, He is our God who graciously grants us simple people the strength to never again be born and die in this world.
commentary: The endless cycle of birth and death is a heavy burden for the soul. The divine gives even the humblest people the spiritual strength to break free from it forever.

translit: muppāḻ kaṭanta muḻuppāḻuk kappālaic ceppātu ceppuṟunam tēcikaṉkāṇ - tappātu
translation: See, He is our Guru who teaches without speaking about that which lies beyond the absolute void transcending the three voids.
commentary: Ultimate reality lies far past anything words can hold. The "three voids" (muppāḻ) are deep stages of spiritual emptiness, and what lies beyond even the absolute void past them is what this Guru teaches. He teaches it in total silence.

translit: tīrā iṭumpait tiripeṉpati yātoṉṟum cērā neṟiyaruḷnam tēcikaṉkāṇ - ārātu
translation: See, He is our Guru who graciously bestows the path where no trace of endless affliction or delusion can ever reach us.
commentary: Ordinary life is full of suffering and deep confusion. The divine teacher sets the soul on a pure path where pain and delusion lose all their power.

translit: nittam teriyā nilaimē viyanamatu cittam teḷivikkum tēcikaṉkāṇ - vittareṉa
translation: See, He is our Guru who brings clarity to our mind that dwells in a state unable to perceive the eternal reality.
commentary: The human mind is clouded by nature and struggles to recognize what is permanent. The Guru clears that fog so the eternal truth can show through.

translit: yātoṉṟum tērā tiruntanamak kivvulakam tīteṉ ṟaṟivitta tēcikaṉkāṇ - kōtiṉṟi
translation: See, he is the teacher who showed us that this world is harmful while we remained oblivious to everything.
commentary: God is our first teacher. While we sat lost in ignorance, he opened our eyes to the traps of worldly life.

translit: ōcai peṟukaṭalcū ḻuṟṟa vulakiṉammai ācai yuṭaṉīṉṟa appaṉkāṇ - mācuṟavē
translation: Flawlessly, see, he is the father who lovingly brought us forth into this world surrounded by the resounding ocean.
commentary: He is our true creator. With flawless love he brings souls into this vast physical world.

translit: vaṉpāy vaḷarkkiṉṟa maṟṟaiyarpō lallāmal aṉpāy namaivaḷarkkum appaṉkāṇ - iṉpāka
translation: Unlike others who raise us harshly and with flaws, see, he is the father who raises us with love.
commentary: Human guardians can be harsh or imperfect. This father raises our souls with nothing but pure affection.

translit: ippāril cēyār itayam malarntammai appā eṉumnaṅkaḷ appaṉkāṇ - ceppāmal
translation: Joyfully, see, he is our father whom the children in this world call "Mother" and "Father" with blossoming hearts.
commentary: He is the parent of every living being. People whose hearts have opened recognize him as both mother and father, and they say so with joy.

translit: eḷḷit tirintālum intā eṉ ṟiṉṉamutam aḷḷik koṭukkunama tappaṉkāṇ - uḷḷikkoṇ
translation: Even if we wander around mocking him without saying a word, see, he is our father who scoops up sweet nectar and gives it to us saying, "Here, take this!"
commentary: His grace comes with no conditions. We can wander away, even mock him, and still he scoops up the sweetest nourishment and holds it out to us.

translit: ṭiṉṟē aruḷvāy eṉattutikkil āṅkunamak kaṉṟē aruḷunama tappaṉkāṇ - naṉṟēmuṉ
translation: If we praise him saying, "Grant your grace this very day," he grants us his grace right then and there; behold our Father.
commentary: A sincere request for grace gets an instant answer. Ask him for it today and he does not put you off to some future time. He gives it right then, the way a loving father would.

translit: kātaravu ceytunalam kaṟpittup piṉperiya ātaravu ceyyunaṅkaḷ appaṉkāṇ - kōtuṟumā
translation: First he shows loving care and teaches us goodness well, and then he provides immense support; behold our Father.
commentary: God takes an active hand in our growth. First he teaches us how to be good. Then he stands behind the life we are trying to build, with the steady guidance of a parent.

translit: vañcamalat tālvarunti vāṭukiṉṟa nantamaiyē añcalañca leṉṟaruḷum appaṉkāṇ - tuñcaleṉum
translation: When we suffer and wither from the highly flawed and deceitful impurities, he blesses us saying, "Fear not, fear not"; behold our Father.
commentary: The impurities of ego and illusion wear us down from the inside and cause deep suffering. When we wither under them, God steps in with "Fear not, fear not," and his grace heals the pain.

translit: nacceṉṟa vātaṉaiyai nāḷumeṇṇi nāmañcum accam keṭuttāṇṭa appaṉkāṇ - niccalumiṅ
translation: Thinking daily of the poisonous torment called death, we are afraid, but he destroys that fear and rules us; behold our Father.
commentary: The fear of death hangs over human life like a poisonous shadow. God lifts that burden off entirely. Once he takes us under his care, the dread of dying gives way to the safety of his presence.

translit: kēyiravum ellum eḷiyēm piḻaittapiḻai āyiramum tāṉpoṟukkum appaṉkāṇ - cēyiraṅkā
translation: Here, day and night, he patiently bears the thousands of mistakes we poor ones commit; behold our Father.
commentary: Day and night we make mistakes, thousands of them. He never turns away in anger. He bears every fault simply because we are his children.

translit: muṉṉam eṭuttaṇaittu muttamiṭṭup pālaruttum aṉṉaiyiṉum aṉpuṭaiya appaṉkāṇ - maṉṉulakil
translation: See, He is the loving Father, possessing more love than the mother who comes forward to lift up, embrace, kiss, and feed us milk.
commentary: Picture a mother lifting her child, holding it close, kissing it and feeding it milk. Vallalar says God's love is greater even than hers.

translit: vaṉmai yaṟappattu mātam cumantunamai naṉmai tarappeṟṟa naṟṟāykāṇ - immaitaṉil
translation: In this enduring world, see, He is the good Mother who endured hardship, carried us for ten months, and gave birth to us to grant us goodness.
commentary: Our existence and our well-being both come from God. Vallalar compares him to a mother who endures the hardship of ten months of pregnancy to bring her child safely into a good life.

translit: aṉṟorunāḷ nampacikaṇ ṭantō tariyātu naṉṟiravilcōṟaḷitta naṟṟāykāṇ - eṉṟumaruṭ
translation: In this present life, see, He is the good Mother who could not bear to see our hunger on that day and fed us rice in the night.
commentary: The divine watches over our daily needs with tender compassion. Just as a mother cannot bear to see her child go hungry and wakes in the night to feed them, God provides for us when we are most vulnerable.

translit: cemmai ilācciṟiya tēvarkaḷpāl cērkkātu nammai vaḷarkkiṉṟa naṟṟāykāṇ - cummaiyeṉa
translation: See, He is the good Mother of eternal grace who raises us, keeping us from joining minor deities who lack perfection.
commentary: People often direct their worship toward lesser gods. Vallalar says the supreme divine acts as a protective mother, steering the soul away from these minor, imperfect deities to keep it safely focused on true grace.

translit: mūḷum peruṅkuṟṟam muṉṉimēl mēṟceyiṉum nāḷum poṟuttaruḷum naṟṟāykāṇ - mūḷukiṉṟa
translation: Even if we deliberately commit great faults that multiply like a heavy burden again and again, see, He is the good Mother who forgives us every day and bestows grace.
commentary: His forgiveness has no end. We may pile up heavy faults on purpose, again and again, and still Vallalar says God remains a mother who forgives us completely every single day.

translit: vaṉṉeṟiyiṟ ceṉṟālum vāveṉ ṟaḻaittunamai naṉṉeṟiyiṟ cērkkiṉṟa naṟṟāykāṇ - cenneṟiyiṉ
translation: Behold the good mother who, even when we stray onto a cruel path, calls us back and sets us on the good path of righteousness.
commentary: Vallalar pictures the divine as a loving mother who never abandons her children. We make mistakes and wander down harmful paths, and God does not punish us for it. Grace calls us back and sets us on the good road again.

translit: nāmtēṭā muṉṉam namaittēṭip piṉputaṉai nāmtēṭac ceykiṉṟa naṟṟāykāṇ - āmtōṟum
translation: Behold the good mother who seeks us out before we seek her, and then makes us seek her continually.
commentary: Grace moves first. It comes looking for us long before we think to search for it, and once that love touches a person, it awakens a longing that keeps them seeking God from then on.

translit: kālam aṟintē kaṉivōṭu nallaruṭpāl ñālam micaiyaḷikkum naṟṟāykāṇ - cālavuṟu
translation: Behold the good mother who knows the right time and tenderly feeds us the milk of good grace upon this earth.
commentary: A mother knows when her baby is hungry. God knows the right moment to nourish a soul, and the milk here is grace, given tenderly so we can grow right here in the physical world.

translit: vempiṇiyum vētaṉaiyum vēcaṟikkai yumtuyarum nampaciyum tīrttaruḷum naṟṟāykāṇ - ampuviyil
translation: Behold the good mother who graciously cures our cruel diseases, agony, weariness, sorrow, and hunger on this beautiful earth.
commentary: For Vallalar, spiritual rescue and physical relief belong together. The same grace that lifts weariness and sorrow also cures disease and fills an empty stomach.

translit: vennīril āṭṭiṭilem meynōkum eṉṟaruḷām naṉṉīril āṭṭukiṉṟa naṟṟāykāṇ - ennīriṉ
translation: Behold the good mother who fears our bodies will ache if bathed in hot water, bathing us instead in the good water of grace.
commentary: A mother tests the bathwater so it won't scald her child. Grace is that gentle and protective. It cleanses the soul without the harsh pain that worldly trials bring.

translit: mēlāy namakku viyaṉulakil aṉpuṭaiya nālā yiramtāyil naṟṟāykāṇ - ēlātu
translation: See the good mother who is supreme to us in this vast world, possessing more love than four thousand mothers combined.
commentary: Pool the affection of four thousand earthly mothers and it still falls short of this one. With that image Vallalar shows God's grace as nurturing and without limit.

translit: vāṭiyaḻu tālem varuttam tariyātu nāṭi-eṭut taṇaikkum naṟṟāykāṇ - nīṭulakil
translation: When we wilt and cry helplessly, see the good mother who, unable to bear our sorrow, seeks us out, lifts us up, and embraces us.
commentary: God does not sit and wait. Like a mother who runs to a crying child, grace comes looking for us when we suffer, and our pain draws an immediate, tender answer.

translit: tāṉpāṭakkēṭṭut tamiyēṉ kaḷikkumuṉṉam nāṉpāṭakkēṭṭuvakkum naṟṟāykāṇ - vāṉpāṭum
translation: Before I, a lonely soul, can listen to him sing and rejoice, see the good mother who rejoices upon hearing me sing.
commentary: The divine delights in our devotion. Before the soul can enjoy hearing the divine voice, God is already glad at the sound of the devotee's simple song, so close and personal is this love.

translit: ñāṉamaṇam ceyyaruḷām naṅkaitaṉait tantunamak kāṉamaṇam ceyvikkum ammāṉkāṇ - tēṉiṉoṭum
translation: See the Lord who gives us the lady of grace, bearing the heavenly fragrance of wisdom, and arranges a fitting marriage for us.
commentary: The image shifts from a nurturing mother to a generous Lord arranging a sacred marriage. He weds the soul to grace itself, pictured as a heavenly bride, and that union brings the wisdom a true spiritual life needs.

translit: iṉpāl amutāti ēkkamuṟa iṉṉaruḷkoṇ ṭaṉpāl viruntaḷikkum ammāṉkāṇ - vaṉpāva
translation: See the Lord who serves us a feast with sweet grace and love, making honey, sweet milk, and celestial nectar pale in comparison.
commentary: Grace is a feast of pure love. Next to it, honey and milk taste bland. Even the legendary nectar of the gods cannot match the taste of compassion and grace.

translit: āḻkaṭalvīḻn tuḷḷam aḻuntum namaiyeṭuttuc cūḻkaraiyil ēṟṟum tuṇaivaṉkāṇ - vīḻkuṇattāl
translation: See, He is the companion who lifts us when our hearts fall and sink in the deep sea, placing us safely on the shore.
commentary: Worldly suffering can feel like drowning in a deep, endless sea. God is the faithful friend who reaches into the water, pulls us out and sets us on solid ground.

translit: iṉpam eṉaittum ituveṉ ṟaṟiyānam tuṉpam tuṭaikkum tuṇaivaṉkāṇ - vaṉpavamām
translation: Through our fallen nature, we do not recognize any joy. See, He is the companion who wipes away our sorrow.
commentary: Our own flaws blind us to real happiness. When we are stuck in that sadness, God comes as a true companion and wipes the pain away.

translit: tīneṟiyiṟ ceṉṟu tiyaṅkukiṉṟa nantamakkut tūneṟiyaik kāṭṭum tuṇaivaṉkāṇ - mānilattil
translation: Trapped in the cruel cycle of birth, we walk the evil path and stand bewildered. See, He is the companion who shows us the pure path.
commentary: Repeated birth breeds confusion and pushes people down harmful paths. God is the guide who finds the bewildered mind and points it toward the pure path of grace.

translit: iṉṟutoṭṭa taṉṟi yiyaṟkaiyāy nantamakkut toṉṟutoṭṭu vantavaruṭ cuṟṟaṅkāṇ - toṉṟutoṭṭē
translation: In this great world, our bond did not begin today. See, He is the family of grace who has naturally been with us from ancient times.
commentary: The bond between the soul and God is eternal. He is our true, ancient family, tied to us by grace long before this present life began.

translit: āyumuṭaṟ kaṉpuṭaittām āruyiriṟ ṟāṉciṟanta nēyamvaitta nammuṭaiya nēcaṉkāṇ - pēyareṉa
translation: Ever since ancient times, He holds a love for our precious soul far greater than the soul's own love for the body. See, He is our beloved.
commentary: We cling to our bodies fiercely. God's love for the soul within runs deeper and older than even that instinct for survival.

translit: vāṅkātu nāmē maṟantālum nammaiviṭṭu nīṅkāta nammuṭaiya nēcaṉkāṇ - tīṅkāka
translation: Even if we relentlessly forget Him, see our lover who never departs from us.
commentary: He stays even when we forget Him completely. Most human bonds need attention from both sides to survive. God's presence is entirely unconditional, and He stays firmly by our side however deeply we ignore Him.

translit: īṭṭukiṉṟa āpattil intā eṉa-aruḷai nīṭṭukiṉṟa nammuṭaiya nēcaṉkāṇ - kūṭṭulakil
translation: In the midst of harmful and mounting dangers, see our lover who reaches out with His grace and says, "Here, take this."
commentary: In a crisis God steps in at once, like a beloved holding out a hand. "Here, take this," He says, and His grace pulls us out of danger.

translit: pulleṉṟa māyaiyiṭaip pōntōṟum nammaiyiṅku nilleṉ ṟiruttukiṉṟa nēcaṉkāṇ - cilleṉṟeṉ
translation: Whenever we wander into the trivial illusion of this crowded world, see our lover who halts us and commands, "Stop right there."
commentary: The world dresses up trivial things as deeply important. When we start chasing these illusions, God steps into our path like a firm guide and tells us to stop before we lose our way.

translit: uṭṭūvum taṉṉaimaṟan tuṇṭālum maṟṟataṟku niṭṭūram ceyyāta nēcaṉkāṇ - naṭṭūrntu
translation: Even if we forget Him who showers a cooling peace within my heart and we merely indulge in eating, see our lover who inflicts no cruelty upon us for that.
commentary: God offers deep inner peace, and we often ignore it to chase the pleasures of the body. Many traditions picture a deity who punishes such forgetfulness. Vallalar's divine lover watches our foolish indulgence and inflicts no cruelty or revenge.

translit: vañcamatu nāmeṇṇi vāḻntālum tāṉciṟitum neñcilatu vaiyāta nēcaṉkāṇ - eñcalilāp
translation: Even if we live harboring deeply planted deceit, see our lover who does not hold it against us in His heart even the slightest bit.
commentary: He holds no grudge, even against our worst flaws. We may live with deceit planted deep in our hearts, and still God does not resent us. His love stays untainted by our moral failures.

translit: pārniṉṟa nāmkiṭaiyāp paṇṭametu vēṇṭiṭiṉum nērniṉ ṟaḷittuvaru nēcaṉkāṇ - ārvamuṭaṉ
translation: Whatever rare thing we who stand on this earth desire, He stands directly before us and grants it. See, He is our loving companion.
commentary: God is an intimate friend. Whatever rare or hard-to-get thing we want in this world, He stands right before us as a loving companion and gives it.

translit: ārntanamak kivviṭattum avviṭattum evviṭattum nērnta-uyir pōṟkiṭaitta nēcaṉkāṇ - cērntumikat
translation: Filled with eager love, we have found Him to be our loving companion, acting as our very own life in this place, that place, and every place. See!
commentary: Here, there, everywhere, He is with us. His love is so complete that He becomes our very life, wherever we go.

translit: tāpañcey kuṟṟam tariṉum poṟuppataṉṟik kōpañ ceyānamatu kōmāṉkāṇ - pāpamaṟa
translation: Even if we accumulate agonizing faults, He patiently bears them and does not become angry. See, He is our King.
commentary: Worldly rulers punish mistakes. This King answers with endless patience, bearing all our painful faults without ever showing anger.

translit: viḷḷumiṟai nāmaṉpu mēvalaṉṟi vēṟṟaracar koḷḷumiṟai vāṅkānam kōmāṉkāṇ - uḷḷamuṟa
translation: To destroy our sins, we declare and offer our love as tribute. See, He is our King who does not extract the taxes collected by other kings.
commentary: Earthly kings demand wealth and goods as taxes. The divine King asks only for our love as tribute, and offering that love sincerely is what clears away our wrongdoings.

translit: uṇṭaḷikkum ūṇuṭaipūṇ ūrā tikaḷtāṉē koṇṭunamak kiṅkaḷikkum kōmāṉkāṇ - maṇṭalattil
translation: Fulfilling the desires of our hearts, He is our King who Himself brings and gives us food to eat and share, clothing, ornaments, towns, and all such things here. See!
commentary: God provides for every part of our earthly life. He Himself gives us food to eat and to share with others, along with clothing, homes and the other comforts of the world.

translit: oṉṟālum nīṅkā tukaṅkaḷ palapalavāyc ceṉṟālum cellānam celvamkāṇ - muṉtāvi
translation: Behold our wealth. It never departs by any means, and it remains undiminished even as countless eons pass. Leaping forward...
commentary: Spiritual wealth is the only treasure that lasts. Worldly riches can be lost or spent. This divine inheritance stays whole however much time passes.

translit: nāṭivaikkum nallaṟivōr nāḷum tavampurintu tēṭivaitta nammuṭaiya celvamkāṇ - māṭiruntu
translation: Behold our wealth. The wise ones of good intellect sought and secured it for us by performing penance every day. Staying close...
commentary: Wise seekers kept up their spiritual discipline day after day to uncover this treasure. They secured it so that everyone who seeks the truth could inherit it.

translit: nāmet taṉaināḷum nalkiṭiṉum tāṉulavāc cēmitta vaippiṉ tiraviyamkāṇ - pūmikkaṇ
translation: Behold the treasure of this accumulated reserve. It never depletes even if we give it away for endless days. Whether here on earth...
commentary: Material wealth runs out when it is shared. Grace does not. The more of this divine love we give to others, the more its endless reserve remains within us.

translit: īṅkuṟiṉum vāṉāti yāṅkuṟiṉum viṭṭakalā tōṅkaruḷāl nammai uṭaiyavaṉkāṇ - āṅkavaṉtaṉ
translation: Behold the one who claims us through his supreme grace. He never leaves us, whether we remain here or in the heavens. And there...
commentary: His supreme grace stays with us wherever we are. Whether a soul lives on earth or in the highest heavens, the divine embrace never lets go.

translit: kaṅkaic caṭaiyaḻakum kātaṉmikum accaṭaimēl tiṅkaṭ koḻuntiṉ tiruvaḻakum - tiṅkaḷtaṉmēl
translation: is the beauty of his matted hair holding the river Ganges, the divine beauty of the tender crescent moon upon that greatly beloved hair, and upon that moon...
commentary: Now Vallalar turns to a joyful vision of the Lord's form. The cosmic river Ganges flows through His matted hair and the gentle crescent moon rests above it, a classic picture of majestic beauty.

translit: cārntilaṅkum koṉṟaimalart tāraḻakum attārmēl ārntilaṅkum vaṇṭiṉ aṇiyaḻakum - tērntavarkkum
translation: The beauty of the radiant garland of konrai flowers adorning Him, and the beautiful array of bees swarming upon that garland.
commentary: A radiant vision of the Lord's form begins with the konrai (golden shower) flowers He wears and the bees drawn to their sweetness. Vallalar shows the divine as something living and fragrant.

translit: nōkkariya nōkkaḻakum nōkkār nutalaḻakum pōkkariya naṉṉutalil poṭṭaḻakum - tēkkutiri
translation: The beauty of His gaze, difficult to comprehend even for realized sages. The beauty of His forehead, and the beauty of the sacred mark upon that fine, unblemished forehead.
commentary: Even the most advanced seekers cannot fathom the depth of His gaze. From the eyes, Vallalar's vision moves to the flawless forehead and the sacred mark upon it.

translit: puṇṭarattiṉ nallaḻakum poṉṉaruḷtāṉ taṉṉeḻilaik kaṇṭavarpāl ūṟṟukiṉṟa kaṇṇaḻakum - toṇṭarkaḷtam
translation: The fine beauty of the three radiant lines of sacred ash. The beauty of His eyes pouring forth golden grace upon those who behold His loveliness.
commentary: Three lines of sacred ash mark the forehead in the traditional way. The real power sits in the eyes, though. They pour out golden grace on anyone who simply looks at the Lord's beauty.

translit: nēcitta neñcamalar nīṭu maṇamukanta nācit tirukkumiḻiṉ nallaḻakum - tēcuṟṟa
translation: The fine beauty of His divine, bud-like nose, breathing in the lasting fragrance from the blossoming hearts of loving devotees.
commentary: Even the Lord's features show how He relates to those who love Him. His nose breathes in the lasting fragrance of devotion blooming in the hearts of the faithful.

translit: mullai mukaiyām muṟuvalaḻa kumpavaḷa ellai vaḷarcev vitaḻaḻakum - nallavarait
translation: The beauty of His radiant smile revealing teeth like jasmine buds, and the beauty of His red lips surpassing the redness of coral.
commentary: Now the smile. Classical Tamil poetry compares bright teeth to white jasmine buds and lips to red coral, and Vallalar uses both to show how warm and approachable the Lord is.

translit: tēveṉṟa tīmpālil tēṉkalantāṟ pōliṉikka vāveṉ ṟaruḷumalar vāyaḻakum - pūvoṉṟum
translation: The beauty of the flower-like mouth that graciously says "Come," sweet as honey mixed in sweet divine milk. The king upon the single flower...
commentary: One word of welcome: "Come." Vallalar likens its sweetness to honey stirred into rich milk. It is pure grace, drawing the soul closer.

translit: kōṉparavum caṅkak kuḻaiyaḻakum aṉparmoḻit tēṉparavum vaḷḷaic ceviyaḻakum - nāṉparavi
translation: ...praises the beauty of the conch earring. The beauty of the leaf-shaped ears gathers the honey of the devotees' words. I stand praising...
commentary: Brahma, the creator seated on a lotus, praises the Lord's conch earring. The ears gather the devotees' words like honey. God really listens to the love His worshippers pour out.

translit: vēṭṭavaiyai niṉṟāṅku viṇṇappam ceyyavatu kēṭṭaruḷum vārceviyiṉ kēḻaḻakum - nāṭṭiluyar
translation: ...and make my requests right there, and the radiant beauty of the long ears graciously listens to them. High in the world...
commentary: Vallalar stands before the Lord and speaks his heart. It comforts him to know that God hears his personal requests.

translit: caivam mutalāyt taḻaikka aruḷcurakkum teyva mukattiṉ tiruvaḻakum - teyvamukat
translation: ...the sacred beauty of the divine face pours forth grace so that Saivism and other traditions flourish. On that divine face...
commentary: Grace from the Lord's face sustains the world's spiritual paths, so that Saivism and other traditions grow and flourish.

translit: tuḷḷam kuḷira uyirkuḷira meykuḷirak koḷḷum karuṇaik kuṟippaḻakum - uḷḷaṟiviṉ
translation: ...the beauty of the compassionate expression cools the mind, cools the soul, and cools the body. The inner knowledge...
commentary: A single compassionate look brings the devotee total peace. It cools mind, body and soul, and relieves the burning heat of worldly suffering.

translit: eḷḷāta mēṉmaiyula kellām taḻaippavoḷir teḷḷār amutac cirippaḻakum - uḷḷōṅkum
translation: The beauty of his clear, ambrosial smile shining to make all the incomparable noble worlds flourish.
commentary: His smile is an ambrosial light that nourishes all creation. Its pure joy makes every world flourish.

translit: cīla aruḷiṉ tiṟattuk kilacciṉaiyām nīla maṇimiṭaṟṟiṉ nīṭaḻakum - mālakaṟṟi
translation: The enduring beauty of his sapphire-blue throat, serving as the seal for the virtuous grace rising within him.
commentary: Siva's throat is blue because, tradition says, he swallowed a deadly poison to save the universe. Vallalar calls this dark mark the seal of his grace, permanent proof of his boundless compassion.

translit: vāḻntoḷirum aṉpar maṉampōlum veṇṇīṟu cūḻntoḷikoṇ ṭōṅkutirut tōḷaḻakum - tāḻntilavāyt
translation: The beauty of his majestic sacred shoulders covered in radiant white ash, glowing like the minds of devotees who live brightly having cast away delusion.
commentary: White ash covers the divine shoulders. Its bright purity is likened to the minds of true devotees, wiped clean of worldly confusion and glowing with clear light.

translit: tāṉōṅkum aṇṭamelām cattamuṟak kūvumoru māṉōṅkum ceṅkai malaraḻakum - ūṉōṅkum
translation: The beauty of his lotus-like red hand holding aloft a deer that cries out loudly for all the vast universes to hear.
commentary: Traditional images show Siva holding a leaping deer in one hand. Vallalar has it cry out to all the universes, a living voice held safely in God's palm.

translit: āṇavattiṉ kūṟṟai aḻikka oḷirmaḻuvaik kāṇavaitta ceṅkamalak kaiyaḻakum - nāṇamuṟṟē
translation: The beauty of his red lotus hand displaying the shining battle-axe to destroy the deadly force of flesh-bound arrogance.
commentary: Another hand holds a shining battle-axe (maḻu). Its work is wholly spiritual. It destroys the deadly grip of ego and arrogance (āṇavam) that binds the soul to physical suffering.

translit: ēṅkum paricuṭaiya empōlvār accamelām vāṅkum apaya malaraḻakum - tīṅkaṭaiyāc
translation: The beauty of the lotus hand showing the sign of refuge, dispelling all the fears of yearning souls like us.
commentary: Lifted, palm facing outward, the Lord's hand makes the traditional Indian gesture of refuge. It tells yearning souls like us to stop being afraid. The protection it promises is complete.

translit: cīrvaravum ellāc ciṟappum peṟavumaruḷ cārvarata voṇkait talattaḻakum - pēraravap
translation: The beauty of the bright palm showing the boon-granting sign, bestowing grace to attain flawless prosperity and every greatness.
commentary: The other hand points downward in the boon-granting gesture, a sign of generosity without limit. Through it grace pours out freely. Anyone who seeks it receives true prosperity and spiritual greatness.

translit: pūṇilaṅka veṇpoṟ poṭiyilaṅka eṉpaṇittār māṇilaṅka mēvutiru mārpaḻakum - cēṇilattar
translation: The beauty of the sacred chest where great snake ornaments shine, white sacred ash gleams, and garlands of bones radiate splendor.
commentary: Everything on this chest speaks of eternity and victory over death. The white ash is the purity left when every worldly attachment has burned away. Snakes and bone garlands mark the Lord as the great ascetic, master of time, fear and mortality.

translit: mēluṭutta āṭaiyelām veḵka viyākkiramat tōluṭutta oṇmaruṅkil tuṉṉaḻakum - pālaṭutta
translation: The fitting beauty of the bright waist wrapped in a tiger skin, making the dwellers of the heavens covet it above all the fine garments they wear.
commentary: A plain tiger skin is the old mark of supreme spiritual power and freedom from the world. The heavenly beings look down and want this rough garment more than their own fine robes. They can see that real majesty belongs to divine detachment.
