translit: kēḻkkōla mēvutiruk kīḷaḻakum akkīḷiṉ kīḻkkō vaṇattiṉ kiḷaraḻakum - kīṭkōlam
translation: The beauty of the sacred waist-cord shining with a milky hue, and the radiant beauty of the loincloth tucked beneath that cord.
commentary: The ruler of the whole universe dresses like the poorest beggar. A single glowing cord at the waist holds up a plain cloth, and that is all. He is free of worldly pride and needs nothing to be beautiful.

translit: oṭṭiniṉṟa meyyaṉpar uḷḷa melāñcērttuk kaṭṭiniṉṟa vīrak kaḻalaḻakum - eṭṭiraṇṭum
translation: The beauty of the heroic anklets that gather and bind together the hearts of the true devotees who cling to Him.
commentary: The heroic anklets carry a magnetic grace. They draw in the hearts of sincere seekers and bind them together in love.

translit: cittikkum yōkiyartam cintaitaṉil tēṉpōṉṟu tittikkum cēvaṭiyiṉ cīraḻakum - cattittu
translation: The excellent beauty of His red feet that taste sweet like honey in the minds of the yogis who attain the realization of eight and two.
commentary: 'Eight and two' points to a classic Tamil mystic teaching. Eight is written as the letter 'a' (அ) and two as 'u' (உ), and together they signify a deep inner vision of the Divine. Yogis who reach this clear state find His presence as sweet and nourishing as honey.

translit: malvaitta māmaṟaiyum mālayaṉum kāṇpariya celvat tiruvaṭiyiṉ cīraḻakum - colvaitta
translation: The excellent beauty of His supreme divine feet that are difficult to see even for the mighty, resounding Vedas and for Vishnu and Brahma.
commentary: The mighty Vedas cannot see these feet, and neither can Vishnu or Brahma. The highest truth lies beyond study and traditional lore.

translit: cemmai maṇimalaiyaic cērnta - marakatampōl ammaiyoru pālvāḻn taruḷaḻakum - ammamikac
translation: The beauty of His grace where the Mother dwells on one side, looking like an emerald joined to a mountain of red rubies praised by words.
commentary: Here the Divine is half male and half female, one perfect whole. His side blazes like a mountain of red ruby. Beside it the Mother glows green, an emerald set against the red.

translit: cīrttinikaḻ cempavaḷac cemmē ṉiyiṉaḻakum pārttiruntāl nammuṭ pacipōṅkāṇ - tīrttaruḷam
translation: Oh mother, the beauty of His highly renowned body of red coral. If we just keep looking at Him, the hunger within us will vanish.
commentary: Beauty like this satisfies the deepest longing we have. Hold the coral-red form in the mind's eye and that is enough. The emptiness inside is gone, and every kind of worldly hunger with it.

translit: koṇṭiruntāṉ poṉmēṉik kōlamatai nāmtiṉamuṅ kaṇṭiruntāl allalelām kaṭṭaṟuṅkāṇ - toṇṭaṭaintu
translation: He possesses a beautiful golden form. If we gaze upon it daily, all our afflictions will be severed, see. Approaching in service,
commentary: Keep His golden form in mind every day and worldly troubles are cut away. Devotion starts with that steady inner seeing.

translit: pāṭṭāl avaṉpukaḻaip pāṭukiṉṟōr pakkaniṉṟu kēṭṭāl viṉaikaḷviṭai kēṭkumkāṇ - nīṭṭāmal
translation: if you stand beside those singing his praises in song and listen, your karmas will take their leave, see. Without delay,
commentary: Stand near true devotees and listen as they sing God's praises, and karma (the accumulated burden of past actions) begins to dissolve. Their pure devotion works as a remedy for anyone who simply stops and listens.

translit: oṉṉār purampoṭitta uttamaṉē eṉṟorukāl coṉṉā lulakat tuyaraṟuṅkāṇ - ennāḷum
translation: if you say just once, 'O Supreme One who crushed the cities of foes', the sorrows of the world will be severed, see. At all times,
commentary: Say it once, with real sincerity, and the sorrows of life are cut through. The crushed cities of His foes are a traditional image of divine power breaking our inner obstacles of ego, illusion and desire.

translit: paṉṉumuḷḷat tuḷḷām paracivamē eṉṟorukāl uṉṉumuṉṉam tīmaiyelām ōṭiṭuṅkāṇ - aṉṉavaṉṟaṉ
translation: before you even finish thinking just once, 'O Supreme Siva dwelling in the praising heart', all evils will flee, see. That Lord's
commentary: God lives right inside the human heart. Turn your thought inward to Him and every inner evil flees before the thought is even finished.

translit: āṭṭiyalkāṟ pūmāṭ ṭaṭaiyeṉṟāl antōmuṉ nīṭṭiyakāl piṉvāṅki niṟkiṉṟāy - ūṭṭumavaṉ
translation: flower-like dancing feet you are told to reach, but alas, you pull back the foot you stepped forward and stand hesitant. He who feeds
commentary: Grace is this easy to receive, one thought or one word, and still the mind hesitates. We take one brave step toward God, then pull the foot back out of fear or worldly distraction.

translit: māṟkaṭavu ḷāmōr makavalaṟak kaṇṭutirup pāṟkaṭalai yīntavaruṭ pāṉmaitaṉai - nūṟkaṭaliṉ
translation: Seeing a great divine child cry, He gave him the sacred ocean of milk. This is His gracious nature. In the ocean of scriptures...
commentary: An ancient story tells of a divine child crying out in hunger for milk. A cup would have done. The Lord gave him the whole celestial ocean of milk, because that is His nature: He answers pure need with overwhelming abundance.

translit: mattiyilnī kēṭṭum vaṇaṅkukilāy aṉpaṭaiyap puttiyuḷōrk kītoṉṟum pōtātō - muttineṟi
translation: you have heard of this, yet you do not bow. Is this one act not enough for wise people to attain love? The path of liberation...
commentary: Vallalar is talking to a stubborn mind that has read countless scriptures and stayed untouched by God's kindness. For someone truly wise, hearing one story of such grace is enough to awaken deep love. Knowing the texts means nothing if the heart never melts.

translit: māṇā arakkaṉ malaikkīḻ iruntētta vāṇāḷvaḻaṅkiyatōr vaṇmaitaṉai - nāṇāḷum
translation: When the flawed demon praised Him from beneath the mountain, He granted him a long life. This is His generosity. Every single day...
commentary: Ravana, the arrogant demon king, tried to lift God's mountain and was crushed beneath it. When he saw his mistake and sang praise from under it, God forgave him at once and granted him a long life. Divine generosity flows freely the moment a flawed person seeks forgiveness.

translit: naṇṇi uraittum nayantilainī aṉpukoḷap puṇṇiyaruk kītoṉṟum pōtātō - puṇṇiyarām
translation: people approach and tell you this, yet you do not desire Him. Is this one act not enough for virtuous people to gain love? The virtuous...
commentary: People tell these stories of forgiveness every single day, and still the listener feels no longing for God. A virtuous person needs no further proof. One act of such mercy should be enough to inspire complete devotion.

translit: cuntararkkuk kaccūril tōḻamaiyait tāṉterikka vantirappuc cōṟaḷitta vaṇmaitaṉai - muntakattil
translation: Sundarar was shown His friendship in Kacchur, where He came, begged for alms of rice, and gave it to him. This is His generosity. Previously in the heart...
commentary: Sundarar, the beloved saint, was treated by God as a close friend. At Kacchur, when he was resting in a temple, exhausted and hungry, God Himself went into the town, begged for rice and brought it back to feed him. This is a God willing to become a beggar out of pure love for a devotee.

translit: pētamaṟak kēṭṭum piṟaḻntaṉaiyē aṉpaṭaiyap pōtamuḷōrk kītoṉṟum pōtātō - pōtavumney
translation: Even after hearing this clearly, you strayed. To cultivate love, is this one instance not enough for the wise? The abundant ghee
commentary: The mind keeps wandering even after hearing such clear stories of grace. One example of God's mercy should be enough to wake true love in anyone wise.

translit: aṅkōr elitāṉ aruntavakal tūṇṭavataic ceṅkōlaṉ ākkiyavac cīrttitaṉai - iṅkōtac
translation: a rat there tried to eat, bumping the lamp bowl. As His fame in making that rat a righteous king is recited here,
commentary: A hungry rat tried to drink the ghee in a temple lamp and accidentally pushed the wick, so the flame burned brighter. For that unintended act of tending the light, God let the rat be reborn as a great and righteous king.

translit: cantatamnī kēṭṭumavaṉ tāḷniṉaiyāy aṉpaṭaiyap puntiyuḷōrk kītoṉṟum pōtātō - muntavarum
translation: you listen constantly, yet you do not meditate on His feet. To cultivate love, is this one instance not enough for the intelligent? The swiftly arriving
commentary: The mind hears the rat's story over and over and still does not think of His feet. If God shows such grace for an accidental deed by a small animal, that alone should move any thinking person to deep devotion.

translit: naṟṟuṇaiyeṉ ṟēttumanta nāvaracark kaṉṟukaṭaṟ kaṟṟuṇaiyōr teppameṉak kāṭṭiyatai - iṟṟeṉanī
translation: good companion, that king of speech praised Him. On that day, He turned the stone pillar in the sea into a floating raft for him. Knowing this is how it happened, you
commentary: The king of speech is the Tamil saint Appar. A hostile ruler tied him to a heavy stone pillar and threw him into the sea. Appar sang a hymn praising the Lord as his good companion, and God made the stone float like a wooden raft to save him.

translit: māvulakil kēṭṭum vaṇaṅkukilāy aṉpaṭaiyap pūvulakark kītoṉṟum pōtātō - tāvunutal
translation: hear it in this great world, yet you do not bow down. To cultivate love, is this one instance not enough for the people of this beautiful earth? The leaping forehead
commentary: The mind knows the story of the floating stone and still refuses to bow in reverence. One account of God rescuing His devoted saint should be all the proof anyone on earth needs to grow a heart full of love.

translit: kaṇcumantāṉ aṉpaṉ kalaṅkā vakaivaikai maṇcumantāṉ eṉṟuraikkum vāymaitaṉaip - paṇpuṭaiyōr
translation: Noble people speak the truth that the Lord who bears the frontal eye carried earth at the Vaigai river so His devotee would not be troubled.
commentary: This verse recalls a famous story of divine compassion. When the Vaigai river flooded, the king ordered every citizen to help build a dam. To save an old, devoted woman from punishment, God took the form of a laborer and carried the earth for her.

translit: māṇavuraip pakkēṭṭum vāyntēttāy meyyaṉpu pūṇaveṉṟāl ītoṉṟum pōtātō - nīṇarakat
translation: Even after hearing them speak of this excellently, you do not aptly praise Him. Is this one truth not enough for you to embrace true love?
commentary: Vallalar asks his own heart how it can stay unmoved. The Lord of the universe humbled Himself to do manual labor for a poor devotee. Knowing that should be enough to awaken true love for God.

translit: tīṅkuṟumā pātakattait tīrttōr maṟaiyavaṉaip pāṅkaṭaiyac ceyta-aruṭ paṇpataṉai - īṅkulakar
translation: He erased the great sin that brings the torment of deep hell and graciously enabled a brahmin to attain salvation.
commentary: Another traditional story: God forgave a brahmin who had committed a terrible crime and raised him to salvation. Grace can wipe away even the darkest past and grant final freedom.

translit: tuṅkam uṟa-uraittuñ cūḻkiṉ ṟilaiyaṉpu poṅkaveṉṟāl ītoṉṟum pōtātō - taṅkiya-ip
translation: Even when the people of this world speak of His grace with great exaltation, you do not consider it. Is this one truth not enough for love to surge within you?
commentary: Hearing of such boundless forgiveness should melt the hardest heart. Vallalar wonders why his mind still hesitates to surrender, when this one act of mercy is proof enough of God's endless love.

translit: pāraṟiyāt tāyākip paṉṟik kuruḷaikaṭku ūraṟiya naṉmulaippāl ūṭṭiyataic - cīraṟivōr
translation: Becoming a mother in a way this enduring world has never known, He fed sweet breast milk to the piglets for the whole town to see. Those who know His glory...
commentary: God took the form of a mother pig and nursed a litter of orphaned piglets, with the whole town watching. His compassion reaches every living creature, whatever its physical form.

translit: colliniṉṟār kēṭṭum tutikkiṉ ṟilaiyaṉpu pulla-eṉṟāl ītoṉṟum pōtātō - nallatirup
translation: Even after hearing those who recounted this, you do not praise Him. To embrace love, is this one truth not enough? His good and sacred...
commentary: Vallalar asks how anyone can hear stories of divine grace and stay unmoved. Knowing the lengths God goes to for us should be enough to wake true love.

translit: pāta malarvaruntap pāṇaṉ taṉakkāḷāyk kōtilviṟa kēṟṟuvilai kūṟiyatai - nītiyuḷōr
translation: ...lotus feet suffered as He became a servant to the bard, carried a load of flawless firewood, and called out its price. The righteous...
commentary: A famous Tamil legend tells how the Lord disguised Himself as a woodcutter and sold firewood to help a devoted musician. He humbled Himself, letting those tender feet walk rough streets, just to serve someone who loved Him.

translit: cāṟṟiniṉṟār kēṭṭumavaṉ tāḷniṉaiyāy meyyaṉpil pōṟṟaveṉṟāl ītoṉṟum pōtātō - pōṟṟukiṉṟa
translation: ...have proclaimed this. Even after hearing it, you do not think of His feet. To praise Him in true love, is this one truth not enough? The praising...
commentary: The Divine stepped down to serve a human being. Hearing that should melt the heart, yet the stubborn mind refuses to dwell on it.

translit: āṭum kariyum aṇilum kuraṅkumaṉpu tēṭuñ cilampiyoṭu ciṟṟeṟumpum - nīṭukiṉṟa
translation: ...cow, elephant, squirrel, and monkey, the love-seeking spider, the tiny ant, and the long...
commentary: Creatures from traditional lore, from the great elephant down to the tiny ant, each showed real devotion. The capacity for spiritual love exists in every living being.

translit: pāmpum civārccaṉaitāṉ paṇṇiyateṉ ṟālpūcai ōmpuvataṟ kiyārtā muvavātār - cōmpuṟunī
translation: ...snake all performed worship to Siva. Knowing this, who would not rejoice to perform worship? You, afflicted by laziness...
commentary: If simple animals could worship Siva, human beings have no excuse for spiritual laziness. We were given higher awareness, so our failure to practice devotion is a tragedy of our own making.

translit: vaṉpeṉpa tellām maṟuttavaṉtāḷ pūcikkum aṉpeṉpati yātō aṟiyāyē - aṉpuṭaṉē
translation: Rejecting all cruelty, it worships his feet. Do you not know what such love is? With such love,
commentary: True love for God begins by giving up all cruelty toward other living creatures. Vallalar asks whether the listener even understands this pure, harmless devotion.

translit: ceñcaṭaikoḷ namperumāṉ cīrkēṭ ṭiraiyaruntā tañcaṭakki yōkam amarntulakiṉ - vañcamaṟa
translation: hearing the glory of our Lord with red matted hair, it stopped eating prey, controlled its five senses, and sat in yoga to end the world's deceit.
commentary: A crane heard of God's glory and gave up its natural habit of hunting prey. It mastered its senses and sat in deep meditation. The story shows that the path to God requires us to stop harming others.

translit: nāraiyē muttiyiṉpam nāṭiyateṉ ṟālmaṟṟai yāraiyē nāṭātār eṉṟuraippēṉ - īramilāy
translation: Thus even a crane sought the bliss of liberation! If this is so, who else would not seek it? O you who lack a tender heart,
commentary: If a simple bird can seek liberation, surely a human being should want it too. Vallalar rebukes the listener for a heart so hard and unfeeling beside this devoted creature.

translit: nīyō ciṟitum niṉaintilai-av viṉpameṉṉai yēyōniṉ taṉmai iruntavitam - ōyāta
translation: you do not think of that bliss even a little. Alas, what is this state of your nature? With unceasing
commentary: Even with the crane's example in front of them, the listener ignores the joy of spiritual life entirely. Vallalar pities this stubborn, careless state of mind.

translit: aṉpuṭaiyār yāriṉumpēr aṉpuṭaiyāṉ namperumāṉ niṉpuṭaiyāṉ nittam nikaḻttukiṉṟēṉ - uṉpuṭaiyōr
translation: love, our Lord has immense love, greater than anyone else who loves. He is right beside you. I declare this to you every day. Those beside you
commentary: The Lord's love is boundless and exceeds any human affection. He stands right beside us, and Vallalar keeps saying so, every day.

translit: aṉpavaṉmēl koṇṭa taṟiyēṉ puṟaccamayat tiṉpuṭaiyā rēṉum iṇaṅkuvarē - aṉpuṭaṉē
translation: I do not understand the love you hold for Him. Even those who delight in outer religions would yield to Him. With love,
commentary: Vallalar is baffled by a stubborn mind that refuses to surrender. Even followers of outer religions would yield to the Lord's greatness.

translit: tāveṉṟāl nallaruḷin tāveṉpāṉ namperumāṉ ā-uṉpāl ōti alukkiṉṟēṉ - nīvaṉpāl
translation: if you ask Him to give, our Lord says, "Here, take this good grace." Ah, I grow weary of preaching to you. You, in your hardness,
commentary: Ask with love and the Lord answers at once with His grace. Nothing is held back. Vallalar grows exhausted explaining something this simple to a hardened heart.

translit: niṉṟāy alatavaṉai nērntuniṉai yāypittar eṉṟālum eṉcoṟ kiṇaṅkuvarē - kuṉṟātu
translation: stand stubbornly and do not resolve to think of Him. Even madmen would heed my words. Unfailingly,
commentary: The mind stays rigid and will not turn toward God. Vallalar finds it absurd, since even a madman would listen to advice this clear.

translit: pittā eṉiṉum piṟappaṟuppāṉ nammuṭaiyāṉ attō uṉakkī taṟaikiṉṟēṉ - caṟṟēṉum
translation: even if you just call Him "Madman", our Lord will sever your cycle of birth. Alas, I speak this to you. Even a little bit,
commentary: God's mercy answers even a casual or disrespectful call. "Madman" (pittā) is a traditional name for the divine in Tamil poetry. Utter only that word and the Lord will end the soul's cycle of rebirth.

translit: kēḷviyilār pōlataṉaik kēḷāy keṭukiṉṟāy vēḷviyilār kūṭṭam viḻaikiṉṟāy - vēḷviyeṉṟa
translation: you do not listen to it, acting like the unlearned, and you ruin yourself. You desire the company of those who make no sacrifice. The sacrifice...
commentary: Ignoring this wisdom leads only to ruin. Vallalar warns against the company of worldly people who make no spiritual effort, because their influence pulls the mind away from grace.

translit: vēlaivaruṅ kāloḷittu mēvukiṉṟāy niṉtalaikkaṅ kōlaivaruṅ kāliṅ koḷippāyē - mālaiyuṟum
translation: When work arises, you hide yourself and slip away. When the warrant of death comes for your head, will you be able to hide here?
commentary: Vallalar speaks straight to his own mind. It always finds a way to dodge spiritual effort and useful work. When death's summons arrives, it will have nowhere to hide.

translit: ippār veṟumpū itunayavēl eṉṟuṉakkuc ceppā muṉamviraintu celkiṉṟāy - appāḻil
translation: Before I can even tell you that this delusion-filled earth is an empty phantom and you should not desire it, you rush forward.
commentary: The material world is a passing illusion. The mind wants its pleasures so badly that it rushes into them before wisdom can get a word of warning out.

translit: cellātē caivaneṟi celleṉṟāl eṉṉuṭaṉum collātu pōymayakkam tōykiṉṟāy - pollāta
translation: When I tell you not to enter that wasteland but to walk the path of Siva, you leave without a word to me and steep yourself in delusion.
commentary: Vallalar sets the wasteland of worldly life against the path of Siva, the road that leads toward the divine. The mind hears this good counsel, says nothing, and walks off to soak itself in confusion.

translit: añcarunteṉ ṟālamuti ṉārkiṉṟāy viṭṭiṭeṉṟāl nañcarunteṉ ṟāṟpōl nalikiṉṟāy - vañcakattil
translation: When told to feed on the five wicked senses, you feast as if on nectar. When told to abandon them, you suffer as if told to drink poison.
commentary: The mind has its priorities backwards. Indulging the five senses tastes like nectar to it. Ask it to give them up and it writhes as though you had handed it poison.

translit: ōṭukiṉṟāy mīḷāmal uṉṉiccai yiṉvaḻiyē āṭukiṉṟāy maṟṟaṅ kayarkiṉṟāy - nīṭulakaic
translation: You run headlong into deceit without ever turning back. You dance along the path of your own desires and then grow utterly exhausted there.
commentary: Chasing passing desires never fills anyone. The mind runs after deceitful worldly goals and dances to its own impulses until it is drained and empty.

translit: cūḻkiṉṟāy vēṟoṉṟil cuṟṟukiṉṟāy maṟṟoṉṟil vīḻkiṉṟāy mēloṉṟil mīḷkiṉṟāy - tāḻvoṉṟē
translation: You scheme about one thing, wander around another, fall into a third, and then return, bringing only degradation.
commentary: The mind never rests. It bounces blindly from one worldly distraction to the next, and all that scheming and wandering only drags a person down into degradation.

translit: īkiṉṟāy vaṉṉeṟiyil eṉṉai valataḻikkap pōkiṉṟāy mīṭṭum pukukiṉṟāy - yōkiṉṟi
translation: You yield to cruel paths to destroy my strength. Devoid of focus, you leave and enter again.
commentary: An unfocused mind tears down a person's spiritual strength. It keeps leaving the path of peace for harsh worldly habits, and so it becomes an enemy inside, draining away every bit of resolve.

translit: oṉṟaimaṟaik kiṉṟāymaṟ ṟoṉṟainiṉaik kiṉṟāyeṉ naṉṟaimaṟaik kiṉṟāy nalikiṉṟāy - veṉṟipeṟum
translation: You conceal one thing while thinking of another. You obscure my welfare and suffer in torment.
commentary: An untrained mind is full of deceit. It hides what it really intends and keeps a person at war with himself. That dishonesty buries the soul's true welfare, and suffering follows.

translit: cēviṟ paramaṉtāḷ cēreṉṟāl maṟṟorucār mēvip palavāy virikiṉṟāy - pāvittuk
translation: When I tell you to reach the feet of the Supreme Lord mounted on the victorious bull, you stray elsewhere and scatter in many directions.
commentary: The bull is Siva's traditional mount, so the Supreme Lord here is Siva. Told to go to His feet, the mind breaks its attention across countless worldly distractions and scatters every other way.

translit: kuṉṟum uṉakkaṉantam kōṭiteṇṭa ṉiṭṭālum oṉṟum iraṅkāy uḻalkiṉṟāy - naṉṟurukāk
translation: Even if I exalt you and bow down endless millions of times, you show no pity at all. You wander aimlessly, completely unsoftened.
commentary: Vallalar begs his own mind for peace, bowing to it endlessly, and still it will not soften. It wanders without purpose and shows no mercy to the soul that longs to rest in the divine.

translit: kalleṉpēṉ uṉṉaik karaṇam kalantaṟiyāk kalleṉṟāl eṉcol kaṭavātē - pullaniṉai
translation: I would call you a stone, you who do not understand by uniting the inner faculties. If you were a stone, you would not disobey my words. You base one,
commentary: Over these verses Vallalar scolds his mind for its stubbornness. He thinks of calling it a stone, then sees the flaw: a stone at least stays where you put it. His mind will not be still and disobeys every attempt to guide it.

translit: vallirumpeṉ pēṉanta vallirumpēl kūṭattil kollaṉkuṟip paiviṭṭuk kōṇātē - allalelām
translation: I would call you hard iron. If you were hard iron, you would not bend in the forge contrary to the blacksmith's intention. All the sorrows
commentary: Now iron. Even the hardest iron softens in the forge and takes the shape the blacksmith intends. The mind refuses to be shaped by a higher will.

translit: kūṭṭukiṉṟa vaṉmaik kuraṅkeṉpēṉ akkuraṅkēl āṭṭukiṉṟōṉ colvaḻiviṭ ṭāṭātē - nīṭṭulakar
translation: you gather together, so I would call you a strong monkey. If you were a monkey, you would not dance straying from the instructions of your master. The people of the vast world
commentary: Next comes the monkey, because the mind keeps gathering up fresh sorrows like a restless monkey. Yet a trained monkey dances exactly as its master commands. Vallalar's mind runs wild and ignores the guidance of the divine.

translit: ēcukiṉṟa pēyeṉpēṉ eppēyum añceḻuttaip pēcukiṉṟōr tammaip piṭiyātē - kūcukiṟpak
translation: abuse you, so I would call you a ghost. No ghost possesses those who chant the five holy letters. Making them shrink back in fear,
commentary: Then a ghost, for the mind torments like one. Traditional belief holds that ghosts are driven away by chanting the five holy letters, the sacred mantra Na-Ma-Si-Va-Ya. The mind is worse, since it keeps up its torment even during holy recitation.

translit: kaṇṭōraik kavvuṅ kaṭuñcuṇaṅkaṉ eṉpaṉatu koṇṭōraik kaṇṭāl kulaiyātē - aṇṭārkkum
translation: I would call you a fierce dog that bites those it sees. That dog does not bark when it sees its master. Even to those who do not approach
commentary: Now a vicious dog that bites whoever it sees. A real dog stays loyal and never barks at its own master. The mind turns on its owner, showing no loyalty to the soul that houses it.

translit: pūvil aṭaṅkāp puliyeṉpēṉ eppuliyum mēvil vayappaṭṭāl etirātē - nōviyaṟṟi
translation: I would call you an untamable tiger on earth. But any tiger, if approached and subdued, will not oppose its master.
commentary: Vallalar turns on his own unruly mind and calls it a tiger. Even a wild tiger can be caught and taught to obey a master. The mind stubbornly refuses to be brought under control.

translit: vīṟukiṉṟa mummatamāl veṟpeṉpēṉ āṅkatuvum ēṟukiṉṟōṉcolvaḻiviṭ ṭēṟātē - cīṟukiṉṟa
translation: I would call you a pain-inflicting, mountain-like elephant frenzied with three kinds of rut. But even that elephant will not stray from the path commanded by its rider.
commentary: Now the mind is a huge elephant in a violent frenzy. Even a crazed elephant still follows the commands of the rider on its back. The mind refuses to be steered at all.

translit: veṉṉaṭaicērmaṟṟai vilaṅkeṉpēṉ evvilaṅkum maṉṉavaṉcēr nāṭṭil vaḻaṅkātē - niṉṉaiyiṉi
translation: I would call you some other roaring beast with a cruel gait. But no wild beast roams freely in a land governed by a true king.
commentary: A cruel, roaming beast is the next comparison, and it falls short too. A strong king can drive wild animals out of his land and restore order. The mind wanders wherever it pleases and respects no inner authority.

translit: eṉṉeṉpēṉ eṉmoḻiyai ēṟṟaṉaiyēl māṟṟuyarnta poṉṉeṉpēṉ eṉvaḻiyil pōntilaiyē - koṉṉuṟanī
translation: What shall I call you now? If you accepted my words, I would call you pure gold of the highest quality. But you do not walk in my path.
commentary: Trained to listen, the mind would be as precious and pure as the finest gold. It refuses the disciplined spiritual path, so that value stays lost.

translit: pōmvaḻiyum poynī purivatuvum poyataṉāl āmviḷaivum poyniṉ ṉaṟivumpoy - tōmviḷaikkum
translation: In vain, the path you take is false. What you do is false. Therefore, the resulting consequence is false. Your knowledge is false, yielding only harm.
commentary: Left to itself, the untrained mind builds its whole reality on illusion. Every path it chooses and every thought it makes is false, and the end is pain and harm.

translit: niṉṉuṭalum poyyiṅku niṉtavamum poynilaiyā niṉṉilaiyum poyyaṉṟi nīyumpoy - eṉṉilivaṇ
translation: Your body is false here. Your penance is false. Your unstable state is false, and you yourself are false. If I consider this, here...
commentary: Vallalar calls the worldly mind's entire existence an illusion. The body, the unstable emotions, even shallow spiritual practice are false once they are cut off from true spiritual reality.

translit: ētum uṇarntilaiyē immāya vāḻkkaiyeṉum vātiliḻut teṉṉai mayakkiṉaiyē - tītuṟunī
translation: You have realized nothing at all. You dragged me into the dispute of this illusory life and deluded me. You who are full of evil...
commentary: The worldly mind understands nothing of the divine. It drags the soul into the arguments and daily distractions of worldly life and leaves it deeply deluded.

translit: vaṉṉēr viṭaṅkāṇiṉ vaṉpeyariṉ muṉporukīṟ ṟeṉṉē aṟiyāmal iṭṭaḻaittēṉ - koṉṉēnī
translation: Seeing you as cruel poison, I unknowingly added a stroke before your cruel name and called you. Uselessly, you...
commentary: The wayward mind is a cruel poison here. Uncontrolled, it brings the soul no clarity and poisons its spiritual progress.

translit: nōva toḻiyā noṟiṟkāma veppiṉiṭai āva taṟiyā taḻuntiṉaiyē - mēvumatil
translation: You sank into the heat of swift lust where pain never ceases, not knowing what would happen. Abiding in that...
commentary: Worldly desire is a burning heat whose pain never ends. The mind plunges into these passing pleasures, blind to the suffering that must follow.

translit: uḷḷeriya mēlām uṇarvum karukavuṭal naḷḷeriya naṭpiṉ nalamvetumpa - viḷvatiṉṟi
translation: Your inside burns, your supreme awareness is scorched, your body burns in the center, and the goodness of friendship withers. Without speaking...
commentary: The fire of worldly desire destroys whatever it touches. Inner peace burns away, higher awareness is scorched, the body is damaged, and genuine friendships wither.

translit: vāṭip pilañceṉṟu vāṉceṉ ṟoḷittālum tēṭic cuṭuṅkoṭiya tīkkaṇṭāy - ōṭi-aṅku
translation: Even if you wither away, descend into the underworld, or rise into the heavens and hide, know that it is a cruel fire that seeks you out and burns you. Running there
commentary: Lust is a fire you cannot hide from. Flee deep underground or high into the heavens, Vallalar says, and it will track you down and burn you.

translit: pērntāl alatu peruṅkāmat tīniṉṉaic cērntā raiyuñcuṭumcen tīkkaṇṭāy - cārntāṅku
translation: and escaping is your only hope. Otherwise, know that this great fire of lust is a blazing red fire that burns even those who associate with you. Approaching
commentary: The only defense against lust is to run from it entirely. Its fire does not stop with one person. It spreads to consume whoever keeps company with them.

translit: cantī yeṉavaruvār tammaic cuṭuṅkāmañ centī yaiyuñ cuṭumōr tīkkaṇṭāy - vantīṅku
translation: as peacemakers, they too are burned by this lust. Know that it is a fire that burns even the blazing red fire itself. Coming here
commentary: Lust burns even those who step in to make peace and help. Vallalar's image for its intensity is striking: a fire so fierce it can burn fire itself.

translit: maṇṇil taṉaikkāṇā vaṇṇam niṉaittālum naṇṇit talaikkēṟu nañcaṅkāṇ - eṇṇaṟṟa
translation: and resolving to remain unseen on earth will not save you. Know that it is a poison that reaches you and rushes straight to your head. Countless
commentary: Hiding away from the world offers no protection. Lust is a fast-acting poison that rushes straight to the head and overwhelms a person's thoughts and self-control.

translit: pōruṟumuṭ kāmap putumayakkam niṉṉuṭaiya pēraṟivaik koḷḷaikoḷum pittaṅkāṇ - cōraṟivil
translation: battles are waged by this strange new delusion of inner lust. Know that it is a madness that plunders your supreme wisdom. In your faltering intellect
commentary: Lust keeps up a constant war inside and fills a person with delusion. Vallalar calls it a madness that plunders supreme wisdom and leaves the intellect weak and faltering.

translit: kaḷḷaṭaikkum kāmak kaṭumayakkam meynneṟikkōr muḷḷaṭaikkum pollā muraṇkaṇṭāy - aḷḷaluṟa
translation: See that the severe delusion of lust, intoxicating like liquor, is an evil obstruction placing thorns on the true path, causing you to sink into the mire.
commentary: Lust works on the mind like liquor, and the first thing it blinds is the truth. Then it throws thorns across the spiritual path and drags the seeker down into the mud.

translit: ētamelām taṉṉuḷ iṭuṅkāmam pātakattiṉ pētamelām oṉṟip piṟappiṭaṅkāṇ - ātaliṉāl
translation: See that lust, which draws all afflictions into itself, is the single birthplace where all varieties of sins unite. Therefore,
commentary: Every kind of sin and suffering starts from lust. It gathers all human afflictions into itself, and from that single root more wrongdoing keeps breeding.

translit: vemmāl maṭantaiyarai mēvavoṇā tāṅkavarkaḷ tammācai iṉṉum tavirntilaiyē - immāya
translation: you must not approach women of cruel delusion. Yet you have still not forsaken your desire for them.
commentary: Vallalar turns on his own mind and asks why it still clings to desire for women. Worldly attraction is a powerful illusion, and he wants it abandoned completely.

translit: maṉṟa vaṇaṅkiṉarcev vāymaṭavār pētaiyarkaḷ eṉṟakoṭuñ coṟporuḷai eṇṇilaiyē - toṉṟulakil
translation: You have not considered the meaning of the severe words declaring that these red-lipped, beautiful women of this illusory world are ignorant.
commentary: Fix your eyes on physical beauty and you are trapped in the ignorance of an illusory world. The mind is scolded for ignoring the severe warnings earlier sages gave about these attachments.

translit: peṇṇeṉ ṟuraippiṟ piṟappēḻum āntuyaram eṇṇeṉṟa nallōrcol eṇṇilaiyē - peṇṇiṅku
translation: In this ancient world, you have not considered the words of the wise who instructed you to realize that merely uttering the word "woman" brings the sorrow of seven births.
commentary: In the ascetic tradition, worldly attachment is the root cause of endless rebirth. So the mind is told to remember the strict words of the wise: even speaking of this desire is enough to pull a person back into the sorrow of seven births.

translit: māmāt tiraiyiṉ varuttaṉameṉ ṟeṇṇiṉai-an nāmārttam ācaiyeṉa nāṭilaiyē - yāmārttam
translation: You considered it the affliction of the great illusion. You did not realize that the meaning of that name is desire.
commentary: Many people think of the great illusion (māyā) as a cosmic force that hides reality. Vallalar brings it much closer to home. The real meaning of that name is simply human desire, and when cravings drive us, we live in a false world.

translit: mantirattum pūcai marapiṉumaṟ ṟevvitamām tantirattum cāyāc caḻakkaṉṟō - mantirattil
translation: Is it not a stubborn evil that does not yield to mantras, to traditional rituals of worship, or to any kind of tantric practice?
commentary: Mantras, rituals and tantric practices are powerless against the grip of lust. It is a stubborn evil that outward spiritual remedies cannot touch. Only a complete change inside brings true purity.

translit: pēypiṭittāl tīrntiṭumip peṇpēy viṭātēcen nāypiṭittāl pōlumeṉṟu nāṭilaiyē - āyviluṉṟaṉ
translation: If a ghost possesses you, it can be cured. But this female ghost will not let go. You did not realize it is like being gripped by a wild dog.
commentary: A healer can drive away a real ghost. The ghost of lust grips the mind the way a wild dog locks its jaws, and it refuses to let go. Deep-rooted sexual obsession is far harder to break than any possession.

translit: ēḻaimai-eṉ ṉeṉpēṉ ivarmayakkam valnarakiṉ tōḻamaiyeṉ ṟantō tuṇintilaiyē - ūḻamainta
translation: What can I say of your ignorance? Alas, you did not firmly understand that infatuation with them is companionship with cruel hell.
commentary: Infatuation is companionship with a cruel hell, and yielding to it brings the soul endless suffering. Vallalar can hardly find words for the ignorance that sees no danger here and treats it casually.

translit: kāriruḷil cellak kalaṅkukiṉṟāy mātarcūḻal pēriruḷil celvataṉaip pērttilaiyē - pāriṭaiyōr
translation: You hesitate and fear to walk in the pitch dark. Yet you have not turned away from walking into the great darkness of women's company.
commentary: We hesitate to walk outside in pitch darkness because we cannot see what lies ahead. Yet people walk blindly into the far greater darkness of lust, which hides the truth from the mind entirely.

translit: eṇvāḷ eṉilañci ēkukiṉṟāy ēntiḻaiyār kaṇvāḷ aṟuppak kaṉintaṉaiyē - maṇvāḻum
translation: If you merely think of a sword, you run away in fear. Yet when the sword-like eyes of women wearing fine jewelry slice into you, you completely melt.
commentary: Desire makes the mind irrational. A man flees in terror at the mere thought of a sword, yet melts when a woman's sharp gaze cuts into him.

translit: ōrāṉai yaikkaṇṭāl ōṭukiṉṟāy mātarmulai īrāṉai yaikkaṇ ṭicaintaṉaiyē - cīrāṉa
translation: If you see a single elephant roaming the earth, you run away. But upon seeing the two elephants that are the breasts of women, you gladly yield.
commentary: Lust overrides even the instinct to stay alive. A man runs for his life from a single wild elephant, then gladly throws himself at the two that poets make of a woman's breasts.

translit: veṟpeṉṟāl ēṟa viraintaṟiyāy mātarmulai veṟpeṉṟāl ēṟa viraintaṉaiyē - poṟpoṉṟum
translation: You never show any haste to climb a magnificent mountain. But if it is the mountain of women's breasts, you rush to climb it.
commentary: Few people volunteer to climb a steep mountain, and in daily life the effort is easily avoided. Driven by attraction, the same mind rushes to exhaust itself.

translit: ciṅkameṉṟāl vāṭit tiyaṅkukiṉṟāy mātariṭaic ciṅkameṉil kāṇat tirumpiṉaiyē - iṅkuciṟu
translation: If they mention a beautiful lion, you wither and tremble in fear. But if it is the lion that is a woman's waist, you turn around to look at it.
commentary: Classical poets often compare a slender waist to a lion. The man who withers in fear at a real one turns happily to look at the metaphor, and spiritual truth is forgotten.

translit: pāmpeṉṟāl ōṭip patuṅkukiṉṟāy mātaralkul pāmpeṉṟāl caṟṟum payantilaiyē - āmpaṇṭaik
translation: If they mention a small snake here, you run and hide. But if it is the snake that is a woman's loins, you are not afraid at all.
commentary: A snake sends people running to hide in panic. When poets compare the curve of a woman's body to a cobra's hood, the same mind approaches without the slightest hesitation, captivated by the illusion.

translit: kīḻkkaṭalil āṭeṉṟāl kēṭkilainī mātaralkul pāḻkkaṭalil kēḷātu pāyntaṉaiyē - kīḻkkatuvum
translation: If told to bathe in the eastern sea, you refuse to listen. Unprompted you plunge into the perilous sea of women's loins.
commentary: Bathing in the eastern sea is a traditional act of religious discipline. Tell the mind to do this simple duty and it refuses. Point it toward lust and it throws itself in uninvited, however exhausting the chase.

translit: kalleṉṟāl piṉṉiṭuvāy kārikaiyār kāṟcilampu kalleṉṟāl mēleḻumpak kaṟṟaṉaiyē - alaḷakam
translation: If told to study, you step back. But if the anklets on the feet of lovely women resound with a jingling noise, you have learned to spring up instantly.
commentary: Two words sound alike here. Told to study (kal), the mind backs away, yet at the jingle (kal) of a woman's anklets it jumps to its feet. That is how easily the senses pull us off the work that matters.

translit: maiyō karumeṉ maṇalō-eṉ pāymāṟi aiyō naraippa taṟintilaiyō - poyyōti
translation: You praise her dark tresses and ask "Is it dark kohl or fine black sand?" Alas, do you not realize it will eventually change and turn gray?
commentary: The mind flatters a woman's dark hair, comparing it to black sand or kohl. Infatuation keeps it from seeing what time will do. All that hair turns gray.

translit: oṇpiṟaiyē oṇṇutaleṉ ṟuṉṉukiṉṟāy uḷḷelumpām veṇpiṟaiyaṉ ṟēyataṉai viṇṭilaiyē - kaṇpuruvam
translation: Speaking falsehoods, you consider her bright forehead to be a radiant crescent moon. You fail to admit that it is merely a white crescent-shaped bone beneath.
commentary: Romantic metaphors hide the stark physical reality of the human body. Poets often compare a woman's beautiful forehead to a glowing crescent moon. Vallalar strips away this flattering illusion to remind the listener that beneath the skin lies nothing more than a curved piece of white bone.

translit: villeṉṟāy veṇmayirāy mēvi utirntiṭuṅkāl colleṉṟāl collat tuṇiyāyē - vallampil
translation: You call her eyebrows a bow. When they turn into white hairs and fall out, you will not dare to speak if asked to describe them.
commentary: A lover likens eyebrows to a hunter's bow. When old age comes and those hairs go white and drop out, all that praise falls silent. Vallalar is warning us not to tie our desire to a body that withers.

translit: kaṭku vaḷai-eṉṟāyk kaṇṇīr ularntumika uṭkuḻiyum pōtil uraippāyē - kaṭkulavu
translation: You called the eyes valai fish. Will you say this when the tears dry up and the eyes sink deep into their sockets?
commentary: In the old poems, darting eyes are swimming fish. Vallalar asks whether the comparison still holds when a person is old, the tears have dried, and the eyes have sunk into the skull.

translit: meykkumiḻē nāciyeṉa veḵkiṉaiyāl veṇmalattāl uykkumiḻuñ cīnta luḷatēyō - eyttalilā
translation: You desired the nose, calling it a kumizh flower on the body. Does the kumizh flower have white mucus and snot being blown out of it?
commentary: The kumizh flower is the poets' image for a well-shaped nose. Vallalar asks plainly whether a real flower runs with mucus and has to be blown. Obsession with the body looks absurd once you remember what the body does.

translit: vaḷḷaiyeṉṟāy vārkātu vaḷḷaitaṉak kuṭpuḻaiyō ṭuḷḷunaram piṉpuṉaivum uṇṭēyō - veḷḷainakai
translation: You called the long ears vallai leaves. Does the vallai leaf have an inner hole and a network of nerves inside it?
commentary: The vallai is a water plant, and poets liken the curve of an ear to its leaf. A leaf has no fleshy hole and no web of nerves inside it. Vallalar keeps stripping the fantasy down to bare anatomy.

translit: mullaiyeṉṟāy mullai muṟittorukōl koṇṭunitam ollai aḻukkeṭuppa tuṇṭēyō - nallatoru
translation: You called the white teeth jasmine buds. Do you break a stick and quickly pick dirt out of jasmine buds every day?
commentary: White teeth as unopened jasmine buds is an old romantic trope. Vallalar answers with daily hygiene. Nobody breaks off a stick to pick food and dirt out of a jasmine bud.

translit: kovvai yeṉa-itaḻaik koḷkiṉṟāy mēlkuḻampum cevvai irattameṉat tērntilaiyē - cevviyakaṇ
translation: You consider the lips to be red kovvai fruit. You have not realized that they are just red blood pooling on the surface.
commentary: The red kovvai gourd stands for full red lips. Look closer, Vallalar says. That redness is blood pooling just under thin skin.

translit: ṇāṭi yeṉakkavuṭkē ācaivaittāy mēlceḻuntōl vāṭiyakkāl eṉṉuraikka māṭṭuvaiyē - kūṭiyatōr
translation: You sought and placed your desire on the cheeks. When the rich outer skin withers, what will you be able to say?
commentary: The whole attraction rests on a thin layer of skin. Ask what becomes of that desire when youth fades and the skin wrinkles.

translit: anta matimukameṉ ṟāṭukiṉṟāy ēḻtuḷaikaḷ entamatik kuṇṭataṉai eṇṇilaiyē - nanteṉavē
translation: You dance around calling that face the moon. Which moon has seven holes in it? You do not consider this.
commentary: The face is the moon, say the poets. Vallalar asks which moon has seven holes (the eyes, ears, nostrils, and mouth), and makes us look straight at raw anatomy.

translit: kaṇṭamaṭṭum kūṟiṉai-ak kaṇṭamaṭṭum aṉṟiyuṭal koṇṭamaṭṭum maṟṟataṉmeyk kūṟaṉṟō - viṇṭavaṟṟait
translation: You praised the neck as a conch. Apart from the neck, isn't the entire body made of the same physical elements?
commentary: Poets praise a smooth neck by comparing it to a conch shell. Vallalar points out that the neck is made of the same ordinary flesh as everything below it.

translit: tōḷeṉ ṟuraittut tuṭikkiṉṟāy avvēykku mūḷoṉṟu veḷḷelumpiṉ mūṭṭuṇṭē - nāḷoṉṟum
translation: You tremble, praising her shoulders as bamboo. Does that bamboo contain a joint of white bone?
commentary: Classical poetry compares curved shoulders to smooth bamboo. Think of the white bone and the joint hidden just under the surface, and the picture breaks.

translit: ceṅkāntaḷ aṅkaiyeṉac ceppukiṉṟāy ammalarkkup poṅkāp palaviraliṉ pūṭṭuṇṭē - maṅkāta
translation: You declare her beautiful hands are red gloriosa lilies. Does that flower have a cluster of jointed fingers attached to it?
commentary: Calling hands red gloriosa lilies leaves out the jointed fingers. Taken together, these verses take the romantic metaphors apart one at a time. Infatuation only lasts while we look away from flesh and its decay.

translit: cevviḷanīr koṅkaiyeṉac ceppiṉaival ūṉṟaṭippiṅ kevviḷanīrk kuṇṭataṉai eṇṇilaiyē - cevvaipeṟum
translation: You speak of breasts as red tender coconuts. You do not consider what kind of tender coconut this lump of hard flesh actually is.
commentary: Poets compare a woman's body to lovely things in nature to stir up desire. Vallalar strips the illusion away. What romantic verse calls a red tender coconut is a lump of hard flesh.

translit: ceppeṉ ṟaṉaimulaiyaic cīcī cilantiyatu tuppeṉ ṟavarkkiyātu collutiyē - vappiṟukac
translation: You call the breasts a perfect casket. Disgusting! What will you say to those who call them a spider's nest?
commentary: The romantic mind sees the body as a casket holding something precious. The spiritual mind sees a trap. It likens the object of lust to a spider's nest that catches the unwary in a web of desire.

translit: cūḻntamulai moṭṭeṉṟē tuḷḷukiṉṟāy kīḻttuvaṇṭu vīḻntamulaik keṉṉa viḷamputiyē - tāḻnta-avai
translation: You leap with joy calling the bound breasts a flower bud. What will you say about breasts that droop and fall downward?
commentary: Physical beauty does not last, and the body ages and changes. Praising the firmness of youth ignores what time does. Sooner or later it pulls all flesh downward, and the spell of attraction breaks with it.

translit: maṇkaṭṭum panteṉavē vāḻntāy mutirntuṭaiyāp puṇkaṭṭi eṉpavarvāyp pottuvaiyē - tiṇkaṭṭum
translation: You lived praising them as a tightly bound ball. Will you cover the mouths of those who call them a swollen and unbroken boil?
commentary: Worldly people celebrate the shape of the body and ignore its biological nature. Those who see clearly find a site of disease and decay. To them it is a swollen, unbroken boil, far from a pretty ball to play with.

translit: annīrk kurumpai avaiyeṉṟāy mēleḻumpum cennīrp puṭaippeṉpār tērntilaiyē - annīrār
translation: You called them tender coconuts full of water. You have not understood those who call them a swelling of rising blood.
commentary: Romance hides the raw anatomy of human life. Under the skin the body is blood and tissue. Seeing that plainly helps cure the mind of its obsessive physical desires.

translit: kaṇṇīr tarumparuvāyk kaṭṭuraippār cāṉṟāka veṇṇīr varalkaṇṭum veṭkilaiyē - taṇṇīrmaic
translation: Even as witnesses speak words that bring tears, you see the flow of white fluids and feel no shame.
commentary: Lust blinds. The fluids of the body are plain to see, witnesses speak of the sorrow worldly attachment brings, and still people chase physical desire without shame.

translit: cāṭiyeṉpāy nī-ayalōr tātuk kaṭattiṭumēṉ mūṭiyeṉpār maṟṟavarvāy mūṭutiyō - mēṭataṉai
translation: You call it a pot of cool water. Others will say it is merely a lid placed on a pot of physical elements. Can you shut their mouths?
commentary: A cooling pot of water is the kind of image poets use for the body. Vallalar says the plain truth is entirely different: it is a container of flesh and basic physical elements.

translit: ālilaiyē eṉpāy aṭarkuṭarō ṭīruḷoṭum tōlilaiyē ālilaikkeṉ collutiyē - nūliṭaitāṉ
translation: You call that mound a banyan leaf. Does a banyan leaf have dense intestines, a liver, and skin? What will you say to the banyan leaf?
commentary: Classical Tamil poetry likens a woman's abdomen to a delicate banyan leaf. Vallalar asks whether a banyan leaf has intestines and a liver. Naming what lies beneath the skin breaks the spell of physical attraction.

translit: uṇṭō ilaiyō-eṉ ṟuṭpukaḻvāy kaitoṭṭuk kaṇṭōrpūṭṭuṇṭeṉpār kaṇṭilaiyē - viṇṭōṅkum
translation: You praise her thread-like waist inwardly, wondering if it even exists. Those who have touched it and seen it will say it is firmly locked. You have not seen this.
commentary: An old poetic trope praises a waist so slender it seems not to exist. That is pure imagination. The body is a solid, ordinary structure.

translit: āḻṅkaṭaleṉ pāymaṭavār alkuliṉaic ciṟcilarkaḷ pāḻṅkiṇaṟeṉ pārataṉaip pārttilaiyē - tāḻṅkoṭiñcit
translation: You call the loins of women an expansive, deep ocean. A few others call it a ruined well. You have not seen that.
commentary: Worldly desire imagines the body as an endless ocean of pleasure. Those who see clearly know it for a trap. They call it a ruined well that gives no true spiritual nourishment.

translit: tērāḻi eṉpāyac cīkkuḻiyai aṉṟuciṟu nīrāḻi yeṉpavarkkeṉ nērutiyē - ārāppuṉ
translation: You call that pit of pus a chariot wheel. What will you say to those who call it a mere ocean of urine?
commentary: The harsh words are deliberate. Ascetic poetry uses blunt physical description to break the spell of sexual desire, and by pointing to pus and urine behind the romantic image of a chariot wheel, Vallalar aims to cultivate deep detachment.

translit: nīrvīḻiyai ācai nilaiyeṉṟāy vaṉmalamtāṉ cōrvaḻiyai eṉṉeṉṟu collutiyē - cārmuṭaitāṉ
translation: You called the unceasing discharge of foul fluids the seat of desire. What will you call the path where hard feces slips out?
commentary: The mind glorifies the source of sexual pleasure and ignores how close it lies to the body's foulest waste. Setting the two side by side forces the seeker to see the body clearly, free of the veil of infatuation.

translit: āṟāc cilainīrkāṉ āṟāy oḻukkiṭavum vīṟāppuṇ eṉṟu viṭuttilaiyē - ūṟākki
translation: Even as the gathering stench and unhealing fluids flow like a river, you did not abandon it, failing to see it as just a dreadful wound.
commentary: The anatomy of desire is pictured as a weeping wound that never heals. Vallalar wants obsessive craving replaced by a blunt awareness of how messy and fragile the body is.

translit: mūlai eṟumpuṭaṉī moyppatañci maṟṟataṉmēl cīlaiyiṭak kaṇṭum terintilaiyē - mēlaiyuṟu
translation: Fearing that flies and corner-dwelling ants will swarm the oozing wound, they cover it with a cloth. Even seeing this, you did not understand its true nature.
commentary: Clothing hides the body's natural secretions from the world. People dress the physical form up to make it appealing and willfully ignore what lies just beneath the fabric.

translit: mēnarakam eṉṟāl vitirppuṟunī mātaralkul kōnarakam eṉṟāl kulaintilaiyē - ūṉamitaik
translation: You tremble at the mention of the great hell in the hereafter. Yet you do not shudder when told that a woman's reproductive organ is the chief of hells.
commentary: People are terrified of an imagined hell after death, yet they eagerly pursue the physical desires that trap the soul in suffering. For the ascetic, unchecked lust is the true hell, because it blinds the mind entirely to spiritual truth.

translit: kaṇṭāl namatācai kaiviṭuvār eṉṟataṉait taṇṭā toḷittiṭavum cārntaṉaiyē - aṇṭātu
translation: You approached them even as they constantly concealed their flaws, fearing, "If men see this, they will abandon their desire for us."
commentary: Physical attraction depends on hiding what the body really is. Desire, Vallalar says, rests on an illusion, kept alive only because people hide their flaws so others stay interested.

translit: pōtaviṭā yākip pulampukiṉṟāy maṟṟataṉpāl mātaviṭāy uṇṭāl matittilaiyē - mātaravar
translation: You lament with an unquenchable thirst for them. Yet you give no thought to the menstrual cycle that occurs within them.
commentary: Obsession refuses to look at the body as it is. Vallalar names the menstrual cycle plainly, a blunt fact meant to break the spell of blind lust.

translit: taṅkuṟaṅkai mellarampait taṇṭeṉṟāy taṇṭūṉṟi veṅkuraṅkiṉ mēvuṅkāl viḷḷutiyē - naṉkilavāy
translation: You praised their thighs as the soft stems of plantain trees. When they grow old, lean on a walking stick, and move like a fierce monkey, will you say the same?
commentary: Comparing thighs to plantain stems ignores what age will do. Vallalar asks whether the same praise will hold when youth gives way to frailty, a walking stick and a stooped gait.

translit: ēynta muḻantāḷaivarāl eṉṟāy pulāṟciṟitē vāyntu varāṟṟōṟku matittilaiyē - cēntavaṭi
translation: You described their knees as the beautiful varal fish. You failed to realize that they are merely a bit of flesh that cannot possibly compare to the varal fish.
commentary: Tamil love poetry often likens a woman's knees to the sleek varal (snakehead) fish. Vallalar strips the metaphor away and leaves the mind looking at ordinary flesh.

translit: taṇṭā maraiyeṉṟāy taṉmai viḷarppaṭaintāl veṇṭā maraiyeṉṟu mēvutiyō - vaṇṭārā
translation: You praised their red feet as cool lotuses. If those feet grow pale and wither, will you then approach them and call them white lotuses?
commentary: Red feet as blooming lotuses is a favorite comparison. Vallalar mocks the habit by asking whether the mind will simply start praising white lotuses once sickness or old age drains the color away.

translit: mēṉāṭṭuñ caṇpakamē mēṉiyeṉṟāy tīyiṭuṅkāl tīnāṟṟam caṇpakattil tērntaṉaiyō - vāṉāṭṭum
translation: You said the body is the fine champaka flower. When it is set on fire, have you ever known a champaka to yield such a burning stench?
commentary: The champaka is a sweet-smelling flower, and poets love to compare the body to it. Vallalar carries the comparison to the cremation pyre. No burning flower gives off the stench of a burning corpse.

translit: miṉṟēr vaṭiveṉṟāy mēlnī uraittavuḷī toṉṟē orupuṭaiyāy ottatukāṇ - oṉṟāccol
translation: You said the form is like a lightning chariot in the sky. Among all the things you have said before, this alone is somewhat fitting.
commentary: Of all the comparisons, this is the one Vallalar allows. Lightning flashes bright and is gone in an instant, and so is a human life.

translit: vēḷvā kaṉameṉṟāy veyyanamaṉ viṭṭiṭuntū tāḷvā kaṉameṉṟāl ākātō - vēḷāṉōṉ
translation: Speak fitting words. You said it is the vehicle of the god of love. If it is called the vehicle of the cruel messengers sent by Yama, would that not be accurate?
commentary: Romantic verse calls the body the vehicle of the god of love. Vallalar offers a darker and truer name: the vehicle claimed by the cruel messengers of Yama, the god of death.

translit: kākaḷamāy iṉkuralaik kaṭṭuraittāy kālaṉeṉpōṉ kākaḷameṉ pārkkeṉ kaḻaṟutiyē - nākaḷavum
translation: You described the sweet voice as the musical horn of the god of love. What will you say to those who call it the trumpet of the one named Yama?
commentary: A sweet voice gets compared to the love god's musical horn. Vallalar hears something else in the sounds of physical life, the trumpet of Yama announcing that death is drawing near.

translit: cāyaimayil eṉṟē tarukkukiṉṟāy cārpirama cāyaiyaḵ teṉpārkkeṉ cāṟṟutiyē - cēyamalar
translation: You boast to the limits of your tongue that her form is like a peacock. What will you say to those who declare it is merely the shadow of clinging illusion?
commentary: Calling her a peacock is an empty boast. To clear spiritual sight the body is only a shadow thrown by worldly illusion, and it blinds us to what is real and eternal.

translit: aṉṉa naṭai-eṉpāy aḵtaṉ ṟaruntukiṉṟa aṉṉanaṭai eṉpārkkeṉ āṟṟutiyē - aṉṉavarai
translation: You say they have a swan-like gait, but it is not so. If people say it is merely the movement of the food they consume, how will you respond?
commentary: The swan-like walk is a stock compliment in poetry. Vallalar asks how the lover would defend it if he remembered that her movement is just a body working on the food it eats.

translit: ōrō viyameṉpāy ōviyamēl āṅkeḻupat tīrā yiranāṭi yāṇṭuṭaittē - pārārnta
translation: You call those women an exquisite painting. If they are a painting, do they possess seventy-two thousand nerves inside?
commentary: Calling a beautiful woman a flawless painting is another stock trope. Vallalar points beneath the skin. No painting holds the seventy-two thousand pulsing nerves that make up a human body.

translit: muṉṉumalark kompeṉpāy mūṉṟoṭaraik kōṭiyeṉat tuṉṉu murōmat tuvāramuṇṭē - iṉṉamutāl
translation: You call them a prominent flowering branch on this wide earth. Yet they have thirty-five million closely packed hair pores.
commentary: The lover sees a delicate flowering branch. Vallalar bluntly reminds him that this petal-smooth form is covered in millions of hair pores.

translit: ceytavaṭi veṉpāyac ceykaimeyyēl nīyavarkaḷ vaitiṭiṉum maṟṟataṉai vaiyāyē - poytavirāy
translation: You say their forms are made of sweet nectar. If that were true, you would not scold them in return even when they scold you. You do not abandon falsehood.
commentary: Lovers like to say their beloved is made of sweet nectar. Vallalar catches the hypocrisy. If she were truly pure sweetness, the man would not lose his temper and shout back when they quarrel.

translit: oḷḷiḻaiyār tammuruvōr uṇkarumpeṉ ṟāyciṟitu kiḷḷiyeṭut tālirattaṅ kīḻvarumē - koḷḷumavar
translation: You say the bodies of these women wearing bright jewels are like edible sugarcane. If you pinch them even slightly, blood will flow down.
commentary: Sweet sugarcane is one more poetic fantasy. Pinch the skin a little, Vallalar says, and what comes out is human blood.

translit: īṭilpeyar nallār eṉanayantāy nāyppeyartāṉ kēṭilperuñ cūraṉeṉpar kēṭṭilaiyō - nāṭilavar
translation: You desired them, thinking their matchless name is "good women." Haven't you heard that even a dog is named "great flawless warrior"? If you examine them...
commentary: Flattering titles do not change what lies underneath. People call women "good" or "beautiful," but these are only labels. Even a common dog may be given a heroic name, Vallalar points out. He asks the mind to stop mistaking poetic convention for truth.

translit: melliyalār eṉpāy mikukaruppa vētaṉaiyai valliyalār yārpoṟukka vallārkāṇ - villiyalpūṇ
translation: You call them "tender-natured women." Who among the strong-natured can bear the intense agony of pregnancy? See this. Wearing the nature of a bow...
commentary: The romantic imagination pictures women as delicate and fragile. Vallalar breaks that picture by pointing to the harsh agony of pregnancy and childbirth. Look past the poetry of tenderness, he says, and see the severe suffering bound up in bearing children.

translit: vēyntāl avarmēl viḻukiṉṟāy ventīyil pāyntālum aṅkōr palaṉuṇṭē - vēyntāṅku
translation: If they adorn themselves, you fall upon them. Even if you leap into a blazing fire, there is some benefit there. Adorned thus...
commentary: Show the mind a decorated body and it loses all self-control. Leaping into a blazing fire would be the better choice, Vallalar says. A fire might at least purify or end the delusion. Blindly chasing attraction only builds a cycle of endless misery.

translit: ceṉṟāl avarpiṉṉarc celkiṉṟāy vempulippiṉ ceṉṟālum aṅkōr tiṟaṉuṇṭē - ceṉṟāṅku
translation: If they walk away, you walk after them. Even if you walk after a fierce tiger, there is some merit there. Going thus...
commentary: Lust turns a person into a helpless follower. Walking behind a fierce tiger would have more merit, Vallalar says, because facing a wild animal takes real courage. Trailing after a lover strips away dignity and yields nothing of spiritual value.

translit: niṉṟāl avarpiṉṉar niṟkiṉṟāy kaṇmūṭi niṉṟālum aṅkōr nilaiyuṇṭē - oṉṟātu
translation: If they stand, you stand behind them. Even if you stand with your eyes closed, there is some state of being there. Without uniting...
commentary: Waiting on an object of desire is a great loss of focus. Vallalar sets this foolish lingering beside standing quietly with closed eyes in meditation, which brings deep stillness. Hanging about in hope of romance wastes a human life.

translit: kaṇṭāl avaruṭampaik kaṭṭukiṉṟāykallaṇaittuk koṇṭālum aṅkōr kuṇamuṇṭē - peṇṭāṉār
translation: When you see them, you embrace their bodies. Even embracing a stone has some merit. Those women:
commentary: Lust sends people chasing bodies in a hollow pursuit. Hugging a lifeless rock, Vallalar says, would be a more meaningful use of that energy.

translit: vaitālum toṇṭu valittāy piṇattoṇṭu ceytālum aṅkōr ciṟappuḷatē - kaitāvi
translation: Even when they scold you, you forcefully serve them. Even serving a corpse has some greatness. Spreading hands:
commentary: Desire strips away self-respect until a person will endure insults to get what they want. Tending a dead body, Vallalar says, holds more dignity than suffering abuse to satisfy lust.

translit: meyttāvum centōl miṉukkāl mayaṅkiṉainī cettālum aṅkōr ciṟappuḷatē - vaittāṭum
translation: You are deluded by the shine of the reddish skin that covers the body. Even dying has some greatness. Applying and sporting:
commentary: Much of attraction is a trick played by the shine of skin. Vallalar counts death itself a better fate than a life fooled by mere flesh.

translit: mañcaḷ miṉukkāl mayaṅkiṉainī maṟṟoḻintu tuñcukiṉum aṅkōr cukamuḷatē - vañciyaraip
translation: You are deluded by the shine of turmeric. Even abandoning everything else and dying has some comfort. Those vine-like women:
commentary: Cosmetics like turmeric give the body a shine that passes for lasting beauty, and the mind falls for it. Giving up the world for the quiet rest of death is better, Vallalar says, than being trapped by such surface tricks.

translit: pārttāṭi ōṭip paṭarkiṉṟāy vennarakaip pārttālum aṅkōr palaṉuṇṭē - cērttārkait
translation: Seeing them, you dance, run, and pursue them. Even facing cruel hell yields some benefit. Joined hands:
commentary: Desperate chasing after pleasure makes a person dance and run about with no dignity left. Vallalar declares that even going to hell is better than this hollow pursuit, since hell at least teaches a lasting spiritual lesson.

translit: toṭṭāl kaḷittuc cukikkiṉṟāy vaṉpūtam toṭṭālum aṅkōr tuṇaiyuṇṭē - naṭṭālum
translation: You rejoice and feel pleasure when you touch. Even if a fierce ghost touches you, there is at least a companion there. Even if you befriend...
commentary: Worldly people delight in sensual touch, and Vallalar answers with an extreme comparison to show how empty it is. Even the touch of a terrifying ghost brings a companion of sorts. Lust leaves the soul entirely alone.

translit: tevviṉmaṭa vārait tiḷaikkiṉṟāy tīviṭattai vavvukiṉum aṅkōr matiyuṇṭē - cevvitaḻnīr
translation: ...ruinous women, you revel with them. Even if you consume deadly poison, there is at least some sense in it. The moisture of red lips...
commentary: Lust pursued blindly is worse than swallowing deadly poison. Poison at least has a clear and definite outcome. Chasing desire ruins spiritual clarity and offers nothing that lasts.

translit: uṇṭāl makiḻvāynī oṇciṟuvar tamciṟunīr uṇṭālum aṅkō ruraṉuṇṭē - kaṇṭākak
translation: ...you drink and rejoice. Even if you drink the urine of bright young children, there is at least some strength gained. Like rock candy...
commentary: Vallalar turns the romance of the kiss completely upside down. Even drinking a child's urine, which traditional medicine sometimes treats as a remedy, gives some real strength. The moisture of a lover's lips gives nothing real at all.

translit: kavvukiṉṟāy avvitaḻaik kārmatukam vēmpivaṟṟaik kavvukiṉum aṅkōr katiyuṇṭē - avviḷaiyar
translation: ...you bite those lips. Even if you bite on dark licorice or neem, there is at least some benefit. Those young women's...
commentary: Passionate kissing loses out to bitter herbs. Biting on dark licorice or bitter neem leaves at least does the body some medicinal good. Sensual passion helps neither body nor soul.

translit: meṉṟīyum miccil viḻaikiṉṟāy nīveṟumvāy meṉṟālum aṅkōr viḷaivuṇṭē - muṉṟāṉai
translation: ...chewed and offered leftovers you deeply desire. Even if you chew with an empty mouth, there is at least some result. The front of the garment...
commentary: Lovers make something romantic of sharing chewed food and leftovers. Vallalar strips that illusion away. Chewing with an empty mouth is the better act, he argues, since moving the jaw at least exercises it, while obsessing over such leftovers only degrades the mind.

translit: paṭṭāl makiḻvu patintāy pataikkavampu paṭṭālum aṅkōr palaṉuṇṭē - kiṭṭāmeyt
translation: You are deeply immersed in the joy of wearing silk. Even if you suffered a scandal that made you tremble in fear, there would be some benefit in that.
commentary: Vanity offers nothing of real value. The person addressed takes deep pride in wearing fine silk. A terrifying public scandal would be better, because suffering at least has the power to wake a person up.

translit: tīṇṭiṭiluḷ ḷōṅkic cirikkiṉṟāy centēḷmuṉ tīṇṭiṭiṉum aṅkōr tiṟaṉuṇṭē - vēṇṭiyavar
translation: When an unattainable physical body touches you, your heart swells and you laugh aloud. Even if a red scorpion had stung you instead, there would be some meaning in that.
commentary: Touch brings a fleeting, foolish joy. A red scorpion's sting would carry more meaning, since sharp pain wakes you to reality at once, while lust only deepens the soul's illusion.

translit: vāykkiṭayā tāṉumoṉṟu vāṅkukiṉṟāy maṟṟataiyōr nāykkiṭiṉum aṅkōr nalaṉuṇṭē - tākkavarkkāyt
translation: You accept whatever trifle is given to feed the mouths of those who desire you. Even if you gave that to a dog instead, there would be some good in it.
commentary: Feeding worldly attachments earns no merit. Taking scraps to please a lover wastes a life. Give that same food to a hungry dog and it becomes compassion (jīvakāruṇyam), and that alone does real spiritual good.

translit: tēṭṭāṇmai ceyvāyat tēṭṭāṇmai yaitteruvil pōṭṭālum aṅkōr pukaḻuṇṭē - vāṭṭāraik
translation: You exhaust yourself gathering wealth for aggressive men. Even if you threw that gathered wealth into the street, there would be some fame in it.
commentary: Wearing yourself out for arrogant, powerful men is a degrading way to live. Better to throw the hard-earned money straight into the street. Tossing it away breaks the grip of greed, and it might even help someone in need.

translit: koṇṭā ruṭaṉuṇavu koḷkiṉṟāy kukkaluṭaṉ uṇṭālum aṅkōr uṟavuṇṭē - miṇṭākum
translation: You share food with the men who have claimed you. Even if you ate with a stray dog instead, there would be some true kinship in that.
commentary: Worldly relationships are often built on control and vanity. A meal with men who treat you as property gives no true connection. Eat with a stray dog and there is real kinship, because that bond rests on plain compassion for a fellow living being.

translit: iṅkivarvāyp pākilaiyai ēṟkiṉṟāy puṉmalattai nuṅkiṉumaṅ kōrnal noṟiluṇṭē - maṅkaiyartam
translation: Here you accept the chewed betel leaf from their mouths. Even if you swallowed foul excrement, there would be some good outcome in that. The women's...
commentary: Vallalar sharply rebukes the mind for degrading itself in pursuit of sensual pleasure. Accepting chewed betel leaf from the mouths of courtesans is so humiliating, he says, that even eating filth would be less shameful. The comparison is grotesque on purpose. It is meant to shock the mind awake from its delusions.

translit: ēttā maṉaikāt tirukkiṉṟāy īmamatu kāttālum aṅkōr kaṉamuṇṭē - pūttāḻvōr
translation: ...unpraised houses you sit and guard. Even if you guarded the cremation ground, there would be some dignity in that. Those adorned with flowers...
commentary: Now he sets guarding a courtesan's house beside guarding a graveyard. Watching over the dead has at least some solemn dignity. Standing watch for lust brings nothing but disgrace.

translit: kāṭṭāk kuralkēṭpāy karttapattiṉ pāḻṅkuralaik kēṭṭālum aṅkōr kiḷaruṇṭē - kōṭṭāvi
translation: ...whose harsh voices you listen to. Even if you listened to the ruinous bray of a donkey, there would be some awakening in that. Yawning...
commentary: To a man lost in desire, these women's voices may sound sweet. Vallalar calls them harsh and deceptive. A donkey's bray would be better to endure, since it might at least startle him into clear awareness.

translit: āḻntā ruṭaṉvāḻa ātarittāy āḻṅkaṭalil vīḻntālum aṅkōr virakuṇṭē - vīḻntāruḷ
translation: ...you desired to live with those deeply sunk in it. Even if you fell into the deep ocean, there would be some way of escape in that. Among those who have fallen...
commentary: Sinking into obsession with worldly pleasure is more dangerous than falling into the ocean. In the sea you can still swim, or someone may pull you out. Drowning in lust leaves the soul no easy escape.

translit: vīṭṭāl mulaiyumetir vīṭṭāl mukamumuṟak kāṭṭāniṉ ṟārkaṇṭum kāyntilaiyē - kūṭṭāṭkuc
translation: ...they stand showing their breasts to one house and their faces to the opposite house. Even seeing this, you do not burn with anger. To the companion...
commentary: Breasts turned to one house, face turned to the house across the street. These women offer themselves to several men at once, loyal to none. Vallalar wonders how the mind can see such plain lack of affection and still cling to them instead of turning away in disgust.

translit: ceykai yiṭumpaṭitaṉ cīmāṉ taṉatupaṇap paikaiyiṭal kaṇṭum payantilaiyē - caikaiyatu
translation: You feel no fear even when you see the wealthy patron hand over his money bag to make her perform the act.
commentary: Seen plainly, worldly desire is crude and transactional. A wealthy patron hands over a bag of money to buy a woman's affection. Vallalar asks the seeker why watching such a shallow exchange does not frighten them away from the same trap.

translit: kaiyāl orucilarkkum kaṇṇāl orucilarkkum ceyyā mayakkukiṉṟār tērntilaiyē - eyyāmal
translation: They bewitch some men with the gestures of their hands and others with their eyes. You have not understood this.
commentary: A glance for some men, a wave of the hand for others. That is all the trap needs. Vallalar cautions the seeker that the spell is an illusion designed to confuse the mind.

translit: īṟikanta ivvakaiyāy immaṭavār ceykaiyelām kūṟuvaṉēl amma kuṭarkuḻampum - kūṟumivar
translation: If I were to endlessly recount all the actions of these women, alas, your guts would churn.
commentary: Describe everything these women do to secure money and attention, Vallalar says, and the listener would be sick to the stomach. The outward glamour hides a bitter truth.

translit: vāyorupāl pēca maṉamorupāl cellavuṭal āyorupāl ceyya aḻivārkāṇ - āya-ivar
translation: Their mouths speak one thing, their minds wander elsewhere, and their bodies do yet another. See that they will perish.
commentary: Deception splits a person inside. These women say one thing to please a patron, think of something else entirely, and let the body do another. Vallalar observes that such a total break from inner truth and sincerity leads only to ruin.

translit: naṉṟaṟiyār tītē nayappār civatalattil ceṉṟaṟiyār pēykkē ciṟappeṭuppār - iṉṟivarai
translation: These women do not know what is good. They desire only evil. They never visit the temple of Siva. They offer grand worship only to demons.
commentary: Their spiritual lives are as misguided as the rest. They keep away from the temple of Siva and offer lavish worship to lower spirits. Those who chase material wealth, Vallalar shows, are drawn to such forces and miss the path of truth completely.

translit: vañcameṉkō vevviṉaiyām valliyameṉ kōpavattiṉ puñcameṉkō mānaraka pūmiyeṉkō - añcuṟumīr
translation: Shall I call it deceit? Shall I call it the tiger of cruel karma? Shall I call it a heap of worldly births? Shall I call it the realm of great hell? Shall I call it a fearsome double-edged
commentary: Vallalar searches for the right name for the trap of worldly desire, and each name is more terrifying than the last: deceit, a predatory tiger, an endless cycle of birth, hell itself.

translit: vāḷeṉkō vāykkaṭaṅkā māyameṉkō maṇmuṭivu nāḷeṉkō veyya namaṉeṉkō - kōḷeṉkō
translation: sword? Shall I call it an indescribable illusion? Shall I call it the final day of the earth? Shall I call it the cruel god of death? Shall I call it an evil affliction?
commentary: The search for a name goes on. Desire becomes an illusion that words cannot hold, a force as destructive as the end of the world or death itself.

translit: cālameṉkō vāṉintra cālameṉkō vīṟāla kālameṉkō niṉpollāk kālameṉkō - ñālamatil
translation: Shall I call it sorcery? Shall I call it a grand celestial illusion? Shall I call it the fierce primordial poison? Shall I call it your terrible fate? In this world,
commentary: Vallalar runs through every comparison he has, likening this force to black magic, grand cosmic deception and a fatal poison. The tension builds before he finally names the snare.

translit: peṇeṉṟāl yōkap periyōr naṭuṅkuvarēl maṇniṉṟār yārnaṭuṅka māṭṭārkāṇ - peṇeṉṟāl
translation: if even great yogis tremble at the word woman, who among those standing on earth will not tremble? At the word woman,
commentary: At last the danger has a name. In traditional ascetic poetry, the figure of a woman represents the ultimate trap of physical lust and worldly entanglement. If highly disciplined yogis fear this snare, ordinary people living in the world have no defense against it.

translit: pēyum iraṅkumeṉpār pēyoṉṟō tāmpayanta cēyum iraṅkumavar tīmaikkē - āyuñcem
translation: they say even a ghost would feel pity. Is it only a ghost? Even the child they bore will feel pity for their wickedness. When examining...
commentary: This entanglement ruins lives completely. The moral collapse is so tragic that it draws pity from malevolent spirits, and even from the person's own children.

translit: poṉṉāl tukilāl puṉaiyā viṭilavarmey eṉṉākum maṟṟitainī eṇṇilaiyē - iṉṉāmaik
translation: What will their bodies become if they are not adorned with gold and fine garments? You have not considered this.
commentary: Much of physical beauty is made by clothes and jewelry. Vallalar tells his mind to look past the decoration and see the body underneath for what it is, something temporary.

translit: kotteṉṟa ammaṭavār kūṭṭam eḻumaikkum vitteṉ ṟaṟintumatai viṭṭilaiyē - totteṉṟu
translation: Even knowing that the company of those women is a cluster of misery and the seed for seven future births, you have not abandoned it.
commentary: Sensual attachment brings misery and traps the soul in the cycle of reincarnation. "Seven births" means that continuous loop of being born again and again. The mind knows the danger and still refuses to let go.

translit: pāca viṉaikkuṭ paṭuttuṟumap pāvaiyarmēl ācaiyuṉak kevvā ṟaṭaintatuvē - nēcamilāy
translation: How did you acquire such desire for those women who enslave and trap you in the actions of worldly attachment?
commentary: Lust binds a person to worldly attachments and to the heavy consequences of their actions. That trap leads straight into spiritual bondage.

translit: niṉṉācai eṉṉeṉpēṉ neyvīḻ neruppeṉavē poṉṉācai mēṉmēlum poṅkiṉaiyē - poṉṉācai
translation: O loveless one, what shall I say of your desire? Like a fire fueled by poured ghee, your desire for gold swells more and more.
commentary: Greed can never be satisfied. Vallalar compares the desire for wealth to a fire fed with ghee (clarified butter). Pour on fuel and the fire burns hotter, and acquiring gold works the same way on the craving for it.

translit: vaittiḻantu vīṇē vayiṟerintu maṇṇulakil ettaṉaipēr niṉkaṇ etirniṉṟār - tattukiṉṟa
translation: How many people have stood before your very eyes in this world, having harbored a desire for gold, lost it, and burned in useless anguish?
commentary: Everyday life shows what greed does. We keep seeing people who give themselves to chasing wealth, only to lose it and suffer deeply. The mind watches these warnings play out right in front of it and ignores them.

translit: poṉṉuṭaiyār tuṉpap puṇariyoṉṟē allatumaṟ ṟeṉṉuṭaiyār kaṇṭiṅ kiruntaṉaiyē - poṉṉiruntāl
translation: Those who possess gold possess only an ocean of sorrow. What else do they have? You have seen this and remained here. If you possess gold,
commentary: Wealth brings nothing but an ocean of sorrow. Hoarded gold means endless anxiety, and people see this painful truth every day and still choose to ignore it.

translit: āṟṟaṉmiku tāyumaṟi yāvakaiyāl vaittiṭavōr ēṟṟaviṭam vēṇṭumataṟ keṉceyvāy - ēṟṟaviṭam
translation: you need a suitable place to hide it so that even your capable mother does not know. What will you do for that? Even if a suitable place
commentary: Wealth breeds paranoia. A person with gold grows so suspicious that they feel forced to hide it even from their own mother, and they never stop worrying about where to keep it safe.

translit: vāyttālum aṅkataṉai vaittaviṭam kāṭṭāmal ēyttāl civacivamaṟ ṟeṉceyvāy - ēykkātu
translation: is found, if someone deceives you by not showing where it was kept, Siva Siva, what will you do? Even if it remains without deceit,
commentary: The fear of being robbed never ends. If the person trusted to hide the wealth steals it instead, the owner is left helpless. "Siva Siva" is a cry of dismay at this worldly trap.

translit: niṉṟālum piṉṉatutāṉ nīṭum kariyāṉa teṉṟāl arakaramaṟ ṟeṉceyvāy - naṉṟāka
translation: if it later turns to mere charcoal, Hara Hara, what will you do? You run away when told to stand
commentary: Material wealth has no stability. If the hoard suddenly loses its value and turns to worthless charcoal, the owner is ruined. "Hara Hara" is the gasp of shock at how quickly worldly security vanishes.

translit: oṉṟorucār nilleṉṟāl ōṭukiṉṟa nī-ataṉai eṉṟum purappataṉuk keṉceyvāy - veṉṟiyoṭu
translation: well and firmly in one place. What will you do to protect it forever? With victory,
commentary: The mind cannot even hold itself steady in one place. Restless and easily distracted, a person has no real power to guard a physical treasure forever.

translit: pērttup puraṭṭip peruñciṉattāl māṟṟalarkaḷ īrttup paṟikkilataṟ keṉceyvāy - pērtteṭukkak
translation: If enemies with great wrath unearth it, overturn it, drag it, and snatch it away, what will you do? To dig it up...
commentary: Buried wealth is never safe. Angry enemies can dig it up and carry it off by force, and the hoarder is left with nothing.

translit: kaipukuttum kāluṭ karuṅkuḷavi ceṅkuḷavi eypukuttak koṭṭiṭiṉmaṟ ṟeṉceyvāy - poypukuttum
translation: ...when you thrust your hand in, if black wasps and red wasps sting you like piercing arrows, what will you do? The falsehood-introducing...
commentary: People used to bury their gold in the earth to hide it. Reach into that dark ground and hidden wasps may sting you. Chasing wealth brings suffering at once, right into the hand.

translit: poṉkāval pūtamatu pōyeṭukkum pōtumaṟit teṉkāval eṉṟālmaṟ ṟeṉceyvāy - poṉkāval
translation: ...demon guarding the gold blocks you when you go to take it and declares, "This is under my guard." What will you do then? As the guarding of the gold...
commentary: Folklore says dark spirits guard buried treasure. Hoarded wealth takes on a life of its own and turns on the one who buried it, refusing them their own gold.

translit: vīṟuṅkāl āṇavamām veṅkūḷi niṉtalaimēl ēṟuṅkāl maṟṟataṉuk keṉceyvāy - māṟumcīr
translation: ...swells with force, if the fierce demon of ego mounts your head, what will you do about it? The shifting...
commentary: Hoarding breeds arrogance. Ego climbs onto the mind like a fierce demon and blinds a person to spiritual truth.

translit: uṉnēyam vēṇṭi ulōpam eṉumkuṟumpaṉ iṉṉē varuvaṉataṟ keṉceyvāy - muṉṉētum
translation: ...rogue called greed comes right now seeking your friendship. What will you do about that? Before anything...
commentary: Last comes greed, a rogue who wants to be your friend and never leaves. That endless wanting for more rots a person's character from the inside.

translit: illā namakkuṇṭō illaiyō eṉṉunalam ellām aḻiyumataṟ keṉceyvāy - nillāmal
translation: The wealth that we, who have nothing, wonder whether we possess or not will entirely perish. What will you do about that? It never stays still.
commentary: Wealth never stays put. We spend our lives worrying whether we have enough, and still our possessions vanish. Vallalar asks what you will do when that moment comes.

translit: āyntōr cilanāḷil āyirampēr pakkalatu pāyntōṭip pōvatunī pārttilaiyē - āyntōrcol
translation: In just a few days, it leaps and runs away to a thousand different people. Have you not seen this? The words of the wise
commentary: Money keeps changing hands. In a few days a fortune can leap from one person to a thousand others, loyal to no one.

translit: kūttāṭ ṭavaicēr kuḻāmviḷintāṟ pōlumeṉṟa cīrttāṭ kuṟaḷmoḻiyum tērntilaiyē - pērttōṭum
