translation: and the excellent verses of the Kural state that wealth is like a crowd gathering at a theater and then dispersing. Have you not understood this? It constantly shifts and runs.
commentary: Vallalar quotes the Tirukkural here. Its verse compares wealth to a crowd at a play, packed together for the show and scattered the moment it ends. Fortune is that restless.

translit: nāṭkolli eṉṟāl naṭuṅkukiṉṟāy nāḷaṟiyā āṭkolli eṉparitai āyntilaiyē - kīḻkkollaip
translation: You tremble at the mention of a poison that kills on a set day. Yet you have not examined the truth that the wise call wealth a killer of men that strikes on no set schedule. In the lower backyard,
commentary: People are terrified of literal poison that takes time to kill. The wise teach that the obsession with wealth is far more dangerous. It is a sudden killer of men that ruins lives without any warning.

translit: paccilaiyāl poṉṉaip paṭaippārēl maṟṟataṉmēl iccaiyuṉak kevvā ṟiruntatuvē - iccaiyilār
translation: if people create gold using green herbs, how can your desire for it persist? Those who are free from desire
commentary: Some try to make gold from green herbs through alchemy. If gold can be made that way, Vallalar asks, how can your burning desire for such artificial wealth last? Peace belongs only to those who have dropped greed altogether.

translit: iṭṭamalam paṭṭaviṭam ellāmpoṉ ṉāmeṉṟāl iṭṭamatai viṭṭaṟkicaintilaiyē - muṭṭakaṟṟap
translation: Even if excrement turns to gold wherever it falls, you refuse to abandon your desire for it. To remove your obstacles,
commentary: Suppose even excrement turned to gold wherever it fell. The craving to hoard it would stay just as base and spiritually empty. That is how badly the obsession blinds.

translit: poṉṉaṭappa taṉṟiyatu pōṉakamē yātiyavāy eṉṉaṭutta toṉṟumiḵ teṇṇilaiyē - innilattil
translation: gold cannot walk, nor can it serve as food or anything else. You do not consider this at all. In this world,
commentary: Gold cannot walk, and it cannot be eaten. People hoard it out of greed and forget that a metal coin will never nourish the body.

translit: nīṇmayakkam poṉmuṉ nilaiyāy ulakiyalām vīṇmayakkam eṉṟataṉai viṭṭilaiyē -nīṇvalayat
translation: the great delusion of gold stands firmly before you. You have not forsaken this vain worldly illusion. In this vast world,
commentary: Riches are an empty worldly illusion. Chasing them keeps the mind in endless confusion and pulls it away from any deeper spiritual reality.

translit: ticcelva miṉṟi iyalātēl ciṟṟuyirkaḷ eccelvam koṇṭiṅ kiruntaṉavē - vecceṉṟa
translation: if you believe life is impossible without this wealth, what wealth do the little creatures possess to survive here?
commentary: Look at the small creatures of the earth. They own no riches and survive perfectly well, which proves false the human belief that life is impossible without wealth.

translit: maṇṇācai koṇṭaṉainī maṇṇāḷum maṉṉarelām maṇṇāl aḻital matittilaiyē - eṇṇātu
translation: You harbor a burning desire for land. You do not reflect on how all the kings who ruled the earth were destroyed by the earth. Without thinking,
commentary: Wanting to own land gets you nothing in the end. Even the mightiest kings who claimed to rule the earth were buried in it, consumed by the very soil they tried to possess.

translit: maṇkoṇṭār māṇṭārtam māyntavuṭal vaikkavayal maṇkoṇṭār tammiruppil vaittilarē - tiṇkoṇṭa
translation: Those who acquired land died. To bury their lifeless bodies, people took the soil of the fields. They did not keep the dead in their own homes.
commentary: A man can spend his whole life gathering property. Death leaves him needing only a patch of field soil for a grave, and all that wealth cannot keep him in his own house once the breath goes.

translit: viṇṇēkuṅ kālaṅku vēṇṭumeṉa īṇṭupiṭi maṇṇēṉuṅ koṇṭēka vallārō - maṇnēyam
translation: When departing to the firm heavens, thinking they might need it there, are they able to take even a handful of earth from here?
commentary: Wealth and property belong to this physical world. When the time comes to leave, nobody carries off even a handful of that beloved soil.

translit: eṉṉateṉṟāṉ muṉṉoruvaṉ eṉṉateṉṟāṉ piṉṉoruvaṉ iṉṉatunī kēṭṭiṅ kiruntilaiyō - maṉṉulakil
translation: One man in the past claimed the land as his own. Another man later claimed it as his own. Have you not heard this while living in this enduring world?
commentary: The earth outlasts everyone who claims it. One generation holds the deed and calls the land its own, and the next steps in and says exactly the same.

translit: kaṇkāṇi yāynīyē kāṇiyallāy nīyirunta maṇkāṇi eṉṟu matittaṉaiyē - kaṇkāṇa
translation: You are merely an overseer. You are not the owner of the land. You considered the piece of earth you occupied as your own property.
commentary: We look after the earth for a short while and are never its masters. To think a piece of land belongs to you for good is to misunderstand how brief your stay here is.

translit: maṇkāṇi vēṇṭi varuntukiṉṟāy nīmēlai viṇkāṇi vēṇṭal viyappaṉṟē - eṇkāṇa
translation: You suffer in your desire for a piece of earthly land. It is no surprise that you do not seek the heavenly estate above.
commentary: Wanting land keeps a person anxious and miserable. Tied to a small patch of earth, he forgets to seek the lasting freedom of the heavenly estate.

translit: antarattil niṉṟāynī antō niṉaiviṭamaṇ antarattil niṉṟa taṟintilaiyē - tantirattil
translation: You stand in the void. Alas! You do not realize that the earth you consider your home also stands in the void.
commentary: We lean on the earth as if it were solid ground. Vallalar reminds us that the planet itself hangs unsupported in empty space, just as we do.

translit: maṇkoṭuppēṉ eṉṟuraikkil vaivār ciṟuvarkaḷum maṇkoṭukkil nītāṉ makiḻntaṉaiyē - vaṇkoṭukkum
translation: If you cunningly tell little children you will give them dirt, even they will scold you. Yet you rejoice when given dirt!
commentary: Worldly wealth is dirt. Offer a child a handful of mud and he will scold you, yet grown men spend their lives chasing land and rejoice when they get it.

translit: vīṭeṉṟēṉ maṟṟataimaṇ vīṭeṉṟē nīniṉaintāy vīṭeṉṟa coṟporuḷai viṇṭilaiyē - nāṭoṉṟum
translation: I spoke of the liberation that grants abundant grace. You thought I meant an earthen house. You did not understand the true meaning of the word.
commentary: The Tamil word vīṭu means both a house and final spiritual liberation. Vallalar offers the supreme state of grace, and the worldly mind hears only a promise of property.

translit: maṇṇāl marattāl vaṉaikiṉṟa vīṭaṉaittum kaṇṇārak kaṭṭaḻital kaṇṭilaiyō - maṇṇāṉa
translation: In any land, have you not seen with your own eyes the complete ruin of all houses built with earth and wood?
commentary: Everything physical falls down in the end. A house of earth and wood gives no permanent shelter, and you have seen this with your own eyes.

translit: mēlvīṭum aṅkuṭaiya vēntarkaḷum mēlvīṭṭap pālvīṭum pāḻātal pārttilaiyō - mēlvīṭṭil
translation: Have you not seen the earthen multi-storied palaces, the kings who own them, and the milky-white mansions all falling into ruin?
commentary: Wealth and power give no protection against time. Grand palaces and the kings inside them meet the same fate as ordinary houses. They crumble back into the dust they were made from.

translit: ēṟuvaṉē eṉpāy iyamaṉ kaṭāmicaivan tēṟuvaṉēl uṉṉācai eṉṉāmō - kūṟiṭumim
translation: You say, "I will ascend." If the god of death comes riding on his buffalo, what will become of your desires? Tell me this.
commentary: People make grand plans and boast of how high they will rise. Death makes a mockery of that greed. When the god of death comes riding his buffalo, every one of those desires is left behind.

translit: maṇṇaḷitta vētiyaṉum maṇviruppam koḷḷāṉēl eṇṇamuṉak kevvā ṟiruntatuvē - maṇṇiṭattil
translation: Even the Creator who made the earth has no desire for the earth. How did such a thought take hold in you?
commentary: Even the Creator who formed the earth does not try to possess it. We made none of it and can keep none of it, yet we are consumed with owning land and wealth. Vallalar finds that absurd.

translit: ākāt turumpiṭattum ācaivaittāy - eṉṉiluṉṟaṉ ēkāp peruṅkāmam eṉcolkēṉ - pōkāta
translation: On this earth, you place your desire even on a useless piece of straw. What can I say about your boundless, immense greed?
commentary: Human greed clings even to a worthless piece of straw. Once the mind starts wanting whatever it sees, useful or not, it never finds rest, and the soul stays trapped in dissatisfaction.

translit: pāpak kaṭaṟkōr paṭukaṭalām pāḻvekuḷik kōpak kaṭalil kuḷittaṉaiyē - tāpamuṟac
translation: You have bathed in the ruinous ocean of wrath, which is a deeper abyss than the inescapable ocean of sins.
commentary: Anger ruins the one who carries it. Vallalar calls wrath an abyss deeper than the ocean of sins. A mind given over to rage loses its clarity and its compassion.

translit: cellā viṭattuc ciṉantītu celliṭattum illataṉil tīyateṉṟa teṇṇilaiyē - mallalpeṟat
translation: Causing distress, anger is evil where it holds no power. Even where it holds power, there is nothing worse than it. You have not reflected on this.
commentary: Anger is poison in every situation. If you are powerless, it torments only you. Given power, it does terrible harm to others. Vallalar says nothing is worse, and asks you to think on it.

translit: taṉṉaittāṉ kākkil ciṉaṅkākka eṉṟataṉaip poṉṉaippōlpōṟṟip pukaḻntilaiyē - tuṉṉi
translation: You did not cherish and praise like gold the teaching that says if you wish to protect yourself, you must guard against anger. Drawing near,
commentary: Vallalar is scolding his own mind. An ancient Tamil teaching says anger destroys the one who holds it, so whoever wants to stay safe must first guard against their own rage. He asks why the mind will not treasure this warning like gold.

translit: akaḻvārait tāṅkum nilampōla eṉṉun tikaḻvāy maiyumnī teḷiyāy - ikaḻvārai
translation: you do not understand the shining truth that tells us to be like the earth that patiently bears those who dig into it. Regarding those who despise us,
commentary: Another famous teaching, this time on patience. The earth silently holds up the very people who dig into it and scar it. His mind has failed to grasp that this shining example shows how to treat those who cause harm.

translit: evvaṇṇam nammai ikaḻvār aṟivōmeṉ ṟivvaṇṇam eṉṉaiveḷi yiṭṭaṉaiyē - tevveṉṉa
translation: you wondered, "How will they insult us? Let us find out." In this manner you exposed me completely. Like an enemy,
commentary: Instead of practicing patience, the restless mind goes looking for trouble, listening for insults and wondering how people will show disrespect. That obsession with what others think drags a person down. It exposes them to pain they never needed to feel.

translit: ōrā vekuḷi yuṭaiyāṉ tavamaṭaiyāṉ tīrāyeṉ pāratuvum tērntilaiyē - pērāniṉ
translation: you failed to realize the saying of the wise that one who harbors unthinking anger will never attain penance and will not be cured. If the Lord inflicts suffering upon you
commentary: Blind anger blocks any true spiritual progress, because rage makes deep meditation and discipline impossible. The wise elders say an angry heart can never heal its own suffering, and the mind has ignored them.

translit: vevviṉaikkī ṭāka-araṉ vemmaipuri vāṉeṉṟāl ivvekuḷi yārmāṭ ṭiruttuvatē - cevvaiyilāy
translation: in proportion to your cruel and unwavering karma, upon whom can you direct this anger? Oh you who lack righteousness!
commentary: Karma is the principle that our past actions shape what we meet now. If the Lord lets suffering reach us, it is our own cruel deeds coming back. We caused it ourselves, so there is no one else to aim our anger at.

translit: ēyntaṉaiyaṉ pōriṭattil iṉṉāmai ceytavaraik kāyntaṉaimaṟ ṟeṉṉapalaṉ kaṇṭaṉaiyē - vāyntaṟivōr
translation: You clashed in conflict and burned with anger against those who caused you harm. What benefit did you see from this? Those with true wisdom...
commentary: Anger and retaliation bring no spiritual benefit. Meeting harm with hatred and conflict is useless and only burdens the soul.

translit: ellā nalamum iḵtēyeṉ ṟēttukiṉṟa kollā nalamciṟituṅ koṇṭilaiyē - pollāta
translation: ...praise the virtue of non-killing as the sum of all goodness. You have not embraced even a trace of this virtue of non-killing. You wicked...
commentary: Non-killing (kollāmai) is the absolute foundation of spiritual life. The wise recognize that refusing to harm others is the greatest of all virtues, yet the ordinary mind fails to embrace even a fraction of this goodness.

translit: vaṉpō ṭirukku matiyilinī maṉṉuyirkkaṇ aṉpō ṭirakkam aṭaintilaiyē - iṉpōṅku
translation: ...fool persisting in cruelty, you have felt no love or compassion for living beings. The joy-abounding...
commentary: A harsh heart cannot hold Jeevakarunyam (compassion for all living beings). Without love and mercy for other lives, a person stays trapped in cruelty and foolishness.

translit: tūymaiyeṉpa tellām tuṇaiyāy aṇaivatutāṉ vāymaiyeṉpa toṉṟē matittilaiyē - tūymaiyilāy
translation: ...truth is the sole companion that brings together all that is called purity. You have not valued this singular path of truth. You impure one...
commentary: Truthfulness is the single quality that gathers all other forms of purity to it. Without a commitment to truth, the mind remains unclean, regardless of what outward religious acts are performed.

translit: māṉorukai ēntiniṉṟa vaḷḷalaṉpar taṅkaḷuḷē nāṉoruvaṉ eṉṟu naṭittaṉaiyē - āṉamaṟṟaip
translation: ...merely play-acted as if you were a true devotee among the lovers of the generous Lord who holds a deer in one hand. As for the other...
commentary: The deer in the Lord's hand is a traditional symbol of Siva's gentle grace. Without compassion, truth, and non-violence, calling oneself a devotee of God is nothing but an empty performance.

translit: pātakaṅka ḷellām paḻakip paḻakiyatil cātakañcey vōril talainiṉṟāy - pātakattil
translation: You repeatedly practiced every kind of sin, standing foremost among those who have perfected them.
commentary: The mind easily makes habits out of wrongdoing. Repeat a fault long enough and you become an expert in it. Look how much effort goes into perfecting flaws that could have gone into seeking what is real.

translit: ōyā vikāra uṇarcciyiṉāl ivvulaka māyā vikāram makiḻntaṉaiyē - cāyātu
translation: In that wickedness, driven by restless and distorted feelings, you delighted in the illusory transformations of this world.
commentary: Restless desires tie awareness to temporary things. Driven by unsteady feelings, people take their joy in the shifting illusions of the physical world, and those fleeting pleasures pull them away from lasting spiritual truth.

translit: nī-iḷamai meyyāy niṉaintāy niṉaippeṟṟa tāyiḷamai ettaṉaināḷ taṅkiyatē - āyiḷamai
translation: Unwavering, you considered youth to be permanent. Holding onto that thought, how many days did your youth actually remain?
commentary: We live as though youth will last forever. That feeling of permanence is a deep delusion. Measured against the vast span of time, the years of youth slip away in a matter of days.

translit: meykoṭutta teṉpāy viruttarkaṭku niṉpōlvār kaikoṭuttup pōvataṉaik kaṇṭilaiyō - meykoṭutta
translation: You claim that youth gave permanence to your body. Have you not seen people like yourself lending a supporting hand to the elderly as they walk?
commentary: The evidence of aging is everywhere. Even while feeling young and invincible, people keep having to help the elderly walk, and that ordinary sight shows plainly how temporary physical strength is.

translit: kūṉoṭumkaik kōlūṉṟik kunti naṭaitaḷarntu kāṉaṭuṅka niṟpavaraik kaṇṭilaiyō - ūṉoṭuṅka
translation: Have you not seen them standing with bodies bent, leaning on walking sticks, hobbling with a faltering gait and trembling legs?
commentary: Old age waits for everyone. Bodies bend, legs tremble, and a walking stick takes the place of independence. Seeing this decline clearly loosens the mind's false attachment to physical beauty and power.

translit: aiyanaṭa veṉṟē arumputalvar muṉcelappiṉ paiya naṭappavaraip pārttilaiyō - veyyanamaṉ
translation: Have you not seen the elderly walking slowly behind while their dear children walk ahead urging them, "Father, walk"? The cruel God of Death
commentary: Children walk ahead calling "Father, walk," and the old man shuffles behind as best he can. Vallalar asks you to look hard at that ordinary scene. The strength of youth does not last.

translit: nāṭaḻaikkac cēṉanari nāyaḻaikka nāṟucuṭu kāṭaḻaikka mūttuniṉṟār kaṇṭilaiyō - pīṭaṭainta
translation: calls them to his realm. Flocks of foxes and dogs call them. The foul-smelling cremation ground calls them. Have you not seen those who stand in such old age? The once proud
commentary: Old age leaves a person standing at the very edge of death, with the god of death, the scavenging foxes and dogs, and the reeking cremation ground all calling for the body. Vallalar uses these grim images to break our illusion that we will last.

translit: meyyularntu nīriṉ viḻiyularntu vāyularntu kaiyularntu niṟpavaraik kaṇṭilaiyō - meyyularntum
translation: body withers. The eyes lose their moisture and dry up. The mouth dries up. The hands wither away. Have you not seen those standing in such a state? Even as the body withers,
commentary: The body we were once proud of dries out piece by piece, eyes, mouth and hands. Vallalar wants you to witness this suffering directly. Watch how the physical form fails us.

translit: cākāṉ kiḻavaṉ taḷarkiṉṟāṉ eṉṟivaṇnī ōkāḷam ceyvataṉai ōrntilaiyō - ākāta
translation: you mock them saying, "This old man does not die, he only languishes." Have you not realized the ridicule you make here? The incurable
commentary: Some of the young and healthy mock the old for lingering in pain, grumbling that the old man just won't die. Vallalar exposes the cruelty of that arrogance. Those youths are laughing at their own future.

translit: kaṇṭamitu pollāk kaṭunōy eṉuṅkumara kaṇṭamiḵ teṉpavaraik kaṇṭilaiyō - koṇṭavuṭal
translation: danger is this severe and cruel disease. Have you not seen people saying, "This is the deadly affliction of youth"? The physical body
commentary: Disease can strike the young too, and destroy them. After the verses on old age, Vallalar shows that youth itself gives no real protection. The body is always open to sudden, deadly affliction.

translit: kuṭṭamuṟak kaikāl kuṟukkumitu pollāta kuṭṭameṉa nōvār kuṟittilaiyō - tuṭṭaviṉai
translation: Have you not noticed those who suffer and cry out, "This is the wicked leprosy that shortens and shrivels our hands and legs"?
commentary: Vallalar asks whether we have truly paid attention to the suffering around us, beginning with those whose hands and legs are shriveled by leprosy. Look closely at their agony. Seeing the real torment of others is the first step toward compassion for all living beings (Jeevakarunyam).

translit: mālaiyiṉum kālaiyiṉum mattiyiṉum kuttumitu cūlaiyeṉa nōvāraic cūḻntilaiyō - cālavumit
translation: Have you not drawn near those who suffer and groan, "This cruel karma pierces us like a sharp spear in the evening, in the morning, and at midday"?
commentary: The questions keep coming. Here it is pain that pierces like a spear morning, noon and evening, day after day. You cannot cultivate compassion while keeping a safe distance from people living in that kind of unbroken agony.

translit: tēka matunaliyac ceyyuṅkāṇ uyvaritām mēkamiḵ teṉpārai mēvilaiyō - tākamuṟac
translation: Have you not reached those who say, "See how this severe wasting disease ruins the body and makes survival impossible"?
commentary: Now come the wasting diseases that slowly strip away life and hope. Vallalar asks whether we have actually gone to people dying in bodily ruin. Spiritual life means witnessing that decline and being present for the dying.

translit: cittanōy ceykiṉṟa cītanōy vātamoṭu pittanōy koṇṭavarpāl pērntilaiyō - mettariya
translation: Have you not moved among those afflicted with diseases of phlegm, wind, and bile that cause burning thirst and deep distress to the mind?
commentary: Vallalar draws on the traditional medicine in which imbalances of phlegm, wind and bile cause severe illness. Such disease rarely stays in the body. It brings burning distress to the mind as well, and he wants us to walk among these sufferers and see how their peace is shattered.

translit: kaippiṇiyum kāṟpiṇiyum kaṭpiṇiyō ṭeṇṇariya meyppiṇiyum koṇṭavarai viṇṭilaiyō - eyppuṭaiya
translation: Have you not spoken to those suffering from severe diseases of the hands, diseases of the legs, diseases of the eyes, and countless other diseases of the body?
commentary: Hands, legs, eyes, and then countless other afflictions of the body. Vallalar asks whether we have spoken to the sufferers themselves. Pity from a distance does not count. Compassion is lived through real, personal contact with people who are unwell.

translit: muṭṭūṟum kaikāl muṭaṅkūṉ mutalāya eṭṭūṟuṅ koṇṭavarai eṇṇilaiyō - taṭṭūṟiṅ
translation: Have you not thought of those who suffer the eight kinds of afflictions, beginning with crippled hands and feet and hunched backs?
commentary: Health is fragile and easily lost. Vallalar turns the mind toward those with crippled hands and feet, hunched backs, and the rest of the eight afflictions. Their pain shows plainly how vulnerable our own bodies are.

translit: keṇṇaṟṟa tuṇṭēl iḷamai oruporuḷāy eṇṇap paṭumōveṉ ṟeṇṇilaiyō - eṇṇattil
translation: If there are countless obstacles here, have you not considered whether youth can be valued as a thing of worth?
commentary: Youth passes quickly and is hemmed in by countless uncertainties. It offers no lasting security, and valuing it as something of permanent worth is a deep mistake.

translit: poyyeṉ ṟaṟavōr pulampuṟavum ivvuṭampai meyyeṉṟu poymmayakkam mēviṉaiyē - kainiṉṟu
translation: Even as the wise lament that it is false, you have embraced the false delusion that this body is true.
commentary: The wise keep warning that this body is false and will perish. Still the mind stubbornly treats it as if it will last forever. That delusion keeps us bound to worldly attachments and away from lasting spiritual truth.

translit: kūkā eṉamaṭavār kūṭi aḻalkaṇṭum nīkātal vaittu nikaḻntaṉaiyē - mākātal
translation: Even seeing women gather and wail aloud in grief, you have lived placing your love on worldly life.
commentary: Witnessing the death of others should wake us up to the reality of our own end. Seeing families weeping bitterly over a lost loved one makes the tragic outcome of worldly attachment clear. Despite seeing this grief firsthand, people continue to pour all their love into a temporary worldly life.

translit: peṇṭiruntu māḻkap piṇaṅkoṇṭu celvāraik kaṇṭiruntum antō kalaṅkilaiyē - paṇṭirunta
translation: Even seeing them carry away the corpse while the wife stays behind and perishes in grief, alas, you remain unshaken.
commentary: A funeral procession is a direct lesson in impermanence. The body is carried off, the wife is left behind broken with grief, and that is how every worldly relationship ends. Vallalar's "alas" is his wonder that even this fails to shake the mind out of its complacency.

translit: ūrār piṇattiṉ uṭaṉceṉṟu nāmmīṇṭu nīrāṭal caṟṟum niṉaintilaiyē - cīrāka
translation: You have not reflected at all on the fact that we follow the corpses of the townspeople, return, and then take a bath.
commentary: People walk in funeral processions for their neighbors, come home, wash, and carry on with life. Vallalar asks how we can keep performing this ritual of death without once realizing that our own time is coming.

translit: iṉṟiruntār nāḷaik kiruppatupoy eṉṟaṟavōr naṉṟirunta vārttaiyumnī nāṭilaiyē - oṉṟi
translation: You do not seek the good words of the sages who declared it a lie to say that those who are here today will still be here tomorrow.
commentary: We keep assuming life will simply go on. Vallalar reminds us that the wise have always called this a dangerous illusion and warned us never to take tomorrow for granted.

translit: uṟaṅkuvatu pōlumeṉṟa oṇkuṟaḷiṉ vāymai maṟaṅkaruti antō maṟantāy - kaṟaṅkiṉ
translation: Alas, harboring ignorance, you forgot the truth of the brilliant Kural which says that death is just like falling asleep.
commentary: The Kural is the classical, deeply revered book of Tamil ethical wisdom. Its famous teaching says dying is as natural and certain as falling asleep. Vallalar asks how we manage to ignore a truth stated so plainly.

translit: nerunal uḷaṉoruvaṉ eṉṉum neṭuñcol maruvum kuṟaṭpā maṟantāy - teruvil
translation: You forgot the Kural verse holding the profound words which state that a man who was alive yesterday is no more today.
commentary: Another Kural verse, this one on how suddenly death comes. A man alive yesterday is gone today, while the rest of us go on living as if we were permanent. That is the bitter irony it sets before us.

translit: iṟantār piṟantā riṟantā reṉuñcol maṟantāy maṟantāy maṟantāy - iṟantār
translation: You forgot, you forgot, you forgot the words echoing in the streets saying that people died, were born, and died again.
commentary: Births and deaths are announced in our own streets every day. Vallalar says "you forgot" three times, and the repetition carries his sorrow at how completely the mind ignores the cycle of death happening right outside our doors.

translit: paṟaiyōcai aṇṭam paṭīreṉ ṟolikka maṟaiyōcai yaṉṟē maṟantāy - iṟaiyōṉ
translation: When the death drum resounds with a crash throughout the universe, you completely forget the sound of the sacred chants. The Lord's
commentary: At the moment of death, the terrifying sound of the funeral drum drowns out everything else. The sacred chants are forgotten then, gone from the dying person's memory.

translit: pulaṉaintumeṉṟaruḷum poṉmoḻiyai māyā malamoṉṟi antō maṟantāy - nilaṉoṉṟi
translation: golden words of grace concerning the five senses you have forgotten. Alas, you united with the impurity of illusion. Fixing on the earth,
commentary: Once we are bound up in the illusions of worldly life, divine wisdom slips out of sight. The teachings that show us how to master the five senses are forgotten completely.

translit: vikkuḷ eḻanīr viṭumi ṉeṉa-ayalōr nekkurukal antō niṉaintilaiyē - mikkaṉalil
translation: when the final hiccups arise, bystanders melt in sorrow and tell others to give you water. Alas, you do not think of this. In the fierce fire,
commentary: The last moments of life are physical and desperate. Relatives gather in sorrow to pour drops of water into the mouth of someone struggling for breath. Yet people live as if this end will never come to them.

translit: neyviṭalpōl uṟṟavarkaṇṇīrviṭ ṭaḻavuyirpal meyviṭalum kaṇṭaṉainī viṇṭilaiyē - ceyviṉaiyiṉ
translation: relatives shed tears and weep like pouring ghee as the life departs from the body. You have seen this, yet you do not realize the truth. Due to past deeds,
commentary: Families weep without end at the deaths we witness. We see life leave a body with our own eyes and still do not wake up to the fact of our own death.

translit: vāḷkaḻiyac ceṅkatirōṉ vāṉkaḻiya nammuṭaiya nāḷkaḻitaṟ kantō naṭuṅkilaiyē - kōḷkaḻiyum
translation: the radiant red sun crosses the sky and its light fades. Alas, you do not tremble knowing that our own days are passing away. The planets pass.
commentary: Each sunset takes another day from our time on earth, and it never comes back. We watch the days go and feel no urgency to seek the divine before our time runs out.

translit: nāḻikaiyōr nāḷāka nāṭiṉaiyē nāḷai-oru nāḻikaiyāy eṇṇi nalintilaiyē - nāḻikaimuṉ
translation: You desired a single hour to stretch into a day, but you did not feel distressed realizing that a whole day could shrink into a single hour.
commentary: The mind bends time to suit its desires. People wish moments of pleasure would stretch on forever, yet how fast their real lifespan is slipping away doesn't trouble them at all.

translit: niṉṟār iruntār nilaikulaiya vīḻntuyirtāṉ ceṉṟār eṉakkēṭṭum tērntilaiyē - piṉṟātu
translation: You hear people say that just an hour ago someone stood and sat, then lost their balance, fell, and their life departed. Even after hearing this, you have not gained clarity.
commentary: Life can end in seconds. We keep hearing of people who were fine one moment and gone the next. The real tragedy is that such warnings do nothing to shake a person out of spiritual laziness.

translit: toṭṭār uṇavuṭaṉē tummiṉār amma-uyir viṭṭār eṉakkēṭṭum veṭkilaiyē - taṭṭāmal
translation: You hear people say that someone touched their food without delay, sneezed, and alas, their life departed. Even after hearing this, you feel no shame.
commentary: Death comes in the middle of the most ordinary moment. Someone sits down to a meal, sneezes, and is gone. Hearing how fragile we are should make anyone ashamed of wasting limited time on petty distractions.

translit: uṇṭār paṭuttār uṟaṅkiṉār pēruṟakkam koṇṭār eṉakkēṭṭum kūcilaiyē - vaṇtārār
translation: You hear people say that someone unhesitatingly ate, lay down, and fell asleep, only to enter the great sleep of death. Even after hearing this, you do not shrink in fear.
commentary: Death can arrive silently, without anyone noticing. People lie down expecting to wake and slip into the final sleep instead. That quiet, constant nearness of death should make a person shudder and seek spiritual truth without delay.

translit: nēṟṟu maṇampurintār nīṟāṉār iṉṟeṉṟu cāṟṟuvatu kēṭṭum taṇantilaiyē - vīṟṟuṟutēr
translation: You hear people announce that those wearing rich garlands married just yesterday, and today they have turned to ash. Even after hearing this, you have not detached yourself from worldly desires.
commentary: Worldly joy is no shield against sudden death. A person can celebrate a wedding one day and be cremated the next. Knowing this should loosen our desperate grip on passing worldly desires.

translit: ūrntār teruvil ulāppōntār vāṉulakam cērntār eṉakkēṭṭum tērntilaiyē - cērntāṅku
translation: You hear people say someone walked in the street, went for a stroll, and then reached the heavenly world, yet you still lack clarity.
commentary: Someone takes an ordinary walk down the street and is gone the next moment. We hear of such deaths all the time, and still we live as if our days had no end, never seeking clarity.

translit: eṉṉē iruntār irumiṉār īṇṭiṟantār aṉṉē eṉakkēṭṭum āyntilaiyē - koṉṉē
translation: You hear the shocked cry that they were just here, they coughed, and they died right on the spot. Even hearing this, you have not reflected on the truth.
commentary: Life hangs by the thinnest thread. A man sits at ease, gives one cough, and dies where he sits. People pass the shocked news along and never stop to think about their own death.

translit: maruvum karuppaikkuḷ vāyntē mutirāk karuvum pitirntutirak kaṇṭāy - karuvoṉ
translation: You have seen an unripened fetus form within the womb, only to dissolve and fall away.
commentary: The fragility starts before birth. A child conceived in the womb can dissolve and be lost before it ever takes shape, and people have seen this with their own eyes.

translit: ṟoṭutiṅkaḷ aiyaintil ovvoṉṟil antō keṭukiṉṟa teṉṟatuvum kēṭṭāy - paṭumin
translation: Alas, you have also heard of the unborn child perishing in the first month, the tenth month, or any month in between.
commentary: Death does not wait for old age. The unborn can perish in the first month, the last, or any month between.

translit: nilaimuṟṟa yōṉi nerukkil uyirpōyp palaṉaṟṟu vīḻntatuvum pārttāy - palaṉuṟṟē
translation: You have seen a fully developed infant lose its life in the crushing pressure of the birth canal and fall lifeless.
commentary: A fully formed infant can survive the whole pregnancy and still die in the pressure of being born. When life is threatened at every stage like this, putting off the search for truth is a sad mistake.

translit: kāveṉṟu vīḻntak kaṇamē piṇamākak kōveṉ ṟaḻuvār kuṟittilaiyō - nōviṉṟip
translation: Have you not noted those who weep loudly as someone falls crying "Save me!" and becomes a corpse that very moment?
commentary: Death can come with no warning at all. A person cries out for help and is a corpse in that same moment. Vallalar wants us to drop the dangerous assumption that there is always more time.

translit: pālaṉeṉṟē aṉṉaimulaip pālaruntum kālaiyilē kālaṉ uyirkuṭikkak kaṇṭilaiyō - mēluvantu
translation: Have you not seen the god of death drinking the life of an infant right when it effortlessly drinks milk from its mother's breast?
commentary: Not even infants are safe. The god of death (Kālan) can take a baby while it nurses peacefully at its mother's breast. Death does not wait for anyone to grow old.

translit: peṟṟār makiḻveytap pēciviḷai yāṭuṅkāl aṟṟāvi pōva taṟintilaiyō - kaṟṟāyap
translation: Have you not known the life breath severing and departing right when a child speaks and plays to the great delight of its parents?
commentary: Death can snatch away young children just as they begin to talk and play. Parents watch their toddlers with immense joy, unaware that the child's life breath can slip away without warning. This continues the warning that youth offers no protection against the end of life.

translit: paḷḷiyiṭuṅ kālavaṉaip pāra namaṉvāyil aḷḷiyiṭun tīmai aṟintilaiyō - paḷḷiviṭum
translation: Have you not known the evil of a child being scooped up and thrown into the mouth of the god of death right when they enroll him in school to learn?
commentary: Now the child reaches school age. On the very day the parents send him to learn, the god of death (Naman) may scoop him up. Every careful plan for his future comes to nothing when death strikes.

translit: kāḷaip paruvamatil kaṇṭār iraṅkiṭa-av āḷaic camaṉkoḷva tāyntilaiyō - vēḷaimaṇa
translation: Have you not examined how the god of death seizes a young man right in his prime after leaving school, leaving onlookers in pity?
commentary: The young man in his prime is no safer. The god of death (Camaṉ) can seize him just after his schooling, and onlookers can only pity the loss. Vallalar walks us through each stage of youth to make one thing plain: begin spiritual practice now, because no one is promised tomorrow.

translit: māppiḷḷai āki maṇamuṭikkum aṉṟavaṉē cāppiḷḷai yātaleṇṇic cārntilaiyē - mēṟpiḷḷai
translation: Did you not consider that the very man who becomes a bridegroom and marries can become a corpse on that same day? You did not think of this and seek the truth.
commentary: A man can marry and die on his wedding day. Since death can arrive at any moment, there is no time to delay seeking the truth.

translit: māṭaiyērp peṇṭuṭaṉil vāḻuṅkāl paṟpalartām pāṭaimēl cērtaliṉaip pārttilaiyō - vīṭaliḵ
translation: While living with a beautiful woman adorned with gold, did you not see so many people being placed upon the funeral bier?
commentary: Family life and its pleasures absorb us easily. We watch others carried off on the bier and still ignore our own death.

translit: tikkaṇamō mēlvan tiṭuṅkaṇamō aṉṟimaṟṟai ekkaṇamō eṉṟārnī eṇṇilaiyē - tokkuṟutōl
translation: Will death come this moment, the next moment, or some other moment? The wise asked this, yet you did not think about it.
commentary: No one knows the hour. The wise have always warned that death could come this second or the next, yet most people never take it to heart.

translit: kūṭeṉkō ivvuṭampaik kōḷviṉainīr ōṭṭilviṭṭa ēṭeṉkō nīrmēl eḻutteṉkō - kāṭeṉkō
translation: Should I call this body covered in skin a cage? Should I call it a palm leaf set adrift in the running stream of grasping karma? Should I call it writing on water? Should I call it a forest?
commentary: The body is fragile and passing, and Vallalar piles up images for it. A palm leaf swept along the river of past actions (karma), writing on water: both vanish easily, and the leaf is tossed wherever the current takes it.

translit: pāḻeṉkō oṉpatuvāyp pāvaiyeṉkō vaṉpiṟavi ēḻeṉkō kaṉmamataṟ kīṭeṉkō - tāḻmaṇṇiṉ
translation: Should I call it a wasteland? Should I call it a puppet with nine openings? Should I call it the harsh sevenfold cycle of birth? Should I call it the vessel for karma?
commentary: The body has nine openings, like a fragile puppet worked by unseen strings. Far from a permanent home, it is a temporary vessel where the soul reaps its past actions through the long cycle of births.

translit: pāṇṭameṉkō veñcarakkup paiyeṉkō pāḻṅkaruma kāṇṭameṉkō āṇavattiṉ kaṭṭeṉkō - kōṇtakaiyār
translation: Shall I call it a clay vessel, a bag of foul wares, a chapter of ruined karma, or a knot of ego? The crooked people's...
commentary: Vallalar holds up the body and tries out names for it: a fragile clay pot, a sack of impurities, the fruit of ruined past deeds, a trap built by the ego (āṇavam). Nothing on that list is permanent or pure. He wants the mind to sit with that.

translit: meyyeṉkō māya viḷaiveṉkō miṉṉeṉkō poyyeṉkō māyap poṭiyeṉkō - meyyeṉṟa
translation: ...body, shall I call it? Shall I call it a product of illusion, a flash of lightning, a lie, or illusory dust? Calling it true...
commentary: Now the body is a flash of lightning, a heap of illusory dust. The Tamil word mey means both 'truth' and 'body', and Vallalar plays on it. We call the body true when it is about the least lasting thing we have.

translit: maṅkalattai maṅkalattāl vāñcit taṉarulakar aṅkavaṟṟai eṇṇā talaintaṉaiyē - taṅkulakil
translation: ...auspiciousness, worldly people desire it through auspicious means. You wandered without giving those things a single thought. In this enduring world...
commentary: Most people treat bodily life as something to celebrate and spend their days chasing what the world calls auspicious. Vallalar scolds his own mind for wandering after the same illusions without once turning toward what is real.

translit: maṟṟitaṉai ōmpi vaḷarkka uḻaṉṟaṉainī kaṟṟataṉai eṅkē kaviḻttaṉaiyē - aṟṟavarai
translation: ...you toiled to protect and nurture this body. Where did you overturn everything you learned? For those who have died...
commentary: All that toil, he tells his mind, just to keep this temporary shell fed and comfortable. Somewhere along the way it threw out the spiritual wisdom it once learned.

translit: ikkaṭ ṭaviḻttiṅ kerimūṭ ṭeṉakkēṭṭum mukkaṭṭum tēṭa muyaṉṟaṉaiyē - ikkaṭṭu
translation: ...even when hearing the command, "Untie this bundle and light the fire here," you still strove to seek the three attachments. This bundle...
commentary: At a funeral someone calls out to untie the body and light the pyre. The mind hears it and still learns nothing about its own death. It goes straight back to the three old attachments: desire for land, wealth and sensual pleasure.

translit: maṇpaṭṭu ventī marampaṭ ṭiṭakkaṇṭum veṇpaṭ ṭuṭukka viraintaṉaiyē - paṇpa ṭṭa
translation: Even after seeing bodies buried in the earth or burned by fierce fire on a wooden pyre, you hasten to wear fine white silk.
commentary: Bodies go into the earth or onto the wooden pyre in front of us, and we still hurry to dress our own in fine white silk. Vallalar wants us to remember where this body is headed before we fuss over decorating it.

translit: aiyā araināṇ aviḻumeṉak kēṭṭuniṉṟum meyyā paraṇattiṉ mēviṉaiyē - eyyāmal
translation: O sir, even after hearing that your waist-thread will be untied at death, you still covet ornaments for this physical body.
commentary: In Indian tradition even the simple string worn around the waist is untied and removed before a body is cremated. If we cannot take even that thread with us, spending a life chasing gold and jewels makes no sense.

translit: kātiṟ kaṭukkaṉ kaḻaṟṟumeṉak kēṭṭuniṉṟum ētiṟ paṇiyiṉiṭat teytiṉaiyē - tātiṟkut
translation: Even after hearing that your earrings will be stripped from your ears at death, you still seek out other jewelry.
commentary: Before the final rites, relatives take the jewelry off the dead. We know ours will be stripped away too. Still we keep wanting more ornaments and hoarding them.

translit: tuṟkanta mākac cuṭuṅkāl mukarntiruntum naṟkantat tiṉpāl naṭantaṉaiyē - puṟkeṉṟa
translation: Even after smelling the foul stench when a body is burned on the pyre, you still chase after sweet perfumes.
commentary: Anyone who has stood at a cremation ground knows the smell of burning flesh. Having smelled it, we still spend our lives masking our own coming decay with sweet perfumes. That is plain foolishness.

translit: vaṉcuvaittī nāṟṟa malamāy varalkaṇṭum iṉcuvaippāl eyti yiruntaṉaiyē - muṉcuvaittup
translation: Even after seeing that richly flavored food ultimately turns into foul-smelling excrement, you remain obsessed with sweet tastes.
commentary: The finest meal ends as foul waste. Every pleasure of the body decays the same way, so a craving for rich flavors should not be allowed to run our lives.

translit: pāṟuṇṭa kāṭṭil palarven tiṭakkaṇṭum cōṟuṇ ṭirukkat tuṇintaṉaiyē - māṟuṇṭu
translation: Even seeing many people burn in the cremation ground where vultures feed, you dared to sit and eat your meal.
commentary: Vultures feed at the burning ground, many bodies burn there, and people go home and sit down to eat. Their own fragile lives do not trouble them at all.

translit: kūmpulakam poyyeṉanāṉ kūvukiṉṟēṉ kēṭṭumiku cōmpaluṭaṉ tūkkan toṭarntaṉaiyē - āmpalaṉōr
translation: I cry out aloud that this perishing world is false. Hearing this, you continued sleeping with great laziness.
commentary: Vallalar shouts it aloud: this perishing world is false. People hear the warning and stay comfortably asleep, lazy in their ignorance and worldly attachments.

translit: nalvāḻvai eṇṇi nayantōr nayavāta ilvāḻvai meyyeṉ ṟiruntaṉaiyē - collāvi
translation: You believed this domestic life to be real, a life rejected by those who contemplate and desire the truly good life.
commentary: Those who seek the truly good life see that ordinary household life is temporary and let it go. Most people take this passing arrangement for the whole reality of their existence.

translit: īṉṟōṉ taṉaināḷum eṇṇāmal ivvuṭampai īṉṟōrai īṉṟōreṉ ṟeṇṇiṉaiyē - īṉṟōrkaḷ
translation: Without ever thinking of the One who truly gave birth to you, you considered those who gave birth to this physical body as your parents.
commentary: Our parents gave birth to the body, and that is all. We take them for our true origin and forget God, the real parent who gave birth to the soul.

translit: nontāl uṭaṉiṉṟu nōvār viṉaippakaitāṉ vantāl atunīkka vallārō - vantāṭal
translation: If you suffer, they will stand by you and feel the pain. But when the enmity of karma arrives, are they capable of removing it?
commentary: Family can stand beside us and feel our pain when we suffer. When karma (the accumulated consequences of our past actions) comes due, they are powerless to remove it.

translit: uṟṟaciṟār nammaṭaiyā tōṭṭukiṟpār teṉṟicaivāḻ maṟṟavaṉvan tāltaṭukka vallārō - ciṟṟuṇavai
translation: Your dear children might drive away what comes near you. But if the god of death arrives from the South, do they have the power to stop him?
commentary: Your children can chase off whatever troubles you day to day. When the god of death comes from the South, they are powerless. No worldly attachment keeps you safe from dying.

translit: īṅkeṉṟāl vāṅki yiṭuvār aruḷamutam vāṅkeṉṟāl vāṅkiyiṭa vallārō - tīṅkakaṟṟat
translation: If you ask them for a little food here, they will fetch it and serve you. But if you ask them to fetch the nectar of grace, are they capable of getting it?
commentary: Ask your family for a meal and they will bring it. The soul's real nourishment is the nectar of divine grace, and no relative can fetch that for you.

translit: tūṇṭā maṉaiyātic cuṟṟamelām cuṟṟiyiṭa nīṇṭāy avarnaṉ ṉeṟittuṇaiyō - māṇṭārpiṉ
translation: Surrounded by a wife and relatives who never urge you to dispel evil, you stand tall in pride. Are they true companions on the good path?
commentary: People are proud of a large, supportive family. Relatives who never urge you to leave bad habits behind and seek the good path are not true companions, however many of them stand around you.

translit: kūṭi aḻattuṇaiyāyk kūṭuvār vaṉṉarakil vāṭiyaḻum pōtu varuvārō - nīṭiyanī
translation: After you die, they will gather as companions to weep. But when you wither and cry in cruel hell, will they come to your side?
commentary: When you die, your family will gather and weep loudly. That shared grief does nothing for a soul suffering in the afterlife. The tears of the living cannot reach the dead.

translit: iccīvar taṉtuṇaiyō īṅkivarkaḷ niṉtuṇaiyō cīccī iteṉṉa tiṟaṅkaṇṭāy - iccīvar
translation: Are you a lasting companion to these beings? Are they true companions to you here? Shame, see what sort of state this is!
commentary: Human relationships are temporary and bound to end. Vallalar's "Shame!" is aimed at wasting a human life leaning on bonds that cannot last. The soul has to look past ordinary family ties to find a permanent connection with the divine.

translit: niṉṉaivaittu muṉceṉṟāl nīceyva teṉṉavarmuṉ innilattil nīceṉṟāl eṉceyvar - niṉṉiyalpiṉ
translation: If they leave you behind and depart first, what will you do? If you depart from this world before them, what will they do? Consider your own nature:
commentary: Death separates everyone. If your loved ones go first, you cannot stop them; if you go first, they cannot save you. Facing this shows how little worldly bonds can actually do.

translit: ettaṉaitāy ettaṉaipēr ettaṉaiyūr ettaṉaivāḻ vettaṉaiyō tēkam eṭuttaṉaiyē - attaṉaikkum
translation: how many mothers, how many people, how many towns, and how many lives have you known? You have taken countless bodies. For all of those bodies,
commentary: The soul has taken countless bodies before this one. Each birth came with its own mother, family and home. This life is one passing arrangement in an endless chain.

translit: avvav viṭaṅkaṭoṟum avvavarai āṇṭāṇṭiṅ kevvev vitattāl iḻantaṉaiyō - avvitattil
translation: in all those various places, you lost those respective people then and there in so many different ways. In that same manner,
commentary: Every one of those bonds ended in separation. You have already left behind more families than you can count, and lost them in every way there is. The soul has been through this loss over and over.

translit: oṉṟēṉum naṉṟāy uṇarntirutti yēlivarai iṉṟē tuṟattaṟ kicaiyāyō - niṉṟōril
translation: if you deeply understood even one of these truths, would you not agree to renounce these current attachments this very day? Among those standing here,
commentary: Take in the scale of those past separations and your present attachments look different. Once you truly see that you will lose this family just as you lost all the others, the clinging stops, and it stops today. Real clarity ends these worldly illusions at once.

translit: tāyār maṉaiyār taṉayarār tammavarār nīyār itaṉai niṉaintilaiyē - cēyēkil
translation: who is the mother? Who is the wife? Who are the children? Who are the relatives? Who are you? You have not reflected on this. If you go far away,
commentary: Mother, wife, child, relative: in the light of spiritual truth these are temporary roles. Vallalar asks who you really are beneath those labels. People suffer because they never reflect on their true nature and take passing bodily ties for their whole identity.

translit: ēṅkuvarē eṉṟāy iyamaṉvariṉ niṉṉuyirai vāṅkimuṭi yiṭṭakattil vaippārō - nīṅkiyivaṇ
translation: You say they will grieve. When death comes and takes your life, will they tie it in a knot and keep it safely in the house?
commentary: The fear of making family members sad often keeps people tied to worldly life. The poem points out that family grief is powerless against death. No amount of human sorrow can keep a soul safe in the house once its time has come.

translit: uṉtantai taṉṟaṉakkiṅ kōrtantai nāṭuvaṉī eṉtantai eṉṟuraippa tevvāṟē - ceṉṟupiṉṉiṉ
translation: Your father himself seeks a father of his own. How can you call him your father?
commentary: Your father is himself a searching soul who came from someone else, looking for a father of his own. Earthly parentage is a temporary arrangement. The only true parent is the divine, and worldly titles of ownership and lineage are an illusion.

translit: taṉmaṉaiyāḷ maṟṟoruvaṉ taṉmaṉaiyāḷ āvaḷeṉil eṉmaṉaiyāḷ eṉpatunī evvaṇamē - naṉmaipeṟum
translation: If a man's wife can become the wife of another man, how can you claim her as your wife?
commentary: Claiming ownership of another person is false. A spouse is an independent soul whose worldly roles change with time and circumstance. Earthly marriage is temporary and cannot define who a soul really is.

translit: naṭpamainta naṉṉeṟinī nāṭā vakaitaṭukkum uṭpakaivar eṉṟivarai ōrntilaiyē - naṭpuṭaiyāy
translation: Have you not realized these people are inner enemies who stop you from seeking the good path of true fellowship?
commentary: Attachment to family often passes itself off as love. Bonds that shut you inside a small, closed circle are hidden enemies. They keep the soul from walking the path of true, universal fellowship with all living beings.

translit: emmāṉ paṭaitta-uyir ittaṉaikkuṭ cilluyirpāl immāl aṭaintatunī eṉṉiṉaintō - vammāṟil
translation: Among all the countless souls created by our Lord, what were you thinking when you developed such deep delusion over just a few?
commentary: God created countless souls. Keeping all your love and loyalty for a handful of relatives while ignoring the rest of creation is deep delusion. Spiritual life means replacing that narrow attachment with Jeevakarunyam (compassion for all living beings) and taking every soul as kin.

translit: empanta mēniṉakkiṅ killaiyeṉṟāl maṟṟaiyavar tampantam evvāṟu taṅkiyatē - campantar
translation: If you have no bond with me here, how did the bond of others take hold of you?
commentary: Vallalar is talking to his own mind. It keeps no faithful bond with his true inner self, yet it gets tangled in worldly relationships with no trouble at all.

translit: aṟṟavaruk kaṟṟacivaṉāmeṉumap poṉmoḻiyai maṟṟaimoḻi pōṉṟu maṟantaṉaiyē - ciṟṟuyirkkuk
translation: You forgot the golden words of Sambandar that Siva belongs to those who have renounced all attachments, treating them just like any other words you have forgotten.
commentary: Sambandar, the revered Tamil poet-saint, taught that God (Siva) is found only by those who let go of worldly desires. The mind has ignored this wisdom of the saints. Vallalar scolds it for tossing that truth aside like ordinary chatter.

translit: kaṟpaṉaiyil kāyppuḷatāyk kāṭṭum pirapañcak kaṟpaṉaiyai meyyeṉṟu kaṇṭaṉaiyē - paṟpalavām
translation: You saw as truth the illusion of the universe, which displays an imaginary harvest to the petty soul.
commentary: The mind takes the physical world as real and permanent. To shallow people the universe promises a rich harvest of pleasures, and that harvest is imaginary.

translit: tūriyattiltōṉṟolipōl tōṉṟik keṭumāyā kāriyattai meyyeṉanī kaṇṭaṉaiyē - cīriyaṟṟum
translation: You saw as truth the effects of maya, which appear and perish like the sound arising from many drums.
commentary: The material world is a passing illusion called maya. A drumbeat booms and then fades into silence, and worldly experience goes the same way. The mind is foolish to take it for lasting reality.

translit: āṭakattil pittaḷaiyai ālit tiṭuṅkapaṭa nāṭakattai meyyeṉṟu nampiṉaiyē - nīṭakattil
translation: You believed as truth the deceitful drama that joyfully passes off brass as excellent gold.
commentary: Worldly life is a con. It passes off cheap brass as precious gold and seems to enjoy doing it. The mind falls for the trick, prizing worthless physical pursuits over real spiritual wealth.

translit: kāyavittai yālak kaṭavuḷ iyaṟṟuminta māyavittai meyyeṉanī vāḻntaṉaiyē - vāyavittai
translation: You lived your life believing that this magic of illusion, which God performs by creating physical bodies, is real.
commentary: God shapes bodies and the material world as a kind of magic. We mistake them for the final truth, and they do not last.

translit: ippaṭaka māyai yiruḷtamamē eṉṉumoru muppaṭakat tuḷḷē muyaṅkiṉaiyē - oppiṟaivaṉ
translation: Ignorance, this expansive Maya, and dark ego, you wallowed helplessly within these three covering veils.
commentary: Three forces trap the soul: ignorance, Maya (the illusion of the material world), and a dark sense of ego. These thick veils keep us wandering helplessly in the dark, cut off from spiritual light.

translit: āṉavoḷi yiṟparaiyām ātapatti ṉāltōṉṟum kāṉaliṉai nīrāyk kaḷittaṉaiyē - āṉakiri
translation: In the light of the incomparable Lord, the sunshine of the Supreme Energy creates a mirage. You delighted in this mirage, believing it to be real water.
commentary: The material world is a mirage thrown up by the intense light of the Divine. Chasing worldly pleasures and achievements, we are the thirsty traveler who takes a trick of the light for water.

translit: yācatti yeṉṟiṭumōr ammaiviḷai yāṭṭeṉumip pācatti ṉuḷḷē paṭarntaṉaiyē - nēcattiṉ
translation: You became entirely entangled in this worldly bondage, which is nothing but the playful act of the Mother known as Kriya Sakti.
commentary: Kriya Sakti is the active, creative energy of the Divine, and worldly life with all its attachments is her play. We suffer because we take the game seriously and let it bind us.

translit: poyyoṉṟuṇ meyyiṟ pukumpāla līlaitaṉai meyyeṉṟu vīṇil virintaṉaiyē - poyyeṉṟu
translation: You wasted your life vainly believing this child's play to be true, a state where the falsehood of worldly attachment mingles with truth.
commentary: Earthly life mixes passing falsehood with eternal truth. To treat this childlike game of attachments as final reality is a tragic waste of a human life. The wise look past the game to the truth behind it.

translit: mīṭṭuniṉṟa līlā viṉōta meṉuṅkataiyaik kēṭṭuniṉṟum antō kiḷarntaṉaiyē - īṭṭiniṉṟa
translation: Even after hearing the story of the wondrous divine play of redemption, alas, you swell with pride.
commentary: The mind is stubborn. People hear how divine grace redeems souls, and still they stay swollen with ego and pride instead of softening into humility.

translit: kālattai vīṇil kaḻikkum paṭimēka cālattai meyyāyt tarukkiṉaiyē - cālattil
translation: You waste your accumulated time in vain. You arrogantly treat the passing illusion of clouds as the truth.
commentary: A human life is a rare, hard-won chance. We spend its allotted time clinging to attachments that shift like clouds, and we treat them as permanent truth.

translit: kaṇmaiyakaṉ ṟōṅkumanta kārattil cemmāppuṟ ṟuṇmaiyoṉṟuṅ kāṇā tuḻaṉṟaṉaiyē - vaṇmaiyilāy
translation: In this illusion, your vision is lost. You swell with pride in the growing darkness. You wander without seeing a single truth. O destitute one!
commentary: Blinded by worldly illusion, the mind can no longer see clearly. Such a person is spiritually bankrupt, wandering proudly through total ignorance without grasping one real truth.

translit: iṅku niṉaipperiyōr eṉṉiṉaippār ēmāppil kaṅku liṉaippakalāyk kaṇṭaṉaiyē - taṅkuṟumit
translation: What will the great ones here think of you? In your delusion, you see the night as the day.
commentary: The wise can only pity such foolishness. Deep delusion makes the mind take darkness for light, so it assumes its false way of living is right.

translit: tēkāti poyyeṉavē tērntār uraikkavumnī mōkātik kuḷḷē muyalkiṉṟāy - ōkōnum
translation: Even when the realized ones declare that this abiding body and all else are false, you still strive within delusion and lust. Oho!
commentary: Realized teachers keep warning that the body and all its pleasures will not last. The mind hears this plain truth and goes right on chasing its passing desires.

translit: kōmuṭikkaṇ tīppaṟṟik koṇṭateṉṟāl maṟṟataṟkup pūmuṭikkat tēṭukiṉṟōr pōṉṟaṉaiyē - māmuṭikkum
translation: If told that the cow's head has caught fire, you are like those who search for flowers to adorn it.
commentary: A cow's head is on fire, and someone goes looking for flowers to decorate it. That is how Vallalar sees us chasing worldly status while our mortal time burns away. The danger is urgent, and we fuss over trivial pleasures.

translit: vāḻvunilai yaṉṟimaippil māṟukiṉṟa teṉṟuraittum vīḻvukoṭuvāḷā viḻukiṉṟāy - tāḻvuṟanum
translation: Even when told that this highly exalted worldly life is impermanent and vanishes in the blink of an eye, you still fall down ruinously in vain.
commentary: Life vanishes in a blink, and we know it. Still we ruin ourselves clinging to wealth and status. Vallalar calls that fall vain, a waste of the little time we have on earth.

translit: viṇṭuṟuṅkai vīṭaṉalāl vēkiṉṟa teṉṉavuṭpōy uṇṭuṟaṅku kiṉṟōrai ottaṉaiyē - toṇṭulakaṅ
translation: When told that your house is burning down in flames and falling to ruin, you are like those who go inside to eat and sleep.
commentary: The burning house is our own decaying body. Vallalar pictures people walking into it to eat and sleep. That is plain denial, because the need for spiritual awakening is urgent and we lose ourselves in daily comforts instead.

translit: kāṉamuyaṟ kompāyk kaḻikiṉṟa teṉkiṉṟēṉ nīnayamuṟ ṟantō nikaḻkiṉṟāy - āṉanummūr
translation: I tell you that this servile world is passing away into nothingness like the non-existent horn of a forest hare, yet alas, you live delightfully attached to it.
commentary: The horn of a forest hare is a traditional phrase for something that simply does not exist. Vallalar says the material world is just as unreal and just as fleeting. His "alas" is real grief, since people still live delighted and attached to it instead of seeking eternal truth.

translit: veḷḷatti ṉālmuḻuki viṭṭateṉṟāl ceṉṟukaṭai koḷḷat tiripavarpōl kūṭiṉaiyē - koḷḷaviṅku
translation: When told that your very town is submerged in a flood, you gather like those who wander out to shop.
commentary: Picture someone whose town is under floodwater strolling out to shop. Vallalar says this is how we behave. Death surrounds us, and we carry on with petty errands and daily business.

translit: kaṇṭaṉavel lāmnilaiyāk kaitavameṉ kiṉṟēṉnī koṇṭavaimuṟ cērak kuṟikkiṉṟāy - uṇṭaḻikka
translation: I tell you that everything seen is a fleeting illusion. You aim to gather together the things you have acquired. To consume and destroy,
commentary: Everything visible will fade, Vallalar warns. The listener keeps hoarding anyway. That is how deeply things that will not last can hold us.

translit: ūḻiveḷḷam vantateṉṟāl uṇpataṟkum āṭutaṟkum ūḻinaṉṉīrōveṉpār ottaṉaiyē - ēḻiyaṟṟum
translation: when I warn that the cosmic deluge has come, you are like those who ask if the floodwater is good for drinking and bathing. Causing the sevenfold births,
commentary: Told that the world-ending deluge has come, people ask whether the water is good for drinking and bathing. Habit has that strong a grip. They miss the danger facing their own soul entirely.

translit: taṟpuvaṉam pōkam taṉukaraṇam eṉkiṉṟa coṟpaṉattil antō tuvaṉṟiṉaiyē - paṟpakalum
translation: alas, you are immersed in the dream of bodies, instruments, worlds, and experiences. Day after day,
commentary: Bodies, mental instruments, worlds, and experiences (taṉu, karaṇam, puvaṉam, pōkam) are the classical categories of physical existence. Vallalar calls absorption in them a dream. We stay asleep in it instead of waking to spiritual reality.

translit: uṇṭaṉavē uṇkiṉṟāy ōrntaṉavē ōrkiṉṟāy kaṇṭaṉavē kaṇṭu kaḷikkiṉṟāy - koṇṭaṉavē
translation: you eat what you have already eaten. You ponder what you have already pondered. You see what you have already seen and rejoice. Holding onto what you have already grasped,
commentary: Eat the same, think the same, see the same, and rejoice each time as if it were new. Worldly life runs on this repetition. Nothing in the cycle feeds the spirit; it only replays old habits.

translit: koṇṭiyaṅku kiṉṟāy kuṟittaṉavē piṟkuṟittup paṇṭaṟiyār pōlap paṭarkiṉṟāy - paṇṭaṟintu
translation: you function. You aim again at what you have already targeted. You wander like those who know nothing of the past. Knowing the past,
commentary: Without spiritual awareness we act as if our own history taught us nothing. We aim again at the same empty goals, repeat the same mistakes, and wander.

translit: collāṭi niṉṟaṉavē colkiṉṟāy maṟṟitaṉai nallōrkaḷ kaṇṭāl nakaiyārō - cellāṉa
translation: You keep repeating the very words already spoken. If good people see this, will they not laugh?
commentary: Repeating words heard from others is the mind on autopilot. With no inner experience behind them, those words look foolish to the genuinely wise, and Vallalar says they will laugh.

translit: kālampōl iṅkunikaḻ kālamumkāṇ kiṉṟiyetir kālamaṟṟum attiṟammēṟ kāṇkuvaiyēl - cālavumuṉ
translation: You experience the present time here just like the past. If you view the future and beyond in that same manner,
commentary: Live mechanically and yesterday looks like today, and tomorrow will look the same. The mind drags old habits into the present and projects them forward without end. Nothing grows in that closed loop.

translit: pōtucelā muṉṉamaṉu pūtiyainī nāṭāmal yātupayaṉ eṇṇi iṉaikiṉṟāy - tītuceyum
translation: what benefit do you expect while you suffer, instead of seeking divine experience before your time runs out?
commentary: Life is short and fragile. Vallalar urges us to seek direct divine experience before death arrives. Clinging to worldly pain in this repetitive cycle gains nothing when realization is possible.

translit: vīṇavattai yellām viḷaikkum tiṟalmūla āṇavatti ṉālē aḻintaṉaiyē - āṇavattil
translation: You are destroyed by the powerful root ego that does evil and produces all these useless states.
commentary: All this wasted time springs from āṇavam (the deep-seated root ego). This primal ignorance traps the soul in empty states of consciousness and wrecks any chance of real spiritual growth.

translit: nīyār eṉa-aṟiyāy niṉṉetiril niṉṟavarai nīyār eṉaviṉavi nīṇṭaṉaiyē - ōyāmal
translation: Trapped in that ego, you do not know who you are. You ask those standing before you, "Who are you?" and prolong this endlessly.
commentary: Gripped by ego, a person has no idea who they are. So they look outward and demand of others, "Who are you?" All that questioning and judging only stretches the ignorance further.

translit: ūṉiṉṟa oṉṟiṉ uḷavaṟiyāy antōnī nāṉeṉṟu colli nalintaṉaiyē - nāṉeṉṟu
translation: Alas, you do not know the secret of the One dwelling in your flesh. You have suffered by constantly declaring yourself as "I."
commentary: Suffering comes straight from the ego. We keep saying "I," asserting our own importance, and never look at the deeper truth of what we are. The divine dwells inside this very body of flesh, and Vallalar says we miss that secret because we are trapped in self-interest.

translit: collutiyō collāyō tuvvāmai peṟṟorunī allaluṟuṅ kālat taṟaikaṇṭāy - allavelām
translation: Will you still say "I" or will you not? Try saying it and see what happens when you are helpless and suffering in times of sorrow.
commentary: Pride looks solid until real suffering arrives. Vallalar dares us to say "I" in a moment of total helplessness and see whether it holds. In deep sorrow the ego has no comfort to give and no salvation to offer.

translit: nī-iṅkē nāṉaṅkē niṟkanaṭu vēkutittāl nī-eṅkē nāṉeṅkē niṉṟaṟikāṇ - nī-iṅku
translation: Leaving all else aside, if you stand here and I stand there, and something suddenly leaps between us, where are you and where am I? Stand still and realize this.
commentary: Our sense of being separate individuals is an illusion. Vallalar pictures two people standing apart when something suddenly leaps between them, and in that shock the boundary dividing them dissolves. Stand still, he says, and see how fast "you" and "I" vanish when reality breaks in.

translit: oṉṟeṭukkac ceṉṟumaṟṟai oṉṟeṭukkak kāṇkiṉṟēṉ iṉṟaṭutta nī-eṅ kiruntaṉaiyē - maṉṟaṭutta
translation: I see you going to pick up one thing, only to pick up another instead. Where were you, who have arrived here today?
commentary: We set out to pick up one thing and come back holding another. That is how little control we have over our own actions, pushed by distraction instead of clear purpose. If the mind scatters this easily, Vallalar asks, where is the true self that claims to be in charge?

translit: tāḷā tarittēniṉ ṟaṉṉaimaṟan tuyyātu vāḷā matattiṉ malikiṉṟāy - kēḷāyic
translation: Without taking refuge in the feet of the Lord of the Hall, forgetting yourself and finding salvation, you needlessly swell with arrogance.
commentary: Liberation asks us to let the ego go completely. The only real safety is surrender at the feet of the Lord of the Hall. Instead, Vallalar warns, people waste their lives inflating a pride that is empty.

translit: cārpiloṉṟu viṭṭoḻintāl cālamakiḻ kiṟpēṉāṉ cōrpukoṇṭu nītāṉ tuyarkiṉṟāy - cārpuperun
translation: If I abandon even a single attachment, I rejoice greatly. You, however, grow weary and suffer sorrow.
commentary: Vallalar is talking to his own restless mind. Each time he lets go of a worldly attachment, his soul feels deep joy. The mind feels only loss and sorrow.

translit: tūveṉṟu nāṉivaṇañ cummā iruntālum vāveṉ ṟeṉaiyum valikkiṉṟāy - ōvuṉṟaṉ
translation: Even if I reject great attachments with disgust and remain perfectly still here, you forcefully drag me along and command me to come.
commentary: The soul longs to sit in detached stillness. The mind will not let him rest and keeps dragging him back into worldly thoughts and actions.

translit: cūḻcciyaṟi yēṉnī cuḻalkiṉṟa pōtellām cūḻcciyilē nāṉum cuḻalkiṉṟēṉ - nīṭciyilnī
translation: I do not understand your schemes. Whenever you spin around, I too am caught and spin within your schemes.
commentary: The mind is all restless energy and endless plotting. Vallalar confesses he is helpless against it. Whenever it starts spinning, he is dragged into the same dizzy motion.

translit: kālacaittāl yāṉum kaṭitil talaiyacaippēṉ mālacaitta niṉpuṇarppiṉ vāṟetuvō - vālumaṇṭak
translation: If you stretch out and merely move your leg, I quickly nod my head in submission. What is the nature of this union with you that stirs up such delusion?
commentary: Vallalar laments how completely his own mind has enslaved him. It barely moves and he obeys at once, trapped in a union that brings nothing but confusion.

translit: kūvattil yāṉōr kuṭanī kayiṟṟōṭum ēvalko ḷumēḻai eṉkēṉō - pāvattil
translation: In the well of this universe, I am but a water pot. Am I to call myself a poor wretch commanded by you and your rope?
commentary: The physical universe is a deep well, and the soul is a water pot. The mind is the rope tied to it, hauling Vallalar up and down at its own command.

translit: cuṟṟuṇṭa nīkaṭalil tōṉṟucuḻi yāka-atil eṟṟuṇṭa nāṉtiraṇam eṉkēṉō - paṟṟiṭunī
translation: You are the whirlpool forming in the swirling sea. Shall I say I am the blade of grass tossed within it? You who grasp,
commentary: God is the vast swirling ocean, and divine will is its whirlpool. The tiny soul is a blade of grass caught in it, carried along by forces far greater than itself.

translit: caṅkaṟpa māñcūṟai tāṉāka nāṉāṭum aṅkaṭ carukeṉ ṟaṟaikēṉō - poṅkuṟṟa
translation: become the whirlwind of intention. Shall I declare I am the dry leaf dancing there? Swelling,
commentary: Divine will is a fierce whirlwind. The soul is a dry leaf with no weight of its own, moving only where the wind of God's intention carries it.

translit: cēlaivirā yōrtaṟiyil celkuḻainī piṉtoṭarum nūliḻaināṉ eṉṟu nuvalkēṉō - māliṭunī
translation: you are the shuttle moving across a loom to weave a cloth. Shall I say I am the thread of yarn trailing behind? You who cause delusion,
commentary: God is the shuttle flying across the loom, weaving the fabric of reality. The soul is the thread trailing behind, pulled exactly where the master weaver guides it.

translit: tuḷḷuṟuppiṉ maṭpakaiñaṉ cuṟṟāḻi yākavatiṉ uḷḷuṟuppē nāṉeṉ ṟuraikkēṉō - eḷḷuṟunī
translation: are the spinning wheel of the potter with its leaping parts. Shall I state that I am the inner form shaped upon it? You who permeate,
commentary: Now the creator is a potter's spinning wheel. The soul is the clay resting at its center, shaped and molded as the divine wheel turns.

translit: pāḻalaivā ṉēkum paruntāka apparuntiṉ nīḻalaināṉ eṉṟu niṉaikēṉō - nīḻaluṟā
translation: are the eagle flying through the vast empty sky. Shall I consider myself the shadow of that eagle? Shadowless,
commentary: An eagle crosses the empty sky and its shadow glides over the ground below. The soul is that shadow. It has no existence or movement of its own and is forever bound to the bird above.

translit: niṉvacamnāṉ eṉṟulaku nintaimoḻi kiṉṟatalāl eṉvacamnī eṉpa tilaikaṇṭāy - eṉvacamnī
translation: The world blames me, claiming I am under your control. Yet you are never under my control. If you were under my control...
commentary: Vallalar turns to his own unruly mind with a painful irony. The world mocks him as a slave to his wandering thoughts, as if his mind ran his life. Yet, he complains, that same mind never once listens to his will.

translit: āṉāl eḷiyēṉuk kākāp poruḷuḷavō vāṉāṭar vantu vaṇaṅkārō - āṉāmal
translation: ...would anything remain unattainable for this poor soul? Would the celestial beings not come and bow down to me?
commentary: A quiet, obedient mind holds enormous spiritual power. If only it would obey him, Vallalar tells it, nothing would be out of reach. Even the celestial beings (vānāṭar, the gods of the heavens) would come and bow.

translit: eṇṇutaṟkum pēcutaṟkum eṭṭāp parañcōtik kaṇṇutalum aṅkaik kaṉiyaṉṟō - eṇṇumiṭat
translation: The Lord with the eye on his forehead, the supreme Jothi beyond all thought and speech, would be like a fruit resting within my palm. When I consider this...
commentary: The 'Lord with the eye on his forehead' is Siva, the supreme reality that thought and speech cannot reach. With a perfectly focused mind, Vallalar says, that supreme Jothi (the divine light) would rest in his palm as easily as a fruit. Direct experience of God is what a still mind finally gives.

translit: teṉceyvē ṉōrkaṇamum eṉcolvaḻi nillāmal koṉceyvēṉ eṉṟu kutikkiṉṟāy - vaṉceyyum
translation: ...what shall I do? You refuse to obey my words for even a single moment, and you leap around threatening to cause ruin.
commentary: Instead of helping, the mind rebels. Vallalar cannot get it to stay still for a single second. It keeps leaping about, threatening to wreck all his spiritual effort.

translit: cintōṭum ōrvaṭavait tīyum karattaṭaippar antō uṉaiyār aṭakkuvarē - vantōṭum
translation: Sages can catch and contain the raging submarine fire of the ocean in their hands. Alas, who can ever control you?
commentary: Taming the mind is the hardest task there is. The vaṭavai is a legendary fire said to burn beneath the ocean, and great sages might hold even that raging fire in their bare hands. The restless mind would still defeat them.

translit: kaccōtam eṉṉak katirōṉ taṉaiyeṭuppar accō uṉaiyār aṭakkuvarē - vaiccōṅku
translation: They lift the radiant sun as if it were a glass mirror. Ah, who can control you!
commentary: Those who have attained spiritual realization can pick up the blazing sun as lightly as a small glass mirror. Vallalar's cry comes back anyway: who can control you?

translit: mūvulakum cērttorutam muṉṟāṉai yiṉmuṭivar āvuṉaiyum iṅkār aṭakkuvarē - mēvupala
translation: They gather the firmly established, exalted three worlds and tie them in the hem of their garment. Ah, who here can control even you!
commentary: The universe shrinks to a trinket. Realized beings can gather the three worlds (heaven, earth, and the lower worlds) and tie them in the hem of their garment, so small does the material universe become to one who has reached the infinite reality of grace. Even they cannot hold the mind.

translit: tēcameṉṟum kālameṉṟum tikkeṉṟum paṟpalavām vācameṉṟum avvav vaḻakkeṉṟum - mācuṭaiya
translation: They speak of many fitting lands, times, and directions, of diverse abodes and their respective customs,
commentary: Now Vallalar turns from the freedom of enlightened souls to the limits of ordinary thinking. People carve up life by time, place, direction and local custom. These are human inventions, and they tie awareness to the physical world.

translit: pōkameṉṟum maṟṟaip pulaṉeṉṟum poyakalā yōkameṉṟum paṟpalavām yūkameṉṟum - mēkameṉṟum
translation: of flawed worldly enjoyments and other sensory pursuits, of yogas where falsehood never leaves, of various deductions,
commentary: Sensory pleasures always leave an emptiness behind. Vallalar says plainly that conventional yoga and worldly reasoning remain rooted in falsehood. They are limited pursuits that pull the soul away from direct experience of divine grace.

translit: vāṉeṉṟum munnīr malaiyeṉṟum maṇṇeṉṟum ūṉeṉṟum maṟṟai uṟaveṉṟum - mēlniṉṟa
translation: and of clouds, the sky, the vast sea, mountains, the earth, the flesh, and other remaining worldly bonds.
commentary: People anchor their identity to the elements around them and to their own flesh, and define themselves by family and social bonds. Every one of these ties, to earth, sky or kin, is a temporary attachment that veils the ultimate truth.

translit: cātiyeṉṟum vāḻveṉṟum tāḻveṉṟum ivvulaka nītiyeṉṟum kaṉma neṟiyeṉṟum - ōtariya
translation: People speak of caste, prosperity, degradation, the justice of this world, and the path of karma.
commentary: People consume their attention with social divisions like caste, worries about wealth or poverty, and debates over karma (the law of cause and effect). Vallalar groups all these social and religious structures together as mere human preoccupations.

translit: aṇṭameṉṟum aṇṭat tacaivum acaivumalāp paṇṭameṉṟum colpavelām paṉmukaṅkaḷ - koṇṭirunta
translation: They speak of the hard-to-describe universe, its movement, and the motionless substance. All these spoken things take many forms.
commentary: Philosophers argue endlessly about how the universe moves and what unmoving reality lies behind it. Their theories multiply into countless forms.

translit: uṉniṉaivi ṉuḷḷē utittiṭ ṭulaviniṟpa enniṉaivu koṇṭōmaṟ ṟivvulakar - ennavaiyum
translation: They arise and move about within your thought alone. What do these worldly people think? Looking at every flaw,
commentary: All these cosmic movements and social systems exist entirely within the thought of the divine. Worldly people miss this simple truth.

translit: tantōṉ evaṉō catumukaṉuṇ ṭeṉpārkaḷ antōniṉ ceykai aṟiyārē - antōnāṉ
translation: they ask who created it. They say the four-faced creator exists. Alas, they do not know your actions. Alas!
commentary: When people see flaws in the world, they invent stories about lesser creator gods, like the four-faced Brahma of Hindu mythology. They fail to see that everything is actually guided by the supreme divine alone.

translit: āmeṉṟāl maṟṟataṉai allaveṉpāy allaveṉṟāl āmeṉpāy eṉṉai alaikkiṉṟāy - nāmaṉpāy
translation: If I say yes, you say no to it. If I say no, you say yes. You toss me about. We lovingly...
commentary: If he says yes, the divine says no; if he says no, it says yes. Vallalar describes an intimate and bewildering dance in which every certainty he tries to pin down is overturned. The mind is tossed back and forth until it stops leaning on ordinary logic.

translit: eṉṟum piṟantiṟavā iṉpam aṭaitumeṉṟāl naṉṟeṉ ṟoruppaṭuvāy naṇṇuṅkāl - toṉṟeṉavē
translation: If I ask that we attain the eternal joy free from birth and death, you agree and call it good. Yet when the time comes to reach it, following ancient habit,
commentary: Vallalar talks to his own mind as if to a fickle companion. It readily agrees to seek freedom from birth and death, then slides back into old worldly habits the moment real effort is asked of it.

translit: celkiṟpāy cellāc ciṟunaṭaiyil tīmaiyelām nalkiṟpāy eṉṉēniṉ naṭpuṭaimai - colkiṟpil
translation: you wander down useless petty paths and yield every kind of evil. What a fine friendship you offer! When I speak,
commentary: The mind pulls the seeker into trivial pursuits that only do harm. Vallalar's praise of its "friendship" is bitter irony, showing what a terrible friend the mind is on the spiritual path.

translit: āvatuvum niṉṉāl aḻivatuvumniṉ ṉāleṉayāṉ nōvatuvum kaṇṭayalil nōkkiṉaiyē - tāvumeṉak
translation: saying my rise is in your hands and my ruin is in your hands, you watch me suffer and simply look elsewhere. To me who suffers,
commentary: Whether a seeker rises or falls depends on where the mind is turned. Vallalar laments that his mind ignores this great responsibility and looks away from his inner suffering.

translit: kāṇavalam peṇṇavalam ākum poruḷavalam ūṇavalam uṟṟārō ṭūravalam - pūṇavalam
translation: the things I see are sorrow, women are sorrow, accumulated wealth is sorrow, food is sorrow, relatives and the town are sorrow, and ornaments are sorrow.
commentary: Every ordinary attachment is named and called sorrow. To a soul desperate for the divine, wealth, romance, standing in the town, family and bodily comfort give nothing but grief.

translit: ūṉavalam aṉṟiyumeṉ uṟṟatuṇai yāmnīyum tāṉavalam eṉṟāleṉ cāṟṟuvatē - nāṉivaṇam
translation: The flesh itself is sorrow. Besides all this, if even you, my close companion, are a source of sorrow, what can I say? Here I am,
commentary: Even the body brings pain and limitation. Then comes the despairing turn: if the mind, which should be his closest inner ally, also betrays him and causes misery, Vallalar has no refuge left at all.

translit: iṉpametu kaṇṭēmāl iccaiyelām tuṉpamatil tuṉpam piṟappeṉṟē cōrkiṉṟēṉ - vaṉpuṭaiya
translation: What joy have we found? All desires bring only sorrow. I grow faint, realizing that birth itself is a sorrow.
commentary: Worldly desire brings only pain. Vallalar is worn out by the realization that being born into this world is itself a deep sorrow.

translit: ippiṟavit tuṉpatti ṉumtitiyil tuṉpamatu cepparitām eṉṟē tikaikkiṉṟēṉ - ceppiṟappiṉ
translation: I stand bewildered, realizing that the sorrow of sustaining this harsh birth is even harder to describe than the sorrow of the birth itself.
commentary: Being born hurts, and keeping this life going day after day hurts more. The heavy burden of sustaining the body leaves Vallalar overwhelmed.

translit: ōyāta tuṉpam uraikka uṭampellām vāyāki ṉumpōta māṭṭātēl - ē-ēnām
translation: Even if my entire body became mouths, it would not be enough to speak of this birth's ceaseless sorrow. Alas!
commentary: No human language can hold the suffering of earthly life. Vallalar cries out that a body made entirely of mouths would still fall short of describing it.

translit: ceyvateṉṉō eṉṟu tiyaṅkukiṉṟēṉ ivvaṇamnāṉ naivatellām kaṇṭu naṭantaṉaiyē - kaivarumiv
translation: "What are we to do?" I despair. You saw me wasting away like this, yet you simply walked past.
commentary: Now Vallalar speaks to God directly, and he feels abandoned. The Divine saw the soul wasting away in despair and walked past without offering relief.

translit: illik kuṭamuṭaintāl yātāmeṉ ṟuṉṉuṭaṉyāṉ collit tirintumeṉaic cūḻntilaiyē - valiyamaṉ
translation: "If this leaky pot breaks, what will happen?" Though I wandered and told you this, you did not embrace me.
commentary: The body is a leaky pot, fragile and always draining its life. Afraid of death, Vallalar pleads with God to embrace and save him before the vessel breaks completely.

translit: nāḷaiyō iṉṟō naṭakkiṉṟa nāṭkaḷilev vēḷaiyō tūtu viṭilavarkaḷ - kēḷaiyō
translation: Listen. Whether it is tomorrow, today, or at any moment in the passing days, when they send the messengers,
commentary: Death keeps no schedule. The messengers sent to claim a life may come today, tomorrow, or at any moment.
