translit: nallōm eṉiṉum naṭavār naṭavārnām cellōm eṉiṉumatu cellātē - vallīryām
translation: they will not walk away, even if we say we are good people. Even if we say we will not go, that refusal will not work. O capable ones,
commentary: Being a good person buys no protection when your time is up, and refusing to leave is useless. Death cannot be turned away at the door.

translit: iṉcoliṉōm iṉṟiṅ kiruntuvaru vōmeṉayām eṉcoliṉum accolelām ēlātē - maṉcoluṭait
translation: whatever sweet words we speak, pleading that we will stay here today and come later, none of those words will be accepted.
commentary: People facing the end often try to bargain for a little more time. Sweet talk and pleading for one more day will not delay it.

translit: tāmaraiyōṉ māṉmutalōr tāmaṟaiyā rāyilaṉṟu nāmaṟaivōm eṉṟal naṭavātē - nāmivaṇam
translation: If Brahma possessing the eternal words, Vishnu, and the other gods themselves cannot escape it, saying we will escape on that day will never work. We, here,
commentary: Even the great traditional gods like Brahma the creator and Vishnu the preserver are bound by time and eventual death. If these powerful beings cannot escape their end, ordinary humans certainly cannot hide from it.

translit: annāḷ varumuṉṉar āti aruḷaṭaiyum naṉṉāḷ aṭaitaṟku nāṭutuṅkāṇ - eṉṉāniṉ
translation: before that day comes, let us seek the auspicious day to attain the primal grace!
commentary: The only answer to this ticking clock is to seek divine grace right now. Whatever time is left should go toward reaching the light before the final day arrives.

translit: ṟōtukiṉṟēṉ kēṭṭum uṟārpōṉ ṟulakiyalil pōtukiṉṟāy yātu purikiṟpēṉ - tītunaṉṟō
translation: I speak. Even after hearing me, you wander in worldly ways like a stranger. What can I do? Whether it is bad or good...
commentary: Vallalar's own soul is grieving over how easily we ignore spiritual truth. The mind hears the call of grace and still drifts off like a stranger, lost in ordinary worldly distractions.

translit: ṭēṟṟavaṭi nāḷuṟavām eṉṉaiviṭṭut tāmatamā nēṟṟaiyuṟa vōṭuṟavu nērntaṉaiyē - cāṟṟumanta
translation: ...you abandoned me, your relation from ancient days, and forged a bond with the dark lethargy of yesterday. That lethargy...
commentary: Our bond with the Divine is ancient, as old as time itself. The mind tosses it aside for yesterday's dark habit of spiritual laziness.

translit: tāmatamē ōravittai tāmatamē āvaraṇam tāmatamē mōka camuttiramkāṇ - tāmatameṉ
translation: ...is pure ignorance. Lethargy is a veil. See that lethargy is an ocean of delusion. Alas...
commentary: Lethargy (tāmatam, spiritual darkness or laziness) is where worldly suffering starts. It is plain ignorance (avittai), and it lays a thick veil (āvaraṇam) over our awareness. Sink into that heaviness and you are in an endless ocean of delusion, with no clarity left.

translit: ṟaiyō orunī ataṉōṭu kūṭiṉaiyāl poyyōnām eṉṟu pukaṉṟatuvē - kaiyāmal
translation: ...you alone have united with it. Were the words we spoke a lie? Without hesitating...
commentary: Having known the light, how could the mind take to darkness so easily? Vallalar feels it as betrayal. Every inner vow to seek the truth starts to look like an empty lie.

translit: oṉṉalarpōl kūṭuvā rōṭorunī kūṭuṅkāl eṉṉainiṉai yāyeṉco leṇṇutiyō - paṉṉuṟuniṉ
translation: ...when you unite with those who gather like enemies, you do not think of me. Will you consider my words? Your...
commentary: Worldly habits crowd around the soul like enemies. Once the mind joins them, it forgets its divine origin and stops listening to the voice of grace.

translit: tītellām nāṉāti cēṭarpala rāyppiramaṉ pōtellām colliṭiṉum pōtātē - ātaliṉāl
translation: Even if one took the form of many thousand-headed serpents and spoke for the entire lifespan of Brahma, it would not be enough to recount all your evils. Therefore,
commentary: The mind's faults and deceptions have no end. In Hindu mythology the serpent Adi Sesha has a thousand heads, and the creator god Brahma lives for ages beyond counting. Give someone a thousand mouths and all that time, Vallalar says, and the list of the wandering mind's evils would still be unfinished.

translit: vaikiṉṟēṉ vāḻttāy matittorunī ceyvatellām ceykiṉṟāy ītōr tiṟamaṉṟē - uykiṟpāṉ
translation: I scold you, yet you consider it praise and continue doing whatever you please. This is no great skill. Seeking salvation,
commentary: Stubborn thing. Scold the mind for its bad habits and it hears praise, then goes on doing exactly as it pleases.

translit: vāṭukiṉṟēṉ niṉṉai matittorunāṉ nīmalattai nāṭukiṉṟāy ītōr nalamaṉṟē - kūṭukiṉṟa
translation: I suffer while trusting you alone, yet you constantly seek out impurities. This is no virtue. Gathering
commentary: The soul leans on the mind to reach salvation, and the mind keeps breaking that trust. It chases illusions and impurities instead of grace. The person is left suffering and stuck.

translit: īṇṭōr aṇuvāy iruntanī eṇṭicaipōl nīṇṭāy iḵtōr neṟiyaṉṟē - vēṇṭānī
translation: as a tiny atom here, you have expanded across the eight directions. This is not a proper path. You who are unwanted
commentary: Formless and small as an atom, the mind still spreads its attention across all eight directions, wandering everywhere after worldly distractions. Left uncontrolled, that sprawl ruins the spiritual path.

translit: maṟṟavarpōl aṉṟē maṉaṉēniṉ vaṇpukaḻai muṟṟumivaṇ ārtāṉ moḻivārē - cuṟṟimaṉam
translation: are not like anyone else, oh mind. Who in this world can fully describe your vast fame?
commentary: The praise is sarcasm. In its power to deceive and distract the mind has no equal, and nobody can measure how cunning it is or how hard it is to master.

translit: tāṉaṭaṅkiṉ ellāc cakamum aṭaṅkumoru māṉaṭaṅkoḷ pāta malarvāykkum - vāṉaṭaṅka
translation: If you subdue yourself, all the worlds will be subdued. You will attain the blooming lotus feet that perform the one great dance spanning the heavens.
commentary: Master the ego and you master the world. When the self falls completely quiet, the soul is ready for the grace of the divine, pictured here as the lotus feet of the cosmic dancer.

translit: ellā nalamum itaṉāl eṉamaṟaikaḷ ellām niṉcīrē eṭuttiyampum - ellārkkum
translation: All the Vedas proclaim your glory, declaring that all goodness comes through this state.
commentary: The Vedas, the ancient sacred texts of India, say the same: true goodness flows from this inner quiet. Vallalar reminds his own mind that the highest scriptures praise the very state it is capable of reaching.

translit: mākamaṅkoṇ ṭuṟṟa maṉōlayamē vāṉkatiyeṉ ṟāmakaṅkaḷ niṉcīr aṟaintiṭuṅkāṇ - ākuminta
translation: Behold how the Agamas declare your glory, stating that for everyone, the stillness of mind attained through the great scriptures is the supreme heavenly path.
commentary: The Agamas, the traditional scriptures governing spiritual practice and worship, teach the exact same truth. For them the highest heavenly path is simply manolayam, the mind come to complete stillness and rest.

translit: naṉmai peṟumēṉmai naṇṇiyanī niṉṉuṭaiya taṉmaiviṭal antō caturala-ip - puṉmaiyelām
translation: You have reached this greatness that yields such goodness. Alas, it is not wise to abandon your true nature.
commentary: Real spiritual progress is easy to throw away. Having reached this deep stillness and the greatness it promises, the mind would be foolish to slip back into its old worldly habits.

translit: viṭṭoḻittu nāṉmoḻiyum meyccukattai naṇṇutinī iṭṭiḻaitta accukantāṉ yāteṉṉil - kaṭṭaḻitta
translation: Cast away all this baseness and attain the true bliss I describe. If you ask what this perfectly formed bliss is, it is the state that breaks all bonds.
commentary: True joy asks us to let go of our lowest impulses. The bliss Vallalar describes is lasting freedom, the kind that arrives once every earthly attachment and limitation has been broken.

translit: vēṭam cukameṉṟum meyyuṇarvai yiṉṟiniṉṟa mūṭam cukameṉṟum muṉpalavām - tōṭamcey
translation: Some say an outer guise is happiness. Some say ignorance devoid of true realization is happiness. They claim the many ancient, fault-producing...
commentary: People mistake many false goals for real spiritual happiness. Vallalar opens his list of these errors with two: holy robes worn for show, and the blind ignorance of those who never look for true realization.

translit: pōkam cukameṉṟum pōkam tarumkaruma yōkam cukameṉṟum uṇṭilaiyeṉ - ṟākañcey
translation: ...enjoyments are happiness. Some say the karma yoga that yields such enjoyment is happiness. Arguing over what is and what is not, they claim the resulting bodily...
commentary: Next come worldly pleasures, along with the ritual works and yogic disciplines meant to secure them. Vallalar sets these aside too, and notes how much time people waste quarreling over them.

translit: pōtam cukameṉṟum poṉṟalcukam eṉṟumvintu nātam cukameṉṟum nāmporuḷeṉ - ṟōtalaḵ
translation: ...awareness is happiness. Some say perishing is happiness. Some say the primal light and primal sound are happiness. Asserting that we ourselves are the ultimate reality, they declare that...
commentary: Several major schools teach liberation as total extinction. Others fix on primal sound and light, or declare the individual self to be the ultimate reality. Vallalar counts all of these as false attainments.

translit: toṉṟē cukameṉṟum uṭkaṇ ṭirukkumanta naṉṟē cukameṉṟum nāmpuṟattil - ceṉṟēkaṇ
translation: ...chanting this alone is happiness. Some say the goodness of looking inward and remaining still is happiness. Going outward, some claim that...
commentary: One kind of seeker withdraws from the world to sit in silent meditation. Another goes outward after powers and mastery over nature. Vallalar calls both the inward escape and the outward conquest false versions of happiness.

translit: ṭāṟṟal cukameṉṟum aṉpaṟiyāc cūṉiyamē ēṟṟa cukameṉṟum ivvaṇṇam - ēṟṟapaṭi
translation: ...seeing and mastering things is happiness. Some say the void devoid of love is the acceptable happiness. In this manner, according to their own preferences...
commentary: A spiritual void is unacceptable because it has no love in it. Real realization is never empty. It overflows with compassion, and any path picked by personal preference, without universal love, is a trap.

translit: vellukiṉṟōr pōṉṟu virinīr ulakiṭaiyē collukiṉṟōr collum cukamaṉṟu - collukiṉṟa
translation: It is not the bliss spoken of by those who speak as if they are conquerors in this world of expansive waters.
commentary: Real bliss has nothing to do with the happiness claimed by those who talk as if they had conquered the world. People who boast of their worldly power and achievements do not know what joy is.

translit: vāṉāti tattuvaṅkaḷ māyttāṇ ṭuṟukiṉṟa nāṉāti mūṉṟiloṉṟu nāṭāmal - āṉāmai
translation: Transcending the renowned elements starting with space, prevailing without seeking the triad starting with 'I', and continually
commentary: Finding real bliss means moving past physical reality and the ego. A person must transcend the building blocks of the material world (the tattvas), beginning with space itself, and let go of the ego entirely, forgetting the sense of "I" and its divisions.

translit: eḷḷum pakalum iravumilā ōriṭattil uḷḷum puṟampum orupaṭittāy - vaḷḷaleṉa
translation: dwelling in a unique space without the slightest trace of day or night, remaining perfectly uniform inside and out, like the generous Lord,
commentary: This joy lies outside time, where day and night make no difference. There a person's inner awareness and outer experience become one, reflecting the boundless grace of the Divine.

translit: vāḻum paracivattiṉ vaṉṉiveppam pōlamuṟṟum cūḻum cukamē cukamkaṇṭāy - cūḻvataṉuk
translation: the true bliss is the bliss that completely envelops you, inseparable like the heat of the fire within the eternal Parasiva. Understand this! To attain it,
commentary: Real bliss surrounds and soaks the whole soul, inseparable from the Supreme Divine (Parasiva). Heat cannot be taken out of a flame. This joy cannot be taken out of the divine presence either.

translit: kevvā ṟiruntāl iyalum eṉilamma ivvā ṟiruntāl iyalātāl - cevvāṟṟil
translation: if you ask how one must be, oh friend, know that it is impossible if you remain as you are.
commentary: You cannot reach this state while clinging to your present worldly habits. It asks for a complete change in how you live and think.

translit: paṟṟaṟṟāṉ paṟṟiṉaiyē paṟṟiyiṭal vēṇṭumatu paṟṟaṟṟāl aṉṟip paliyātāl - paṟṟaṟṟal
translation: We must hold fast to the One without attachments. That will not succeed unless we ourselves become detached. The state of detachment...
commentary: To hold fast to the Divine, which has no attachments, we must become free of attachments ourselves. Here begins a chain of steps leading inward. The first link is plain: there is no real connection with God while we cling to the things of the world.

translit: vētaṉaiyāl īṅku viriyum cakappaḻakka vātaṉaipōy nīṅkilaṉṟi vārātāl - vātaṉaiyum
translation: ...will not come unless the latent tendencies of worldly habits, which expand here through suffering, depart and disappear. These latent tendencies...
commentary: Detachment is a deep inner shift. It comes only when we shed the rooted habits and tendencies (vātaṉai) built up through worldly life. These desires keep pulling us outward, and in the end they bring us suffering.

translit: īṉamantō ivvulakam eṉṟaruḷai nāṭukiṉṟa ñāṉamvantāl aṉṟi naliyātāl - ñāṉamatu
translation: ...will not perish unless the wisdom comes that seeks grace, realizing that this world is base. That wisdom...
commentary: Worldly habits fade only when true wisdom (ñāṉam) dawns. That wisdom is a clear recognition that ordinary worldly life cannot satisfy. Once a person really sees this, their attention turns on its own from worldly pursuits toward divine grace.

translit: pōkamuṟṟum poyyeṉavē pōtum aṉittiyavi vēkamuṟṟāl aṉṟi viḷaṅkātāl - ākavaḵ
translation: ...will not become clear unless we attain the discrimination of impermanence, realizing that all worldly enjoyments are entirely false. Therefore, that discrimination...
commentary: Wisdom rests on the ability to tell the real from the passing, called discrimination (vivēkam). It means seeing that every worldly pleasure will end. Until we perceive clearly that such joys cannot sustain us, the wisdom that seeks grace cannot take root.

translit: tuṇṇavantāl pōlumivaṇ uṟṟuvicā rittiṭumōr eṇṇamvantāl aṉṟi icaiyātāl - eṇṇamatu
translation: ...will not be attained unless a thought arises to inquire deeply here, as eagerly as a hungry person coming to eat. And that thought...
commentary: Seeing the world's impermanence starts with one burning thought. A person must feel an urgent need to question and understand their own existence. This hunger for deep inquiry (vicāram) has to be as sharp as a starving person's craving for food.

translit: paṅkamaṭain tāravaiyaip pārātu cātukkaḷ caṅkamaṭain tālaṉṟic cārātāl - iṅkataṉāl
translation: Grace is not attained unless you shun the assembly of the flawed and join the gathering of the virtuous. Therefore, in this world,
commentary: The company we keep directly shapes our spiritual path. Grace comes only when a person leaves the assembly of the flawed and joins the gathering of the virtuous.

translit: vīḻmukatta rākinitam veṇṇī ṟaṇintaṟiyāp pāḻmukattōr tampāl paṭarntuṟaiyēl - pāḻmukattil
translation: do not approach or stay with those dejected people whose ruined faces have never known the daily wearing of white holy ash. On those ruined faces,
commentary: In the Saiva tradition, wearing sacred white ash is a fundamental mark of devotion and purity. Vallalar warns against associating with people who reject this daily practice, describing them as spiritually ruined and deeply dejected.

translit: pēyāṭa uḷḷaṟiyāp pittāṭa niṉṉuṭaṉē vāyāṭu vōrpāl maruvinillēl - nīyāṭip
translation: ghosts and ignorant madness dance. Do not associate with those who merely argue with you. Causing you to waver,
commentary: Endless argument has no place in spiritual life. Vallalar tells the seeker to avoid people who only want to dispute. Their minds, he observes, are clouded by ignorance and madness, and they are not looking for truth at all.

translit: pētit tiṭavum piṟaḻntiṭavum niṉṉuṭaṉē vātit tiṭuvōrpāl vāyntuṟaiyēl - cātittuc
translation: divide, and deviate, they debate with you. Do not remain in their company. Asserting their doubts,
commentary: Constant debate breeds confusion and doubt. People who argue for the sake of arguing split your focus until you wander off the path you chose.

translit: caivameṅkē veṇṇīṟṟiṉ cārpeṅkē meyyāṉa teyvameṅkē eṉpavaraic cērntuṟaiyēl - uyvateṅkē
translation: do not join those who ask where Saivism is, where the refuge of white holy ash is, and where the true God is. Where is salvation for them?
commentary: Cynicism kills spiritual growth. Vallalar says plainly that a seeker must avoid those who mock the Saiva path, the refuge of holy ash, and the existence of the true God. He observes that such skeptics have closed the door to their own salvation.

translit: tīrāc civanintai ceytuciṟu tēvarkaḷai nērāyp pitaṟṟuvarpāl nērntuṟaiyēl - ōrāmal
translation: Do not associate with those who commit endless blasphemy against Siva and prattle constantly about petty gods.
commentary: Vallalar warns the seeker to stay away from people who obsess over minor deities (ciṟu tēvarkaḷ). He considers ignoring the supreme divine reality in favor of these lesser powers to be a grave error.

translit: eḷḷeṉṟum teyvameṉpa tillai ituteḷintu koḷḷeṉṟum tuḷḷukiṉṟōr kūṭṭamuṟēl - naḷḷoṉṟu
translation: Do not join the gathering of those who thoughtlessly jump around claiming there is no God even the size of a sesame seed and demanding you accept this conclusion.
commentary: Then comes the opposite extreme, atheism. Vallalar rejects the company of those who aggressively declare that there is no divine presence in the universe at all. True spiritual life requires recognizing the reality of ArutPerunJothi (the Supreme Grace Light).

translit: nāmeṉṟum nammaiyaṉṟi naṇṇum piramamillai āmeṉṟum colpavarpāl ārntuṟaiyēl - tāmoṉṟa
translation: Do not stay close to those who assert that we are the absolute center and there is no Supreme Reality to attain other than ourselves.
commentary: A quieter arrogance comes next. He advises avoiding those who claim that humans are the absolute center of existence and that there is no Supreme Grace to attain. He sees this belief as a trap that replaces genuine devotion with self-worship.

translit: ellā aṟivum emataṟivē eṉṟuraikkum pollā valakkārar poyukavēl - pullāka
translation: Do not delight in the lies of wicked and arrogant people who claim that all knowledge is exclusively their own knowledge.
commentary: Intellectual pride blocks the way too. Vallalar calls these people wicked and arrogant for believing their own minds hold all possible knowledge, and he tells us to take no pleasure in their lies.

translit: aṟpamē maṟṟavelām āyilaḻiyākkāya kaṟpamē vattuveṉpār kaṇṇaṭaiyēl - ciṟcilavām
translation: Do not seek the presence of those who dismiss everything else as trivial grass and claim the alchemy for an immortal body is the only true reality.
commentary: Some seekers chased secret medicines and alchemy for physical immortality (kāya kaṟpam). While Vallalar teaches that the human form can in the end be transformed into light, he rejects those who view physical longevity as the only goal while treating compassion and devotion as worthless. A deathless body is the result of supreme grace, never a mere chemical trick.

translit: cittikaḷē vattuveṉpōrc cērntuṟaiyēl paṉmāyā cattikaḷē vattuveṉpōr cārpaṭaiyēl - pottiya-ic
translation: Do not live in the company of those who declare that supernatural powers are the supreme reality. Do not seek the support of those who declare that the many powers of illusion are the supreme reality.
commentary: Supernatural powers and the many powers of illusion are not what we are here for. Vallalar warns against keeping company with people who chase these abilities, as such pursuits distract from the supreme reality.

translit: caṉmamē tōṟṟum taramām tiramaṉitta kaṉmamē vattuveṉpōr kaṇṇuṟaiyēl - kaṉmamiku
translation: Do not stay near those who say that this bound birth is the highest state and that impermanent karma is the supreme reality.
commentary: Birth and the round of worldly action (karma) pass away, so they cannot be the supreme reality. Vallalar advises keeping away from people who hold this mindset, as they mistake temporary conditions for the eternal.

translit: mākam katiyeṉpār māṭṭuṟaiyēl palpōka yōkam poruḷeṉpā rūṭuṟaiyēl - ēkamkoḷ
translation: Do not dwell with those engaged in heavy karma who say that the great heaven is the ultimate refuge. Do not mingle with those who say that yoga of manifold enjoyments is the true goal.
commentary: Heavenly rewards and yoga practiced for worldly enjoyment are false goals. Vallalar tells us to steer clear of those who promote them.

translit: maṇṇeṉpār vāṉeṉpār vāymuc cuṭareṉpār peṇṇeṉpār maṟṟavartam pēruraiyēl - maṇṇiṉpāl
translation: Some say the unified reality is earth, some say the sky, some say the three luminaries, and some say the female energy. Do not even speak the names of such people.
commentary: The supreme reality cannot be reduced to physical elements like earth and sky, celestial lights, or female energy. Vallalar instructs us to distance ourselves entirely from people who teach that these limited forms are the ultimate truth.

translit: maṉṉuraiyāc cillōr maranteyvam eṉpārmaṟ ṟeṉṉuraiyār īṇṭavarpāl eytiyiṭēl - maṉnalaṅkaḷ
translation: Speaking foolish words on earth, some say a tree is God, and what else might they not say? Do not approach them here.
commentary: Worshipping ordinary objects like trees as God is foolishness. Vallalar warns against approaching anyone who promotes such confused, limited ideas of the divine.

translit: pūttāl ciṟuvarkaḷum pūcā palameṉpār tēṟṟār civapūcai ceyyārāyp - pūttāvi
translation: Even little children declare that blossoming is the reward of worship. The ignorant do not perform the worship of Siva.
commentary: Blossoming of the soul is the natural fruit of true worship. It is so plain that even little children say it. Still, those without wisdom walk right past it and never turn their hearts to Siva.

translit: vīṟukiṉṟa pūcaiyileṉ vīṇeṉṟu vīṇpāḻvāyk kūṟukiṉṟa pēyarkaḷpāl kūṭiyuṟēl - māṟukiṉṟa
translation: Do not associate with the demons who babble with empty, ruined mouths, saying, "What is the use of this worship where the blossoming soul flourishes? It is a waste."
commentary: Avoid the cynics who mock devotion. Vallalar calls them demons with ruined mouths, because they dismiss the soul's blossoming as a waste of time. Keep out of their company altogether.

translit: nīṭkōla vāḻkkaiyelām nīttiṭuvōṉ poṉaṟaikkut tāṭkōl iṭuvāraic cārntuṟaiyēl - nīṭkōla
translation: Do not stay close to those who put a lock on the golden room of the Lord, who eradicates all this ever-changing, enduring worldly life.
commentary: The golden room is the Lord's own presence, where He frees the soul from the endless changes of worldly life. Some people act as if they hold the key and can lock others out of that grace. Vallalar says not to stay near such gatekeepers.

translit: meyyoḻukkat tārpōl veḷiniṉ ṟakattoḻiyāp poyyoḻukkat tārpāl poruntiyuṟēl - poyyoḻukkil
translation: Do not associate with those of false conduct, who appear outwardly like people of enduring true conduct, but do not eradicate the falsehood within.
commentary: Hypocrisy is a spiritual dead end. Some people put on a show of perfect behavior while the falsehood inside stays rooted. True conduct pulls that falsehood out from within, and those who only pretend make dangerous company on the path.

translit: poynnūl pataṟip pulampukiṉṟa pittarkaḷpāl annūl virumpi aṭaintalaiyēl - kainnērntu
translation: Do not desire and wander after those madmen who, rooted in false conduct, nervously babble false scriptures.
commentary: Do not seek wisdom from false teachers who live unethically. Vallalar dismisses their texts as false scriptures (poynnūl) and calls the men who obsessively recite them madmen. He tells the seeker never to waste time wandering after people whose outward religious babbling masks a life of false conduct.

translit: kōṭātu kōṭi koṭuttālum caivaneṟi nāṭā tavaravaiyai naṇṇiyiṭēl - kōṭātu
translation: Even if they offer ten million in wealth, do not approach the assembly of those who do not seek the Saiva path.
commentary: The seeker must stay completely away from people who reject the spiritual path of truth. Do not seek their company or join their gatherings, no matter how much money or worldly advantage they might offer.

translit: kollā viratamatu koḷḷāraik kāṇiloru pullāka eṇṇip puṟampoḻika - ellāmum
translation: If you see those who do not unswervingly hold the vow of non-killing, consider them as a mere blade of grass and cast them aside.
commentary: The vow never to kill another living being is absolute. Vallalar says that anyone who refuses to hold this vow of non-killing should be treated as utterly insignificant and left behind. This is his core teaching of Jeevakarunyam (compassion for all life), which he holds as the foundation of all spiritual progress.

translit: ākanavil kiṉṟateṉnam aiyaṉukkaṉ pillārai nīkaṉavi lēṉum niṉaiyaṟka - ēkaṉaṭik
translation: Why say anything more? Do not think even in your dreams of those who have no love for our Lord.
commentary: Shut out entirely those who have no love for the Lord. Vallalar wants the distance so complete that they do not enter even your dreams.

translit: kaṉpē vaṭivāy aruḷē uyirāyppē riṉpē uṇarvāy icaintārum - aṉpākik
translation: There are those who have gathered at the feet of the One Lord with love as their form, grace as their life, and supreme bliss as their consciousness.
commentary: True devotees are remade by their bond with the Lord. Love is their very form, grace is their life, and supreme bliss fills their whole awareness.

translit: kaṇṭikaiyē pūṇiṟ kalavaiyē veṇṇīṟāyk koṇṭikavāc cārpu kuṟittārum - toṇṭuṭaṉē
translation: Becoming love itself, they wear rudraksha beads as their ornaments and pure white ash as their fragrant paste. They seek the inseparable refuge of the Lord through devoted service.
commentary: They wear rudraksha beads (seeds used in prayer) and pure white ash as living signs of love. Through constant service they seek a refuge in the Lord that never leaves them.

translit: vāymalarāl mālai vakuttaloṭu nammiṟaikkut tūymalarāl mālai toṭuppārum - cārmalarōṉ
translation: There are those who weave garlands of pure flowers for our Lord, along with crafting garlands of poetic words from their blossoming mouths.
commentary: Two offerings here. Devotees string real flowers, and they compose songs of praise, which Vallalar calls garlands woven by the mouth.

translit: ērnanta ṉappaṇikaṇ ṭiccaiyuṟa nammiṟaikkuc cīrnanta ṉappaṇikaḷ ceyvōrum - nārnantāt
translation: There are those who perform excellent flower garden services for our Lord, maintaining them so beautifully that even Brahma on his lotus sees their work and desires to do it himself.
commentary: Other devotees tend the gardens that grow those flowers. Their work is so beautiful, Vallalar says, that Brahma the creator looks down from his lotus and wishes he could do it himself.

translit: tīyiṉmeḻu kāccintai cērnturuki nammiṟaivāḻ kōyilmeḻu kāniṉṟa koḷkaiyarum - mēyiṉarait
translation: There are those who hold to the practice of washing and smearing the floors of the temple where our Lord lives, their minds melting like wax in the fire of unceasing love.
commentary: Washing and smearing the temple floors is humble work. Vallalar looks at what happens inside the one doing it, the heart melting with love as wax melts in fire.

translit: tāyil vaḷarkkum tayavuṭaiya namperumāṉ kōyil viḷakkum kuṇattōrum - tūya-aruḷ
translation: There are those of noble character who clean the temple of our Lord, whose compassion nurtures those who seek Him far better than a mother.
commentary: Others sweep and clean the temple. They serve a Lord whose compassion for those who seek Him is greater than a mother's.

translit: iṉpuṭaṉē tīpamutal ellāc cariyaikaḷum aṉpuṭaṉē ceytaṅ kamarvārum - aṉpuṭaṉē
translation: There are those who joyfully perform all acts of temple service through pure grace, starting with lighting lamps, and who reside there doing these works with love.
commentary: Vallalar gathers all these physical acts under cariyai (external temple service). Lighting the lamps and all the rest, the devotees do them with love and joy, never as a mere duty.

translit: aṇṇiyamēl aṉpark kamutīta lāticiva puṇṇiyamē nāḷum purivōrum - puṇṇiyamām
translation: Those who daily perform meritorious deeds for Siva, such as offering nectar-like food to the great devotees who draw near...
commentary: Feeding others sits at the center of Vallalar's teaching. For him, offering pure, nourishing food to the devotees who come near is the truest kind of spiritual merit.

translit: tēṉē amutē civamē civamē-em māṉē-eṉ ṟētti makiḻvārum - vāṉāṉa
translation: Those who rejoice, praising Him: "O Honey! O Nectar! O Siva! O Siva! O our Lord!"...
commentary: Honey, nectar: the devotees reach for the sweetest words they have. Knowing God is a joy, and it nourishes like food.

translit: maṉṉē aruṭkaṭalē māṇikka mē-eṅkaḷ aṉṉē-eṉ ṟuṉṉi amarvōrum - naṉṉēyap
translation: Those who sit in meditation, thinking: "O King of the heavens! O Ocean of Grace! O Ruby! O our Mother!"...
commentary: Beside the titles of majesty, king and ocean of grace, God is called Mother. Vallalar returns again and again to this tender maternal love as the heart of the divine nature.

translit: paṇṇīr moḻiyāl parintētti āṉantak kaṇṇīrkoṇ ṭuḷḷam kaḷippōrum - uṇṇīril
translation: Those who praise Him with deep affection using words of great love sweet as music, their hearts rejoicing with tears of bliss...
commentary: True worship overflows. The devotees weep for pure joy, praising God in words as sweet as music.

translit: paṇṭukaṇṭum kāṇāp pariciṉarāyp poṉmēṉi kaṇṭukaṇṭu nāḷum kaḷippōrum - toṇṭaṭaiyum
translation: Those who, as if they had never seen it before despite seeing it in the past, gaze upon His golden form again and again, rejoicing every day...
commentary: The sight of God never grows familiar. They look at His golden form every day and feel the wonder of the very first time.

translit: poṟpatikam eṉṟeṇṇip pōṟṟi-oru mūvarkaḷiṉ coṟpatikam koṇṭu tutippōrum - coṟpaṉattum
translation: Those who revere them as golden hymns and offer praise using the sacred verses composed by the three saints. And those who, even in their dreams,
commentary: The "three saints" are the revered ancient Tamil poets Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar. Devotees sing their hymns and treat every word as precious gold.

translit: mācakattil cērkkāta māṇikkam eṉṟatiru vācakattai vāyāl malarvōrum - vācakattiṉ
translation: recite with their lips the Thiruvasagam, viewing it as a ruby unparalleled in this great world. And those who,
commentary: Manikkavasagar composed the Thiruvasagam, a book of Tamil devotional poetry. Devotees treasure it as a flawless ruby and keep its verses on their lips even in sleep.

translit: maṉṉicaippāl mēlōr vakuttētti niṉṟatiru iṉṉicaippā āti icaippōrum - maṉṉicaippiṉ
translation: sing the sweet sacred songs such as the Thiruvisaippa, which exalted saints composed and praised with enduring melodies. And those who,
commentary: The Thiruvisaippa is another sacred collection of Tamil praise poetry. Devotees sing these old songs to the sweet, enduring music the saints first gave them.

translit: nalvāḻ varuḷukiṉṟa namperumāṉ māṉmiyaṅkaḷ colvōrum kēṭṭut toḻuvōrum - colvāynta
translation: speak the glories of our Lord who grants a good life, and those who listen to them and worship. And those who, with fitting words,
commentary: Worship is shared here. Some recount the loving acts of God, and others gather round to listen and bow.

translit: tātāveṉ ṟaṉpuṭaṉē cāmakī taṅkaḷmutal vētāka maṅkaḷ virippōrum - vētāntam
translation: affectionately call him the Supreme Giver and expound the Vedas and Agamas, beginning with the chants of the Sama Veda. And those who,
commentary: The Vedas and Agamas are ancient Sanskrit scriptures. Starting with the musical Sama Veda, devotees chant and explain them with love, praising God as the giver of all things.

translit: cērntōrk karuḷum civamē poruḷeṉṟu tērntē civapūcai ceyvōrum - ārntētti
translation: Realizing that Sivam alone is the ultimate truth who grants grace to those who reach Him, some perform worship of Siva with overflowing praise.
commentary: The Divine (Sivam) alone is the lasting truth, and He gives grace to anyone who draws near. Knowing this, these devotees perform outer worship with joyful, overflowing praise.

translit: naṉṉeñcē kōyileṉa namperumāṉ taṉṉaivaittu maṉṉum civanēyam vāyntōrum - muṉayaṉṟaṉ
translation: Some install our Lord in their good hearts, treating them as His very temple, and possess enduring love for Siva.
commentary: Inner worship needs no building. These devotees make their pure hearts His temple and seat the Lord inside, where their love for Him stays deep and steady.

translit: añceḻuttel lāmkēṭkil añceḻuttām emperumāṉ añceḻuttāl arccit tamarvōrum - añceṉavē
translation: Hearing all the letters of ancient Brahma, some abide in worship using the five sacred letters of our Lord, who is Himself those five letters.
commentary: Siva's five sacred syllables (Na-Ma-Si-Va-Ya) carry immense spiritual power. The devotees worship with this mantra alone, knowing the Lord is Himself formed of these five letters. That meditation lifts them above ordinary worldly knowledge.

translit: viñcum poṟiyiṉ viṭayamelām namperumāṉ ceñcun tarappatattil cērttōrum - vañcamcey
translation: Some gather all the worldly objects of the five overwhelming senses and place them at the beautiful, red feet of our Lord.
commentary: The five senses keep pulling the mind toward the world. These seekers take every desire and every sensation and surrender them all at the Lord's beautiful feet.

translit: poyvē taṉainīkkum puṇṇiyaṉpāl tammuyirai naivē taṉamākkum nallōrum - ceyvēlai
translation: Some good people offer their very souls as sacred food to the holy Lord who removes deceitful, false agony.
commentary: An offering usually means food set before an altar. These good people offer the soul itself, giving their whole lives to God, and so are freed from the illusions and pains of the world.

translit: nīṭa naṭattaloṭu niṟṟalmutal namperumāṉ āṭal aṭittiyāṉam ārntōrum - vāṭalaṟat
translation: Those who remain completely absorbed in meditating on the dancing feet of our Lord through all their prolonged actions, from walking to standing, without ever fading.
commentary: Devotion does not need closed eyes and a still body. These seekers keep their minds on the Lord's dancing feet, the sign of His energy and grace, while they walk or stand about their ordinary business. Whatever the body is doing, the inner gaze holds.

translit: tūya naṉaviṟ cuḻuttiyoṭu namperumāṉ nēyam nikaḻttum neṟiyōrum - māyamuṟu
translation: Those on the path who manifest their love for our Lord in the pure state of wakeful sleep.
commentary: 'Wakeful sleep' is a state where the busy mind falls as quiet as in deep sleep, yet the person stays fully awake to God. From that stillness these seekers pour out their love to the Lord.

translit: māṉatuvāy niṉṟa vayamnīkkit tāṉaṟṟut tāṉatuvāy niṟkum takaiyōrum - vāṉamatil
translation: Those of noble nature who shed the grip of the illusory ego, lose their separate self, and stand as the Divine itself.
commentary: The biggest wall between us and God is the idea of a separate self. These people shed the ego entirely. When the personal 'I' dissolves, what remains is a clear reflection of the Divine.

translit: vāṉaṅkaṇ ṭāṭum mayilpōṉṟu namperumāṉ tāṉaṅkaṇ ṭāṭum tavattōrum - mōṉamoṭu
translation: Those ascetics who dance upon seeing the abode of our Lord, just like a peacock dancing upon seeing the sky.
commentary: In traditional poetry the peacock dances when it sees dark clouds gathering to bring life-giving rain. These ascetics feel that same spontaneous joy. When they finally behold the Lord's dwelling place, they cannot help breaking into dance.

translit: tāḻcaṭaiyum nīṟum carikōva ṇakkīḷum vāḻcivamum koṇṭu vativōrum - āḻnilaiya
translation: Those who dwell in silence, wearing low-hanging matted hair, sacred ash, a torn loincloth, and carrying the living presence of Siva.
commentary: These are wandering ascetics who have renounced the world. They keep inner silence and carry only the barest marks of their path: matted hair, sacred ash, a torn cloth. The living presence of God is all they own.

translit: vāriyalai pōṉṟacutta māyaiyiṉāl āmpūta kāriyaṅka ḷātiyelām kaṇṭoḻittu - ūriyaṅkat
translation: Seeing and discarding all the elemental products and everything else born of impure illusion that surge like ocean waves,
commentary: The climb starts by recognizing the restless products of impure illusion (acutta māyai) and letting them go. They are the physical and mental distractions that surge like ocean waves and keep the soul bound.

translit: tañcam tarumalarōṉ tattuvamām pūtaṅkaḷ aiñcum poṟiyañcum añcaṟivum - añceṉumōr
translation: and the five elements, the five sensory organs, and the five faculties of knowledge, which are the principles of the lotus-born Brahma who grants refuge to keep the world functioning,
commentary: Next come the building blocks of physical life: the five elements, the five senses and the five faculties of knowledge. Vallalar places all of these under Brahma, the traditional creator god, and the seeker has to leave them behind.

translit: vākkumutal aiñcumaṟṟu mālōṉtaṉ tattuvamām ūkkum kalaimutalām ōrēḻum - nīkki-appāl
translation: and the five organs of action beginning with speech, and the seven stimulating principles beginning with kala that belong to Vishnu, setting all these aside and moving beyond,
commentary: The organs of action and the seven principles of limitation (kalai) go next. Vallalar assigns these to Vishnu, the traditional preserver god. The true path steps right past the domains of these conventional deities.

translit: mēvi viḷaṅkucutta vittaimutal nātamaṭṭum tāvi vayaṅkucutta tattuvattil - mēvi-akaṉ
translation: reaching the radiant pure principles that extend from pure knowledge up to the primal sound, abiding in them and then transcending them,
commentary: Higher up are the pure principles, from pure knowledge (cutti vittai) to the primal sound (nātam). Even these are not the goal. The soul passes through them and moves on.

translit: ṟappāl aruḷkaṇ ṭaruḷāl tamaittāmkaṇ ṭappāl paraveḷikaṇ ṭappāluk - kappālum
translation: and beyond that seeing Grace, and by that Grace seeing one's own Self, and beyond that seeing the supreme space, and moving even beyond that,
commentary: Past every principle, physical and spiritual, the soul meets Grace. Only by that Grace does it see its own true Self. From there it sees the supreme space and keeps going, further still.

translit: tīrāc cuyamāyc citāṉanta māmoḷiyaip pārā irunta paṭiyiruntu - pērātu
translation: Beholding the unending, self-existent light of conscious bliss, remaining exactly in that state without swerving,
commentary: Real focus means resting wholly in the divine light. Vallalar describes beholding the eternal, joyful light of God and staying fixed there, never wavering.

translit: kaṇṭatuveṉ ṟoṉṟum kalavātu tāmkalantu koṇṭaciva yōkiyarām koṟṟavarum - aṇṭariya
translation: and not mixing with anything that is seen, they have merged completely. Such are the sovereign Siva yogis. And the unapproachable,
commentary: These masters do not cling to anything the eyes can see. Vallalar calls them Siva yogis (those united with the Divine), for their awareness has merged entirely with God.

translit: cattuvattil cattuvamē tammuruvāyk koṇṭupara tattuvattiṉ niṟkum takavōrum - attuvattil
translation: worthy ones who take the purest goodness within goodness as their very form and stand in the supreme reality. On that path,
commentary: The highest truth is reached when a person becomes pure goodness through and through. These worthy ones have purified their nature so completely that they stand firm in the supreme reality.

translit: tītum cukamum civaṉceyaleṉ ṟeṇṇivanta yātum camamā iruppōrum - kōtupaṭak
translation: considering both suffering and joy as the action of Siva, there are those who remain perfectly equanimous toward whatever comes. And those who have transcended the flawed
commentary: Peace comes from seeing every event as Siva's own doing. Knowing that joy and suffering both come from God, these people meet whatever happens with an even, calm mind.

translit: kūṟum kuṟiyum kuṇamum kulamumaṭi īṟum kaṭaiyum ikantōrum - vīṟukiṉṟa
translation: spoken symbols, attributes, lineages, beginnings, ends, and all boundaries. Glorious...
commentary: Every earthly identity and division falls away in this state. Vallalar explains that human categories like family lineage, physical traits, and spoken symbols are flawed limits that must be entirely left behind.

translit: cēnti ṉaṭaintavelāñ cīraṇikkac cērcitta cānti yuṭaṉē carippōrum - cāntipeṟat
translation: There are those who wander with an acquired tranquility of mind, gracefully assimilating everything they have attained. To achieve peace,
commentary: Real peace means taking in deep experiences without losing your balance. These sages wander the world with quiet minds, carrying what they have attained with complete calm.

translit: tammaiyuṟum cittevaiyum tāmuvattal ceyyāmal cemmaiyuṭaṉ vāḻum tiṟalōrum - emmaiyiṉum
translation: capable ones live righteously without taking any delight in the miraculous powers that come to them. At all times,
commentary: As a seeker advances, extraordinary or miraculous powers sometimes come. The truly capable live upright lives and take no pride or pleasure in them. They know such distractions can ruin their spiritual progress.

translit: ārāmai ōṅkum avākkaṭalnīr māṉkuḷampiṉ nīrāka nīnti nilaittōrum - cērātu
translation: steadfast ones swim across the swelling ocean of insatiable desire as if it were merely a puddle in a deer's hoofprint. Unattached,
commentary: Desire is usually pictured as a vast, dangerous ocean that swallows people whole. For the steadfast, crossing that endless sea of craving is as easy as stepping over the little puddle left in a deer's hoofprint.

translit: tamporuḷaik kaṇṭē catāṉanta vīṭṭiṉiṭaic cemporuḷaic cārnta tiṟattōrum - maṇporuḷpōyt
translation: worthy ones realize their true essence and unite with the perfect Reality in the abode of eternal bliss. Letting go of earthly things,
commentary: Lasting freedom turns on realizing what the soul truly is. Having found that inner essence, worthy seekers unite with the perfect divine Reality and settle into permanent joy.

translit: tāyar eṉamātar tammaiyeṇṇip pālarpittar pēyareṉa naṇṇum periyōru - mīyataṉiṉ
translation: great ones consider all women as their mothers and behave like children, madmen, or spirits.
commentary: Advanced masters leave ordinary social rules behind. They see every woman as a mother and have dropped all worldly attachment, so they move through life freely. To ordinary society they may look like innocent children, wild madmen, or wandering spirits.

translit: eypparicām ōrtiraṇam evvulakum ceytaḷikka meypparicañ ceyyavalla vittakarum - meyppaṭavē
translation: The masters capable of applying the true touch to a mere blade of grass, empowering it to create and sustain all worlds; truly,
commentary: Such masters hold a power beyond imagining. One divine touch from them could empower a simple blade of grass to create and sustain whole worlds.

translit: yāvum aṟintum aṟiyārpōṉ ṟeppoḻutum cāvum piṟappum tavirntōrum - ōvaliṉṟi
translation: knowing everything, they act as if they know nothing, and they have forever escaped birth and death; endlessly,
commentary: They know everything and still carry themselves as if they knew nothing. Having reached that pure awareness, they are done with birth and death for good.

translit: vaitiṭiṉum vāḻka-eṉa vāḻtti upacāram ceytiṭiṉum taṉmai tiṟampārum - meyvakaiyil
translation: whether abused, they bless their abusers to prosper, or whether served with honors, their nature does not waver; in truth,
commentary: Treat them however you like and their balance holds. Insult them and they answer with genuine blessings. Shower them with praise and honors, and their inner peace does not stir.

translit: tēṟā vulakam civamayamāyk kaṇṭeṅkum ēṟā tiḻiyā tiruppōrum - māṟātu
translation: seeing the confused world as entirely permeated by the Divine, they remain everywhere without rising in pride or falling in despair; unchangingly,
commentary: Where others see only a confused world, they see the Divine filling every part of it. Because God is everywhere for them, they are never lifted by pride or pushed down by sorrow.

translit: mōṉantāṉ koṇṭu muṭintaviṭat tōṅkupara māṉantā tītat tamarntōrum - tāmnantāc
translation: embracing silence, they are established in the transcendent supreme bliss that rises at the ultimate state; themselves unfading,
commentary: Their final state is a deep inner silence. Resting there, they know a supreme bliss far beyond ordinary human awareness.

translit: cātukkaḷ āmavartam caṅka makattuvattaic cātukka ḷaṉṟiyevar tāmaṟivār - nītukkam
translation: Who but the sages can know the greatness of the assembly of sages?
commentary: Only a sage can truly recognize the power of a gathering of holy people. A worldly mind has no way to measure an assembly given over to the Divine.

translit: nīṅki-aṉṉōr caṅkattil niṉṟumakiḻn tēttinitam āṅkavartāṭ kuṟṟēval āyntiyaṟṟi - ōṅkuciva
translation: Shed your sorrow and stand in their assembly. Rejoice and praise them daily. Carefully perform devoted service to their feet.
commentary: Find these holy people and serve them. That is the cure for worldly sorrow, and serving the wise keeps a seeker grounded and glad in practice.

translit: pañcāṭ carattaip pakararuḷē nāvāka eñcāp parivuṭaṉē eṇṇiyaruḷ - ceñcōtit
translation: Chant the supreme five-letter mantra of Siva. Make grace itself your tongue and meditate on it with unfailing devotion.
commentary: The five-letter mantra is Na-Ma-Si-Va-Ya, the sacred syllables of Lord Siva. Chanting it should never be a mechanical repetition of sounds. Make divine grace itself your tongue, and the prayer becomes pure love and focus.

translit: tātoṉṟu tumpaimuṭit tāṇu-aṭi yoṉṟimaṟṟai yātoṉṟum nōkkā tamaintiṭuka - tīteṉṟa
translation: Unite with the feet of the eternal Lord of red radiance who wears the pollen-filled thumpai flower on his crown. Remain still, looking at absolutely nothing else.
commentary: Traditional poetry pictures Lord Siva wearing the small white thumpai flower on his head. What Vallalar asks for is complete single-mindedness. Fix the mind entirely on this radiant presence and shut out every other distraction.

translit: pāḻvāḻvu nīṅkap pativāḻvil eññāṉṟum vāḻvāyeṉ ṉōṭum makiḻntu.
translation: Shed this evil and ruined worldly life. You will live joyfully with me forever in the divine life.
commentary: Fleeting desires and selfishness ruin worldly life. Let go of those illusions and the divine life opens, with eternal joy and true spiritual companionship.

sections.title: Venba Verses on Love for Siva

translit: muṉṉavaṉē yāṉai mukattavaṉē muttinalam coṉṉavaṉē tūymeyc cukattavaṉē - eṉṉavaṉē ciṟparaṉē aiṅkaraṉē ceñcaṭaiyañ cēkaraṉē taṟparaṉē niṉtāḷ caraṇ.
translation: Primal Lord, elephant-faced One, One who taught the goodness of liberation, One of pure true bliss, my own Lord, supreme consciousness, five-handed One, One crowned with red matted hair, supreme Being. I surrender to your feet.
commentary: Vinayakar, the elephant-faced god of beginnings, comes first. Tradition invokes him before anything else to clear obstacles from the way. Vallalar praises him as supreme consciousness, the one who teaches the goodness of liberation, and surrenders at his feet.

translit: vīṟuṭaiyāy vēluṭaiyāy viṇṇuṭaiyāy veṟpuṭaiyāy nīṟuṭaiyāy nēyarkaṭan neñcuṭaiyāy - kūṟu mutalvā-ōr āṟu mukavā mukkaṇṇaṉ putalvāniṉ tāḷeṉ pukal.
translation: Lord of majesty, wielder of the spear, Lord of the heavens, Lord of the mountain, One adorned with sacred ash, One who dwells in the hearts of loving devotees. Proclaimed primal Lord, six-faced One, son of the three-eyed Siva. Your feet are my refuge.
commentary: Now Murugan, the six-faced son of Siva who carries the sacred spear. He is lord of majesty and of the mountains, yet the home he chooses is the heart of whoever loves him. To take refuge at his feet is to trust him completely.

translit: cīrcāṉṟa vētac ceḻumporuḷē ciṟcorupap pērcāṉṟa uṇmaip piramamē - nērcāṉṟōr nāṭum paracivamē nāyēṉuk kaṉpuniṉpāl nīṭum paṭinī nikaḻttu.
translation: Rich essence of the excellent Vedas, true Brahman renowned as the embodiment of pure consciousness, supreme Siva sought by upright wise ones. Grant that love for you grows endlessly in me, a lowly cur.
commentary: Wise seekers and the ancient scriptures all reach for this pure truth and try to describe it. Vallalar calls himself a lowly dog and asks for one thing only. Let his love for God keep growing without end.

translit: niṉaippittā nittā nimalā eṉanī niṉaippittāl ēḻai niṉaippēṉ - niṉaippiṉ maṟappittāli yāṉum maṟappēṉ evaiyum piṟappittāy eṉṉāleṉ pēcu.
translation: Eternal One, pure One. If you make me remember, I, a poor wretch, will remember. If you make me forget my thoughts, I will forget. You created everything. Tell me, what can I do on my own?
commentary: We have no power of our own here. If God makes us remember, we remember, and if God lets us forget, we forget. Since the Divine created everything, effort on our own achieves nothing, and Vallalar says so plainly.

translit: uruvāy uruvil uruvāki ōṅki aruvāy aruvil aruvāy - oruvāmal niṉṟāyē niṉṟa niṉaikkāṇpa tevvāṟō eṉtāyē eṉtantai yē.
translation: You stand as form, as form within form. Rising high, you stand as the formless, as the formless within the formless. You stand unceasingly. How am I to see you who stands thus? You are my mother and my father.
commentary: God is in every physical shape and wholly beyond shape, form within form and formless within formless. No human mind can hold both at once. Vallalar does not try. He calls God his mother and father, and the infinite becomes an intimate relationship of pure love.

translit: veñcañ calamā vikāram eṉumpēykku neñcam paṟikoṭuttu niṟkiṉṟēṉ - añcaleṉa eṇtōḷ iṟaiyē eṉaiyaṭimai koḷḷamaṉam uṇṭō ilaiyō urai.
translation: I stand having surrendered my heart to the demon called the great distortion of cruel sorrow. O Lord with eight shoulders, tell me whether or not you have the mind to say "Do not fear" and take me as your servant.
commentary: Sorrow and inner turmoil have seized his heart like a demon, and Vallalar admits it. He addresses Siva by the traditional image of the Lord with eight shoulders. Then, exposed and honest, he asks straight out whether God will offer comfort and accept him.

translit: appāluṉ cittam aṟiyēṉ eṉakkammai appāniṉ tāḷaṉṟi yārkaṇṭāy - ippāril cāti-uru vākkun taḷai-aviḻttut taṉmayamām cōti-uru vākkun tuṇai.
translation: Beyond this I do not know your will. O my Mother and Father, who is there for me other than your feet? In this world, you are the companion who unties the bonds that create forms of caste and shapes me into a form of Jothi that shares your nature.
commentary: Vallalar calls the divine his mother and father and leaves everything to God's will. He praises the Lord as the companion who unties the bonds of caste. God is the true companion who unties these worldly bonds. Once freed from such divisions, the soul is transformed into a body of pure light, taking on the very nature of Jothi.

translit: pēraṟivāl kaṇṭum periyōr aṟiyārēl yāraṟivār yāṉō aṟikiṟpēṉ cīrkoḷ veḷiyāy veḷikkuḷ veḷiyāy oḷikkuḷ oḷiyāki niṉṟa uṉai.
translation: If even the great ones cannot know you despite seeing with supreme intelligence, who else can know you? Could I possibly know you? You stand as the glorious space, as the space within space, and as the light within light.
commentary: Even the wisest beings cannot grasp God with intellect alone. So how could Vallalar manage it by his own effort? He gives the divine no fixed physical form. He sees it as the endless space within space and the radiant light within all light.

translit: vantittēṉpiṭṭukanta vaḷḷalē niṉṉaṭiyāṉ cintittēṉ eṉṟal cirippaṉṟō - pantattāñ cintucintip pitteṉatu cintaiyuṇiṉ poṉṉaruḷē vantucintip pittal maṟantu.
translation: O benevolent Lord who rejoiced in the sweet flour offering, it is truly a joke for me, your servant, to say "I worshipped you" or "I thought of you." I forget that it is your golden grace alone that enters my mind and makes me think, scattering the thoughts born of worldly bondage.
commentary: Vallalar recalls the ancient story of Siva accepting a sweet flour offering from a poor devotee. Then he calls it a joke for anyone to claim credit for worshipping or thinking of God. Human effort alone achieves nothing. God's golden grace enters the mind, clears away worldly attachments, and creates the very capacity for devotion.

translit: tēṉeṉṟa iṉcol terintuniṉaip pāṭukiṉṟēṉ nāṉeṉ ṟuraittal nakai-aṉṟō - vāṉniṉṟa oṇporuṇī uḷḷam uvantaruḷāl iṉcollum vaṇporuḷum ītal maṟantu.
translation: Is it not a joke to say that I select sweet words like honey and sing of you myself? I forget that you, the luminous truth standing in the heavens, rejoice in your heart and bestow both these sweet words and their rich meaning through your grace.
commentary: Even the poetry that praises God is God's own gift. Vallalar laughs at the idea that he is the one choosing sweet words for his songs. The real author is the divine truth, whose grace happily supplies both the language and the deep meaning behind every verse.

translit: aṇṭaṅka ḷō-avaṟṟiṉ appālō ippālō paṇṭaṅka ḷōciṟ paraveḷiyō - kaṇtaṅka vemperumāl nīttavartam meyyuḷamō taiyaloṭum emperumāṉ nīvāḻ iṭam.
translation: My Lord, where is the place you live with the Goddess? Is it the universes, or beyond them, or on this side? Is it the material realms, or the supreme space of consciousness? Or is it the true hearts of those who have cast off fierce illusion, standing visible to the eye?
commentary: Vallalar wonders where God truly lives with the Goddess. He runs through the possibilities: the physical universe, whatever lies beyond it, the pure space of consciousness. His answer leans toward the clear heart of someone who has abandoned all illusion.

translit: pūtameṅkē maṟṟaip pulaṉeṅkē palluyiriṉ pētameṅkē aṇṭameṉum pēreṅkē - nātameṅkē maṉvaṭiva meṅkē maṟaiyeṅkē vāṉporuṇī poṉvaṭivam koḷḷāta pōtu.
translation: O supreme celestial reality, when you do not assume your golden form, where are the elements? Where are the senses? Where are the distinctions among the countless souls? Where is the very name "universe"? Where is the primal sound? Where are the enduring forms, and where are the scriptures?
commentary: Everything in creation hangs on God choosing to take form. Without that golden form there would be no elements, no senses, no scriptures, no universe at all.

translit: pēruruvō cōtip piḻampākum ciṉmayattiṉ cīruruvō tēvar tiruvuruvam - nēruruvil cālpuṟaccēr aṇṭa carācaraṅkaḷ ellāmnum kālviraṟpāl niṉṟoṭuṅkuṅ kāl.
translation: When all the moving and unmoving things of the universes gather perfectly and dissolve at your toes, what is your divine form, O Lord? Is it a massive physical form? Or is it the magnificent form of pure consciousness that stands as a blazing mass of light?
commentary: At the end of time, all moving and unmoving things dissolve back into God, gathered at his toes. Vallalar asks what form the divine takes at that absolute moment. A giant physical body? Or pure consciousness blazing as a mass of light?

translit: iṉṟō pakalō iravō varunāḷil eṉṟō aṟiyēṉ eḷiyēṉē - maṉṟōṅkum tāyaṉaiyāy niṉṉaruḷām taṇṇamutam uṇṭuvantu nāyaṉaiyēṉ vāḻkiṉṟa nāḷ.
translation: O mother who stands exalted in the Hall, I am a humble soul and I do not know. Is it today, by day or by night, or some day yet to come? When is the day that I, who am like a dog, will come to drink the cool nectar of your grace and truly live?
commentary: The timing of grace is a mystery to the soul. Addressing God as a loving mother, Vallalar longs to know when he will finally drink the cool nectar of grace and truly live. Today, tonight, or some unknown day ahead, he cannot tell.

translit: maṇṇācai veṟpē maṟikaṭalē poṉṉācai peṇṇācai oṉṟē-eṉ pērācai - naṇṇācai viṭṭār pukaḻum viṭaiyāynāṉ poyyācaip paṭṭāl varumē patam.
translation: O Lord riding the bull, praised by those who have abandoned clinging desires! My desire for land is a towering mountain. My desire for gold is a churning ocean. My desire for women is my greatest desire. If I harbor such false desires, will I ever attain the supreme state?
commentary: Worldly attachments block the path to spiritual freedom. Vallalar confesses to feeling overwhelmed by massive desires for land, wealth, and physical pleasure. He knows that as long as he harbors these false attachments, he cannot reach the supreme state.

translit: tantaiyāy eṉṉuṭaiya tāyāyt takaicāṉṟa cintaiyāy eṉṉarumait tēcikaṉāy - muntaiyāy nīṭu maṟaimutalāy niṉṟāyeṉ ṉēneñcam vāṭumeṉai āṭkoḷḷā vāṟu.
translation: You stand as my father, my mother, my noble mind, my precious guru, the ancient one, and the source of the enduring Vedas. Why do you not claim me while my heart withers?
commentary: Vallalar calls God his whole world: father, mother, mind, teacher, the ancient source of the Vedas. Then he asks a very human question. If God is already this close and plays every caring role, why does he wait while his devotee's heart withers instead of stepping in?

translit: ūṭṭukiṉṟa valviṉaiyām uṭkayiṟṟāl uḷḷiruntē āṭṭukiṉṟa nītāṉ aṟintilaiyō - vāṭṭukiṉṟa añcupula vēṭark kaṟivaip paṟikoṭutteṉ neñcupularn tēṅku nilai.
translation: You animate me from within using the inner string of forceful karma that compels experience. Do you not know my state? I have lost my awareness to the five tormenting sense-hunters, and my heart dries up and pines.
commentary: God is the puppeteer here, pulling the inner string of karma (the accumulated results of past actions that drive a person's current experiences). If God moves him from the inside, how could God overlook his suffering? The five senses are cruel hunters that have ambushed his awareness, and Vallalar is left drained, begging for relief.

translit: āmō alavō aṟiyēṉ ciṟiyēṉāṉ tāmō taraṉum catumukaṉum - tāmē aṭiyā tarikkum aracēniṉ ēval aṭiyārkuṟ ṟēvalaṭi yaṉ.
translation: I, a lowly one, do not know if this is proper or not. O King whose feet are revered by Vishnu and four-faced Brahma themselves! I am the servant performing menial tasks for the devotees under your command.
commentary: Brahma and Vishnu, the creator and preserver gods of the Hindu pantheon, bow at the supreme Lord's feet. Vallalar comes before that Lord in utter humility, claiming no greatness of his own. His only standing is the humble work he does for the people who serve God.

translit: uṉṉāl eṉakkāva tuṇṭatunī kaṇṭatuvē eṉṉāl uṉakkāva tētuḷatu - coṉṉālyāṉ tantārvat tōṭum talaimēṟkoṇ ṭuykiṟpēṉ entāyiṅ koṉṟumaṟi yēṉ.
translation: You know the benefit I receive from you. What benefit do you receive from me? If you tell me, I will offer it, bear your command on my head with devotion, and be saved. O my Father, I know nothing here.
commentary: Between the soul and God, the account looks entirely one-sided. Everything good Vallalar has comes from God, and he cannot see what a frail human being could give back. So he asks simply to be told, promising to carry out the command gladly and be saved.

translit: ceṉṟuraippār collil ciṟiyāṉ payamaṟiyāṉ eṉṟuraippār āṅkatumaṟ ṟeṉṉaḷavē - maṉṟakattōy añcēl viḻiyārai antakaṉeṉ pārmoḻiyai añcēṉ ciṟitum aṟintu.
translation: If messengers approach you, they will say this lowly one knows no fear. That applies perfectly to my measure. O Lord of the Hall! I know well and do not fear in the slightest the words of those who call people with beautiful carp-like eyes blind.
commentary: Worldly people might complain to God that Vallalar is fearless and arrogant, and he proudly agrees. He has no fear at all of ignorant critics who look at people with clear spiritual vision and call them blind. Those who cannot see the truth will not intimidate him.

translit: entāyniṉ aṉpartamak kiṉṉamutam iṭṭēttic cintā nalamoṉṟuñ ceytaṟiyēṉ - nantāc cuvaruṇṭa maṇpōlum cōṟuṇṭēṉ maṇṇil evaruṇ ṭeṉaippōl iyampu.
translation: My Father, I do not know how to do a single good deed of feeding sweet nectar to your devotees and praising them. Like mud consumed by a ruinous wall, I merely ate food. Tell me, who on earth is like me?
commentary: This verse expresses deep regret for a life lived without serving others. Vallalar says the highest good is feeding those devoted to God, a practice rooted in jīvakāruṇyam (compassion for all living beings). Instead of sharing, he compares himself to mud packed into a crumbling wall, consuming food without offering anything of value in return.

translit: uppirunta ōṭō ōtiyō ulāppiṇamō veppirunta kāṭō viṉaiccumaiyō - ceppaṟiyēṉ kaṇṇappa rukkuk kaṉiyaṉaiyāy niṟpaṇiyā tuṇṇap parukkum uṭampu.
translation: Is it a pot that held salt, a chameleon, a wandering corpse, a burning cremation ground, or a burden of karma? I cannot say. O Lord who was like a sweet fruit to Kannappar, this body fattens itself by eating without bowing to you.
commentary: A body that eats only to grow fat and never turns to God is of no real use. Vallalar asks whether such a body is anything more than a walking corpse or a heavy load of past actions (karma). Against it he sets the fierce love of Kannappar, the famous hunter-saint who gladly offered his own eyes to God.

translit: ēlār maṉaitoṟumpōy ēṟṟelumpun tēyaneṭuṅ kālāyt tirintuḻaluṅ kālkaṇṭāy - mālākit toṇṭē valañceykaḻal tōṉṟalē niṉkōyil kaṇṭē valamceyyāk kāl.
translation: These feet wander endlessly, begging at the houses of the uncharitable until their bones wear away. O Lord whose ankleted feet are served by Vishnu with deep devotion, these are the feet that fail to circumambulate your temple upon seeing it.
commentary: Look how much human strength goes into mere survival. People walk until their bones wear out, begging favors from the uncharitable, yet will not take a few simple steps around God's temple in reverence.

translit: ēcum piṟarmaṉaiyil ēṅka-avar īyumaraik kācum peṟavirikkum kaikaṇṭāy - mācunta viṇṭuñ ciraṅkuṉikkum vittakaṉē niṉtalattaik kaṇṭuñ ciraṅkuviyāk kai.
translation: These hands stretch out in yearning to receive a mere half-coin from those who scold me at their houses. O wise Lord before whom Vishnu bows his head to dispel his blemishes, these are the hands that fail to join in reverence above the head upon seeing your sacred shrine.
commentary: We stretch out our hands readily for pennies from people who insult us. Those same hands, Vallalar notes, stay stubbornly at our sides before the divine and will not fold together above the head in worship.

translit: veṅkōṭai ātapattiṉ vīḻnīr vaṟantularntu maṅkōṭai yātal vaḻakkaṉṟō - eṅkōniṉ cīrcintāc cēvaṭiyiṉ cīrkēṭṭum āṉanta nīrcintā vaṉkaṇ nilai.
translation: Is it not natural for a stream to dry up and vanish in the fierce heat of summer? O my King, such is the state of my cruel eyes. Even after hearing the glory of your perfect, red feet, they do not shed tears of bliss.
commentary: In the Tamil tradition, real devotion runs deep in the heart and often shows itself in tears of pure joy. Vallalar likens eyes that stay dry on hearing of God's greatness to a shallow stream vanishing in the summer heat. He calls them cruel because they have shut themselves off from love.

translit: vāyaṉṟēl vemmalañcel vāyaṉṟēl mānaraka vāyaṉṟēl valveṟināy vāyeṉpām - tāyeṉṟē ūḻttātā ēttum uṭaiyāy civa-eṉṟē vāḻttātār nāṟṟappāḻ vāy.
translation: O Master whom the ancient Creator praises as Mother. The foul and ruined mouth of those who do not praise you by chanting "Siva" is not a mouth. It is the passage where foul excrement exits. It is the gate to the great hell. We will call it the mouth of a fierce mad dog.
commentary: The voice is meant for praising God. A mouth that never speaks the sacred name of Siva loses all its dignity, and Vallalar is blunt about what it becomes: a passage for bodily waste, a gateway to hell, the foaming mouth of a mad dog. The body has value only when it is turned toward the divine.

translit: vīṭṭār iṟainī viṭaimēl varumpavaṉi kāṭṭā taṭaitta katavaṉṟō - nāṭṭāti nallat tuḷaiyā naticcaṭaiyāy eṉṉuñcīrc cellat tuḷaiyāc cevi.
translation: O Lord of the liberated. The ear that does not let in the glorious praise chanting, "O Lord with the river in your matted hair, O Origin of the worlds", is truly a closed door. It shuts out the sight of your procession arriving upon the bull.
commentary: The ear is there to take in sacred praise. One that refuses to hear God's glory is nothing but a locked door. Keep it shut, and we close ourselves off from the arrival of God's grace in our lives.

translit: pullaṅ kaṇanīrp puḻaiyeṉkō puṟṟeṉkō collum pacumaṭ ṭuḷaiyeṉkō - colluñcīr vīyāta piññakappēr melliṉattiṉ nallicaitāṉ tōyāta nācit tuḷai.
translation: The nostril that does not soak in the sweet music of the soft syllables of your unfading, glorious name, Piññaka. Shall I call it a worthless hole leaking mucus? Shall I call it an anthill? Or shall I call it a mere hole poked in wet clay?
commentary: Even the breath belongs to devotion. Piññaka is a name for Siva that refers to his matted hair. A nose that does not draw in the sweet rhythm of this name is a hole poked in wet clay, or a hollow anthill leaking mucus. Without that spiritual breath, the body is empty clay.

translit: tōṟṟamilāk kaṇṇuñ cuvaiyuṇarā nāvutikaḻ nāṟṟam aṟiyāta nāciyumōr - māṟṟamuntāṉ kēḷāc ceviyuṅkoḷ kīḻmukamē nīṟṟaṇitāṉ mūḷātu pāḻtta mukam.
translation: The ruined face that does not wear the holy ash is a base face holding blind eyes, a tongue that tastes nothing, a nose that smells no fragrance, and ears that hear no word.
commentary: Holy ash worn on the face is a visible sign of reverence. A face without it is spiritually dead. Its eyes, ears and nose may work perfectly, yet they are blind, deaf and numb, because they fail to perceive the divine reality right in front of them.

translit: māṉṟām ulaka vaḻakkiṉ paṭimatittu mūṉṟā vakirntē muṭaināṟa - ūṉṟā malakkūṭai ēṟṟukiṉu māṇātē teṉpāl talakkūṭal tāḻāt talai.
translation: The head that does not bow down in the southern shrine of Kudal will never become worthy, even if one follows confused worldly customs, parts the hair in three ways, and carries a foul-smelling basket of filth upon it.
commentary: Bowing in humility before the divine is the highest use of the head. Kudal is an ancient name for the sacred southern city of Madurai. People spend great effort grooming their hair and following vain worldly fashions, and without reverence all that care only decorates a temporary basket of decaying flesh.

translit: kalleṉkō nīraṭaikkuṅ kalleṉkō kāṉkoḷkaruṅ kalleṉkō kāḻvayirak kalleṉkō - colleṉkō iṉṟā leṉilō eṭuttāḷem mīṉṟāṇēr niṉtāḷ niṉaiyāta neñcu.
translation: Shall I call it a stone? A stone that dams water? A black stone of the forest? A hard diamond stone? What shall I say? The heart that does not think of your feet, which uplifted and ruled me like the mother who bore me.
commentary: A heart that forgets the grace nurturing us like a mother is as cold and lifeless as rock. Vallalar cannot even settle on which hard stone fits it best. God's feet stand for that uplifting, maternal compassion.

translit: collukiṉṟa uḷḷuyiraic cōrvuṟ ṟiṭakkuḷirntu kollukiṉṟa nañcil koṭitaṉṟō - ollumaṉṟat temmāṉiṉ tāṭkamala meṇṇātu pāḻvayiṟṟil cummā aṭaikkiṉṟa cōṟu.
translation: The food aimlessly stuffed into the ruined stomach without thinking of the lotus feet of our Lord in the fitting hall is surely crueler than the cold poison that weakens and kills the inner life breath.
commentary: Eating merely to satisfy physical hunger without remembering the divine is worse than swallowing deadly poison. Mindlessly stuffing food into the stomach kills the inner spiritual life just as surely as cold venom kills the body. The fitting hall refers to the space of divine presence where grace is found.

translit: cōrpaṭaittuc cōṟeṉṟāl toṇṭaivikkik koṇṭunaṭu mārpaṭaittuc cāvukiṉum mānaṉṟē - cīrpaṭaikka eṇṇuvār eṇṇum iṟaivāniṉ tāḷēttā tuṇṇuvār uṇṇum iṭattu.
translation: O Lord meditated upon by those who seek excellence! It is far better to grow weak, ask for rice, choke in the throat, and die of a blocked chest, than to eat in the home of those who eat without praising your feet.
commentary: Starving to death is a better fate than sharing a meal with those who live without gratitude for the divine. Vallalar would rather choke on a handful of begged rice than eat in the home of someone who ignores God. Whom we share food with touches our own inner life directly.

translit: ōkō koṭitē uṟumpulaiyar illiṉiṭat tēkō vataittuṇ ceyalaṉṟō - vākōrtam vāḻmaṉaiyil cellātu vaḷḷaṉiṉai ēttātār pāḻmaṉaiyil ceṉṟuṇ patu.
translation: Alas, how cruel! Going to eat in the ruined house of those who do not praise you, the generous Lord, instead of going to the prosperous houses of the virtuous, is surely like the act of going to the home of the base ones who slaughter and eat.
commentary: Sharing food with people who lack devotion is as spiritually destructive as taking part in the violent slaughter of animals. Real prosperity belongs to the homes of the virtuous who praise God. Choosing to eat in a godless house brings the stain of deep cruelty onto oneself.

translit: vīyumiṭu kāṭṭakattuḷ vēmpiṇattiṉ ventacaiyaip pēyumuṭaṉ uṇṇa-uṇṇum pēṟaṉṟō - tōyumayal nīṅka-aruḷ ceyvōyveṇṇīṟaṇiyār tīmaṉaiyil āṅkavarō ṭuṇṇu matu.
translation: O Lord who grants grace to dispel clinging delusion! Eating in the evil house with those who do not wear the sacred white ash is exactly like the fate of eating the burnt flesh of a blazing corpse in the cremation ground alongside ghosts.
commentary: Eating with those who abandon spiritual practice is as horrifying as feasting on a burnt corpse in a graveyard among ghosts. The sacred white ash is the traditional mark of devotion and purity. Sit close with people lost in delusion and your own clarity clouds over.

translit: kaṇkuḻaintu vāṭum kaṭunarakiṉpēruraikkil oṇkuḻantai yēṉumulai uṇṇātāl - taṇkuḻaiya pūṇṭātārk koṉṟaip puricaṭaiyōy niṉpukaḻai vēṇṭātār vīḻntu viraintu.
translation: If one speaks the name of the fierce hell where eyes grow weary and wither, even a bright infant will stop feeding at the breast. O Lord wearing cool ear-ornaments and a braided matted hair adorned with golden konrai garlands! Those who do not desire your glory will swiftly fall into that hell.
commentary: The hell awaiting those who turn from God is so terrible that its name alone would make a nursing infant stop feeding. Vallalar chooses that image to show how dangerous it is to ignore the divine presence.

translit: kaṇṇutalē niṉtāḷ karutārai nēcikka eṇṇutalē ceyyēṉmaṟ ṟeṇṇuvaṉēl - maṇṇulakil āmiṭattu niṉṉaṭiyārk kācaiyurait tillaiyeṉpār pōmiṭattiṟ pōvēṉ pularntu.
translation: O Lord with an eye on the forehead! I will never even think of loving those who do not meditate on your feet. If I ever hold such a thought, let me wither and go to the place destined for those on earth who raise the hopes of your devotees and then deny them.
commentary: A sincere seeker keeps the heart well away from anyone who does not revere God. Vallalar treats crossing that line as a grave failure. For himself he would ask the same fate as those who raise the hopes of true devotees and then betray them.

translit: aṅkaṇaṉē niṉṉaṭikkōr aṉpilaraic cārntōrtam vaṅkaṇamēvaippatiṉāṉ vaittēṉēl - aṅkaṇattil nīrpōl eṉatu nilaikeṭuka niṟpaḻicoṟ ṟārpō laḻika taḷarntu.
translation: O gracious Lord! I will never maintain friendship with those who associate with people lacking love for your feet. If I do keep such company, let my state perish like water poured into a drain. Let me grow weary and be destroyed like those who speak blame against you.
commentary: Vallalar draws the line further still. He refuses friendship even with those who merely keep company with people who lack love for God. Losing that protection wastes a life completely, like clean water poured away into a drain.

translit: pūvaiviṭṭup pulleṭuppār pōluṉ tiruppātat tēvaiviṭṭu vempiṟavit tēvarkaḷaik - kōvaiyiṭṭuk kūvuvār maṟṟavaraik kūṭiyiṭēṉ kūṭuvaṉēl ōvuvā rāvaluṉai.
translation: Like people discarding flowers to pluck grass, some abandon the service of your holy feet to string together praises for gods bound by cruel birth. I will not associate with them. If I do join them, my longing for you will cease.
commentary: Worshipping lesser deities instead of the supreme Lord is as foolish as throwing away beautiful flowers to pick common grass. These minor gods are themselves still trapped in the cycle of physical birth and death, making them unable to offer true spiritual liberation. Keeping company with people who settle for such a poor substitute would only wear away a seeker's longing for the true divine.

translit: yātō kaṉaṟkaṇ yamatūtar kāyccukarun tātō taḻaṟpiḻampō tāṉaṟiyēṉ - mītōṅku nāṭṭārtārk koṉṟai naticcaṭaiyōy añceḻuttai nāṭṭātār vāykku nalam.
translation: O Lord whose matted hair bears the river and the konrai garland praised by the exalted people! I do not know what awaits the mouths of those who do not establish the five letters. Is it the fire-eyed messengers of Yama, or the black iron they heat up, or a mass of flames? I truly do not know.
commentary: The "five letters" are Na-ma-ci-vā-ya, the central five-syllable mantra of devotion to Lord Siva. A mouth that never speaks it faces a terrible fate at the hands of Yama, the god of death. The fire and hot iron picture the agony of a life lived without remembering the divine.

translit: eṉṉeñcōr kōyil eṉakkoṇṭōy niṉniṉaiyār taṉṉeñcō kallāmac cāmpiṇattār - vaṉneñcil cārntavarkkum maṟṟavarait tāṉōkki vārttaicola nērntavarkkum kallākum neñcu.
translation: You have made my heart a temple. The hearts of those who do not think of You are stones, and they are dead corpses. The hearts of those who associate with such hard-hearted people, and the hearts of those who look at them and happen to speak with them, will also turn to stone.
commentary: God's presence makes a loving heart into a temple. Without the thought of God, a heart hardens to stone and the person walks around like a corpse. Even a casual word with such people is risky, because their hardness slowly creeps into your own heart.

translit: veḷḷamutum tēṉum viyaṉkarumpum mukkaṉiyiṉ uḷḷamutum teḷḷamutum ovvātāl kaḷḷamilā niṉṉaṉpar tampukaḻiṉ nīḷmaturan taṉṉai-iṉi eṉṉeṉpa taiyā iyampu.
translation: Pure nectar, honey, grand sugarcane, the sweet essence of the three fruits, and clear nectar cannot compare to the deep sweetness of the glory of Your deceitless devotees. O Lord, tell me what to call it now.
commentary: Tamil poetry has its standard measures of sweetness: honey, sugarcane, the essence of the three fruits (mango, jackfruit, and banana), and heavenly nectar. Every one of them falls short of the glory of sincere devotees. Praising those who love God without deceit gives a joy Vallalar cannot even name.

translit: paṇṇāluṉ cīriṉaiccam pantarcola veḷḷelumpu peṇṇāṉa teṉpār peritaṉṟē - aṇṇā-ac caivavaṭi vāñāṉa campantar cīruraikkil teyvavaṭi vāñcāmpar cērntu.
translation: People say that when Sambandar sang Your glory in musical verse, white bones turned into a woman. That is no great feat, O Lord. If one speaks the glory of Sambandar who is the embodiment of Saiva wisdom, even ashes will gather and take a divine form.
commentary: Tradition tells how the child saint Sambandar sang a hymn that turned cremated bones back into a living girl. Vallalar calls that miracle no great feat. Sambandar is wisdom embodied, and merely speaking his praise could make scattered ashes gather into a divine form.

translit: eṅkōvē yāṉpukali emperumāṉ taṉmaṇattil aṅkōr poruṭcumaiyāḷ āṉēṉēl - iṅkēniṉ tāḷvarunta vēṇṭēṉ taṭaipaṭṭēṉ ātaliṉin nāḷvarunta vēṇṭukiṉṟēṉ nāṉ.
translation: My King! If I had been a bearer of provisions there at the wedding of our Lord of Pukali, I would not need to trouble Your feet here. Since I was hindered from that, I am forced to suffer and entreat You today.
commentary: The Lord of Pukali is the saint Sambandar, whose life ended when a divine fire appeared at his wedding and absorbed everyone present into liberation. Vallalar wishes he had been there, even as a humble servant carrying supplies. Having missed that chance, he must suffer in this world and beg for grace today.

translit: pūvuk karaiyarumvāṉ puṅkavarum pōṟṟutiru nāvuk karaiyareṉu naṉṉāma - mēvuṟṟa toṇṭarkku nīkaṭṭuc cōṟeṭuttāy eṉṟaṟintō toṇṭarkkut toṇṭaṉeṉpār col.
translation: You carried packed food for the devotee who bears the good name Tirunāvukkaraiyar, who is praised by Brahma on the lotus and the heavenly celestials. Tell me, is it because they knew this that people call You the servant of Your servants?
commentary: Tradition says God took on a disguise to carry packed food for the exhausted saint Tirunavukkaraiyar on a long journey. Vallalar marvels at such humility in the divine. He wonders whether this is why people call God the servant of his own servants, seeing how far the Lord goes for those who love him.

translit: emparavaiyōmaṇ ṇiṭantalaintāṉ cuntaraṉār tamparavai vīṭṭut talaikkaṭaiyāy - vempaṇaiyāy vāyiṟ paṭiyāy vaṭiveṭukka nērntilaṉē māyappeyar nīṇṭa māl.
translation: The tall Vishnu of illusory names dug the earth and wandered endlessly. Yet he never got the chance to take the form of the front entrance, the warm bed, or the doorstep in the house of Sundarar's wife Paravai.
commentary: Legend says Vishnu took the form of a boar and dug through the earth to find the bottom of Siva's fiery column, and failed completely. For his beloved devotee Sundarar, though, Siva humbled himself to act as a mere messenger, waiting at the doorway of Sundarar's wife Paravai. The intimacy Siva offers his true devotees lies far beyond the reach of the other gods.

translit: naṇṇit talaiyāl naṭakkiṉṟōm eṉpateṅkaḷ maṇṇil paḻaiya vaḻakkaṅkāṇ - paṇṇiṟcol ammaiyār vāmattōy āyiṉumuṉ kāraikkāl ammaiyār pōṉaṭantār ār.
translation: Saying we walk forward on our heads is an old custom on our earth. You hold the Mother of musical words on your left side. Yet who has ever walked on their head like the Mother of Karaikkal did before you?
commentary: Karaikkal Ammaiyar, one of the earliest poet-saints, is said to have traveled to Siva's home at Mount Kailash walking on her head, refusing to defile the holy ground with her feet. People speak of walking on their heads as a figure of reverence. She actually did it. Vallalar looks at that total surrender and asks whether anyone else has ever matched it.

translit: vēta muṭivō viḷaṅkā kamamuṭivō nāta muṭivō navilkaṇṭāy - vātamuṟu mācakarkkuḷ nillā maṇiccuṭarē māṇikka vācakarkku nī-uraitta vāṟu.
