O experience of the ripened Supreme of knowledge and bliss. O King of the dance, ripening as the Supreme in the space of consciousness. O celestial tree bearing the ripened fruit of compassion. O God of the wealth of grace, ripening and growing sweet every day within the yoga of yogis who have matured in the strength of supreme wisdom.
commentary: Ripening runs through every line. God is the fully ripened fruit of all spiritual searching, the sweet end of the seeker's effort, whether that effort is truth, wisdom, or the inner stillness of yoga (spiritual discipline). Most of all God is the ripe fruit of compassion, growing sweeter every day in the hearts of those who practice supreme wisdom.

translit: aṇṭamelām kaṇṇākak koḷiṉum kāṇṭaṟ kaṇuttuṇaiyum kūṭāveṉ ṟaṉanta vētam viṇṭalaṟi ōlamiṭṭup pulampa mōṉa veḷikkuḷveḷi yāyniṟaintu viḷaṅkum oṉṟē kaṇṭavaṭi vāyakaṇṭa mayamāy eṅkum kalantuniṉṟa peruṅkaruṇaik kaṭavu ḷē-em caṇṭaviṉait toṭakkaṟacciṉ mayattaik kāṭṭum caṟkuruvē civakuruvē cāntat tēvē.
translation: The endless scriptures cry out, roar, and lament that even if one turned all the universes into eyes, they could not perceive you even an atom's worth. O One who fills and shines as the space within the space of silence. O God of immense compassion who takes visible forms while remaining the boundless whole, mingling everywhere. O true Guru who reveals the nature of pure consciousness to sever the bonds of our fierce karma. O supreme Guru. O God of peace.
commentary: The ancient scriptures confess they cannot see even an atom of God, however hard they look. The divine is found instead as the vast silence within silence. As the true guru (spiritual teacher), God reveals the soul's own pure awareness and cuts through the fierce bonds of karma (the accumulated consequences of past actions).

translit: pētamuṟā meyppōta vaṭiva mākip peruṅkaruṇai niṟampaḻuttuc cāntam poṅkic cītamikun taruḷkaṉintu kaṉintu māṟac ciṉmayamāy niṉmalamē maṇantu nīṅkā ātaravō ṭiyaṉmavuṉac cuvaimēṉ mēṟkoṇ ṭāṉanta racamoḻukki aṉpāl eṉṟum cētamuṟā taṟiñaruḷan tittit tōṅkum ceḻumpuṉitak koḻuṅkaṉiyē tēva tēvē.
translation: Taking the form of non-dual true wisdom, you ripen with the color of immense compassion, overflow with peace, cool profoundly, and ripen deeply with grace. You transform into pure consciousness and emit the fragrance of flawless purity. With unceasing affection and the ever-growing taste of natural silence, you drip the essence of bliss. You forever taste sweet and flourish with love in the indestructible hearts of the wise. O rich, sacred, and luscious fruit. O God of gods.
commentary: Wisdom here is alive, colored by immense compassion and brimming with peace. As the soul grows in silence and pure awareness, it tastes God as a sweet, nourishing fruit. That sweetness never fades in the indestructible hearts of the wise.

translit: uṭalkuḷira uyirtaḻaikka uṇarcci ōṅka uḷaṅkaṉiya meyyaṉpar uḷḷat tūṭē kaṭalaṉaiya pēriṉpam tuḷumpa nāḷum karuṇaimalart tēṉpoḻiyum kaṭavuṭ kāvē viṭalariya empōlvār itayan tōṟum vētānta maruntaḷikkum viruntē vētam toṭalariya veḷimuḻutum paravi ñāṉac cōtivirit toḷirkiṉṟa cōtit tēvē.
translation: O divine grove pouring down the honey of the flower of compassion daily within the hearts of true devotees, cooling their bodies, making their lives flourish, heightening their awareness, and ripening their hearts so that supreme bliss overflows like an ocean. O feast offering the medicine of Vedanta in every heart of people like us who are hard to leave behind. O Deity of Light shining and expanding the light of wisdom, spreading across the entirely unreachable space.
commentary: The divine presence is a living force that brings deep physical and spiritual relief to the true devotee. It pours down the honey of compassion, healing the heart with the ultimate truths of scripture (Vedanta) and filling unreachable spaces with the light of wisdom.

translit: kiriyaineṟi akaṟṟimaṟai muṭivil niṉṟu kēḷāmal kēṭkiṉṟa kēḷvi yēcoṟ kariyavaṟai viṭuttunava nilaikku mēlē kāṇāmaṟ kāṇkiṉṟa kāṭciyē uḷ ariyanilai oṉṟiraṇṭiṉ naṭuvē caṟṟum aṟiyāmal aṟikiṉṟa aṟivē eṉṟum uriyacatā nilainiṉṟa uṇarcci mēlōr uṉṉāmal uṉṉukiṉṟa oḷiyām tēvē.
translation: Removing the path of rituals and standing at the crown of the Vedas, you are the sound heard without hearing. Leaving behind the chamber that defies words and rising above the nine states, you are the vision seen without seeing. In the rare inner state between one and two, you are the knowledge known without knowing in the slightest. O Deity of Light, thought of without thinking by the exalted ones of awareness who eternally stand in their rightful permanent state.
commentary: True spiritual realization leaves physical senses and religious rituals entirely behind. The divine is experienced directly through pure awareness: a sound heard without physical hearing, a vision seen without physical sight, and a truth known without the active effort of the mind.

translit: coṟpōtaṟ karumperiya maṟaikaḷ nāṭit toṭarntutoṭarn tayarntiḷaittut tuḷaṅki ēṅkip piṟpōta viraintaṉpar uḷattē ceṉṟa peruṅkaruṇaip peruvāḻvē peyarā teṉṟum taṟpōta oḻiviṉiṭai niṟaintu poṅkit tatumpivaḻin tōṅkiyellān tāṉē yākic ciṟpōtat takampuṟamum kōttu niṉṟa civāṉantap perukkēmeyc celvat tēvē.
translation: The great Vedas, hard to reach through words, sought you, pursued you constantly, grew tired, exhausted, bewildered, and yearned. As they fell behind, you rushed into the hearts of devotees, O great life of immense compassion. Remaining forever unmoving, you fill the void where self-awareness ends, swelling, overflowing, surging, and becoming everything yourself. O flood of divine bliss threading the inside and outside of supreme wisdom, O Deity of true wealth.
commentary: The grandest scriptures chase God in words until they tire out and fall behind. Meanwhile He has already run into the hearts of those who love Him. That bliss fills only the space left once the self is wiped out completely.

translit: poṅkupala camayameṉum natika ḷellām pukuntukalan tiṭaniṟaivāyp poṅki ōṅkum kaṅkukarai kāṇāta kaṭalē eṅkum kaṇṇākak kāṇkiṉṟa katiyē aṉpar taṅkaniḻal parappimayal cōṭai yellān taṇikkiṉṟa taruvēpūn taṭamē ñāṉac ceṅkumuta malaravaru matiyē ellām ceyyavalla kaṭavuḷē tēva tēvē.
translation: All the surging rivers of various religions enter and merge into you as you swell and rise up in fullness, O limitless shoreless ocean. O refuge seeing everywhere as an eye. O tree spreading a golden shade to cool all the exhaustion of delusion. O flower-filled pond. O moon arriving to make the red water-lily of wisdom bloom. O God capable of doing everything, God of gods.
commentary: The world's many religions are only rivers that in the end empty into the shoreless ocean of the divine. Once they merge into this vastness, their separate boundaries disappear entirely. He is also the refuge, a tree whose golden shade cools a mind worn out by delusion.

translit: vāṉkāṇā maṟaikāṇā malarōṉ kāṇāṉ mālkāṇāṉ uruttiraṉum matittuk kāṇāṉ nāṉkāṇā iṭattataṉaik kāṇpēm eṉṟu nallōrkaḷ navilkiṉṟa nalamē vēṭkai māṉkāṇā uḷakkamala malarttā niṉṟa vāṉcuṭarē āṉanta mayamē īṉṟa āṉkāṇā iḷaṅkaṉṟāy alaman tēṅkum aṉpartamaik kalantukoḷum amalat tēvē.
translation: The sky cannot see you, the Vedas cannot see you, Brahma on the lotus cannot see you, Vishnu cannot see you, and Rudra cannot conceive and see you. You are the goodness the virtuous speak of, saying they will see you in the place where 'I' is unseen. O heavenly flame blooming the heart-lotus unseen by the deer of desire. O embodiment of bliss. O flawless God who unites with devotees who wander and yearn like a young calf unable to find the mother cow.
commentary: The gods who create, preserve and destroy (Brahma, Vishnu, and Rudra) cannot see Him. The good say He is found only where the 'I' goes unseen. When a devotee frets like a calf that cannot find its mother, God comes and unites with them, flawless.

translit: meyññāṉa viruppattil ēṟik kēḷvi mītēṟit teḷinticcai viṭutal ēṟi aññāṉa maṟṟapaṭi ēṟi uṇmai aṟintapaṭi nilai-ēṟi atunāṉ eṉṉum kaiññāṉaṅ kaḻaṉṟēṟi maṟṟa ellām kaṭantēṟi mavuṉaviyaṟ katiyil ēṟi eññāṉam aṟatteḷintōr kaṇṭuṅ kāṇēm eṉkiṉṟa anupavamē iṉpat tēvē.
translation: Ascending in the desire for true knowledge, ascending further through listening and gaining clarity, ascending by abandoning desire, ascending as ignorance is destroyed, ascending to the state of knowing the truth, ascending by shedding the limited knowledge that claims "I am That," ascending by transcending all else, and ascending to the state of absolute silence. Those who have completely cleared away all conditioned knowledge reach this state. Even having seen it, they declare, "We have not seen it." O God of bliss, You are this very experience.
commentary: Vallalar lays out a ladder, and each rung sheds some form of human knowing. Desire goes, ignorance goes, and finally even the old spiritual claim "I am That." At the top is a silence so complete that those who reach it say they have not seen it.

translit: paṟṟaṟiyā muttartamai ellām vāḻaip paḻampōla viḻuṅkukiṉṟa paramē mācu peṟṟaṟiyāp perumpatamē patattaik kāṭṭum perumāṉē āṉantap pēṟṟiṉ vāḻvē uṟṟaṟiyā tiṉṉumiṉṉum maṟaika ḷellām ōlamiṭṭut tēṭaniṉṟa oṉṟē oṉṟum kaṟṟaṟiyāp pētaiyēṉ taṉakkum iṉpam kaṉintaḷitta aruṭkaṭalē karuṇait tēvē.
translation: O Supreme who swallows like a ripe banana all the liberated beings who know no attachment! O great state that has never known a blemish! O Lord who reveals this state! O life of blissful attainment! O One whom all the Vedas still search for with loud cries, unable to reach and know You! O ocean of grace who tenderly bestowed bliss even to an ignorant fool like me who has learned nothing! O God of compassion!
commentary: Learning does not get you there. The Vedas (ancient sacred texts) still cry out searching for Him, while He tenderly gives bliss to an untaught fool like Vallalar. Liberated souls free of attachment He swallows as easily as a ripe banana.

translit: meyyuṇarnta vātavūr malaiyaic cutta veḷiyākkik kalantukoṇṭa veḷiyē muṟṟum poyyuṇarnta emaippōlvār tamakkum iṉpam purintaruḷum karuṇaiveḷḷap poṟpē aṉpar kaiyuṟaintu vaḷarnellik kaṉiyē uḷḷam karaintukarain turuka-avar karutti ṉūṭē uyyuneṟi oḷikāṭṭi veḷiyum uḷḷum ōṅkukiṉṟa cuyañcuṭarē uṇmait tēvē.
translation: O Space that turned the truth-realizing mountain of Vadavur into pure space and merged with him! O golden flood of compassion that grants bliss even to beings like me who have known only falsehood! O gooseberry fruit resting in the hands of devotees! As their hearts melt and melt away, You show the light of the saving path within their thoughts. O self-luminous flame rising both inside and outside! O God of truth!
commentary: The divine light makes itself perfectly clear to those whose hearts melt with devotion. Vallalar uses the image of a gooseberry resting in the palm of the hand, a traditional idiom for something undeniable and plain to see. He recalls how God merged with the saint of Vadavur (the great poet Manikkavasagar), turning his physical body into pure space, and says this same compassionate grace saves even those who have lived in falsehood.

translit: olivaṭivu niṟañcuvaikaḷ nāṟṟam ūṟṟam uṟutoḻilkaḷ payaṉpalavē ṟuḷavāy eṅkum malivakaiyāy evvakaiyum oṉṟāy oṉṟum māṭṭātāy ellāmum valla tākic calivakaiyil lātamutaṟ poruḷē ellām taṉmayamāy viḷaṅkukiṉṟa taṉiyē āṇpeṇ alivakaiyal lātavakai kaṭantu niṉṟa aruṭcivamē civapōkat tamainta tēvē.
translation: You exist abundantly everywhere as forms of sound, colors, tastes, smells, tangible sensations, actions, and various outcomes. You are one with everything, yet You remain untouched by anything. O First Principle, capable of all things and free from any wavering! O Unique One who shines as the essence of all things! O Grace-Siva who stands beyond the categories of male, female, and intersex! O God established in the bliss of Siva!
commentary: Every sound, color, taste, smell and touch is God, every action and every result too, yet nothing touches Him. He shines as the essence of all things. Vallalar places this Grace-Siva beyond male, female, and intersex.

translit: pērāya aṇṭaṅkaḷ palavum piṇṭa pētaṅkaḷ paṟpalavum piṇṭāṇ ṭattiṉ vārāya palaporuḷum kaṭalum maṇṇum malaiyuḷavum kaṭaluḷavum maṇalum vāṉum ūrāta vāṉmīṉum aṇuvum maṟṟai uḷḷaṉavum aḷantiṭalām ōkō uṉṉai ārālum aḷappariteṉ ṟaṉanta vētam aṟaintiḷaikka atitūra mākun tēvē.
translation: One can measure the many great universes, the countless variations of bodies, the many objects that exist beyond bodies and universes, the sea, the earth, the things upon the mountains, the things within the sea, the sand, the sky, the stationary stars in the sky, the atom, and all other existing things. Oh, countless Vedas speak until they grow weary, declaring that You are immeasurable by anyone. O God who remains infinitely far away!
commentary: You can measure the universe down to the atom, count the stars and the grains of sand. God cannot be measured by anyone. The Vedas (ancient scriptures) wear themselves out trying, and He stays infinitely beyond their reach.

translit: kaṟpaṅkaḷ palakōṭi cellat tīya kaṉaliṉaṭu ūciyiṉmēl kālai ūṉṟip poṟpaṟamey uṇaviṉṟi uṟakka miṉṟip pularntelumpu pulappaṭa-aim poṟiyai ōmpi niṟpavaruk koḷittumaṟaik koḷittu yōka nīṇmuṉivark koḷittamarark koḷittu mēlām ciṟpatattil ciṉmayamāy niṟaintu ñāṉat tiruvāḷar uṭkalanta tēva tēvē.
translation: For many crores of aeons, people stand on one foot atop a needle amidst fierce fire. Their bodies lose all beauty. They go without food and sleep. They wither until their bones show as they subdue the five senses. You hide from those who stand in such severe penance. You hide from the Vedas. You hide from the great sages of yoga. You hide from the immortals. Yet You fill the supreme state of consciousness as pure awareness, mingling within the hearts of the wise masters of gnosis, O God of gods!
commentary: Standing on a needle amid fire for countless aeons, starving until the bones show, will not reach God. He hides from such penance, from the scriptures, from the sages of yoga and from the immortals. He fills instead the hearts of those who have come to true wisdom and pure awareness.

translit: maṭṭakaṉṟa neṭuṅkālam maṉattāl vākkāl matittiṭiṉum pulampiṭiṉum vārā teṉṟē kaṭṭakaṉṟa meyyaṟivōr karaṇam nīkkik kalaiyakaṟṟik karuviyelām kaḻaṟṟi māyai viṭṭakaṉṟu karumamala pōtam yāvum viṭuttoḻittuc cakacamala vīkkam nīkkic cuṭṭakaṉṟu niṟka-avar tammai muṟṟum cūḻntukalan tiṭuñcivamē turiyat tēvē.
translation: Knowing You will not come even if praised and lamented in mind and word for a boundless eternity, the true knowers who have shed attachments set aside their inner instruments. They remove the arts. They detach all faculties and leave maya far behind. They completely discard karma, impurity, and intellectual pride. They remove the swelling of the innate ego and stand free of all objectifying thought. Then You completely surround and merge with them, O Sivam, O God of the transcendent state!
commentary: No amount of prayer or pleading, in mind or in word, will bring God to you. Those who truly know understand this, so they strip away the ego, intellectual pride, the illusion of the material world (maya), and the weight of past actions (karma). When the mind stops making God an object of thought, the supreme reality (Sivam) surrounds them and merges with them completely.

translit: urunāṉkum arunāṉkum naṭuvē niṉṟa uru-aruva moṉṟumivai uṭaṉmēl uṟṟa orunāṉkum ivaikaṭanta oṉṟu māyav voṉṟiṉaṭu vāynaṭuvuḷ oṉṟāy niṉṟē irunāṉkum amaintavarai nāṉki ṉōṭum eṇṇāṉkiṉ mēliruttum iṟaiyē māyaik karunāṉkum poruṇāṉkum kāṭṭu mukkaṭ kaṭavuḷē kaṭavuḷarkaḷ karutun tēvē.
translation: You are the four forms with shape, the four formless ones, and the single form-formless one in the middle. You are the four above these and the One beyond them all. You stand in the center of that One, and as the One within the center! O Lord who establishes those equipped with the eight qualities above the thirty-six principles! O three-eyed God who reveals the four wombs of maya and the four substances! O God meditated upon by the gods!
commentary: God is every state of being: the forms, the formless, and what lies beyond both. He lifts pure souls above the thirty-six principles that make up the universe. From the very center of reality He moves outward into every shape, physical and spiritual.

translit: pāṅkuḷanām teritumeṉat tuṇintu kōṭip paḻamaṟaikaḷ taṉittaṉiyē pāṭip pāṭi īṅkuḷateṉ ṟāṅkuḷateṉ ṟōṭi yōṭi iḷaittiḷaittut toṭarntutoṭarn teṭṭun tōṟum vāṅkupara veḷimuḻutum nīṇṭu nīṇṭu maṟaintumaṟain toḷikkiṉṟa maṇiyē eṅkum tēṅkupara māṉanta veḷḷa mēcac citāṉanta aruṭcivamē tēvē tēvē.
translation: Confidently declaring they will know Your nature, ten million ancient Vedas sing over and over. They run back and forth, claiming You are here and You are there. They grow exhausted, yet they continue to pursue You. Every time they reach out, You expand further and further across the entire supreme space, receding and hiding Yourself, O Gem! O flood of supreme bliss brimming everywhere! O Sivam of Grace manifesting as truth, consciousness, and bliss! O God of gods!
commentary: The ancient scriptures cannot capture the truth of God. Millions of texts try to define the divine, pointing here and there in exhaustion, but the divine presence always expands beyond their grasp. God is an endless flood of grace and bliss that recedes from intellectual pursuit and reveals itself only as infinite truth and consciousness.

translit: eḻuttaṟintu tamaiyuṇarnta yōkar uḷḷat tiyalaṟivām taruviṉilaṉ peṉumōr ucci paḻuttaḷintu mavuṉanaṟuñ cuvaimēṟ poṅkip patamporunta anupavikkum paḻamē māyaik kaḻuttarintu karumamalat talaiyai vīcum kaṭuntoḻilōr tamakkēnaṟ karuṇai kāṭṭi viḻuttuṇaiyāy amarntaruḷum poruḷē mōṉa veḷiyiṉiṟai āṉanta viḷaivān tēvē.
translation: In the tree of natural awareness within the hearts of yogis who have known the sacred letters and realized themselves, love ripens into a fruit at the very peak. Reaching the proper state, they experience this fruit overflowing with the fragrant taste of silence. O Fruit! Showing immense compassion to those of fierce resolve who sever the neck of maya and toss away the head of karmic impurity, You sit gracefully as their supreme companion, O Reality! O God who is the harvest of bliss filling the space of silence!
commentary: Awareness grows in the heart like a tree, and love is the fruit that ripens at its top. Seekers who fiercely cut away the world's illusions and their own impurities taste that fruit in deep, blissful silence. God then sits beside them as their closest companion and fills the silence with joy.

translit: uruttirarnā raṇarpiramar viṇṇōr vēntar uṟukaruṭar kāntaruvar iyakkar pūtar maruttuvaryō kiyarcittar muṉivar maṟṟai vāṉavarkaḷ mutalōrtam maṉattāl tēṭik karuttaḻintu taṉittaṉiyē ceṉṟu vētaṅ kaḷaiviṉava maṟṟavaiyuṅ kāṇēm eṉṟu varuttamuṟṟāṅ kavarōṭu pulampa niṉṟa vañcaveḷi yē-iṉpa mayamām tēvē.
translation: O elusive space, O God of pure bliss. Rudras, Vishnus, Brahmas, the king of the celestials, mighty Garudas, Gandharvas, Yakshas, Bhutas, Maruts, yogis, siddhas, sages, and other heavenly beings search for you with their minds. Exhausted in thought, they go one by one to ask the Vedas. The Vedas reply that they too have not seen you, and they stand there grieving and lamenting alongside them.
commentary: Every rank of heaven is in that list: Rudras, Vishnus, Brahmas, siddhas, sages and the rest. All of them search with the mind and come up empty. They go to the Vedas for help, and the Vedas admit they are just as lost and weep beside them. The divine is entirely beyond the reach of traditional deities, learned sages, and religious lore. Yet to those who approach with a loving heart, this elusive presence reveals itself as pure bliss.

translit: pāyiramā maṟai-aṉantam aṉantam iṉṉum pārttaḷantu kāṇṭumeṉap palkāṉ mēvi āyiramā yiramukaṅka ḷālum paṉṉāḷ aḷantaḷantōr aṇuttuṇaiyum aḷavu kāṇā tēyiraṅki aḻutuciva civaveṉ ṟēṅkit tirumpa-aruṭ paraveḷivāḻ civamē īṉṟa tāyiraṅki vaḷarppatupōl empōl vārait taṇṇaruḷāl vaḷartteṉṟum tāṅkun tēvē.
translation: O Siva who dwells in the supreme space of grace. The great endless Vedas approached you many times, thinking they could look, measure, and see you. For many days they measured and measured using thousands upon thousands of faces, but they could not find your measure even by the size of an atom. Despairing and weeping, they yearned, cried "Siva Siva", and retreated. O God, like a mother who gives birth to a child and raises it with tender care, you raise and endlessly support those like us with your cool grace.
commentary: The Vedas went at it with thousands of faces, measuring day after day, and could not find God's measure even by the size of an atom. They wept, cried "Siva Siva", and turned back. Ordinary devotees get a different welcome. Like a mother raising the child she bore, God raises those who come with simple love and holds them up with cool grace, and the complicated texts never enter into it.

translit: antaramiṅ kaṟivōmaṟ ṟataṉil aṇṭam aṭukkaṭukkāy amainta-uḷa vaṟivōm āṅkē untuṟumpal piṇṭanilai aṟivōñ cīvaṉ uṟṟanilai aṟivōmaṟ ṟaṉaittu nāṭṭum entainiṉa taruḷviḷaiyāṭ ṭantō antō eḷḷaḷavum aṟintilōm eṉṉē eṉṟu muntaṉanta maṟaikaḷelām vaḻutta niṉṟa muḻumutalē aṉparkuṟai muṭikkum tēvē.
translation: "We know the vast space here. We know the secret of how the universes are layered within it. We know the states of the many physical bodies evolving there. We know the states of the souls. But O our Father who established all this, alas, we do not comprehend even a sesame-seed measure of your divine play of grace." Saying so, all the ancient endless Vedas stand praising you. O absolute Supreme, O God who fulfills the needs of your devotees.
commentary: The Vedas know a great deal. They can explain cosmic space, the layering of universes, the states of bodies and of souls. Then they confess they do not grasp even a sesame seed's worth of the divine play of grace. That understanding belongs to the devotees, and their needs are met by a caring God directly, whatever the cosmic charts may say.

translit: tōṉṟupara cākkiramum kaṇṭōm antac coppaṉamum kaṇṭōmmēl cuḻutti kaṇṭōm āṉṟapara turiyanilai kaṇṭōm appāl atukaṇṭōm appālām atuvum kaṇṭōm ēṉṟa-upa cāntanilai kaṇṭōm appāl iruntaniṉaik kāṇkilōm eṉṉē eṉṟu cāṉṟavupa niṭaṅkaḷelām vaḻutta niṉṟa taṉmayamē ciṉmayamē cakacat tēvē.
translation: "We have seen the supreme waking state. We have seen the supreme dream state. We have seen the supreme deep sleep state. We have seen the exalted supreme fourth state. We have seen what lies beyond that. We have also seen what lies even further beyond. We have seen the profound state of absolute peace. Yet we do not see you who dwell beyond all these. How can this be?" Saying so, all the noble Upanishads stand praising you. O embodiment of reality, O embodiment of pure consciousness, O God who is our natural state.
commentary: The Upanishads, the philosophical texts of ancient India, claim to have seen every summit of awareness, from waking through dream and deep sleep to the fourth state and the absolute peace beyond it. Still they cannot find the One who dwells past all of it. Vallalar calls that One our natural state. It waits beyond every yogic achievement.

translit: parikkiraka nilaimuḻutun toṭarntōm mēlaip paravintu nilaiyaṉaittum pārttōm pācam erikkumiyaṟ paranāta nilaikkaṇ mella eytiṉōm appālum eṭṭip pōṉōm terikkariya veḷimūṉṟum terintōm eṅkum civamēniṉ ciṉmayamōr ciṟitum tēṟōm tarikkariteṉ ṟākamaṅka ḷellām pōṟṟat taṉiniṉṟa paramporuḷē cāntat tēvē.
translation: "We traced through all the encompassing states. We saw all the higher states of the supreme light. We gently reached the natural state of the supreme sound that burns away all bonds. We extended our reach even beyond that. We perceived the three incomprehensible spaces. Yet O Siva, nowhere do we comprehend even a fraction of your pure consciousness. You are impossible to grasp." Saying so, all the Agamas praise you. O Supreme Reality who stands without equal, O God of peace.
commentary: The Agamas, ancient manuals of ritual and spiritual practice, describe climbing through supreme light, through the supreme sound that burns away bonds, and into three spaces no one can perceive. After all that height they confess they cannot grasp a fraction of Siva's pure consciousness.

translit: maṇakkumalart tēṉuṇṭa vaṇṭē pōla vaḷarparamā ṉantamuṇṭu makiḻntōr ellām iṇakkamuṟak kalantukalan tatīta mātaṟ kiyaṟkainilai yātatutāṉ emmāṟ kūṟum kaṇakkuvaḻak kaṉaittiṉaiyum kaṭanta tantō kāṇparitiṅ kevarkkumeṉak kalaika ḷellām piṇakkaṟaniṉ ṟōlamiṭat taṉittu niṉṟa perumpatamē matātītap periya tēvē.
translation: Like bees that drank the nectar of fragrant flowers, all those who rejoiced by drinking the growing supreme bliss merge harmoniously and become the transcendent state. What is its natural condition? All scriptures lament in unison, crying out, "Alas, it has transcended all the accounts and descriptions we give! It is hard for anyone to perceive it here." You stand alone as the great state, O great God beyond religions.
commentary: The divine experience lies completely beyond the reach of language and holy books. The scriptures themselves admit they cannot capture or measure this supreme state. God exists entirely above and beyond all religions, offering a direct experience of bliss that words cannot contain.

translit: potuveṉṟum potuvilnaṭam puriyā niṉṟa pūraṇaciṟ civameṉṟum pōtā ṉanta matuveṉṟum piramameṉṟum parama meṉṟum vakukkiṉṟōr vakuttiṭuka atutāṉ eṉṟum ituveṉṟum cuṭṭavoṇā tataṉāl cummā iruppatuvē tuṇiveṉakkoṇ ṭirukkiṉ ṟōrai vituveṉṟataṇṇaḷiyāl kalantu koṇṭu viḷaṅkukiṉṟa peruveḷiyē vimalat tēvē.
translation: Let those who classify define it as the common space, the perfect conscious Siva dancing in that common space, the honey of wisdom and bliss, Brahman, or the Supreme. Since it can never be pointed out as this or that, some hold the conviction that simply remaining still is the way. You mingle with such people through your cool grace like the moon. You shine as the great expanse, O pure God.
commentary: Scholars and sects try to define the divine with names like Siva, the perfect consciousness, or Brahman, the supreme reality. Because the absolute truth cannot be boxed into these categories, the purest response is to remain perfectly still in mind and body. The divine light fills this absolute stillness with its cooling grace.

translit: arumaṟaiyā kamaṅkaḷmutal naṭuvī ṟellām amaintamaintu maṟṟavaikkum appā lākik karumaṟainta uyirkaḷtoṟuṅ kalantu mēvik kalavāmal paṉṉeṟiyum kaṭantu ñāṉat tirumaṇimaṉ ṟakattiṉpa uruvāy eṉṟum tikaḻkaruṇai naṭampuriyum civamē mōṉap perumalaiyē parama-iṉpa nilaiyē mukkaṭ perumāṉē ettiṟattum periya tēvē.
translation: You dwell in the beginning, middle, and end of the rare Vedas and Agamas, yet you remain beyond them. You mingle and unite with all souls obscured by karma, yet you remain unattached. Transcending countless paths, you exist as the form of bliss within the holy gem hall of wisdom. O Siva who forever performs the dance of compassion! O great mountain of silence! O state of supreme bliss! O three-eyed Lord! O God great in every way.
commentary: God lives in the beginning, middle and end of the Vedas and Agamas and is still beyond them. The same Lord mingles with souls weighed down by karma, the burden of past actions, and stays untouched by that burden. Beyond countless paths, Siva dances the dance of compassion in the hall of wisdom.

translit: eṉṉuyirnī eṉṉuyirkkōr uyirum nī-eṉ iṉṉuyirkkut tuṇaivaṉī eṉṉai īṉṟa aṉṉainī eṉṉuṭaiya appa ṉī-eṉ arumporuḷnī eṉṉitayat taṉpu nī-eṉ naṉṉeṟinī eṉakkuriya uṟavu nī-eṉ naṟkurunī eṉaikkalanta naṭpu nī-eṉ taṉṉuṭaiya vāḻvunī eṉṉaik kākkun talaivaṉnī kaṇmūṉṟu taḻaitta tēvē.
translation: You are my life. You are the life of my life. You are the companion to my sweet life. You are the mother who bore me. You are my father. You are my rare treasure. You are the love in my heart. You are my good path. You are my rightful relation. You are my good Guru. You are the friendship united with me. You are my very life. You are the Lord who protects me. O God flourishing with three eyes.
commentary: Read the list slowly. Life, life of life, mother, father, treasure, love, path, kin, Guru (spiritual teacher), friend. God takes the place of every bond a person has, and whatever love and protection we have known from people flows from this one source.

translit: tāṉākit tāṉalla toṉṟu millāt taṉmaiyaṉāy evvevaikkun talaiva ṉāki vāṉāki vaḷiyaṉalāy nīru māki malar talaiya ulakāki maṟṟu mākit tēṉākit tēṉiṉaṟuñ cuvaiya tākit tīñcuvaiyiṉ payaṉākit tēṭu kiṉṟa nāṉāki eṉṉiṟaiyāy niṉṟōy niṉṉai nāyaṭiyēṉ evvāṟu naviṟṟu māṟē.
translation: You become yourself and exist as the nature where there is nothing other than you. You are the Lord of all things. You become the sky, the wind, the fire, the water, the expansive earth, and everything else. You become honey, the fragrant taste of honey, and the resulting experience of that sweet taste. You become the seeking 'I' and stand as my Lord. How can I, a lowly dog, adequately speak of you?
commentary: Nothing exists that is not God. Sky, wind, fire, water and earth are God, and so is honey, its taste, and the joy of tasting it. Even the 'I' that goes searching is God. When the seeker sees that the one searching is also the one sought, ordinary speech gives out, and Vallalar, calling himself a lowly dog, asks how he could ever speak of God.

translit: āṉēṟum perumāṉē aracē eṉṟaṉ āruyiruk korutuṇaiyē amutē koṉṟait tēṉēṟu malarccaṭai-eñ civaṉē tillaic ceḻuñcuṭarē āṉantat teyva mē-eṉ ūṉēṟum uyirkkuḷniṟai oḷiyē ellām uṭaiyāṉē niṉṉaṭiccīr uṉṉi aṉpar vāṉēṟu kiṉṟārnāṉ oruvaṉ pāvi maṇṇēṟi mayakkēṟi varuntuṟ ṟēṉē.
translation: Lord who rides the bull! King! The single companion of my precious life! Nectar! Our Siva with matted hair wearing honey-filled konrai flowers! Rich flame of Thillai! God of bliss! The fullness of light within the life residing in my flesh! Master who owns everything! Thinking of the glory of your feet, devotees ascend to heaven. I alone, a sinner, have become rooted in the earth, mounted on delusion, and I suffer.
commentary: Devotees think on the glory of Siva's feet and rise. Vallalar feels left behind, stuck in the earth and drunk on delusion. He calls Siva the rich flame of Thillai (the sacred temple town of Chidambaram) and the light filling the life that lives in his own flesh. The ache is in watching others reach grace while he stays rooted below.

translit: ceñcaṭai-em perumāṉē ciṟumāṉ ēṟṟa ceḻuṅkamalak karattavaṉē civaṉē cūḻntu mañcaṭaiyum matiṟṟillai maṇiyē oṟṟi vaḷarmaruntē eṉṉuṭaiya vāḻvē vēṭkai añcaṭaiya vañciyarmāl aṭaiya vañcam aṭaiyaneṭun tuyaraṭaiya akaṉṟa pāvi neñcaṭaiya niṉaitiyō niṉaiti yēlmeyn neṟiyuṭaiyār neñcamarnta nīta ṉaṉṟē.
translation: Our Lord with red matted hair! You whose rich lotus hands hold a small deer! Siva! Gem of Thillai enclosed by walls touched by clouds! The medicine flourishing in Otriyur! My life! I am a sinner who strayed far, caught in the five desires, trapped in lust for deceitful women, filled with falsehood, and plunged into deep sorrow. Will you ever think to enter my heart? If you do, you are indeed the just one seated in the hearts of those on the true path.
commentary: Vallalar confesses everything: the five desires, lust for deceitful women, falsehood, deep sorrow. Then he asks whether Siva would ever think to enter a heart like that. If God does, it proves the One seated in the hearts of the true is just, and that divine mercy has no limit.

translit: aṉṉaiyiṉum peritiṉiya karuṇai ūṭṭum āramutē eṉṉuṟavē aracē inta maṉṉulakil aṭiyēṉai eṉṉē tuṉpa valaiyilakap paṭa-iyaṟṟi maṟaintāy antō poṉṉaimatit tiṭukiṉṟōr maruṅkē cūḻntu pōṉakamum poyyuṟavum poruntal āṟṟēṉ eṉṉai-uḷaṅ koḷḷutiyō koḷki lāyō eṉceyvēṉ eṉceyvēṉ eṉcey vēṉē.
translation: Rare nectar feeding me a grace sweeter than a mother's! My kin! King! Why did you cause me to fall into the net of sorrow in this enduring world and then hide yourself? Alas! I cannot bear to gather around those who value only gold, accepting their food and their false friendship. Will you accept me in your heart or will you not? What will I do? What will I do? What will I do?
commentary: The pain of living among people who care only for wealth and hollow friendships is overwhelming. Vallalar questions why a God whose compassion is sweeter than a mother's love would let him fall into such a harsh world and then vanish. He is left pleading to be taken in, utterly exhausted by the superficial lives around him.

translit: paṭittēṉpoy ulakiyaṉūl entāy nīyē paṭippittāy aṉṟiyumap paṭippil iccai oṭittēṉnāṉ oṭittēṉō oṭippit tāypiṉ uṉṉaṭiyē tuṇaiyeṉanāṉ uṟuti yākap piṭittēṉmaṟ ṟatuvumnī piṭippit tāyip pētaiyēṉ niṉṉaruḷaip peṟṟōr pōla naṭittēṉem perumāṉī toṉṟum nāṉē naṭittēṉō allatunī naṭippit tāyō.
translation: I studied books of false worldly ways. My Father, you made me study them. Furthermore, I broke my desire for those studies. Did I break it? You made me break it. Then I firmly grasped your feet as my only support. You made me grasp them too. I, an ignorant one, acted like those who have received your grace. Our Lord, did I act this part on my own, or did you make me act it?
commentary: Vallalar traces every step back to God. He studied false worldly books, and God made him study them. He lost the taste for them, and God did that too. Even his firm grip on the Lord's feet, even his playing the part of a graced devotee, he cannot claim as his own. The whole script was God's, and nothing is left for him to take credit for.

translit: mattēṟi alaitayirpōl vañca vāḻkkai mayalēṟi viruppēṟi matatti ṉōṭu pittēṟi uḻalkiṉṟa maṉattāl antō pēyēṟi nalikiṉṟa pētai yāṉēṉ vittēṟi viḷaivēṟi makiḻkiṉ ṟōrpōl mēlēṟi aṉparelām viḷaṅku kiṉṟār ottēṟi uyirkkuyirāy niṟainta eṅkaḷ uṭaiyāṉē itutakumō uṇarki lēṉē.
translation: Like curd agitated by a churning rod, my mind wanders, overcome by the delusion of deceitful life, by desires, by arrogance, and by madness. Alas, I have become a fool tormented as if possessed by a ghost. Like those who rejoice as seeds sprout and yield a rich harvest, all your devotees ascend high and shine. Our Master who dwells fully and equally as the life of all lives! Is this fair? I do not understand.
commentary: Picture curd being churned by a rod. That is the mind under desire, arrogance and madness, tossed about like someone possessed. Meanwhile the devotees rise and shine like farmers glad at a good harvest. Vallalar asks the Lord who lives equally as the life of all lives whether this imbalance is fair, and says plainly that he does not understand.

translit: matiyaṇinta muṭikkaṉiyē maṇiyē ellām valla-aruṭ kuruvēniṉ malarttāḷ vāḻttik katiyaṇintār aṉparelām aṭiyēṉ oṉṟum kaṇṭaṟiyēṉ karumattāl kalaṅki antō potiyaṇintu tirintuḻalum ēṟu pōlap poyyulakil poycumantu pulampā niṉṟēṉ tutiyaṇinta niṉṉaruḷeṉ ṟaṉakku muṇṭō iṉṟeṉilip pāviyēṉ colva teṉṉē.
translation: O fruit on the crown adorned with the crescent moon! O gem! O all-powerful Guru of grace! All your devotees praised your flower-feet and attained the supreme state. I know nothing at all. Confused by karma, alas, I wander like a bull carrying a heavy burden. I stand lamenting in this false world, bearing falsehoods. Does your much-praised grace exist for me too? If it is not given today, what can this sinner say?
commentary: Everyone else has made it. Vallalar watches the devotees reach the supreme state while he stays behind in a false world, wandering like a bull under the load of karma (the accumulated consequences of past actions). He pleads to know whether God's grace will reach him too, and whether it will come today.

translit: eṉṉaracē eṉṉuyirē eṉṉai īṉṟa eṉtāyē eṉkuruvē eḷiyēṉ iṅkē taṉṉaracē celutti-eṅkum uḻalā niṉṟa cañcalaneñ cakattālē tayaṅki antō miṉṉaracē peṇṇamutē eṉṟu mātar veyyaciṟu nīrkkuḻikkaṇ viḻavē eṇṇi koṉṉaraicēr kiḻakkuruṭaṉ kōlpōl vīṇē kuppuṟukiṉ ṟēṉmayalil koṭiya ṉēṉē.
translation: O my king! O my life! O my mother who bore me! O my Guru! Here I am, a poor wretch languishing. My restless heart wanders everywhere, asserting its own rule. Alas, calling women "queen of lightning" and "nectar of womanhood", I think only of falling into the hot little puddle of urine. I am cruel. I fall headlong into this delusion uselessly, like the walking stick of a blind old man.
commentary: The restless mind keeps trying to rule itself, and it drags the soul away from God into delusion. Vallalar's language about lust is stark on purpose. The flattering names men give women only mask a base bodily function. Overcome by these urges, he feels as useless as a blind old man's dropped walking stick tumbling into the dirt.

translit: alvilaṅku ceḻuñcuṭarāy aṭiyār uḷḷat tamarntaruḷum civakuruvē aṭiyēṉ iṅkē ilvilaṅku maṭantaiyeṉṟē entāy anta iruppuvilaṅ kiṉai-oḻittum eṉṉē piṉṉum malvilaṅku parattaiyartam ācai eṉṉum valvilaṅku pūṇṭantō mayaṅki niṉṟēṉ pulvilaṅkum ituceyyā ōkō intap pulaināyēṉ piḻaipoṟukkil putitē aṉṟō.
translation: O Siva Guru! You sit in the hearts of your devotees as the rich flame that dispels darkness. Here I am a servant. O my father, I called a wife "a shackle of the house" and broke that iron shackle. Yet what did it achieve? I then took on the strong shackle of desire for prostitutes. Alas, I stand bewildered. Even low beasts do not act like this. Oh, if you forgive the mistakes of this base dog, would that not be something entirely new?
commentary: Renouncing worldly life achieves nothing if the heart stays bound by desire. Vallalar confesses a bitter irony: he broke the "iron shackle" of marriage, then locked himself into a stronger one, the desire for prostitutes. Even animals show more restraint. So he begs the flame in his heart for a forgiveness he has not earned, which would be something entirely new.

translit: vaṉkoṭumai malanīkki aṭiyār tammai vāḻvikkuṅ kuruvēniṉ malarttāḷ eṇṇa muṉkoṭuceṉ ṟiṭumaṭiyēṉ taṉṉai inta mūṭamaṉam ivvulaka muyaṟci nāṭip piṉkoṭuceṉ ṟalaittiḻukkutantō nāyēṉ pēypiṭitta pittaṉaippōl pitaṟṟā niṉṟēṉ eṉkoṭumai eṉpāvam entāy entāy eṉṉuraippēṉ eṅkuṟuvēṉ eṉcey vēṉē.
translation: O Guru! You remove the harsh, cruel impurities and grant true life to your devotees. I step forward to meditate on your flower-feet. Yet this foolish mind seeks worldly pursuits. It drags me backward and pulls me about. Alas, I am a dog. I stand babbling like a madman possessed by a ghost. What cruelty is this! What sin is this! O my father, my father! What can I say? Where can I go? What can I do?
commentary: Spiritual practice is often a tug-of-war with a stubborn mind. Each time Vallalar steps forward to meditate on God's feet, his own thoughts drag him back toward worldly pursuits. Split like this, he babbles like a man possessed and can only cry out to his Father in helplessness.

translit: uykuvittumeyyaṭiyār tammai ellām uṇmainilai peṟa-aruḷum uṭaiyāy iṅkē maikuvitta neṭuṅkaṇṇār mayakkil āḻntu varuntukiṉṟēṉ allāluṉ malarttāḷ eṇṇik kaikuvittuk kaṇkaḷilnīr poḻintu nāṉōr kaṇamēṉum karutiniṉaik kalanta tuṇṭō ceykuvittuk koḷḷutiyō koḷki lāyō tiruvuḷattai aṟiyēṉeṉ ceyku vēṉē.
translation: O Master! You save all true devotees and graciously grant them the state of truth. Here I sink into the delusion of women with long, kohl-rimmed eyes and suffer. Have I ever folded my hands, poured tears from my eyes, meditated on your flower-feet, and merged with you even for a single moment? Will you reform me and make me yours, or will you not? I do not know your divine will. What can I do?
commentary: True devotion needs a heart that melts completely into God. Looking back on a life spent in sensory pleasures, Vallalar asks whether he has ever given even one moment of tearful surrender. He has no pride left to stand on. Whether he will be reformed and claimed is left wholly to the divine will, and he does not know which way it leans.

translit: aruḷveḷiyil āṉanta vaṭivi ṉālniṉ ṟāṭukiṉṟa peruvāḻvē aracē inta maruḷvalaiyil akappaṭṭa maṉattāl antō matikalaṅki meynnilaikkōr vaḻikā ṇātē iruḷneṟiyil kōliḻanta kuruṭṭū maṉpōl eṇṇātel lāmeṇṇi ēṅki ēṅki uruḷcakaṭak kālpōluñ cuḻalā niṉṟēṉ uyyumvakai aṟiyēṉiv votiya ṉēṉē.
translation: O great life dancing in the space of grace in a form of bliss! O King! Caught in this net of delusion by my mind, alas, my intellect is bewildered. Finding no path to the true state, I am like a blind and mute man who has lost his walking stick on a dark path. I think unimaginable thoughts and pine away. I keep spinning like the wheel of a rolling cart. This useless one does not know the way to be saved.
commentary: A mind caught in its own net of delusion leaves the intellect bewildered. Vallalar is the blind and mute man who has dropped his walking stick on a dark path. Without grace, awareness just spins in place like a cart wheel and never finds the way to the true state.

translit: kaṟṟavaḷai taṉakkumuṇa vaḷikkum uṉṟaṉ karuṇainilai taṉai-aṟiyēṉ kaṭaiyēṉ iṅkē eṟṟavaḷai eṟumpēpōl tirintu nāḷum iḷaittuniṉa taruḷkāṇā tentāy antō peṟṟavaḷaik kāṇāta piḷḷai pōlap pētuṟukiṉ ṟēṉceyyum piḻaiyai nōkki iṟṟavaḷaikkēḷviṭalpōl viṭuti yēlyāṉ eṉceyvēṉ eṅkuṟuvēṉ eṉcol vēṉē.
translation: I do not know your state of compassion that provides food even to the frog trapped inside a rock. I am the lowest. Wandering here like an ant caught on a stick burning at both ends, I grow weary every day without seeing your grace, O my Father. Alas, I am bewildered like a child that cannot see the mother who gave it birth. If you look at my faults and abandon me like a husband abandoning his destitute wife, what will I do, where will I go, and what will I say?
commentary: God's compassion feeds even the frog sealed inside a solid rock. Against that grace Vallalar feels like an ant on a stick burning at both ends, with nowhere safe to run. He begs God not to weigh his faults and turn away, and asks instead for the comfort a mother gives her lost child.

translit: aṭimaiceyap pukuntiṭumem pōlvār kuṟṟam āyiramum poṟuttaruḷum aracē nāyēṉ koṭumaiceyu maṉattālē varunti antō kuraṅkiṉkai mālaiyeṉak kulaiyā niṉṟēṉ kaṭumaiceyap piṟartuṇintāl aṭimai taṉṉaik kaṇṭiruttal aḻakaṉṟē karuṇaik kentāy ceṭimaiyuḷap pātakaṉēṉ eṉcey vēṉniṉ tiruvuḷattai aṟintilēṉ tikaikkiṉ ṟēṉē.
translation: O King who forgives a thousand faults in those like us who come to serve you! Suffering because of my cruel mind, alas, I am ruined like a flower garland in the hands of a monkey. If others dare to deal harshly with your servant, it is not fitting for you to merely watch, O my compassionate Father. I am a sinner with an evil heart. What will I do? I do not know your divine will, and I stand bewildered.
commentary: Give a monkey a flower garland and it tears it apart. A restless mind does the same to any peace it touches. Vallalar knows his own mind is cruel and prone to error, so he asks God to protect him from the world's harshness, reasoning that a true master does not stand by while his servant is mistreated.

translit: kūmpāta meynneṟiyōr uḷattē eṉṟum kuṟaiyāta iṉpaḷikkum kuruvē ācait tāmpālē yāppuṇṭu varunti nāyēṉ taiyalār maiyaleṉum calati āḻntu ōmpāmal uvarnīruṇ ṭuyaṅku kiṉṟēṉ uṉṉaṭiyar akkaraimēl uvantu niṉṟē tīmpāluñ carukkaraiyun tēṉum neyyum tēkkukiṉṟār itutakumō tēva tēvē.
translation: O Guru who grants undiminishing bliss in the hearts of those on the unfading true path! Tied by the rope of desire, I suffer. Sinking into the ocean of infatuation for women, I drink salt water and languish. Your devotees stand joyfully on the opposite shore, brimming with sweet milk, sugar, honey, and ghee. Is this fitting, O God of gods?
commentary: Chasing worldly desire is like drinking salt water. The thirst only gets worse. Tied by the rope of desire, Vallalar drowns in that ocean, while the devotees who have crossed to the far shore of grace feast on sweet milk, sugar, honey and ghee. He asks the God of gods whether this is fitting.

translit: veḷḷamaṇi caṭaikkaṉiyē mūva rāki virintaruḷum orutaṉiyē viḻala ṉēṉaik kaḷḷamaṉak kuraṅkāṭṭum āṭṭa mellām kaṇṭiruntum iraṅkilaiyēl kavalai yālē uḷḷamelin tuḻalkiṉṟa ciṟiyēṉ piṉṉar uyyumvakai evvakaiyī tuṉṉun tōṟum poḷḷeṉamey viyarkka-uḷam pataikkac cōpam poṅkivaḻi kiṉṟatunāṉ poṟukki lēṉē.
translation: O sweet fruit wearing the flood on your matted hair! O unique one who expands to become the three chief gods and bestows grace! If you merely watch all the dances the monkey of my deceitful mind forces upon this worthless one and do not take pity, how will this lowly person, wandering with a heart weakened by worry, ever be saved? Whenever I think of this, my body suddenly sweats, my heart palpitates, and my grief overflows. I cannot bear it.
commentary: Vallalar addresses the one supreme God who expands to become the three chief Hindu deities (Brahma, Vishnu, and Siva). The fear of never reaching grace hits his body hard, with sudden sweating, a pounding heart, and grief that spills over. Without divine pity, he stays a helpless hostage to his own deceitful mind.

translit: eṉaiyaṟiyāp paruvattē āṇṭu koṇṭa eṉṉaracē eṉkuruvē iṟaiyē iṉṟu maṉaiyaṟiyāp piḻaikarutu makiḻnaṉ pōla matiyaṟiyēṉ ceypiḻaiyai maṉattuṭ koṇṭē taṉaiyaṟiyā mukattavarpōl iruntāy entāy taṭaṅkaruṇaip peruṅkaṭaṟkut takumō kaṇṭāy aṉaiyaṟiyāc ciṟukuḻavi yāki iṅkē aṭināyēṉ araṟṟukiṉṟēṉ antō antō.
translation: My King, my Guru, the Lord who took me as your own at an age when I knew nothing of myself! Today, like a husband holding against his wife an unwitting mistake made in the home, you keep in your heart the error I committed in my ignorance. My Father, you remain like a stranger showing no recognition. Consider if this befits the vast great ocean of mercy. I, a lowly dog at your feet, cry out aloud here like a little infant who does not know its mother. Alas, alas.
commentary: God is an ocean of mercy, yet he keeps his distance over a mistake made in ignorance, like a husband who holds a small household slip against his wife. This is the Lord who claimed Vallalar in his earliest youth, before he knew anything of himself. Now Vallalar cries out like an infant who cannot find its mother.

translit: tīviṉainal viṉaiyeṉumvaṉ kayiṟṟāl intac cīvarkaḷai āṭṭukiṉṟa tēvē nāyēṉ ēviṉainēr kaṇmaṭavār maiyaṟ pēyāl iṭaruḻantum calippiṉṟi eṉṉē iṉṉum nāviṉai-eṉ pālvaruntik karaṇṭu kiṉṟa nāykkumnakai tōṉṟaniṉṟu nayakkiṉ ṟēṉāṉ āviṉaiviṭ ṭerutukaṟan tiṭuvāṉ cellum aṟivilikkum aṟiviliyēṉ āṉa vāṟē.
translation: O God who makes these souls dance using the strong ropes of bad and good deeds! I, a dog, suffer torments from the demon of infatuation for women with arrow-like eyes, yet I feel no weariness. What is this? I still stand desiring them, drawing laughter even from a dog that exhausts its tongue gnawing at me. I have become a greater fool than the fool who leaves the cow and goes to milk a bull.
commentary: Good and bad deeds are the ropes by which God makes souls dance. Caught in that pull, Vallalar keeps chasing desire that brings only torment, and he never tires of it. Even a dog would laugh. He calls himself a bigger fool than the man who walks past the cow to milk a bull.

translit: emperumāṉ niṉviḷaiyāṭ ṭeṉcol kēṉnāṉ ētumaṟi yācciṟiyēṉ eṉaittāṉ iṅkē cempuṉalāl kuḻaittapulāl cuvarcūḻ pottaic ciṟuvīṭṭil iruṭṭaṟaiyil ciṟaicey tantō kampamuṟap pacittaḻaluṅ koḷunta antak karaṇamutal poṟipulappēy kavarntu cūḻntu vampiyaṟṟak kāmāti araṭṭar ellām maṭipiṭittu varuttaveṉṟō vaḷarttāy entāy.
translation: My Lord, what can I say of your play? I am a lowly one who knows nothing. My Father, did you nurture me only to imprison me here in the dark room of a frail little house surrounded by walls of flesh mixed with red blood? Alas, while the fire of hunger burns and makes me tremble, the demons of the inner faculties, the sensory organs, and the senses surround and seize me to cause mischief, and ruffians like lust grab my garments to torment me. Is it for this you raised me?
commentary: The body here is a frail, dark prison made of flesh and blood. Inside it the soul burns with hunger while the senses and inner faculties seize it, and lust and the other desires grab at its clothes like street ruffians. It gets no peace. Vallalar asks his Father whether this is what he was raised for.

translit: amparattē āṉanta vaṭivāl eṉṟum āṭukiṉṟa māmaṇiyē aracē nāyēṉ imparattam eṉumulaka naṭaiyil antō iṭaruḻantēṉ paṉṉeṟiyil eṉai-i ḻuttē pamparattiṉ āṭiyalaip paṭuttum intap pāvimaṉam eṉakkuvayap paṭuva tillai komparaṟṟa iḷaṅkoṭipōl taḷarntēṉ eṉṉaik kuṟikkoḷḷak karututiyō kuṟitti ṭāyō.
translation: O great gem, O King, who dances forever in the supreme space with a form of bliss! I, a dog, have suffered afflictions in the ways of this world defined by earthly attachments. Alas, this sinful mind drags me along many paths, making me spin and suffer like a top, and it refuses to come under my control. I have wilted like a tender vine lacking a supporting branch. Do you intend to take notice of me, or will you not?
commentary: God dances forever in perfect bliss, and the human mind will not rest at all. It drags Vallalar down many worldly paths, spinning him like a child's top, and he cannot bring it under control. Worn out, he droops like a young vine with no branch to lean on, and asks whether God means to take notice of him.

translit: kaṇṇuṭaiya nutaṟkarumpē maṉṟil āṭum kāraṇakā riyaṅkaṭanta kaṭavu ḷēniṉ taṇṇuṭaiya malaraṭikkōr ciṟitum aṉpu cārntēṉō cemmarampōl taṇinta neñcēṉ peṇṇuṭaiya mayalālē cuḻalkiṉ ṟēṉeṉ pētaimaiyai eṉpukalvēṉ pēya ṉēṉaip puṇṇuṭaiya puḻuvirumpum puḷḷeṉ kēṉō pulaiviḻaintu nilaiveṟuttēṉ pulaiya ṉēṉē.
translation: O sweet sugarcane with an eye on your forehead! O God who dances in the Hall, transcending cause and effect! Did my heart, hardened like a dead log, ever feel even a little love for your cool, flower-like feet? I spin in infatuation for women. How can I express my ignorance? Should I call my demonic self a bird that desires the worms in a festering wound? Desiring base things, I rejected my true state. I am truly a lowly wretch.
commentary: A heart without love for God is as hard and dry as a dead log. Vallalar addresses Siva in his traditional form, the dancer in the Hall with an eye of wisdom on his forehead, and turns in disgust on his own infatuation with women. His clinging to base pleasures is like a bird eagerly hunting worms in a festering wound.

translit: poṉṉuṭaiyār iṭampukavō avarkaṭ kēṟkap poymmoḻikaḷ pukaṉṟiṭavō potipōl intak koṉṉuṭaiyā uṭalparukkap pacikkuc cōṟu koṭukkavō kuḷirkkāṭai koḷavō vañca miṉṉiṭaiyār muṭaicciṟunīrk kuḻikkaṇ antō vīḻntiṭavō tāḻntiḷaittu viḻikka vōtāṉ eṉṉuṭaiyāy eṉṉuṭaiyāy eṉṉai iṅkē eṭuttuvaḷart taṉai-aṟiyēṉ eṉcol vēṉē.
translation: Was it to enter the homes of the wealthy? Was it to speak lies that please them? Was it to feed rice to this useless sack of a body so it swells? Was it to acquire clothes against the cold? Was it to fall, alas, into the foul pits of deceitful women with waists like lightning? Was it to sink low, grow weary, and stare blankly? O my Master, my Master! I do not know why you lifted me up and raised me here. What can I say?
commentary: A human birth is given for seeking God, and most of us spend it chasing money, flattering the rich and fattening the body. Vallalar lines up these ordinary pursuits and asks his Master plainly why he was raised up at all, if this is all it comes to. The gap between the gift and its use weighs on him.

translit: varukaṇattu vāḻntiṭumō viḻumō inta malakkūṭeṉ ṟaṟiñarelām varuntak kēṭṭum arukaṇaittuk koḷappeṇpēy eṅkē mēṭṭuk kaṭaittiṭaveṇ cōṟeṅkē āṭai yeṅkē irukaṇukku viyappeṅkē vacati yāṉa iṭameṅkē eṉṟutirin tiḷaittēṉ allāl orukaṇattum uṉainiṉainta tuṇṭō eṉṉai uṭaiyāṉē evvakaināṉ uyyum māṟē
translation: Even after hearing the wise lament in sorrow asking whether this cage of filth will survive the next moment or fall, I only wandered and grew weary. I kept asking: where is a demonic woman to embrace? Where is white rice to stuff this stomach? Where are clothes? Where are spectacles for my two eyes? Where is a comfortable place? Other than this, did I think of you even for a single moment? O my Master, how will I ever find salvation?
commentary: Even knowing that death could come at any moment, the human mind remains obsessed with physical comforts and desires. Vallalar laments how easily we ignore the fragility of the body. Instead of seeking grace, he says, we waste our brief time worrying about food, clothing, and pleasure, leaving no room for spiritual salvation.

translit: poṉmalaiyō ciṟiteṉappē rācai poṅkip puvinaṭaiyil paṟpalakāl pōntu pōntu neṉmalaiyō nitimalaiyō eṉṟu tēṭi nilaikulainta taṉṟi-uṉai niṉaintu nēṭi maṉmalaiyō māmaṇiyō maruntō eṉṟu vaḻuttiyatē illai-inta vañca neñcam kaṉmalaiyō irumpōcem maramō pāṟaik karuṅkallō parāymuruṭṭuk kaṭṭai yēyō.
translation: Great greed surged in me, making even a mountain of gold seem small. Wandering again and again along worldly paths, I searched for a mountain of paddy or a mountain of wealth, and I lost my stability. This deceitful heart never thought of you, sought you, or praised you as the enduring mountain, the great gem, or the healing medicine. Is this heart a rocky mountain? Is it iron? Is it red hardwood? Is it a black boulder? Or is it a rough block of dead wood?
commentary: Greed hardens the heart. Vallalar's mind chased mountains of paddy and wealth until it lost its footing, and never once turned to God as the enduring mountain, the great gem, the healing medicine. So he asks what it is made of. Stone, iron, hardwood or dead wood would explain it.

translit: tammaimaṟan taruḷamutam uṇṭu tēkkum takaiyuṭaiyār tirukkūṭṭam cārntu nāyēṉ vemmaiyelām tavirntumaṉaṅ kuḷirak kēḷvi viruntarunti meyyaṟivām vīṭṭil eṉṟum cemmaiyelām tarummauṉa aṇaimēṟ koṇṭu ceṟi-iravu pakaloṉṟum teriyā vaṇṇam immaiyilē emmaiyiṉum kāṇāc cutta iṉpanilai aṭaivēṉō ēḻai yēṉē.
translation: Will I, a poor wretch, join the holy assembly of those worthy souls who forget themselves and drink the nectar of grace to their fill? Will I, a lowly dog, shed all my burning sorrow, cool my mind, and feast on the banquet of spiritual instruction? In the house of true knowledge, will I rest upon the couch of silence that grants all perfection, unaware of dense night or day? Will I attain in this very life that pure state of bliss unseen anywhere else?
commentary: Real joy is found among those who have forgotten themselves in grace, and in the deep silence that grace brings. Vallalar longs to set down his burning sorrows and reach that pure bliss in this very life. He pictures it as a feast of spiritual teaching, and as rest on a couch of silence where night and day no longer divide.

translit: aṭiyaṉēṉ piḻaiyaṉaittum poṟuttāṭ koṇṭa aruṭkaṭalē maṉṟōṅkum aracē innāḷ koṭiyaṉēṉ ceypiḻaiyait tiruvuḷ ḷattē koḷḷutiyō koṇṭukulaṅ kuṟippa tuṇṭō neṭiyaṉē mutaṟkaṭavuṭ camukat tōrtam neṭumpiḻaikaḷ āyiramum poṟuttu māyai oṭiyanēr niṉṟaperuṅ karuṇai vaḷḷal eṉamaṟaikaḷ ōtuvatiṅ kuṉaittā ṉaṉṟē.
translation: O ocean of grace who forgave all my faults and took me into your service! O King who reigns high in the Hall! Will you take the faults committed today by this cruel one into your divine heart? Will you hold them against me and condemn my lineage? O Supreme One! The Vedas proclaim you here as the infinitely compassionate benefactor who forgave thousands of great faults committed by those in the presence of the primal gods, standing forth to destroy illusion.
commentary: God's compassion has no limit and can forgive every human flaw. Vallalar asks that today's mistakes not be held against him. The Vedas themselves call the Lord the benefactor who forgave thousands of great faults, and he holds on to that. This grace has always stepped in to destroy illusion and bring us back to the truth.

translit: kaṇmayakkum pēriruṭṭuk kaṅkuṟ pōtil karuttaṟiyāc ciṟuvaṉai-ōr kaṭuṅkā ṉattē uṇmayakkam koḷaviṭuttē oruvaṉ piṉpōm orutāypōl māyai-iruḷ ōṅkum pōtiṉ maṇmayakkam peṟumviṭayak kāṭṭil antō matiyilēṉ māḻāntu mayaṅka nītāṉ vaṇmaiyuṟṟa niyatiyiṉpiṉ eṉṉai viṭṭē maṟaintaṉaiyē paramēniṉ vaṇmai eṉṉē.
translation: Like a mother who in the blinding darkness of night abandons her innocent child in a harsh forest to faint in bewilderment and runs after a man, You left me! When the darkness of illusion swelled, You left me, a fool, to languish and suffer bewilderment in the forest of sensory objects that bring worldly delusion. You abandoned me to powerful destiny and hid Yourself. O Supreme, what kind of grace is Yours?
commentary: Vallalar compares himself to a child left by its mother in a dark, terrifying forest while she runs after a lover. The forest is the bewildering world of the senses, and the lover is the rigid, unfeeling law of destiny. How, he asks God, can such abandonment be called grace? A complaint this startling shows how deep his despair runs when he feels cut off from the divine presence.

translit: naṟṟāyum piḻaikuṟikkak kaṇṭōm inta nāṉilattē maṟṟavaryār nāṭār vīṇē paṟṟāyum avartamainām paṟṟōm paṟṟil paṟṟāta paṟṟuṭaiyār paṟṟi uḷḷē uṟṟāyuñ civaperumāṉ karuṇai oṉṟē uṟupiḻaikaḷ ettuṇaiyum poṟuppa teṉṟuṉ poṟṟāḷai virumpiyatu maṉṟu ḷāṭum poruḷē-eṉ piḻaiyaṉaittum poṟukka vaṉṟē.
translation: We have seen in this world that even a good mother finds fault. Who else would not seek them out needlessly? We do not cling to those who scrutinize such things. Only the compassion of Lord Siva, grasped and realized within by those holding detached attachment, forgives whatever faults arise. O Reality dancing in the Hall! I desired Your golden feet so that You would forgive all my faults.
commentary: Human love, even at its best, keeps conditions. Even a good mother finds fault with her child, Vallalar says, and others will go looking for faults to find. So he turns to Siva, whose compassion alone forgives every mistake we make. He seeks those golden feet knowing that grace keeps no ledger of our flaws.

translit: eṇṇiyanam eṇṇamelām muṭippāṉ maṉṟuḷ emperumāṉ eṉṟumakiḻn tiṟumān tiṅkē naṇṇiyamaṟ ṟaiyartammai uṟāmai pēci naṉkumati yātirunta nāyi ṉēṉait taṇṇiyanal aruṭkaṭalē maṉṟil iṉpat tāṇṭavañcey kiṉṟaperun takaiyē eṅkaḷ puṇṇiyaṉē piḻaikuṟittu viṭutti yāyil poyyaṉēṉ eṅkuṟṟeṉ purivēṉ antō.
translation: Believing that our Lord in the Hall will fulfill all my intentions, I rejoiced and felt proud. I spoke disdainfully of others who approached and I, a dog, showed them no respect. O cool ocean of good Grace! O Great One performing the blissful dance in the Hall! O our Merit! If You note my faults and abandon me, where will this liar go and what will I do, alas?
commentary: Spiritual pride can pass for devotion. Vallalar confesses that being sure of God's favor made him arrogant and dismissive of others. He begs not to be held to account for it, because if grace were withdrawn, where could a liar like him go?

translit: aṉpartiru vuḷaṅkōyi lākakkoṇṭē aṟputacciṟ capaiyōṅkum aracē iṅku vaṉpariṭaic ciṟiyēṉai mayaṅka vaittu maṟaintaṉaiyē āṉanta vaṭivōy niṉṉait tuṉpavaṭi vuṭaippiṟaril pirittu mēlōr turiyavaṭi viṉaṉeṉṟu coṉṉa vellām iṉpavaṭi vaṭaintaṉṟē entāy antō eṉṉaḷaveṉ colkēṉiv vēḻai yēṉē.
translation: O King reigning in the wondrous Hall of Wisdom, taking the sacred hearts of devotees as Your temple! You left me, a lowly one, bewildered among cruel people and hid Yourself. O Form of Bliss! The great ones distinguished You from those of sorrowful nature and declared You the form of the supreme state. Are these words truly understood only when attaining the form of bliss? O my father, alas, what can this poor wretch say about my condition?
commentary: The sages teach that God is pure bliss, but that fact is little use to someone surrounded by cruelty and confusion. Vallalar asks whether anyone can understand God's blissful nature without tasting it firsthand. Until that change comes, words and concepts give no real comfort.

translit: puṟṟōṅkum aravamellām paṇiyāk koṇṭu poṉmēṉi taṉilaṇinta poruḷē māyai uṟṟōṅku vañcamaṉak kaḷva ṉēṉai uḷaṅkoṇṭu paṇikoḷva tuṉakkē okkum maṟṟōṅkum avarellām perumai vēṇṭum vaṉmaṉattar eṉaivēṇṭār vaḷḷa lēnāṉ kaṟṟōṅkum aṟivaṟiyēṉ palavāc collum karuttaṟiyēṉ eṉakkaruḷak karutu vāyē.
translation: O Reality who takes the serpents rising from anthills as ornaments and wears them on Your golden body! It befits only You to accept this thief whose deceitful mind swells with illusion, keeping me in Your heart and taking my service. All those other eminent ones seek greatness. Hard-hearted people do not want me. O benevolent Lord! I do not possess the exalted knowledge gained through learning. I do not understand the intention behind speaking many words. You must decide to bestow Your grace upon me.
commentary: Siva is traditionally shown wearing venomous snakes as ornaments. Vallalar draws a moving point from it. The God who holds serpents close is the only one who would accept a man full of deceit. The world wants greatness, while grace welcomes the broken, the confused and those without scriptural learning.

translit: aruḷuṭaiya paramporuḷē maṉṟi lāṭum āṉantap peruvāḻvē aṉpu ḷōrtam teruḷuṭaiya uḷamuḻutum kōyil koṇṭa civamēmey aṟivuruvām teyva mē-im maruḷuṭaiya maṉappētai nāyi ṉēṉcey vaṉpiḻaiyaic ciṟitēṉum matitti yāyil iruḷuṭaiya pavakkaṭalviṭ ṭēṟēṉ eṉṉai ēṟṟuvataṟ keṇṇuka-eṉ iṉpat tēvē.
translation: O Supreme Reality of Grace! O great life of bliss dancing in the Hall! O Sivam who makes a temple of the perfectly clear hearts of those filled with love! O God whose form is true knowledge! If you consider even slightly the harsh faults committed by me, a dog with a deluded mind, I will never escape and climb out of the dark ocean of birth. O my God of joy, please resolve to lift me up.
commentary: Sivam, the divine reality, dances in the Hall and makes a temple of hearts filled with love. Vallalar knows his own mind is deluded and full of errors, so he asks God to look past them entirely. Judged strictly, he fears, he would never be lifted out of the dark ocean of birth.

translit: tuṉiyāl uḷantaḷarn tantō turumpil cuḻalukiṉṟēṉ iṉiyā yiṉumiraṅ kātōniṉ cittamen tāyiteṉṉa aṉiyāya mō-eṉ ṉaḷaviṉniṉ pāltaṇ ṇaruḷilaiyō caṉiyāmeṉ valviṉaip pōtaṉai yō-eṉkol cāṟṟuvatē.
translation: Wearied by sorrow, alas, I spin like a speck of dust in the wind. Will your heart not take pity on me even now? My Mother, what injustice is this? Do you have no cool grace for me? Is this the torment of my cruel karma striking like Saturn? What can I say?
commentary: Sorrow tosses Vallalar about like a speck of dust in the wind. He asks whether his karma (the accumulated consequences of past actions) is striking him the way Saturn is said to strike. He calls God Mother, tenderly, and still cannot understand why the cool relief of grace is held back.

translit: eṉṉē muṟaiyuṇ ṭeṉilkēḷvi uṇṭeṉpar eṉṉaḷavil iṉṉē ciṟitum ilaiyēniṉ pālitaṟ keṉceykuvēṉ maṉṉēmuk kaṇṇuṭai māmaṇi yē-iṭai vaipparitām poṉṉēmiṉ ṉērcaṭait taṉṉē rilāppari pūraṇaṉē.
translation: They say where there is an appeal, there is a hearing. Yet for me, even now, you grant no such inquiry. What shall I do about this? O King. O great gem with three eyes. O precious gold that cannot be put away. O Lord with lightning-like matted hair. O peerless perfect whole.
commentary: People say every sincere cry to God is heard, yet Vallalar's own appeals meet silence. He keeps calling Siva by his familiar names, the three-eyed King and the priceless gem. Even while he questions God's fairness, the adoration never leaves his voice.

translit: taṇṭāta cañcalaṅ koṇṭēṉ nilaiyai-it tāraṇiyil kaṇṭār iraṅkuvar kēṭṭār urukuvar kaṅkaitiṅkaḷ tuṇṭār malarccaṭai entāy iraṅkilai tūymaiyilā aṇṭār piḻaiyum poṟuppōy ituniṉ aruṭkaḻakē.
translation: I am caught in unceasing sorrow. In this world, those who see my state feel pity. Those who hear of it melt in compassion. O my Mother whose matted hair is adorned with the Ganges, the crescent moon and blossoms, you do not pity me. You pardon even the faults of impure enemies. Is this fitting for your grace?
commentary: His suffering is so plain that ordinary people who see it or hear of it are moved to pity. The irony stings. Human beings show him compassion, while the divine Mother who pardons even impure enemies ignores his pain. Vallalar asks God to his face whether this indifference is fitting for grace.

translit: poyyām ulaka naṭainiṉṟu cañcalam poṅkamukkaṇ aiyā-eṉ uḷḷam aḻalār meḻukot taḻikiṉṟatāl paiyār arava maticcaṭai yāycem pavaḷaniṟac ceyyāy eṉakkaruḷ ceyyāy eṉileṉṉa ceykuvaṉē.
translation: Trapped in the false ways of the world, my sorrow surges. O three-eyed Father, my heart melts and perishes like wax in fire. O Lord with hooded snakes and the moon in your matted hair. O radiant one the color of red coral. If you do not grant me grace, what shall I do?
commentary: The ways of the world feel false to Vallalar, and living among them melts his heart like wax in a fire. He pictures Siva with hooded snakes and the moon in his matted hair, red as coral. Without grace he sees no way to bear the weight of it.

translit: viṭamilai yērmaṇi kaṇṭāniṉ caiva viratañceyyat tiṭamilai yē-uṭ ceṟivilai yē-eṉṟaṉ cittattuniṉ naṭamilai yē-uṉṟaṉ naṇpilai yē-uṉai nāṭutaṟkōr iṭamilai yē-itai eṇṇilai yēcaṟ ṟiraṅkilaiyē.
translation: O Lord whose throat holds poison like a beautiful gem. I have no strength to practice your holy vows. I have no inner focus. Your dance is not in my mind. I do not have your friendship. I have no place to seek you. You do not consider my plight. You do not pity me even a little.
commentary: Vallalar confesses a complete lack of spiritual discipline, focus, and connection to the divine. He addresses a God known for drinking deadly poison to save the universe, highlighting the divine capacity for extreme mercy. Stripped of all religious achievements, he asks for pity precisely because he is entirely unable to help himself.

translit: viṇṇuṭai yāyveḷḷi veṟpuṭai yāymati mēvucaṭaik kaṇṇuṭai yāyneṟṟik kaṇṇuṭai yāyaruṭ kaṇṇuṭaiyāy paṇṇuṭai yāyticaip paṭṭuṭai yāyiṭap pālilaruṭ peṇṇuṭai yāyvantip piṭṭuṭai yāyeṉ peruñcelvamē.
translation: O You who possess the heavens. O You who possess the silver mountain. O You who hold the moon in your matted hair. O You who possess the forehead eye. O You who possess the eye of grace. O You who possess the melody. O You who wear the directions as your silk garment. O You who hold the graceful Woman on your left side. O You who partook of the sweet pittu offered by Vandi. O my great wealth.
commentary: Vallalar calls on Siva through his traditional forms and stories. Here is the Lord of the silver mountain, wearing the directions as his silk, sharing his form with the Goddess on his left side. He remembers the old story of God coming as a humble laborer to eat the sweet cake called pittu offered by an old woman named Vandi. All these images build to a plain declaration of love. God is his great wealth.

translit: viṭaiyuṭai yāymaṟai mēluṭai yāynati mēviyaceñ caṭaiyuṭai yāykoṉṟait tāruṭai yāykaram tāṅkumaḻup paṭaiyuṭai yāyaruṭ paṇpuṭai yāypeṇ paravaiyiṉpāl naṭaiyuṭai yāyaruḷ nāṭuṭai yāypatam nalkukavē.
translation: O You who possess the bull mount. O You who hold the supreme Vedas. O You who possess the red matted hair where the river rests. O You who wear the garland of konrai flowers. O You who hold the battle-axe weapon in your hand. O You who possess the quality of grace. O You who walked as a messenger to the woman Paravai. O You who possess the realm of grace. Grant me your holy feet.
commentary: The litany of Siva's features goes on, from the river in his matted hair to his garland of sacred konrai flowers. Vallalar also recalls the beloved story of God walking the streets at midnight as a messenger for a devoted saint, to settle a lover's quarrel with a woman named Paravai. A God who came that close to his devotees can surely grant Vallalar the same intimate grace, and his holy feet.

translit: kīḷuṭai yāypiṟaik kīṟṟuṭai yāyeṅ kiḷaittalaimēl tāḷuṭai yāyceñ caṭaiyuṭai yāyeṉ taṉaiyuṭaiyāy vāḷuṭai yāymalai māṉuṭai yāykalai māṉuṭaiyāy āḷuṭai yāymaṉṟuḷ āṭṭuṭai yāyeṉṉai āṇṭaruḷē.
translation: O You who wear the loincloth. O You who wear the sliver of the crescent moon. O You whose feet rest upon the heads of our kin. O You who have red matted hair. O You who possess me. O You who hold the sword. O You who have the daughter of the mountain. O You who hold the leaping deer. O Master who rules over me. O You who perform the dance in the hall. Rule me and grant your grace.
commentary: The imagery centers on Siva the dancer, holding the leaping deer and dancing in the sacred hall. In the middle of these grand visions comes a very personal plea. Vallalar asks the Master to take hold of his life, rule it, and shower him with grace.

translit: nāṉpaṭum pāṭu civaṉē ulakar navilumpañcu tāṉpaṭu mōcollat tāṉpaṭu mō-eṇṇat tāṉpaṭumō kāṉpaṭu kaṇṇiyiṉ māṉpaṭu māṟu kalaṅkiniṉṟēṉ ēṉpaṭu kiṉṟaṉai eṉṟiraṅ kāyeṉṉil eṉceyvaṉē.
translation: O Siva, would even the beaten cotton spoken of by worldly people endure the suffering I endure? Can it be expressed in words? Can it be conceived in thought? I stand bewildered like a deer caught in a forest snare. If you do not show mercy and ask why I suffer, what will I do?
commentary: Praise breaks off into anguish. Vallalar says even cotton beaten and torn apart does not suffer what he suffers, and he stands bewildered like a deer caught in a snare. No word or thought can hold this pain. All he begs is that God show mercy by simply asking him why he is hurting.

translit: poyyō aṭimai uraittalen tāyeṉṉuṭ pōntiruntāy aiyōniṉ uḷḷat taṟintataṉ ṟō-eṉ avalamellām kaiyōṭa vallavar ōrpati ṉāyiraṅ kaṟpaniṉṟu meyyō ṭeḻutiṉun tāṉaṭaṅ kāta viyappuṭaittē.
translation: My Father, are the words of this slave a lie? You have entered and reside within me. Alas, are not all my miseries known in your heart? Even if swift scribes stood for ten thousand aeons and wrote diligently, my suffering holds an immensity that cannot be contained.
commentary: God lives inside Vallalar, so God already knows every detail of his misery firsthand. The pain is so vast that swift scribes writing for ten thousand aeons could not record it all. He appeals to that inner presence, asking his Father to act on the plain truth of his sorrow.

translit: tēṉcollum vāyumai pākāniṉ taṉṉait terintaṭuttōr tāṉcolluṅ kuṟṟaṅ kuṇamākak koḷḷun tayāḷuveṉṟē nāṉcolva teṉṉaipoṉ nāṇcollum vāṇitaṉ nāṇcollumav vāṉcollum emmalai māṉcollum kaimmalai māṉcollumē.
translation: O Lord who shares half his form with Umai whose mouth speaks words of honey! You are the compassionate one who takes the faults spoken by those who know and approach you as virtues. Why should I be the one to say this? The golden wedding thread says it. Saraswati's wedding thread says it. The vast sky says it. Our mountain daughter says it. The elephant daughter says it.
commentary: God's compassion runs so deep that he takes even the faults of those who approach him as virtues. Vallalar says he need not prove this himself. The whole universe and the heroines of the ancient stories already bear witness to that mercy.

translit: veṉṟē mutalaiyum mūrkkarum koṇṭatu mīḷaviṭār eṉṟē uraippariṅ keṉpōṉṟa mūṭarmaṟ ṟillainiṉpēr naṉṟē uraittuniṉ ṟaṉṟē viṭuttaṉaṉ nāṇileṉmaṭ ṭiṉṟēyak kaṭṭurai iṉṟē-eṉ colva tiṟaiyavaṉē.
translation: They say a conquering crocodile and a stubborn fool will not let go of what they have grasped. There is no fool here like me. Having spoken your name perfectly and stood firm, I let it go that very same day. I have no shame. In my case, that proverb has become false today. What can I say, O Lord?
commentary: A proverb says a stubborn fool never lets go of what he has grabbed. Vallalar's foolishness is worse. He grasped the sacred name of God and let it slip away the very same day.

translit: kaikkiṉṟa kāyum iṉippām viṭamum kaṉa-amutām poykkiṉṟa kāṉalum nīrāmvaṉ pāvamum puṇṇiyamām vaikkiṉṟa ōṭuñcem poṉṉāmeṉ keṭṭa maṉatuniṉcīr tuykkiṉṟa nalla maṉatāva tillai-eṉ colluvaṉē.
translation: Bitter unripe fruit becomes sweet. Poison becomes heavy nectar. The false mirage becomes water. Cruel sin becomes merit. A common begging bowl becomes pure gold. But my ruined mind never becomes a good mind that enjoys your glory. What can I say?
commentary: Bitter fruit turns sweet, poison turns to nectar, a common begging bowl turns to gold. Vallalar laments that the one change he desperately needs, his ruined mind turning to enjoy God's glory, seems the only impossible one.

translit: vīṇē poḻutu kaḻikkiṉṟa nāṉuṉ viraimalarttāḷ kāṇēṉkaṇ ṭāraiyuṅ kāṇkiṉṟi lēṉcaṟṟum kāṇaṟkaṉpum pūṇēṉ tavamum puriyēṉ aṟamum pukalkiṉṟilēṉ nāṇēṉ vilaṅkiḻi yāṇē yeṉuṅkaṭai nāyiṉaṉē.
translation: I waste my time in vain. I do not see your fragrant lotus feet. I do not look upon those who have seen them. I do not embrace the love to see them even a little. I do not perform austerities. I do not speak of charity. I have no shame. I am the lowest dog, lower than a beast.
commentary: Vallalar measures his life against the basic practices of a spiritual path: seeking God, keeping company with those who have seen Him, self-discipline and charity. He finds none of them in his days. The sense of unworthiness crushes him, and he calls himself lower than a beast.

translit: nāṉōr eḷimai aṭimaiyeṉ ṟōnallaṉ allaṉeṉṟu tāṉōniṉ aṉpar takāteṉpar īteṉṟu tāṉiṉaittō ēṉōniṉ uḷḷam iraṅkilai iṉṉu miraṅkilaiyēl kāṉōṭu vēṉkol kaṭalviḻu vēṉkolmuk kaṇṇavaṉē.
translation: Is it because I am a poor slave? Is it because I am not a good person? Did you think your devotees would say this is improper? Why does your heart show no pity? If you still show no pity, will I run into the forest? Will I fall into the sea? O three-eyed Lord!
commentary: Feeling totally abandoned, Vallalar wonders whether his low status or bad character is what keeps God's grace away. Desperation brings him to the edge. He threatens to run into the wild forest or throw himself into the sea if the three-eyed Lord (Siva) will not show him pity.

translit: miṉpōluñ ceñcaṭai vittaka ṉē-oḷi mēviyacem poṉpōlu mēṉi-em puṇṇiya ṉē-eṉaip pōṟṟippeṟṟa taṉpōlun tāytantai āyiram pērirun tālumantō niṉpōlum aṉpuṭai yāreṉak kārinta nīṇilattē.
translation: O wise Lord with red matted hair like lightning. O virtuous Lord with a body like luminous red gold. Even if there are a thousand mothers and fathers like those who cherished and bore me, alas, who on this vast earth possesses love for me like Yours?
commentary: The love of the divine vastly exceeds human affection. Even a thousand loving parents combined cannot match the boundless care the Lord holds for a single soul.

translit: aṉpāleṉ taṉṉai-iṅ kāḷuṭai yāyiv vaṭiyavaṉēṉ niṉpāleṉ tuṉpa neṟippāl akaṟṟeṉṟu niṉṟatallāl tuṉpāl iṭaraip piṟarpāl aṭuttoṉṟu coṉṉatuṇṭō eṉpāl iraṅkilai eṉpāṟ kaṭalpiḷḷaik kīntavaṉē.
translation: You rule me here with love. I, this devotee, stood before You asking You to remove me from the path of suffering. Other than that, have I ever approached others and spoken a word about the troubles caused by misery? You who gave the ocean of milk to the child who asked for milk, You show no pity to me.
commentary: Real devotion takes every trouble straight to the Lord and never goes begging to the world. Vallalar has done exactly that. He recalls the old story of the crying child who asked for milk and was given the whole ocean of milk, and he asks why a God so generous now seems to withhold pity from him.

translit: eṉpōṉ maṉitarai ēṉaṭup pēṉeṉak keyppilvaippām poṉpōl viḷaṅkum puricaṭai yāṉṟaṉaip pōyaṭuttēṉ tuṉpōr aṇuvum peṟēṉiṉi yāṉeṉṟu collivantēṉ muṉpōl parāmukañ ceyyēl aruḷuka mukkaṇaṉē.
translation: Why would I approach human beings who are like me? I went and approached the Lord with twisted matted hair shining like gold, my treasure in times of weariness. I came declaring I will not experience even an atom of suffering anymore. Do not look away in indifference as You did before. Bestow Your grace, O three-eyed Lord.
commentary: Other people are bound by the same limits as he is, so leaning on them for final relief is useless. The Lord is the one treasure to draw on when weariness sets in. Vallalar pleads with Him to stop turning away and grant the grace that removes suffering entirely.

translit: poṉṉuṭai yārtamaip pōyaṭup pāyeṉṟa puṉmaiyiṉōrk keṉṉuṭai yāṉṟaṉai yē-aṭup pēṉitaṟ keḷḷaḷavum piṉṉiṭai yēṉavar muṉṉaṭai yēṉeṉap pēcivantēṉ miṉṉiṭai mātumai pākā-eṉ cōkam vilakkukavē.
translation: Base people told me to go and approach the wealthy. I replied to them saying I will approach only my Lord, I will not retreat from this even by the measure of a sesame seed, and I will not stand before those wealthy people. O Lord who shares half Your form with Uma, the lady with a waist like lightning. Dispel my sorrow.
commentary: The world's usual advice is to go seek favors from the rich and powerful. Vallalar refuses it flatly. He will not retreat from relying on the Lord by so much as a sesame seed, and he will never lower himself to beg from wealthy mortals.

translit: cātakat tōrkaṭkut tāṉaruḷ vēṉeṉil tāḻntiṭumā pātakat tōṉukku muṉṉaruḷ īntatep pāṉmaikoṇṭō tītakat tēṉeḷi yēṉā yiṉumuṉ tiruvaṭiyām pōtakat tēniṉaik kiṉṟēṉ karuṇai purintaruḷē.
translation: If You say You will grant grace only to those who perform spiritual practices, by what nature did You previously grant grace to a great sinner? Though I harbor evil within and remain lowly, I meditate on the lotus flower of Your holy feet. Bestow Your compassion upon me.
commentary: Vallalar holds the Lord to His own record. Great sinners have been saved before, so grace cannot belong only to disciplined practitioners. However flawed and unworthy someone feels, a mind fixed on His holy feet can still receive His full compassion.

translit: aruḷaṟi yācciṟu tēvarun tammai aṭuttavarkaṭ kiruḷaṟi yāviḷak keṉṟālum neñcam iraṅkukiṉṟār maruḷaṟi yāpperun tēvēniṉ taṉṉaṭi vantaṭuttēṉ teruḷaṟi yācciṟi yēṉāyi ṉuñceyka cīraruḷē.
translation: Even minor deities who do not know grace show compassion in their hearts to those who approach them, even if they are merely called lamps that dispel darkness. O great God who knows no delusion, I have come and approached your feet. Even though I am a lowly one who knows no clarity, grant me your excellent grace.
commentary: Even lesser gods show mercy to those who come to them for help. The supreme God, free of all delusion, will surely grant grace to a seeker. So Vallalar comes straight to His feet, admitting he lacks clarity and trusting completely in that compassion.

translit: arumporu ḷē-eṉ aracē-eṉ āruyirk kākavanta perumporu ḷē-aruṭ pēṟē civāṉantam peṟṟavarpāl varumporu ḷēmukkaṇ māmaṇi yēniṉ vaḻiyaruḷāl tarumporu ḷēporuḷ eṉṟuvan tēṉeṉait tāṅkikkoḷḷē.
translation: O rare treasure! O my King! O great treasure who came for the sake of my precious life! O gift of grace! O treasure who comes to those who have attained the bliss of Siva! O great gem with three eyes! I have come realizing that the treasure given by your continuous grace is the true treasure. Support me.
commentary: Vallalar piles up names of affection: rare treasure, my King, gift of grace, three-eyed gem. The only real wealth in this world is the continuous grace of God. Worldly possessions mean nothing beside it, and he surrenders completely, asking to be held.

translit: caraṅkār mukantoṭut teyvatu pōleṉ ṟaṉaiyulakat turaṅkā riruṭperu vātaṉai yāliṭar ūṭṭuneñcak kuraṅkāl melintuniṉ nāman tuṇaiyeṉak kūṟukiṉṟēṉ iraṅkār tamakkum iraṅkukiṉ ṟōyeṟ kiraṅkukavē.
