translation: Like shooting an arrow from a bow, the monkey of my mind feeds me affliction through the great torment of dark worldly attachments that never sleep. Weakened by this, I speak your name as my support. O you who show compassion even to those who show no compassion, show compassion to me.
commentary: The mind is a restless monkey, forever attacking the soul with worldly attachments. Worn out by that inner fight, Vallalar clings to God's name to survive. His appeal rests on one trait of the Lord. A God who pities even the pitiless will surely pity a soul that is struggling.

translit: kūṟuṟṟa kuṟṟamun tāṉē makiḻvil kuṇameṉavē āṟuṟṟa ceñcaṭai aṇṇalkoḷ vāṉeṉpar āṅkataṟku vēṟuṟṟa tōrkari vēṇṭuṅko lō-eṉṉuḷ mēvi-eṉṟum vīṟuṟṟa pātat tavaṉmiṭaṟ ṟēkari mēviyumē.
translation: They say the Lord with the red matted hair bearing the river will joyfully accept even spoken faults as virtues. Is any other witness needed for that? The witness is right there on the throat of the one whose majestic feet dwell forever within me.
commentary: God is merciful enough to accept our flaws joyfully, as if they were virtues. For proof Vallalar points to the dark mark on the Lord's throat. In the traditional story Siva drank a deadly poison to save the universe from destruction, took the world's very worst into Himself, and turned it into a permanent sign of His grace.

translit: cūṟpaṭu mēka niṟattōṉum nāṉmukat tōṉumeṉṉaip pōṟpaṭum pāṭunal lōrcolak kēṭkum poḻutumaṉam vēṟpaṭum puṇṇil kalaṅki-an tōnam viṭaiyavaṉpūṅ kāṟpaṭun tūḷinam mēṟpaṭu mō-oru kāleṉṉumē.
translation: When I hear good people tell of how the one with the color of a pregnant raincloud and the four-faced one suffer just like me, my mind is agitated like a wound pierced by a spear. Alas, it asks, will the dust from the beautiful feet of our Lord who rides the bull ever fall upon us?
commentary: Vishnu and Brahma, the gods of protection and creation, are themselves subject to suffering and sorrow. Hearing that these great deities struggle just as humans do fills Vallalar with sharp anxiety. It leaves him sure that his only real safety is the dust of the supreme Lord's feet, the classic symbol of spiritual shelter.

translit: vāḷēy neṭuṅkaṇṇi emperu māṭṭi varuṭumalart tāḷē varunta maṇikkūṭaṟ pāṇaṉ taṉakkaṭimai āḷē eṉaviṟa kēṟṟuviṟ ṟōyniṉ ṉaruḷkiṭaikkum nāḷēnaṉ ṉāḷanta nāṭkā yiranteṇṭaṉ nāṉceyvaṉē.
translation: Our Lady with long sword-like eyes gently strokes your flower-like feet. Yet you let those feet suffer to become a servant to the musician of beautiful Madurai. You carried and sold firewood, declaring yourself his servant. The day I receive your grace is the true good day. I offer a thousand prostrations to that day.
commentary: Out of love for a devotee, God will endure physical hardship. Vallalar recalls the story of the Lord taking the form of a lowly woodcutter, letting His tender feet suffer to help a temple musician in Madurai. The day such a humble, loving God gives him grace will be the greatest day of his life.

translit: aṭuttār tamai-eṉṟum mēlōr viṭārkaḷ avarkkuppiccai eṭuttā yiṉumiṭu vārkaḷeṉ pārataṟ kēṟkaccoṟpūt toṭuttār oruvarkkuk kaccūri lēpiccaic cōṟeṭuttuk koṭuttāyniṉ pēraruḷ eṉcollu kēṉeṇ kuṇakkuṉṟamē.
translation: Great people never abandon those who seek their refuge. The wise say they will even beg for alms to feed them. True to those words, you gathered alms of cooked rice in Kaccūr and fed the one who strung garlands of poetry for you. How can I describe your immense grace, O mountain of eightfold attributes?
commentary: A truly noble person would rather beg in the streets than let a dependent go hungry. God acts exactly so. Vallalar recalls the tradition of the Lord gathering alms in Kaccūr just to feed a poet who sang for Him, and he marvels at a grace that lowers itself this far to serve others.

translit: nāṭiniṉ ṟēniṉai nāṉkēṭṭuk koḷvatu naṇṇumpattuk kōṭiyaṉ ṟē-oru kōṭiyiṉ nūṟṟoru kūṟumaṉṟē tēṭiniṉ ṟēputaip pōrun taruvarniṉ cīrniṉaintuṭ pāṭiyan tōmaṉam vāṭiniṉ ṟēṉmukam pārttaruḷē.
translation: Seeking you, what I ask for is not a hundred million. It is not even one hundredth of a single million. Even misers who hoard their wealth will give something to those who seek it. I sing your glories from within. Alas, I stand here with a withered heart. Look at my face and bestow your grace.
commentary: What Vallalar asks is tiny beside the vast wealth of grace. Even greedy misers part with a small coin when someone begs them directly. Singing with a withered heart, he asks only that God look at his face and give a fraction of that boundless compassion.

translit: tāyāki ṉuñcaṟṟu nēran tarippaḷnan tantaiyainām vāyāra vāḻttiṉum vaiyiṉum taṉṉiṭai vantitunī īyāy eṉilaruḷ vāṉeṉ ṟuṉaiyaṭut tēṉumaiyāḷ nēyā maṉamiraṅ kāyā-eṉ eṇṇam neṟippaṭavē.
translation: Even a mother might hesitate for a moment. But whether we praise our father wholeheartedly or scold him, he will grant our request if we approach him and say, "Give this to me." Trusting this, I approached you. O beloved of Uma! Will your heart not take pity on me so my thoughts may find the right path?
commentary: God is the perfect father, answering His children whether they come with praise or with anger. A mother might hesitate for a moment. A father gives as soon as he is asked. Vallalar comes to the Lord with exactly that trust and asks that his restless thoughts be guided onto the right path.

translit: naṭumpāṭṭai nāvalaṉ vāyttirup pāṭṭai nayantiṭṭanī kuṭumpāṭṭai mēṟkoṇṭa eṉtamiḻp pāṭṭaiyum koṇṭeṉuḷḷat tiṭumpāṭṭai nīkkilai eṉṉiṉun tuṉpat tiḻukkuṟṟunāṉ paṭumpāṭṭai yāyiṉum pārttiraṅ kāyem parañcuṭarē.
translation: You rejoiced in the sacred verses sung by the eloquent poet of Navalur. Even if you do not accept my Tamil verses, sung by one burdened with family life, and do not remove the affliction in my heart, at least look at the suffering I endure as I fall into sorrow. Take pity on me, O our Supreme Light.
commentary: God has always cherished the sacred songs of great saints, like the famous poet of Navalur mentioned here. Vallalar feels inadequate because he writes his Tamil poetry while still caught up in the heavy burdens of ordinary family life. He pleads that even if the Supreme Light rejects his imperfect songs, the Divine should still take pity on his very real suffering.

translit: ēṭṭāluṅ kēḷayal eṉpārai nāṉcirit teṉṉaiveṭṭip pōṭṭālum vēṟiṭam kēḷēṉeṉ nāṇaip puṟamviṭuttuk kēṭṭālum eṉṉai uṭaiyā ṉiṭañceṉṟu kēṭpaṉeṉṟē nīṭṭālum vāyuraip pāṭṭāluñ colli niṟuttuvaṉē.
translation: I laugh at those who tell me to ask elsewhere for support. Even if they cut me down, I will not ask anywhere else. Casting aside my shame, if I ask, I will go to the Lord who owns me and ask him. I will establish this firmly by speaking at length and by singing it with my mouth.
commentary: Vallalar says he will only ever ask God for help, flatly refusing to seek favors from mortal patrons. Even under threat of death, his reliance on the divine is absolute. He is willing to cast aside all worldly pride to beg from the Lord who truly owns him. He pledges to sing and declare this single-minded devotion for everyone to hear.

translit: cīrkkiṉṟa kūṭalil pāṇaṉuk kāṭpaṭac ceṉṟa-annāḷ vērkkiṉṟa vemmaṇal eṉtalai mēlvaikku mellaṭikkup pērkkiṉṟa tōṟum uṟuttiya tō-eṉap pēci-eṇṇip pārkkiṉṟa tōṟumeṉ kaṇṇē-eṉ uḷḷam pataikkiṉṟatē.
translation: On that day when you went to submit to the musician in famous Madurai, did the hot sweating sand hurt your soft feet, which you place on my head, with every step you took? Speaking and thinking of this, my heart throbs in anguish every time I reflect upon it.
commentary: A traditional story tells how Siva walked through the hot sands of Madurai to help a troubled musician. Vallalar cannot get past the picture of those soft feet, the same feet he holds on his head, stepping on that burning ground. Every time he thinks of it, his heart throbs with anguish. His love for God is that personal, and that protective.

translit: nīyē-eṉ tantai aruḷuṭai yāyeṉai nērntupeṟṟa tāyēniṉ pāliṭat temperu māṭṭi-it taṉmaiyiṉāl nāyēṉ ciṟituṅ kuṇamilaṉ āyiṉum nāṉumuṅkaḷ cēyē eṉaippuṟam viṭṭāl ulakañ cirittiṭumē.
translation: You are my father. O gracious one, our great lady at your left side is the mother who lovingly bore me. Because of this, even though I am a dog with no good qualities at all, I am your child. If you cast me out, the world will laugh.
commentary: God is his father, and the goddess at his side is the mother who bore him. Vallalar feels as flawed as a stray dog, yet he is still their child, and parents don't discard their own. Cast him out and the world will mock them. He leans on the fierce bonds of family to demand their grace.

translit: teruḷum poruḷumniṉ cīraru ḷē-eṉat tērntapiṉyāṉ maruḷum puvaṉat toruvarai yēṉu matittatuṇṭō veruḷum puviyil tuyarāl kalaṅki vetumpukiṉṟēṉ iruḷum karumaṇi kaṇṭā aṟintum iraṅkilaiyē.
translation: After realizing that your supreme grace is both true wisdom and true wealth, have I ever respected anyone else in this deluded world? I am distressed by sorrow and suffer in this frightening world. O Lord with a dark jewel-like throat, even knowing this, you show no pity.
commentary: Once Vallalar saw that divine grace is the only real wisdom and the only real wealth, he stopped seeking anyone's approval in this deluded world. He still suffers, and the world still frightens him. He calls Siva the Lord with the dark throat, recalling the ancient story where God swallowed poison to save the universe. A God of such immense pity stays silent while his own devotee suffers, and Vallalar wants to know why.

translit: peṇṇāṉ mayaṅkum eḷiyēṉai āḷap peruṅkaruṇai aṇṇāniṉ uḷḷam iraṅkāta vaṇṇam aṟintukoṇṭēṉ kaṇṇār ulakileṉ tuṉpamel lāmveḷi kāṇilinta maṇṇā pilattoṭu viṇṇāṭuṅ koḷḷai vaḻaṅkumeṉṟē.
translation: O Lord of great compassion, I have realized why your heart does not show pity to rule over this lowly one bewildered by women. You know that if all my sorrows are revealed in this visible world, both this earthly realm with its underworld and the heavenly world will overflow with lamentation.
commentary: Vallalar imagines a poetic reason for God holding back his pity. His inner sorrow is so vast, he says, that if God acknowledged it and brought it all into the open, the weight of it would overwhelm the universe. Earth, the underworld and the heavens would drown in tears.

translit: neṟikoṇṭa niṉṉaṭit tāmaraik kāṭpaṭṭu niṉṟa-eṉṉaik kuṟikoṇṭa vāḻkkait tuyarām periya koṭuṅkalippēy muṟikoṇ ṭalaikka vaḻakkō vaḷartta muṭakkiḻanāy veṟikoṇṭa tēṉum viṭattuṇi yāriv viyaṉilattē.
translation: I stand enslaved by your righteous lotus feet. Is it just for the great cruel demon of worldly suffering to possess and torment me? Even if a crippled old dog they raised goes mad, no one in this vast world would dare abandon it.
commentary: Someone who raised a crippled old dog would not abandon it, even if it went mad. Vallalar uses that humble picture to make his case for God's protection. He has given himself entirely to God, so why should he be left to the madness and torment of worldly life?

translit: matiyāmal āraiyum nāṉiṟu māntu makiḻkiṉṟatem patiyām uṉatu tiruvaruṭ cīruram paṟṟiyaṉṟō etiyār paṭiṉum iṭarppaṭ ṭalaiya-iv vēḻaikkeṉṉa vitiyā iṉippaṭa māṭṭēṉ aruḷcey viṭaiyavaṉē.
translation: I proudly rejoice and disregard everyone else, only because I hold fast to the supreme strength of your divine grace, our Lord. Is it the fate of this poor soul to wander in hardship no matter what troubles arise? I will not suffer anymore. Grant your grace, O rider of the bull.
commentary: Spiritual confidence can look like arrogance. Vallalar does disregard worldly opinion and rejoice in it, and he says the reason is his complete reliance on divine grace, with no ego behind it. Addressing God as the rider of the bull (Siva's sacred mount, Nandi), he declares he has suffered enough and asks for his hardships to end now.

translit: kaṟkōṭṭai neñcarun tampāl aṭuttavar kaṭkuccummāc coṟkōṭṭai yāyiṉum kaṭṭuvar niṉṉait tuṇintaṭuttēṉ aṟkōṭṭai neñcuṭai yēṉuk kiraṅkilai aṉṟulavā neṟkōṭṭai īntavaṉ nīyallai yōmukkaṇ niṉmalaṉē.
translation: Even those with hearts like stone fortresses will build at least a fortress of empty words for those who approach them. I approached you with resolute faith. You show no pity for me, whose heart is a fortress of darkness. Are you not the one who once granted an inexhaustible granary of paddy? O pure one with three eyes!
commentary: Even the most hard-hearted people will usually offer a few polite, empty words to someone begging for help. God has given Vallalar nothing, not even that, though he came with firm faith. So he calls on the pure one with three eyes (Siva) and points to his record of miraculous generosity: once he gave a hungry devotee an endless supply of grain.

translit: ātikka māyai maṉattēṉ kavalai aṭuttaṭuttu vātikka nontu varuntukiṉ ṟēṉniṉ vaḻakkameṇṇic cōtikka eṉṉait toṭaṅkēl aruḷat toṭaṅkukaṇṭāy pōtikka vallanaṟ cēyumai yōṭeṉṉuḷ pukkavaṉē.
translation: My mind is ruled by primal illusion. I ache and suffer as anxieties afflict me time and again. Do not begin to test me according to your usual custom. Begin instead to grant your grace. You have entered my heart along with Uma and your noble son who is capable of teaching!
commentary: Suffering and anxiety have pushed Vallalar to his limit. He begs God to stop the agonizing trials saints are usually put through and to grant grace right away. God has already settled in his heart alongside the goddess Uma and their wise son Murugan. To Vallalar, that means the time for testing is over.

translit: piṟaimuṭit tāṇṭoru peṇmuṭit tōrpiḷḷaip pērmuṭitta niṟaimuṭit tāṇṭavañ cevvēṇi ceytiṭa nittamaṉṟiṉ maṟaimuṭit tāṇṭavañ ceyvōyeṉ pālaruḷ vaitteḷiyēṉ kuṟaimuṭit tāṇṭukoḷ eṉṉē palamuṟai kūṟuvatē.
translation: You rule with the crescent moon on your head, bear a woman on your head, and are crowned with a child's fame. As your red matted hair sways in a perfect dance, you perform your dance at the summit of the Vedas in the eternal hall. Bestow your grace upon me, end the deficiencies of this poor wretch, and rule over me. Why must I ask this so many times?
commentary: Siva's cosmic dance takes place at the very peak of the Vedas, the ancient sacred scriptures. The picture is the traditional one, with a crescent moon on his head and the river goddess Ganga caught in his matted hair. Vallalar is worn out with longing. Why must he beg so many times for his flaws to be erased?

translit: naṭaṅkoṇṭa poṉṉaṭi nīḻalil nāṉvantu naṇṇumaṭṭum tiṭaṅkoṇṭa niṉpukaḻ allāl piṟarpukaḻ ceppavaiyēl viṭaṅkoṇṭa kaṇṭat taruṭkuṉṟa mē-ima veṟpuṭaiyāḷ iṭaṅkoṇṭa teyvat taṉimuta lē-em iṟaiyavaṉē.
translation: O hill of grace with a poison-bearing throat! O unique divine source who holds the daughter of the Himalayas on your left side! O our Lord! Until I come and reach the shadow of your dancing golden feet, do not let me speak the praise of others rather than your enduring praise.
commentary: A prayer for single-minded devotion. Vallalar asks that his voice praise only God and never flatter worldly people for favors. He calls on Siva as the Lord with the poison-bearing throat who shares his form with the goddess, and asks to be kept this way until he reaches the shelter of God's dancing feet.

translit: viḻikkañca ṉantarum miṉṉārtam vāḻkkaiyil vīḻntayalōr moḻikkañci uḷḷam poṟātuniṉ nāma moḻinteḷiyēṉ kuḻikkañci pōṉmayaṅ kiṉṟēṉ aruḷak kuṟittilaiyēl paḻikkañci ṉōyiṉṉum eṉpaḻik kañcap paṭumuṉakkē.
translation: I fell into the life of lightning-like women who wear dark collyrium on their eyes. Fearing the gossip of others, my heart unable to bear it, I poor soul utter your name. I am bewildered like gruel poured into a pit. If you do not resolve to grant me grace, you who fear blame will have to face the blame for my ruin.
commentary: Lost in worldly distractions and afraid of public shame, Vallalar turns his desperation into a bold demand. God fears blame. Let this poor soul perish, and God's own name as a savior is ruined, with the blame landing on the Lord himself.

translit: cēlvaikkum kaṇṇumai pākāniṉ cittam tiruvaruḷeṉ pālvaikku mēliṭar ellām eṉaiviṭṭap pālnaṭakkak kālvaikku mēnaṟ cukavāḻveṉ mītiṉil kaṇvaikkumē mālvaikku māyaikaḷ maṇvaikku mētaṅkaḷ vāytaṉilē.
translation: O Lord who shares your form with Uma of fish-like eyes! If your will bestows divine grace upon me, all afflictions will step away and depart from me. A good life of bliss will set its eyes on me. The illusions that cause delusion will put dirt in their own mouths.
commentary: Divine grace is the one force needed to clear away suffering. The moment God decides to grant it, Vallalar says, worldly afflictions will simply step aside and true joy will take over his life. The illusions that once confused his mind will be left defeated, with dirt in their own mouths.

translit: orumātu peṟṟa makaṉporuṭ ṭāka uvantumuṉṉam varumāma ṉāki vaḻakkurait tōyeṉ vaḻakkuraittaṟ kirumā nilattatu pōlvēṭaṅ kaṭṭa iruttikolō tirumāl vaṇaṅkum patattava yāṉuṉ ciṟuvaṉaṉṟē.
translation: For the sake of a son born to a woman, you joyfully came forward in the past as an uncle and argued his case. Are you waiting to wear a disguise on this vast earth to argue my case? O Lord whose feet are worshipped by Thirumal! Am I not your little son?
commentary: Intimacy lets a devotee speak playfully to God. Vallalar recalls the old story where God disguised himself as an uncle to testify for a devotee in a village court. Is the Lord taking so long because he's preparing another disguise? Then he reminds him, whose feet even great deities like Thirumal (Vishnu) worship, that he is God's own little son.

translit: muṉṉañca muṇṭa miṭaṟṟara cēniṉ muḻukkaruṇai aṉṉañ cukampeṟa uṇṭumuṉ pālaṉ paṭaintilatāl kaṉṉeñca mōkaṭṭai vaṉṉeñca mō-eṭṭik kāyneñcamō eṉṉeñcam eṉṉeñca mōteri yēṉitaṟ keṉceyvatē.
translation: O King with the throat that swallowed poison in the past! Even after happily eating the food of your complete grace, my heart has not attained love for you. Is my heart made of stone, or hard wood, or the bitter poison-nut? What kind of heart is my heart? I do not know. What can I do about this?
commentary: The spiritual path needs a heart that melts with love, and Vallalar grieves that his stays cold. He has eaten the sweet food of divine grace and still lacks true devotion. Is his heart dead stone, he wonders, or hard wood, or a bitter poison-nut? He doesn't know, and he doesn't know what to do about it.

translit: vāṉam viṭātuṟu kālpōleṉ taṉṉai vaḷaintukoṇṭa māṉam viṭātitaṟ keṉceyku vēṉniṉṉai vantaṭuttēṉ ūṉam viṭātuḻal nāyēṉ piḻaiyai uḷaṅkoṇṭiṭēl ñāṉam viṭāta naṭattōyniṉ taṇṇaruḷ nalkukavē.
translation: Like the wind that never leaves the sky, worldly pride surrounds me and refuses to let go. What can I do about this? I have come seeking refuge in you. Do not take to heart the faults of this dog who wanders endlessly in error. O Lord whose dance is inseparable from wisdom, please grant your cool grace.
commentary: Pride is hard to see and harder to shake. Vallalar compares it to the wind that never leaves the sky, invisible and wrapped around him on every side. He cannot break free by his own effort, so he throws himself on grace and asks the Lord of wisdom for shelter.

translit: nāyuñ ceyāta naṭaiyuṭai yēṉukku nāṇamumuḷ nōyuñ ceyāniṉṟa vaṉmiṭi nīkkinaṉ nōṉpaḷittāy pēyuñ ceyāta koṭuntavat tālpeṟṟa piḷḷaikkunal tāyum ceyāḷinta naṉṟikaṇ ṭāyceñ caṭaiyavaṉē.
translation: My conduct is worse than a dog's. Yet you removed the harsh poverty that caused me shame and inner affliction, granting me the path of good penance. Even a good mother would not do such a kindness for a child she obtained through fierce austerities that a demon could not endure. Behold this, O Lord with red matted hair!
commentary: Divine grace surpasses even the fiercest maternal love. Looking back at his own unworthiness, Vallalar says God saved him from crushing poverty and inner turmoil when he felt his behavior was worse than a street dog's. He marvels that God showed him a kindness greater than any human mother could ever offer.

translit: uruvatti lēciṟi yēṉāki yūkatti loṉṟumiṉṟit teruvatti lēciṟu kālvīci yāṭiṭac ceṉṟa-antap paruvatti lēnal aṟivaḷit tē-uṉaip pāṭacceytāy aruvatti lē-uru vāṉōyniṉ taṇṇaḷi yārkkuḷatē.
translation: When I was small in stature, devoid of any understanding, swinging my little legs and running to play in the street: at that very age, you granted me true knowledge and made me sing of you. O Lord who took form within the formless, who else possesses your cool mercy?
commentary: Vallalar was a small boy, swinging his legs and running off to play in the street, when God gave him true knowledge and made him sing. He had no understanding of the world yet. So he calls the Lord the one who took form within the formless, the infinite stepping into a little boy's ordinary day with a mercy no one else has.

translit: māṉeḻun tāṭuṅ karattōyniṉ cānta maṉattilciṉan tāṉeḻun tālum eḻuka-eṉ ṟē-eṉ taḷarvai-ellām ūṉeḻun tārkkaniṉ pāluraip pēṉaṉṟi ūrkkuraikka nāṉeḻun tālumeṉ nā-eḻu mōmoḻi nalkiṭavē.
translation: O Lord whose hand holds the leaping deer! Even if anger rises in your peaceful heart, let it rise. I will declare all my weariness to you until my very flesh cries out. Even if I stand up to tell the townspeople instead, my tongue will not rise to speak the words.
commentary: Every pain goes straight to God. Vallalar will cry out until his very flesh aches, and if that stirs anger in the Lord's peaceful heart, let it rise. Complaining to the people around him is out of the question. His reliance on God is so complete that even if he stood up to try, his tongue would not move.

translit: vaṉameḻun tāṭuñ caṭaiyōyniṉ citta makiḻtalaṉṟic ciṉameḻun tālum eḻuka-eṉ ṟē-eṉ ciṟumaiyainiṉ muṉameḻun tāṟṟuva tallāl piṟarkku moḻintiṭa-eṉ maṉameḻun tālumeṉ vāyeḻu mō-uḷḷa vāṟituvē.
translation: O Lord whose matted hair dances with the rising waters! Even if anger rises instead of joy in your heart, let it rise. I pour out my baseness only before you. Even if my mind resolves to tell others, my mouth will not open to speak. This is the truth.
commentary: Vallalar says it again, more firmly. God is the only rightful witness to his flaws and suffering, and even if his mind decides to tell others, his mouth will not open. The Lord whose matted hair dances with the rising waters holds a vast and chaotic force in check. Only such a one can receive a person's heaviest sorrows.

translit: ciṟpara mē-eñ civamē tiruvaruḷ cīrmikunta kaṟpaka mē-uṉaic cārntōrk kaḷikkuniṉ kaivaḻakkam aṟpamaṉ ṟēpala aṇṭaṅ kaḷiṉaṭaṅ kātateṉṟē naṟpara ñāṉikaḷ vācakat tālkaṇṭu nāṭiṉaṉē.
translation: O Supreme Consciousness! O our Sivam! O wish-fulfilling tree abounding in the wealth of divine grace! Your custom of giving to those who reach You is not small, and it cannot be contained within many universes. Realizing this through the words of good supreme sages, I sought You out.
commentary: God's generosity to those who reach him cannot be contained even in many universes. Vallalar calls the divine Sivam (the supreme reality) and a wish-fulfilling tree. He came seeking precisely because the great sages promised this boundless giving.

translit: varuñcelluḷnīrmaṟut tālum karuṇai maṟāta-eṅkaḷ peruñcelva mē-eñ civamē niṉaittoḻap peṟṟumiṅkē taruñcel arikku marampōl ciṟumait taḷarnaṭaiyāl aruñcellal mūḻkiniṟ kiṉṟēṉ ituniṉ aruṭkaḻakē.
translation: Even if the passing clouds withhold their water, Your compassion never fails, O our great wealth! O our Sivam! Though I am blessed to worship You, I stand here sinking in intense sorrow with a feeble gait born of smallness, like a tree eaten by termites. Is this beautiful to Your grace?
commentary: God's compassion is more reliable than the rain, yet Vallalar feels hollowed out by sorrow like a termite-eaten tree. So he asks a pointed question. Does it look good for divine grace to let a devoted worshipper suffer this deeply?

translit: karumuka nīkkiya pāṇaṉuk kēkaṉa kaṅkoṭukkat tirumukam cēraṟ kaḷittōyeṉ ṟuṉṉait terintaṭutteṉ orumukam pārttaruḷ eṉkiṉṟa ēḻaik kutavilaiyēl urumukavārkkum viṭaiyōy evarmaṟ ṟutavuvarē.
translation: You gave a sacred letter to the Chera king to grant gold to the musician and dispel his sorrow. Knowing this, I approached You. If You do not help this poor one who begs You to look at my face just once and bestow grace, O Lord who rides the roaring bull, who else will help me?
commentary: The story is a famous one in Tamil tradition. God sent a sacred letter to the Chera king so that a struggling musician would receive gold and be rid of his sorrow. Vallalar knows it and comes with a direct appeal: if God stepped into the world to end one man's poverty, who else can a desperate soul turn to?

translit: maruppā vaṉattuṟṟa māṇikku maṉṉaṉ maṉamaṟintōr tiruppā curañceytu poṟkiḻi īntaniṉ cīrniṉaintē viruppā niṉaiyaṭut tēṉeṉak kīntiṭa vē-iṉṟeṉṉai karuppāniṉ cittam tiruppāyeṉ mītu kaṟaikkaṇṭaṉē.
translation: Knowing the king's mind, You composed a sacred verse and gave a purse of gold to the young bachelor in the fragrant forest. Thinking of Your excellence, I eagerly approached You. Will You not turn Your heart toward me today to bestow Your gifts upon me, O dark-throated Lord?
commentary: Another old story. Knowing the king's mind, God composed a sacred verse so a poor young man could receive a purse of gold. Vallalar holds up that track record of generosity and asks for the same attention today.

translit: pīḻaiyai mēvumiv vāḻkkaiyi lēmaṉam pētuṟṟa-iv ēḻaiyai nīviṭa lāmō aṭimaik kiraṅkukaṇṭāy māḻaiyaippōṉmuṉṉart tāṅkoṇṭu vaittu vaḷartta-iḷa vāḻaiyait tāmpiṉṉar nīrviṭa liṉṟi maṟuppatuṇṭē.
translation: In this life filled with distress, can You abandon this poor one whose mind is bewildered? Have mercy on Your servant. Having taken and tenderly raised a young banana plant like gold at first, would anyone later deny it water?
commentary: No one who raised a young banana plant like gold would later refuse it water. Vallalar puts this to God as an intimate, logical plea. Having nurtured him so carefully and brought him this far, the Lord cannot abandon him to the distress of worldly life.

translit: karuttaṟi yācciṟi yēṉpaṭun tuṉpak kalakkamellām uruttaṟi yāmai poṟuttaruḷ īpavar uṉṉaiyaṉṟit tiruttaṟi yārpiṟar aṉṟēmeṉ kaṉṟiṉ ciṟumai-oṉṟum eruttaṟi yātunaṟ cētā aṟiyum iraṅkukavē.
translation: I am a lowly one who lacks understanding. Other than you, who will tolerate all the sorrowful turmoil I suffer without showing anger at my ignorance, and grant me grace? Others do not know how to correct me. A bull does not know the distress of a tender calf; only the good mother cow knows it. Show me mercy.
commentary: A bull takes no notice of a tender calf's distress. Only the mother cow knows it. Vallalar says ordinary people are like that bull, unable to understand his deep sorrow, while God, like the mother, knows his pain and answers with true mercy.

translit: vāṉvēṇṭik koṇṭa maruntōmuk kaṇkoṇṭa vaḷḷaluṉṉai nāṉvēṇṭik koṇṭatu niṉṉaṭi yārkku nakaitarumī tēṉvēṇṭik koṇṭaṉai eṉpār itaṟkiṉṉum ēṉiraṅkāy tāṉvēṇṭik koṇṭa aṭimaikkuk kūḻiṭat tāḻppatuṇṭē.
translation: O nectar desired by the heavens! O generous three-eyed Lord! My pleading with you makes your devotees laugh. They ask why I keep begging for this. Why do you still withhold your mercy? Do you delay pouring porridge for a slave you yourself have taken?
commentary: A master is responsible for feeding the servant he has taken. Vallalar has surrendered completely, so why is he still waiting? He is left begging for the plain porridge of divine mercy, and the delay makes him a laughingstock to others.

translit: paiyurait tāṭum paṇippuyat tōytamaip pāṭukiṉṟōr uyyurait tāvuḷḷa tillateṉ ṟillatai uḷḷateṉṟē poyyurait tālum taruvār piṟaratu pōlaṉṟināṉ meyyurait tālum iraṅkāmai niṉṉaruḷ meykkaḻakē.
translation: O Lord whose shoulders bear dancing hooded snakes! To survive, those who sing of you might speak falsely, claiming what exists does not exist and what does not exist exists, and others will still reward them. Unlike that, even when I speak the truth, you show no mercy. Is this fitting for the beauty of your true grace?
commentary: The world often pays flatterers who tell desperate lies to wealthy patrons just to survive, calling what exists nonexistent and what does not exist real. Vallalar sees a bitter irony in his own case. He tells God the honest truth about his suffering and gets silence, and he asks whether that silence truly matches the beauty of divine grace.

translit: maṭalvaṟṟi ṉālum maṇamvaṟṟu ṟāta malareṉa-eṉ uṭalvaṟṟi ṉālumeṉ uḷvaṟṟu mōtuyar uḷḷavellām aṭalvaṟṟu ṟātaniṉ tāṭkaṉṟi īṅkaya lārkkuraiyēṉ kaṭalvaṟṟi ṉālum karuṇaivaṟ ṟātamuk kaṇṇavaṉē.
translation: Just as a flower retains its fragrance even when its petals wither, will my inner self dry up even if my body wastes away? I will not speak of all my enduring sorrows to strangers here, but only to your victorious feet. O three-eyed Lord whose compassion never runs dry even if the oceans evaporate!
commentary: A flower keeps its fragrance after the petals dry. Vallalar says his inner self is the same, still full of feeling while his body wastes away from sorrow. True devotion outlasts the body's decay. He vows to share his pain only with God, trusting a compassion that will not run dry even if the oceans evaporate.

translit: eḷḷiruk kiṉṟataṟ kēṉuñ ciṟitiṭa miṉṟi-eṉpāṉ muḷḷiruk kiṉṟatu pōluṟṟa tuṉpa muyakkamellām veḷḷiruk kiṉṟavar tāmuṅkaṇ ṭāreṉil mēvi-eṉṟaṉ uḷḷiruk kiṉṟaniṉ tāṭkōtal eṉem uṭaiyavaṉē.
translation: Without leaving even a tiny space the size of a sesame seed, all the sorrowful turmoil I suffer pierces my flesh like thorns. If even outsiders have seen this, what need is there to report it to your feet that reside within me, O my Lord?
commentary: The pain leaves no space even the size of a sesame seed. Vallalar feels it like thorns through every inch of his flesh. Even strangers on the outside can see his agony, he says, so there is no need to explain it aloud to God, who lives inside his heart and must already know it perfectly.

translit: poṉkiṉṟupūtta caṭaiyāyiv vēḻaikkuṉ poṉṉaruḷām naṉkiṉṟu nītaral vēṇṭuman tōtuyar naṇṇi-eṉṉait tiṉkiṉṟa tēkoṭum pāmpaiyum pāluṇac ceytukolār eṉkiṉṟa ñālam iḻukkurai yāteṟ kiraṅkiṭiṉē.
translation: O Lord with matted hair blooming like gold! You must grant the goodness of Your golden grace to this poor soul today. Alas, sorrow approaches and consumes me. The world says people will feed milk even to a cruel snake and spare its life. If You take pity on me, the world will not speak ill of You.
commentary: Sorrow is eating him alive. People feed milk even to a deadly snake and let it live, out of plain compassion. If human beings show that much mercy to a dangerous creature, nobody will fault God for taking pity on a suffering soul.

translit: vāymūṭik kolpavar pōlē-eṉ uḷḷattai vaṉtuyarām pēymūṭik koṇṭateṉ ceykēṉ mukattil piṟaṅkukaiyaic cēymūṭik koṇṭunaṟ pāṟkaḻak kaṇṭun tikaḻmulaiyait tāymūṭik koḷḷuva tuṇṭō aruḷuka caṅkaraṉē.
translation: Like those who kill by smothering the mouth, the ghost of intense sorrow has smothered my heart. What will I do? When a child covers its face with its little hands and cries for good milk, will a mother cover her breasts and refuse it? Bestow Your grace, O Sankara!
commentary: Grief smothers the heart the way a killer smothers a mouth. Vallalar answers it with the plainest picture of compassion there is, a mother and her crying child. No mother hides her milk from her baby, so God (Sankara, a name for the Divine) must not hold back grace from a soul this desperate.

translit: kōḷvēṇṭum ēḻai maṉattiṉai vēṟuṟṟuk koṭṭakkoḷḷit tēḷvēṇṭu mōcuṭat tīvēṇṭu mōvatai ceytiṭa-ōr vāḷvēṇṭu mōkoṭun tuṉpē atileṇ maṭaṅkukaṇṭāy āḷvēṇṭu mēleṉṉai āḷvēṇṭum eṉṉuḷ añaroḻittē.
translation: Does one need a fiery scorpion to sting this poor afflicted mind? Does one need fire to burn it? Does one need a sword to torment it? Cruel sorrow is eight times worse than all those things. If You want a subject, You must rule me and eradicate the grief within me.
commentary: Mental anguish is worse than any physical torture. A scorpion's sting, a fire, a sword wound are nothing beside the weight of sorrow inside. The only cure Vallalar asks for is that God take full ownership of his mind and rule it directly.

translit: viṭaiyilai yō-ataṉ mēlēṟi eṉmuṉ viraintuvarap paṭaiyilai yōtuyar ellām tuṇikkap pataṅkoḷaruṭ koṭaiyilai yō-eṉ kuṟaitīra nalkak kulavumeṉtāy puṭaiyilai yō-eṉ taṉakkākap pēca-em puṇṇiyaṉē.
translation: Do You have no bull? Do You have no retinue to mount it and rush before me? Do You have no gift of grace at Your feet to sever all my sorrow? Is my celebrated Mother not by Your side to speak for me and grant relief from my flaws, O virtuous Lord?
commentary: When help is slow, it feels like neglect. Vallalar asks whether God has lost his bull, his traditional mount, or his power to grant relief. Surely the Divine Mother still stands beside him, ready to speak up for her suffering child.

translit: naṟaiyuḷa tēmalark koṉṟaikoṇ ṭāṭiya naṟcaṭaimēl piṟaiyuḷa tēkaṅkaip peṇṇuḷa tēpiṟaṅ kuṅkaḻuttil kaṟaiyuḷa tē-aruḷ eṅkuḷa tē-ik kaṭaiyavaṉēṉ kuṟaiyuḷa tē-eṉ ṟaraṟṟavum caṟṟuṅ kuṟittilatē.
translation: On Your good matted hair adorned with fragrant honey-filled cassia flowers rests the crescent moon. The maiden Ganga is there. On Your shining neck is the dark stain. Where is Your grace? Even as this lowly one cries out loudly about his flaws, You do not take the slightest note of it.
commentary: God wears all his famous symbols: the crescent moon, the river goddess Ganga in his hair, and the dark stain on his neck from the poison he swallowed. Every ornament is in place. The one thing this soul needs is missing, and his loud cries go unanswered, so he is left asking where the grace has gone.

translit: ciṉattālum kāmatti ṉālumeṉ taṉṉait tikaippikkumim maṉattāl uṟuntuyar pōtāmai eṉṟu matittuccuṟṟum iṉattālum vāḻkkai iṭumpaiyi ṉālum iḷaikkavaittāy aṉattāṉ pukaḻum patattōy ituniṉ aruṭkaḻakē.
translation: This mind bewilders me with anger and lust. You considered the sorrow caused by this mind insufficient, and so you made me languish through my surrounding relatives and the afflictions of worldly life. O Lord whose feet are praised by the swan-riding Brahma, is this beautiful to your grace?
commentary: The mind already torments him with anger and lust, and worldly attachments only add to the pain. Vallalar asks, a little playfully, whether it suits God's grace to pile on relatives and the troubles of daily life when the inner struggle is hard enough. Brahma, the creator god who rides a swan, is named to show that even the highest cosmic powers praise the Lord's feet.

translit: pullaḷa vāyiṉum īyārtam vāyil pukuntupukaḻc collaḷa vāniṉ ṟirappōr irakkanaṟ coṉṉaṅkaḷaik kallaḷavāttaru kiṉṟōrtam pāluṅ karuticceṉṟōr nellaḷa vāyiṉum kēḷēṉniṉ pālaṉṟi niṉmalaṉē.
translation: People go to the doors of those who do not give even a blade of grass and beg with words of praise. Some give good gold in abundance to those who beg. I will not go to them to ask for even a single grain of paddy. I will ask only from you, O pure one.
commentary: Relying on God alone means refusing to beg from human patrons, however rich or generous they are. Vallalar will not flatter the wealthy for even a single grain of rice. He looks only to the Pure One for what he needs and turns his back on worldly rewards.

translit: piṟaicūḻnta vēṇi muṭikkaṉi yē-em peruñcelvamē kaṟaicūḻnta kaṇṭattem kaṟpaka mēnutaṟ kaṭkarumpē maṟaicūḻnta maṉṟoḷir māmaṇi yē-eṉ maṉamuḻutum kuṟaicūḻntu koṇṭateṉ ceykēṉ akaṟṟak kuṟittaruḷē.
translation: O fruit upon the crescent-adorned matted hair! Our great wealth! Our wish-fulfilling tree with a dark-stained neck! O sweet sugarcane with an eye on the forehead! O great jewel shining in the hall surrounded by the Vedas! My entire mind is engulfed by faults. What shall I do? Please resolve to remove them by your grace.
commentary: Old images of Siva fill this prayer, the wish-fulfilling tree and the sweet sugarcane among them. The dark-stained neck recalls the story of Siva swallowing poison to save the world, and the eye on the forehead stands for supreme spiritual vision. Overwhelmed by his own faults, Vallalar cries out to this vast, compassionate presence to sweep his mind clean.

translit: kaṇkaṭṭi āṭum paruvatti lēmulai kaṇṭa-oru peṇkaṭṭi yāḷa niṉaikkiṉṟa ōrciṟu piḷḷaiyaippōl eṇkaṭṭi yāṉuṉ aruḷviḻain tēṉciva ṉē-eṉneñcam puṇkaṭṭi yāyalaik kiṉṟatu maṇkaṭṭip pōlutirntē.
translation: Like a little boy playing blindman's buff who dreams of embracing a grown woman, I formed a thought and desired your grace, O Siva. My heart has become a festering wound, and it wanders and crumbles like a clod of earth.
commentary: Longing for grace can run far ahead of spiritual maturity. Vallalar pictures himself as a little boy playing a blindfold game who suddenly wants the embrace of a grown woman. Reaching for something so far beyond him leaves his heart a raw wound, crumbling like a clod of earth.

tamil: பொய்விட்ட நெஞ்சுறும் பொற்பதத் தைய இப் பொய்யனைநீ
translit: meyviṭṭa vañcaka neñcāl paṭuntuyar venneruppil neyviṭṭa vāṟinta vāḻkkaiyiṉ vātaṉai nēriṭṭatāl poyviṭṭa neñcuṟum poṟpatat taiya ip poyyaṉainī kaiviṭ ṭiṭaniṉai yēlaruḷ vāykaru ṇaikkaṭalē.
translation: The sorrow caused by this deceitful mind that has forsaken truth is like pouring ghee into a hot fire, and the torments of worldly life have confronted me in this way. O Lord whose golden feet abide in hearts devoid of falsehood, do not think of abandoning this liar. Bestow your grace, O ocean of compassion.
commentary: Worldly troubles feed the mind's sorrow the way ghee, or clarified butter, makes a hot fire blaze higher. The Lord's feet rest in hearts free of falsehood, and Vallalar openly confesses his own heart is deceitful. He begs the ocean of compassion to pour out grace and not abandon him.

translit: aruṭkaṭa lē-ak kaṭalamu tē-av vamutattuṟṟa teruṭcuvai yē-ac cuvaippaya ṉēmaṟaic ceṉṉiniṉṟa poruṭpata mē-ap patattara cēniṉ pukaḻniṉaiyā iruṭkuṇa māyai maṉattē ṉaiyumuvan tēṉṟukoḷḷē.
translation: O ocean of grace! O nectar of that ocean! O clear and sweet taste of that nectar! O fruit of that taste! O state of truth standing at the crest of the Vedas! O king of that state! Joyfully accept even me, I whose mind is filled with the dark illusion that never thinks of your glory.
commentary: The address goes deeper step by step, from the ocean of grace to its nectar, to the taste of that nectar, and on to the fruit that taste brings. This grace is the highest truth, standing at the crest of the Vedas. Vallalar asks to be accepted anyway, though his mind is clouded by illusion and forgets that glory.

translit: aṇṭaṅkaṇ ṭāṉum aḷantāṉum kāṇṭaṟ kariyavaniṉ kaṇṭaṅkaṇ ṭārkkuñ caṭaimēl kuṟainta kalaimatiyiṉ tuṇṭaṅkaṇ ṭārkkum payamuḷa tō-eṉac cūḻntaṭaintēṉ toṇṭaṉkaṇ ṭāḷpala teṇṭaṉkaṇ ṭāyniṉ tuṇaiyaṭikkē.
translation: O Lord who is difficult to see for the creator of the worlds and the one who measured them! Do those who have seen your dark throat and the crescent moon on your matted hair have any fear? Thinking this, I approached you. Rule over this servant. I offer countless prostrations to your two feet.
commentary: The dark throat and the crescent moon are the marks of a God who suffers to protect others. Whoever has seen them has nothing left to fear. Trusting this shelter, Vallalar surrenders completely, knowing this divine truth lies far beyond the reach of the creator and preserver gods.

translit: tēṭṭakkaṇ ṭērmoḻip pākā ulakil cilarkuraṅkai āṭṭakkaṇ ṭēṉaṉṟi akkuraṅ kālavar āṭaccaṟṟum kēṭṭukkaṇ ṭēṉilai nāṉēḻai neñcak kiḻakkuraṅkāl vēṭṭukkoṇ ṭāṭukiṉ ṟēṉitu cāṉṟa viyappuṭaittē.
translation: O Lord who shares half your form with the Goddess whose words are as sweet as honey! In this world, I have seen people making monkeys dance. I have never heard or seen people dancing to a monkey's direction. Yet I dance, driven by the desires of the old monkey of my poor heart. This is a profound wonder.
commentary: The restless mind is often called a monkey. People train a monkey to dance on command, and Vallalar has never heard of a monkey making people dance. Yet that is his state. He dances to the wild desires of the old monkey in his own heart.

translit: pōkaṅkoṇ ṭārtta aruḷār amutap puṇarmulaiyaip pākaṅkoṇ ṭārtta paramporu ḷēniṉ pataniṉaiyā vēkaṅkoṇ ṭārtta maṉattāliv vēḻai melintumikac cōkaṅkoṇ ṭārttuniṟ kiṉṟēṉ aruḷat toṭaṅkukavē.
translation: O Supreme Reality who shares half your form with the Goddess whose breasts brim with the nectar of grace! My fierce and rushing mind never thinks of your feet. Exhausted by this mind, I stand here as a poor wretch, crying aloud in deep sorrow. Please begin to bestow your grace.
commentary: A runaway mind brings exhaustion and sorrow. Vallalar's fierce, rushing thoughts never turn to the Lord's feet, and he stands crying aloud for grace to begin. He makes his plea to the Supreme Reality who shares half his form with the Goddess, the nurturing presence of grace.

translit: iṉṟala vēneṭu nāḷāka ēḻaik ketirttatuṉpam oṉṟala vēpala eṇṇila vē-uṟ ṟuraittatayal maṉṟala vēpiṟar naṉṟala vēyeṉa vantakayak kaṉṟala vēpacuṅ kaṉṟaṭi yēṉṟaṉaik kāttaruḷē.
translation: My sorrows did not begin today. The troubles confronting this poor wretch over a long time are many and countless. The assembly where I told my grief is foreign to me. Others say my state is not good. I am not the offspring of a vile beast. I am a tender calf, your servant. Please protect and bless me.
commentary: Vallalar feels alone and misunderstood. His troubles are old and countless, and when he tells his grief, the gathering is foreign to him and people only judge his state. So he turns to God for shelter, calling himself no offspring of a vile beast but an innocent, helpless calf seeking its true guardian.

translit: paṭipaṭṭa māyaiyiṉ pāṟpaṭṭa cālap parappiṟpaṭṭē miṭipaṭṭa vāḻkkaiyiṉ mēṟpaṭṭa tuṉpa vicārattiṉāl aṭipaṭṭa nāṉuṉak kāṭpaṭṭum iṉṉum alaitalnaṉṟō piṭipaṭṭa nēriṭaip peṇpaṭṭa pākap peruntakaiyē.
translation: O great Lord whose half is the woman with a waist so slender it can be grasped. I am caught in the vast expanse of illusions belonging to Maya. I am battered by the overwhelming sorrows of an impoverished life. Even after surrendering to you, is it right that I still wander in distress?
commentary: Caught in the illusions of māyā (worldly delusion) and battered by poverty, Vallalar asks why a soul that has already surrendered should still suffer. He wants to know how it can be right to leave a devoted servant wandering in distress.

translit: uṭaiyāyeṉ viṇṇappam oṉṟuṇṭu kēṭṭaruḷ uṉṉaṭiccīr taṭaiyātum iṉṟip pukalvatal lālic cakattiṭaināṉ naṭaiyāl ciṟumaikoṇ ṭantō piṟarai naviṉṟavarpāl aṭaiyā maiyuneñ cuṭaiyāmai yuntan taruḷukavē.
translation: O Master, I have one plea. Listen and grant it. In this world, I wish to praise the glory of your feet without any hindrance. Grant me the grace to never stoop to a petty life, to never praise others, to never seek them out, and to never let my heart be broken.
commentary: Vallalar asks for one boon: to sing God's praises without ever stooping to flatter wealthy patrons. He begs the Lord to guard his dignity, so that he never has to seek out worldly people for help and his heart is never broken by humiliation.

translit: tañcameṉ ṟēniṉṟa nāyēṉ kuṟaiyait taviruṉakkōr pañcamiṉ ṟē-ula kellāniṉ cīraruṭ pāṅkukaṇṭāy eñcaniṉ ṟēṟkuṉai yallāl tuṇaipiṟi tillai-itu vañcamaṉ ṟēniṉ pataṅkāṇka mukkaṇ maṇiccuṭarē.
translation: O jewel-flame with three eyes. Remove the flaws of this wretch who stands crying for refuge. You suffer no scarcity. All the worlds are the realm of your supreme grace. For me who stands bereft, there is no companion but you. This is no deceit. I swear upon your feet.
commentary: Desperation turns into an oath. Vallalar swears upon the Lord's feet that he has no other refuge. God lacks nothing, he points out, while he himself stands completely empty, and he insists that his total dependence is the plain truth.

translit: poṟuttālum nāṉceyum kuṟṟaṅkaḷ yāvum poṟāteṉainī oṟuttālum naṉṟiṉik kaiviṭṭi ṭēleṉ ṉuṭaiyavaṉnī veṟuttālum vēṟilai vēṟṟōr iṭattai virumpi-eṉṉai aṟuttāluñ ceṉṟiṭa māṭṭēṉ eṉakkuṉ aruḷiṭamē.
translation: Whether you bear all the faults I commit or refuse to bear them and punish me, it is fine. Do not abandon me now. You are my Lord. Even if you despise me, I have no one else. Even if you cut me off and wish for me to seek another place, I will not go. Your realm of grace is my only home.
commentary: True surrender accepts whatever God chooses to do. Vallalar will take forgiveness or harsh punishment, as long as the Lord does not abandon him. Even if he is rejected and ordered away, he will not leave the home he has found in grace.

translit: cēlvarum ērviḻi maṅkaipaṅ kā-eṉ ciṟumaikaṇṭāl mēlvaru nīvarat tāḻttālum uṉṟaṉ viyaṉaruṭpoṟ kālvaru mē-iḷaṅ kaṉṟaḻat tāyppacuk kāṇiṉmaṭip pālvaru mēmulaip pālvaru mēpeṟṟa pāvaikkumē.
translation: O Lord whose half is the woman with beautiful eyes like carp. If you see my distress, even if you delay coming to me, your vast and golden grace will stream toward me. When a mother cow sees her young calf crying, milk flows from her udder. When a mother sees her child, her breast milk flows.
commentary: Grace answers suffering the way a mother's body answers a crying child. Even if the Lord seems to delay, Vallalar trusts that grace will come on its own. A cow's milk flows when her calf cries, and a mother's milk flows when she sees her baby. He is that certain.

translit: vaṉpaṭṭa kūṭalil vāṉpaṭṭa vaiyai varampiṭṭaniṉ poṉpaṭṭa mēṉiyil puṇpaṭṭa pōtil puvinaṭaiyām tuṉpaṭṭa vīraran tōvāta vūrartam tūyaneñcam eṉpaṭṭa tō-iṉṟu kēṭṭa-eṉ neñcam iṭipaṭṭatē.
translation: In the harsh city of Koodal, when you raised the banks of the heavenly Vaigai river and your golden form suffered a strike, what must the pure heart of the heroic Vadavurar have felt, he who endured the sorrow of worldly existence? Hearing of this today, my own heart shatters.
commentary: A famous ancient story tells of the divine coming to earth as an ordinary laborer and being struck with a cane by a king. Vallalar imagines that blow landing on God and wonders how it must have broken the heart of the great saint Manikkavasagar, called here Vadavurar. The thought of that pain, so long ago, shatters his own heart today.

translit: nīrcintum kaṇṇum nilaicintum neñcamum nīṇaṭaiyil cīrcintu vāḻkkaiyum tēṉcinti vāṭiya cemmalarpōl kūrcintu puntiyum koṇṭuniṉ ṟēṉuṭ kuṟaicintumvā ṟōrcintu pōlaruḷ nērcintaṉ ēttum uṭaiyavaṉē.
translation: I stand here with eyes shedding tears, a heart losing its balance, a life losing its virtue on this long worldly path, and a mind losing its sharpness like a red flower withered after shedding its honey. O Lord praised by the righteous, bestow your grace like a vast ocean to wash away the flaws within me.
commentary: Spiritual exhaustion drains the mind and heart. Vallalar sees his fading awareness as a red flower that has shed its honey and withered. He asks the Lord to wash away his flaws with grace as vast as the ocean.

translit: koṭikoṇṭa ēṟṟiṉ naṭaiyum caṭaiyum kuḷirmukamum tuṭikoṇṭa kaiyum poṭikoṇṭa mēṉiyum tōluṭaiyum piṭikoṇṭa pākamum pēraruḷ nōkkamum peykaḻalum kuṭikoṇṭa naṉmaṉam eṉmaṉam pōṟkuṟai koḷvatiṉṟē.
translation: A good mind enshrined with the gait of the bull bearing your banner, your matted hair, your cool face, your hand holding the small drum, your ash-smeared body, your garment of skin, your form sharing the Goddess, your gaze of supreme grace, and your adorned anklets will never harbor flaws like my mind does.
commentary: Fill the mind with the Lord's form and no room is left for flaws. Vallalar lists the traditional features of Siva, from the ash-smeared body to the gaze of supreme grace, as a focus for devotion. A mind anchored in them stays pure, and he admits his own is not yet such a mind.

translit: vitikkum patikkum patinati ārmati vēṇippati titikkum patikkum patimēṟ katikkun tikaḻpativāṉ tutikkum patikkum pati-ōṅku māpati coṟkaṭanta patikkum paticiṟ patiyem patinam pacupatiyē.
translation: He is the Lord of the creator, the Lord of the sustainer, and the Lord wearing the river and the moon in his matted hair. He is the radiant Lord of the higher realms, the supreme Lord praised by the heavens, and the Lord of the state beyond words. He is the Lord of the space of consciousness. He is our Lord, our Pasupati.
commentary: One Lord stands behind every action and every level of reality. He governs the creator, the sustainer and the highest heavens alike. And that same supreme being is Lord of our own inner consciousness, guiding each soul.

translit: eṉaiyaṭain tāḻttiya tuṉpac cumaiyai iṟakkeṉavē niṉaiyaṭain tēṉaṭi nāyēṟ karuḷa niṉaitikaṇṭāy viṉaiyaṭain tēmaṉa vīṟuṭain tēniṉṟu vēṟṟavartam maṉaiyaṭain tēmaṉam vāṭaluṉ toṇṭar marapallavē.
translation: I have come to you asking you to lift the burden of sorrow that has overwhelmed and sunk me. See that you resolve to bestow grace upon this lowly dog. It is not the tradition of your devotees to succumb to karma, to lose their strength of mind, and to stand withering at the doorsteps of strangers.
commentary: A true devotee leans on grace alone and does not go begging to worldly people. Sorrow can weigh heavy enough to crush the spirit. Even so, standing at strangers' doors for relief breaks with the tradition of the Lord's devotees, and Vallalar brings his burden straight to God.

translit: vaṉampōy varuvatu pōlēvaṉ celvar maṉaiyiṭattē tiṉampōy varumic ciṟiyēṉ ciṟumaic ceyalatupōyc ciṉampōyk koṭumpakaik kāmamum pōyniṉ tiṟanikaḻttā iṉampōyk koṭiya maṉampōy iruppateṉ ṟeṉṉaracē.
translation: My King! Every day I, a lowly person, visit the houses of the hard-hearted wealthy and return as if walking into a barren forest. When will this lowly behavior end? When will anger and the cruel enemy of lust depart? When will the company of those who do not speak of your greatness leave me? When will my cruel mind perish so I can remain in peace?
commentary: Vallalar compares his daily visits to the houses of hard-hearted rich men to walking through a barren forest. Begging there is tiring and empty. He longs to be free of it, free of anger and lust, and free of people who never speak of the Lord's greatness.

translit: peṟṟā ḷaṉaiyaniṉ kuṟṟēval ceytu piḻaikkaṟiyāc ciṟṟāḷ palariṉum ciṟṟā ḷeṉumeṉ ciṟumaitavirt tuṟṟāḷ kilai-eṉiṉ maṟṟār tuṇai-eṉak kuṉkamalap poṟṟāḷ aruṭpukaḻk kaṟṟāyntu pāṭap purintaruḷē.
translation: You are like the mother who bore me. I do not know how to survive by doing your humble service. If you do not remove my lowliness of being the lowest among many lowly servants and accept me, who else is my support? Grant your grace so I may learn, deeply reflect upon, and sing the gracious glory of your golden lotus feet.
commentary: Vallalar addresses God as the mother who bore him. He feels helpless, the lowest of lowly servants, and asks where else he could turn if God rejects him. All he wants now is the grace to study, reflect on and sing the glory of the Lord's golden feet.

translit: annāṇai yātunañ cēṟṟayaṉ mālmaṉai yātiyartam poṉṉāṇaik kātta aruṭkaṭa lēpiṟar puṉmaṉaipōy innāṇai yāvakai eṉṉāṇaik kāttaruḷ ēḻaikkuniṉ taṉṉāṇai aiyaniṉ tāḷāṇai vēṟu caraṇillaiyē.
translation: Ocean of grace! On that day you consumed the poison without hesitation and protected the golden marriage threads of the wives of Brahma, Vishnu, and the other gods. Protect my honor today so I do not suffer by visiting the petty houses of others. I swear upon you, Lord. I swear upon your feet. This poor one has no other refuge.
commentary: An old story tells how Siva drank a deadly poison to save the universe, protecting the lives of the other gods and sparing their wives from widowhood. Vallalar asks the same compassionate Lord to spare him the daily humiliation of begging at the houses of petty people for his survival. He swears upon God's feet that he has nowhere else to go.

translit: pavacāta ṉampeṟum pātakar mēvumip pāriṭainal civacāta ṉattarai ēṉpaṭait tāyat tiruvilikaḷ avacāta ṉaṅkaḷaik kaṇṭiva ruḷḷam aḻuṅka-eṉṟō kavacā taṉameṉak kaimmā ṉuriyaik kaḷittavaṉē.
translation: You who joyously wear the elephant skin as your precious armor! Why did you create people with true Saiva virtues on this earth filled with sinners who pursue worldly attachments? Did you create them so their hearts would grieve watching the futile ways of those who lack your grace?
commentary: Good people suffer when they must live among the cruel and worldly. Vallalar asks God why he puts spiritually minded people in such a selfish world. He wonders if it was only so their hearts would grieve, watching others waste their lives on empty attachments. The elephant skin in the opening line comes from the story of Siva defeating a demonic elephant and wearing its hide as armor.

translit: nāṉceyta puṇṇiya miyātō civāya nama-eṉavē ūṉceyta nāvaikkoṇ ṭōtappeṟ ṟēṉeṉai oppavarār vāṉceyta nāṉmukat tōṉum tiruneṭu mālumaṟṟait tēṉceyta kaṟpakat tēvaṉum tēvaruñ ceyyaritē.
translation: What good deeds have I done? I am blessed to chant "Sivaya Nama" with my fleshy tongue. Who is equal to me? The four-faced Brahma who created the heavens, the tall and sacred Vishnu, Indra of the honey-yielding Kalpaka tree, and the other gods all find this hard to achieve.
commentary: Sivaya Nama means homage to Siva, and Vallalar counts the chance to chant it as the highest blessing there is. To say it with an ordinary tongue of flesh makes him luckier, he feels, than the greatest gods in heaven, Brahma the creator and Vishnu the preserver among them. Even those mighty beings struggle to reach the simple, pure devotion this prayer asks for.

translit: uṟṟā yiṉumaṟaik kōrvari yōyeṉai uṟṟuppeṟṟa naṟṟā yiṉumiṉi yāṉēniṉ nallaruḷ nalkileṉṉai viṟṟā yiṉuṅkoḷa vēṇṭukiṉ ṟēṉeṉ viruppaṟintum caṟṟā yiṉumiraṅ kātōniṉ cittam tayānitiyē.
translation: O Treasure of Compassion, though You are close, You are rare for the Vedas to comprehend. You are sweeter than the good mother who bore me. If You grant Your good grace, I beg You to take me as Your own, even if You must sell me. Knowing my desire, does Your heart not feel even a little pity?
commentary: Sweeter than the mother who bore him, yet beyond anything the Vedas (ancient Hindu scriptures) can grasp. That is the Lord Vallalar speaks to. He offers himself as property, to be claimed or even sold, so long as God takes him. Then comes the hurt question. All this longing, and not one drop of pity yet?

translit: vāṉmā ṟiṉumoḻi māṟāta māṟaṉ maṉaṅkaḷikkak kāṉmāṟi yāṭiya kaṟpaka mēniṉ karuṇaiyeṉmēl tāṉmā ṟiṉumviṭṭu nāṉmāṟi ṭēṉpeṟṟa tāykkumulaip pāṉmāṟi ṉumpiḷḷai pāṉmāṟu mō-atil palliṭumē.
translation: O wish-fulfilling tree, You switched your dancing foot to delight the heart of the Pandyan king whose word never fails even if the heavens fail. Even if Your grace toward me changes, I will not let go and change my devotion. Even if the mother who bore a child runs out of breast milk, will the child's nature change? It will only bite the empty breast with its teeth.
commentary: Long ago the Lord changed his dancing foot to delight a Pandyan king whose word held even if the heavens failed. If God bends that far for love, Vallalar will not bend at all. Grace may seem to change toward him, but his devotion won't. He is the hungry infant at a dry breast, biting it rather than turning away, because there is nowhere else to go.

translit: aṉpari tāmaṉat tēḻaiyaṉ yāṉtuya rālmelintē iṉpari tāmic ciṟunaṭai vāḻkkaiyil ēṅkukiṉṟēṉ eṉpari tāpa nilainī aṟintum iraṅkilaiyēl vaṉpari tāntaṇ aruṭkaṭa lē-eṉṉa vāḻveṉakkē.
translation: I am a poor wretch with a heart lacking love. Wasted by sorrow, I languish in this petty life where joy is rare. If You do not show pity despite knowing my pitiful state, what kind of life is this for me, O cool ocean of grace?
commentary: Vallalar admits his heart is poor in love and worn thin by sorrow. He has nothing to offer, so he throws himself on mercy alone. If the cool ocean of grace knows his state and still does not pity him, he asks what kind of life is left to him.

translit: maikaṇṭa kaṇṭamum māṉkaṇṭa vāmamum vaittaruḷil kaikaṇṭa nī-eṅkum kaṇkaṇṭa teyvam karutileṉṟē meykaṇṭa nāṉmaṟṟaip poykaṇṭa teyvaṅkaḷ mēvuvaṉō neykaṇṭa ūṇviṭṭu nīrkaṇṭa kūḻukkeṉ nēṭuvatē.
translation: You bear the dark poison in Your throat and hold the deer in Your left hand. Your grace is a proven truth. I have realized the reality that You are the visible deity everywhere. Will I seek out other false gods? Abandoning a feast rich with ghee, why would I yearn for watery gruel?
commentary: Poison dark in the throat, a deer in the left hand: these are Siva's familiar marks, and Vallalar treats his grace as something already tested and proven. He has found the living God visible everywhere. He plainly calls all other gods false. Turning to them now would be like leaving a feast rich with ghee for a bowl of watery gruel.

translit: vēṇikku mēloru vēṇivait tōymuṉ virumpi-oru māṇikku vētam vakuttē kiḻi-oṉṟu vāṅkittanta kāṇikkut tāṉaraik kāṇimaṭ ṭāyiṉum kāṭṭukaṇṭāy pāṇikkumōtarum pāṇivan tēṟṟavar pāṉmaikaṇṭē.
translation: You placed the river like a braid upon Your braided hair. Long ago, You lovingly expounded the Vedas and procured a purse of gold for the young bachelor. Please show me at least a fraction of that generosity. Will Your giving hand delay, seeing the nature of those who come and beg?
commentary: Vallalar asks for only a fraction of what others have received. The Lord who wears the river in his matted hair once lovingly taught the Vedas to a young student and got him a purse of gold. God's hand moves quickly when it sees genuine need. Why should it hesitate now?

translit: maṟaikkoḷit tāyneṭu māṟkoḷit tāyticai māmukaṅkoḷ iṟaikkoḷit tāyiṅ katilōr paḻiyilai eṉṟaṉmaṉak kuṟaikkoḷit tālum kuṟaitīrt taruḷeṉak kūviṭumeṉ muṟaikkoḷit tālum aracēniṉ pālpaḻi mūṭiṭumē.
translation: You hid from the Vedas. You hid from great Vishnu. You hid from Brahma, the lord with great faces pointing in all directions. There is no blame in that. But if you hide from my mind's grievances, and if you hide from my rightful cry begging you to resolve my flaws and grant grace, O King, blame will surely fall upon you.
commentary: The Vedas, Vishnu and Brahma all failed to find the Lord, and Vallalar finds no fault in that. Staying hidden from the mighty is fair. Hiding from a suffering soul's sincere cry would be a real failure of compassion, and he says the blame would fall on God. A true king does not abandon a desperate subject.

translit: muṉmaḻai vēṇṭum paruvap payirveyil mūṭikkeṭṭa piṉmaḻai pēynteṉṉa pēṟukaṇ ṭāyantap peṟṟiyaippōl niṉmaḻai pōṟkoṭai iṉṟaṉṟi mūppu neruṅkiyakkāl poṉmaḻai pēynteṉṉa kaṉmaḻai pēynteṉṉa pūraṇaṉē.
translation: What benefit is there if it rains after the seasonal crops, which needed early rain, have withered under the scorching sun? Just like that, if your rain-like generosity is not given today, what does it matter if it rains gold or if it rains stones when old age approaches, O Perfect One?
commentary: A farmer needs rain while the crop is growing. Rain on a withered field brings nothing. Vallalar wants grace now, while there is still life to spend on it. If God waits until old age has ruined the body, a shower of gold and a shower of stones would come to the same thing.

translit: nīḷā taravukoṇ ṭeṉkuṟai yāvum nikaḻttavumnī kēḷā tavaṉeṉa vāḷā irukkiṉṟa kēṇmai-eṉṉō cūḷāta mukkaṇ maṇiyē viṭēluṉaic cūḻnta-eṉṉai āḷākak koḷḷiṉum mīḷā narakat taḻuttiṉumē.
translation: Even as I express all my grievances with deep longing, what kind of friendship is this where you remain silent as if you have not heard? O unblemished three-eyed gem! Whether you accept me as your servant or plunge me into inescapable hell, do not abandon me, for I cling to you.
commentary: Vallalar speaks to God with the bluntness of an old friend. He has poured out every grievance and gets silence, as if the Lord had not heard, and he calls that a poor kind of friendship. Then, in the same breath, he surrenders. Make him a servant or push him into a hell with no way out, he will cling either way.

translit: vaḷaṅkaṉṟu māvaṉat tīṉṟataṉ tāyiṉṟi vāṭukiṉṟa iḷaṅkaṉṟu pōlciṟu vāḻkkaiyil niṉaruḷ iṉṟi-antō uḷaṅkaṉṟu nāṉceyva teṉṉē karuṇai utavukaṇṭāy kaḷaṅkaṉṟu pēraruṭ kāreṉṟu kūṟum kaḷattavaṉē.
translation: Like a young calf wilting without the mother who bore it in a barren great forest, I languish in this petty life without your grace. Alas, what can I do with a bruised heart? Grant me your compassion, O Lord whose dark neck is hailed as the dark raincloud of supreme grace.
commentary: A soul separated from divine grace feels as helpless as an orphaned calf wandering in a barren forest. Vallalar appeals to God's ultimate compassion by referencing the ancient story of Siva, whose neck turned dark from swallowing a deadly poison to save the universe. He asks for that exact same self-sacrificing mercy to heal his own bruised heart.

translit: kāṟṟukku mēlviṭṭa pañcāki uḷḷam kaṟaṅkacceṉṟē cōṟṟukku mēṟkati iṉṟeṉa vēṟṟakan tōṟumuṇpōr tūṟṟukku mēlperun tūṟilai āṅkeṉ tuyarameṉum cēṟṟukku mēlperuñ cēṟilai kāṇaruṭ cevvaṇṇaṉē.
translation: There is no slander greater than the slander upon those whose minds spin like cotton tossed in the wind, who believe there is no refuge higher than food, and who eat in every stranger's house. Likewise, see that there is no mire greater than the mire of my sorrow, O red-hued Lord of grace!
commentary: People with no aim beyond the next meal, minds blown about like cotton in the wind, eating at every stranger's door, bear the worst kind of disgrace. Vallalar sets his sorrow beside theirs. No mire is deeper than the one he is sinking in, and he begs the red-hued Lord of grace to see it and feed him with something higher.

translit: antō tuyaril cuḻaṉṟāṭum ēḻai avalaneñcam cintōta nīril cuḻiyō iḷaiyavar ceṅkaitoṭṭa pantō ciṟuvartam pampara mōkoṭṭum pañcukolō vantō ṭuḻalum turumpō-eṉ colvatem māmaṇiyē.
translation: Alas! My poor miserable heart spins in sorrow. Is it a whirlpool in the ocean waters? Is it a ball bounced by the red hands of young women? Is it a spinning top of little boys? Is it beaten cotton? Is it a piece of straw whirling about? What can I say, my great Gem?
commentary: Vallalar cannot even settle on what his heart is like. A whirlpool, a ball in a girl's hands, a boy's spinning top, beaten cotton, a straw in the wind: he tries each and none is enough. Seeing that restlessness plainly is where the plea for stability begins.

translit: poṉvaca mōpeṇka ḷiṉvaca mōkaṭaṟ pūvacamō miṉvaca mō-eṉum meyvaca mō-eṉ vitivacamō taṉvaca mōmalan taṉvaca mō-eṉ cavalaineñcam eṉvaca mō-illai niṉvacam nāṉeṉai ēṉṟukoḷḷē.
translation: Is my feeble heart controlled by gold, by women, or by the earth surrounded by the sea? Is it controlled by this body that flashes like lightning? Is it controlled by my fate? Is it controlled by itself, or by impurity? It is certainly not under my control. I am under your control. Please accept me.
commentary: Gold, women, land, a body as brief as lightning, fate, impurity. Vallalar runs through every power that might be steering his feeble heart. Wherever the control lies, it is not with him. So he hands himself over to the Lord and asks to be accepted.

translit: nāṉaṭaṅ kātoru nāṭceyum kuṟṟa naṭakkai-ellām vāṉaṭaṅ kātinta maṇṇaṭaṅ kātu matikkumaṇṭam tāṉaṭaṅ kāteṅkun tāṉaṭaṅ kāteṉat tāṉaṟintum māṉaṭaṅ kāṭṭu maṇi-eṉai āṇṭatu māviyappē.
translation: Even knowing that the faulty deeds I restlessly commit in a single day cannot be contained in the sky, cannot be contained on this earth, cannot be contained in the esteemed universe, and cannot be contained anywhere, the Gem who holds a leaping deer in his hand took me into his governance. This is a great wonder.
commentary: In a single day Vallalar commits more faults than sky, earth or the whole universe could hold. The Lord knew this, the Gem with a leaping deer in his hand, and took him in anyway. Vallalar can only call it a great wonder.

tamil: தாம்பா யினும் ஒரு தாம்பாயி னுங்கொடு தாம்பின்செல்வார்
translit: pāmpā yiṉumuṇap pālkoṭup pārvaḷarp pārmaṉaippāl vēmpāyi ṉumveṭṭal ceyyār vaḷartta veruṭcikkaṭāt tāmpā yiṉum oru tāmpāyi ṉuṅkoṭu tāmpiṉcelvār tēmpāy malarkkuḻaṟ kāmpāka eṉṉaiyum cērttukkoḷḷē.
translation: Even if it is a snake, people give it milk to drink and raise it. Even if a neem tree grows by their house, they do not cut it down. Even if a goat they raised turns wild, they secure it with a rope and follow behind it. Please gather me up too, like a stem for the honey-dripping flowers worn in flowing tresses.
commentary: People bear with what they have raised. They give milk to a snake, leave the bitter neem by the house standing, and when the goat they reared turns wild they rope it and follow behind. Vallalar asks God for the same patience with him. Let him be gathered in like a plain stem that holds honey-dripping flowers in a woman's hair.

translit: neruppukku muṭṭaiyum kūḻkkiṭa uppaiyum nēṭiccelvōr paruppukku neyyumoṇ pālukku vāḻaip paḻamuṅkoḷḷat teruppukku vāroṭu cērkileṉ ṉāmic ciṟunaṭaiyām iruppukku vēṇṭiya nāṉciva yōkarpiṉ eytileṉṉē.
translation: For those who go seeking a spark for their fire and salt for their gruel, what does it matter if they join those who enter the street to get ghee for their dal and bananas for their pure milk? I desire only a meager livelihood for this brief earthly existence. What does it matter if I walk behind the great Siva yogis?
commentary: A poor person after a spark for the fire and salt for the gruel loses nothing by walking with those buying ghee for their dal and bananas for their milk. Vallalar wants only enough to get through this brief life. Walking behind the great Siva yogis (spiritual masters devoted to Siva) can only do him good, however small his own needs seem.

tamil: விம்மத மாக்கினும் வெட்டினும் நன்றுன்னை விட்ட அதன்
translit: emmata māṭṭu mariyōyeṉ pāvi iṭumpaineñcai mummata yāṉaiyiṉ kāliṭ ṭiṭaṟiṉum moyaṉaṟkaṇ vimmata mākkiṉum veṭṭiṉum naṉṟuṉṉai viṭṭa ataṉ vemmata nīṅkaleṉ cammataṅ kāṇev vitattiṉumē.
translation: O Lord rare to reach through any religion! It is good even if my sinful and suffering heart is trampled under the feet of a rutting elephant, or destroyed in a blazing fire, or chopped into pieces. I agree that its fierce pride in abandoning you must be eradicated by any means whatsoever.
commentary: The divine cannot be reached through any religion. Vallalar would welcome his heart being trampled by an elephant, burned in fire or chopped to pieces, if that is what it takes to root out the fierce pride that keeps it separated from God.

translit: kallāta puntiyum antōniṉ tāḷil kaṇappoḻutum nillāta neñcamum pollāta māyaiyum nīṇmatamum kollāmal koṉṟeṉait tiṉṉāmal tiṉkiṉṟa koḷkaiyai-iṅ kellām aṟinta uṉakkeḷi yēṉiṉ ṟicaippateṉṉē.
translation: Alas! My unlearned intellect, my heart that does not rest at your feet even for a moment, wicked illusion, and endless pride kill me without killing and devour me without eating. You know everything here. What is there for poor me to tell you today?
commentary: Ignorance, illusion and pride leave no wounds you can see, yet they eat a person from the inside. That is what "kill me without killing" means. God already knows everything that happens here, so Vallalar sees no use in explaining his torment.

translit: tevvaḻi ōṭum maṉattēṉuk kuṉṟaṉ tiruvuḷantāṉ ivvaḻi ēkeṉ ṟiruvaḻik kuḷviṭṭa tevvaḻiyō avvaḻi yēvaḻi cevvaḻi pāṭaniṉ ṟāṭukiṉṟōy vevvaḻi nīrppuṇaik keṉṉē ceyaliv viyaṉilattē.
translation: My mind runs in hostile ways. Your divine will commanded me to go this way and placed me on one of the two paths. Whichever path that is, that becomes my path. O Lord who dances to the singing of beautiful melodies! What independent action can a raft take in a fierce river current on this vast earth?
commentary: A raft in a fierce current goes where the water takes it. Vallalar sees himself the same way under the divine will. Whichever of the two paths God has placed him on, that becomes his path, and he follows it completely.

translit: kaṇṇār nutaṟceṅ karumpēniṉ poṉṉaruṭ kāṉmalarai eṇṇāta pāvi-iṅ kēṉpiṟan tēṉniṉai ēttukiṉṟōr uṇṇāta ūṇum uṭukkā uṭaiyum uṇarccicaṟṟum naṇṇāta neñcamum koṇṭula kōrmuṉṉar nāṇuṟavē.
translation: O sweet red sugarcane with an eye on your forehead! I am a sinner who does not think of the fragrant flower feet of your golden grace. Why was I born here? I live with food that those who praise you would never eat, clothes they would never wear, and a heart completely devoid of true feeling, only to face shame before the people of the world.
commentary: Vallalar calls Siva by the eye on his forehead and owns his shame. He eats and dresses in ways no devotee would, and his heart feels nothing. A human birth spent like that is wasted, which is why he asks what he was born for.

translit: ammā vayiṟṟerik kāṟṟēṉ eṉaniṉ ṟaḻutalaṟac cummā-ac cēymukan tāypārt tirukkat tuṇivaḷkolō immā nilattamu tēṟṟāyi ṉuntan tiṭuvaḷmukkaṇ emmāṉiṅ kēḻai aḻumukam pārttum iraṅkilaiyē.
translation: When a child stands crying and screaming, "Mother, I cannot bear this burning in my stomach," would a mother dare to sit idly and just watch her child's face? Even if she had to beg for ambrosia on this vast earth, she would get it and feed the child. O our Lord with three eyes! You see the crying face of this poor one here, yet you show no pity.
commentary: A mother whose child cries from hunger will not sit and watch. She would beg for the rarest nectar to feed it. Vallalar cries to God with that same desperation and asks why the three-eyed Lord, the true parent, looks at his crying face and shows no pity.

translit: ōyāk karuṇai mukilē nutaṟkaṇ oruvaniṉpāl tōyāk koṭiyaven neñcattai nāṉcuṭu collaiccolli vāyāl cuṭiṉun terintila tē-iṉi valvaṭavait tīyāl cuṭiṉumeṉ antō ciṟitun terivataṉṟē.
translation: O unceasing cloud of compassion! O unique one with an eye on your forehead! My cruel, harsh heart does not immerse in you. Even if I scorch it with my mouth by speaking burning words, it understands nothing. What if I burn it now with the fierce oceanic fire? Alas, it will not realize even a little.
commentary: Siva is an unceasing cloud of compassion, yet Vallalar's heart will not soak in it. He has scolded it with burning words and it learned nothing. Even the fierce fire of the ocean, he fears, could not burn the ignorance out of a mind this hard.

translit: mālaṟi yāṉmala rōṉaṟi yāṉmaka vāṉaṟiyāṉ kālaṟi yāṉmaṟṟai vāṉōr kaṉaviṉuṅ kaṇṭaṟiyār cēlaṟi yāviḻi maṅkaipaṅ kāniṉ tiṟattaimaṟai nālaṟi yā-eṉil nāṉaṟi vēṉeṉal nāṇuṭaittē.
translation: Vishnu does not know. Brahma on the lotus does not know. Indra does not know. The wind god does not know. The other celestials have never seen or known you even in their dreams. O sharer of the lady whose eyes are more beautiful than carp! If the four Vedas do not know your nature, it brings me shame to claim I know you.
commentary: Vishnu, Brahma, Indra, even the wind god: none of them knows the Supreme, and the other celestials have not seen him even in dreams. If the four Vedas cannot grasp his nature, Vallalar says, it would be shameful arrogance for an ordinary person to claim he knows.

translit: āṟiṭṭa vēṇiyum āṭṭiṭṭa pātamum ammai-oru kūṟiṭṭa pākamum kōttiṭṭa koṉṟaiyum kōlamikka nīṟiṭṭa mēṉiyum nāṉkāṇum nāḷeṉ ṉilaittalaimēl ēṟiṭṭa kaikaḷkaṇ ṭāṇavap pēykaḷ iṟaṅkiṭumē.
translation: The matted hair bearing the river, the dancing foot, the side shared as half with the Mother, the strung garland of konrai flowers, and the beautiful form smeared with holy ash. On the day I behold these, seeing my hands raised in reverence above my steady head, the demons of arrogance will step down and depart.
commentary: Seeing God directly breaks the ego. Vallalar pictures Siva in full, with the Ganges in his matted hair, the dancing foot, half his body shared with the Divine Mother, the konrai garland and the form white with holy ash. On the day he sees this, his hands will rise above his head in reverence, and the demons of arrogance will step down and flee.

translit: alluṇṭa kaṇṭat taracēniṉ cīrtti amutamuṇṭōr kolluṇṭa tēvartaṅ kōḷuṇṭa cīreṉum kūḻuṇparō colluṇṭavāyiṉar pulluṇpa rō-iṉ cuvaikkaṇṭeṉum kalluṇṭa pērkaruṅ kalluṇpa rō-ik kaṭaliṭattē.
translation: O King with a throat as dark as night! Will those who have consumed the nectar of your glory ever eat the gruel of the afflicted wealth belonging to mortal gods who suffer death? Will people with mouths accustomed to eating fine rice graze on grass? Will those who have tasted sweet rock sugar ever eat black stones in this sea-girt world?
commentary: Once someone tastes real grace, worldly rewards lose their pull. Vallalar puts it in kitchen terms. A mouth used to fine rice will not graze on grass, and no one who has had rock sugar goes back to chewing black stones. Whoever has drunk the nectar of Siva's glory will not settle for the fleeting wealth of lesser gods who themselves die.

translit: kārē eṉumaṇi kaṇṭatti ṉāṉpoṟ kaḻalaiyaṉṟi yārē tuṇainamak kēḻaineñ cē-iṅ kiruntukaḻu nīrē eṉiṉun taraṟkañcu vāroṭu nīyuñceṉṟu cērēl iṟukac civāya nama-eṉac cintaiceyyē.
translation: O poor heart! Other than the golden feet of the Lord with a sapphire throat resembling a dark cloud, who is our refuge? Do not go and associate with misers here who hesitate to give even the leftover water used to wash rice. Hold fast and meditate upon the mantra Sivaya Nama.
commentary: Some people will not part with even the water left from washing rice. Vallalar warns his own heart away from such misers. Apart from the golden feet of the Lord with the dark throat there is no refuge, so he tells his mind to turn from the world and hold tight to the five-syllable mantra Sivaya Nama (salutations to Siva).

translit: valaippaṭṭa māṉeṉa vāṭpaṭṭa kaṇṇiyar maiyaleṉṉum pulaippaṭṭa pēykku vilaippaṭṭa nāṉmati pōyppulampa vilaippaṭṭa immaṉam antō-iv vēḻaikkeṉ ṟeṅkiruntu talaippaṭṭa tō-itaṟ keṉceyku vēṉmukkaṭ caṅkaraṉē.
translation: Like a deer caught in a net, I sold myself to the vile ghost of infatuation for women with sword-like eyes. My intelligence abandoned me and I wailed. Alas, from where did this corrupted mind come to afflict this poor wretch? What will I do about this, O three-eyed Sankara?
commentary: Desire traps the mind the way a net traps a deer, and the good sense goes. Vallalar says he sold himself to the vile ghost of infatuation. He cries to Sankara (Siva, the lord of tranquility), asking what to do with a mind like this.

translit: kuruntāmeṉ cōka maṉamāṉa piḷḷaik kuraṅkukkiṅkē varuntā ṇavameṉṉu māṉiṭap pēyoṉṟu māttiramō peruntā matameṉ ṟirākkatap pēyum piṭittatentāy tiruntā ataṉkutip peṉoru vāykoṇṭu cepparitē.
translation: The human ghost of tormenting ego possessed the baby monkey of my sorrowful mind. The demon ghost of deep lethargy possessed it too, my Father. Its untamed leaping is impossible to describe with my single mouth.
commentary: A monkey is restless by nature. Vallalar's mind is a baby monkey, and two ghosts have hold of it, the human ego and deep spiritual lethargy. Pushed by arrogance and dullness at once, it leaps so wildly that one mouth cannot describe it.

translit: peṇmaṇi pākap perumaṇi yē-aruṭ peṟṟikoṇṭa viṇmaṇi yāṉa viḻimaṇi yē-eṉ viruppuṟunal kaṇmaṇi nērkaṭa vuṇmaṇi yē-oru kālmaṇiyait tiṇmaṇik kūṭalil viṟṟōṅku teyva cikāmaṇiyē.
translation: O great gem sharing half your form with the jewel of a woman! O pupil of the eye that became the gem of the grace-filled sky! O divine gem matching the beloved pupil of my yearning eye! O supreme jewel of the gods who once sold gems in the sturdy, gem-filled city of Madurai!
commentary: Jewel after jewel. Vallalar praises God as the supreme gem, shining in many forms of light and value. The Lord shares half his body with the Goddess, the perfect unity of masculine and feminine grace. There is also the old Tamil legend of the Lord walking the streets of Madurai disguised as a gem merchant, bringing the divine right into the ordinary marketplace.

translit: alaiyeḻut tunteṟum ainteḻut tāluṉṉai-arccikkiṉṟōr kalaiyeḻut tumpukaḻ kāleḻut tiṟkuk kaṉivirakkam ilaiyeḻut tumpiṟap pīṭeḻut tuṅkoṇṭa eṅkaḷpuḻut talaiyeḻut tuñcari yāmō nutaṟkaṇ taṉimutalē.
translation: O unique Supreme Being with an eye on your forehead! Devotees worship you with the five syllables that destroy the waves of karma. Will the destiny inscribed on our worm-like heads, burdened by the writing of worldly birth and station, ever equal the tender mercy of your sacred feet praised by the letters of all arts?
commentary: The five sacred syllables of the Panchakshara mantra (Na-Ma-Si-Va-Ya) are chanted to wash away the crushing waves of past actions. In Indian tradition, a person's fate is written invisibly on the forehead at birth. Vallalar sets his own wretched, worm-like head against the merciful feet of God and asks if that mercy can ever overwrite the worldly struggles written there.

translit: āṭcikaṇ ṭārkkuṟṟa tuṉpattait tāṉkoṇ ṭaruḷaḷikkum māṭcikaṇ ṭāyentai vaḷḷaṟ kuṇameṉpar maṟṟataṟkuk kāṭcikaṇ ṭēṉilai āyiṉum uṉṉaruṭ kaṇṭattilōr cāṭcikaṇ ṭēṉkaḷi koṇṭēṉ karuṇait taṭaṅkaṭalē.
translation: O vast ocean of compassion! They say the glorious nature of my Father, the supreme benefactor, is to take on the suffering of those who realize his rule and grant them grace. I have not seen direct proof of this. However, I saw a witness in your grace-filled throat and I rejoiced.
commentary: They say true compassion takes on the suffering of others to save them. Vallalar playfully says he has never seen proof, then finds his witness in the Lord's throat. When a world-destroying poison rose from the ocean, Siva swallowed it to protect all living beings, and he holds that venom in his throat forever as a sign of his boundless mercy.

translit: kaṇkoṇṭa neṟṟiyum kārkoṇṭa kaṇṭamum kaṟpaḷikkum peṇkoṇṭa pākamum kaṇṭēṉmuṉ māṟaṉ pirampaṭiyāl puṇkoṇṭa mēṉip puṟaṅkaṇṭi lēṉap puṟattaikkaṇṭāl oṇkoṇṭa kallum urukumeṉ ṟō-iṅ koḷittaṉaiyē.
translation: I saw your forehead bearing an eye, your neck bearing the dark poison, and your side bearing the lady who grants virtue. I did not see the back of your body, wounded long ago by the cane strikes of the Pandya king. Did you hide it here thinking that if I saw that back, even a bright hard stone would melt?
commentary: Vallalar sees the third eye, the throat dark with swallowed poison, and the side shared with the goddess. The back he cannot see. That back carries the marks of the Pandya king's cane, a brutal beating the Lord took for a poor devotee in the ancient story. Vallalar wonders whether God keeps it hidden because one look at what he suffered for love would melt a heart of stone.

translit: vēykkup porumeḻil tōḷuṭait tēvi viḷaṅkumeṅkaḷ tāykkuk kaṉintoru kūṟaḷit tōyniṉ tayavuminta nāykkuk kiṭaikkum eṉa-oru cōtiṭam nalkilavar vāykkup paḻattoṭu carkkarai vāṅki vaḻaṅkuvaṉē.
translation: You tenderly gave a portion of yourself to the goddess, our radiant mother whose beautiful shoulders rival bamboo. If someone offers a prediction saying your compassion will reach this dog, I will buy fruit and sugar and offer them to their mouth.
commentary: The Lord loves the goddess so tenderly that he shares half of his very body with her. Vallalar wants only a fraction of that tenderness. He calls himself a dog, in the traditional poetry of humility, and promises sweet fruit and sugar to anyone who can predict that divine compassion will finally reach him.
