translit: kāṇṭattiṉ mēvum ulakīrit tēkam karumpaṇaipōl nīṇṭatti leṉṉa nilaiyala vē-itu niṟṟalpacum pāṇṭattil nīrniṟṟal aṉṟō namainam pacupatitāṉ āṇṭattil eṉṉa kuṟaiyōnam mēṟkuṟai āyiramē.
translation: O people of the world living in this realm! What does it matter if this body grows tall like thick sugarcane? It is not permanent. Its endurance is like water standing in an unbaked clay pot. If our Lord of souls rules us, what is the flaw? The thousands of flaws are upon us.
commentary: A strong, tall body looks like something to rely on, but Vallalar warns that physical life is entirely fragile. He compares it to water held in a pot of raw, unbaked clay: sooner or later the water dissolves the pot and it collapses. So do not trust the body. Submit to God, and remember that the flaws belong to our mortal nature and not to the divine.

translit: vēṇikkaṇ nīrvaitta tēvē maturai viyaṉteruvil māṇikkam viṟṟacem māṇikka mē-eṉai vāḻvittatōr āṇippoṉ ṉēteḷ ḷamutēniṉ ceyya aṭimalarkkuk kāṇikkai yākkikkoṇ ṭāḷvāy eṉatu karuttiṉaiyē.
translation: O God who placed the river in your matted hair! O red ruby who sold rubies in the wide streets of Madurai! O pure gold who gave me life! O clear nectar! Make my mind an offering to your red lotus feet and rule me.
commentary: An ancient Madurai legend pictures God wandering the streets disguised as a gem merchant, a red ruby selling rubies. Vallalar brings him no physical wealth. He offers his own mind as the precious gift and asks the Lord to take complete charge of his life.

translit: mākalai vāṇar piṟaṉpāl emakkum maṉaikkumkaṭṭa nīkalai tā-oru mēkalai tā-uṇa neṉmalaitā pōkalai yā-eṉap piṉtoṭar vāravar pōlmaṉaṉī ēkalai īkalar ēkampa vāṇa riṭañcelkavē.
translation: Great scholars of arts follow another person saying, "Give clothes for me and my wife to wear, give a waist-belt, give a mountain of paddy to eat, do not leave us." O mind, do not go like them to those who do not give. Go to the Lord who dwells in Ekambaram.
commentary: Even highly educated scholars demean themselves, trailing after wealthy patrons and begging for food, clothing and security. Vallalar commands his own mind to stop chasing worldly people who are stingy in the end. Go straight to the Lord of Ekambaram, he tells it. That patron provides without fail.

translit: ūrtaru vārnalla ūṇtaru vāruṭai yuntaruvār pārtaru vāruḻaṟ kērtaru vārpoṉ paṇantaruvār cōrtaru vāruḷ ḷaṟivuke ṭāmal cukippataṟkiṅ kārtaru vārammai yārtaru pākaṉai yaṉṟineñcē.
translation: People will give vehicles, good food, and clothing. They will give land, plows for farming, gold, and money. But to remain joyful without losing inner awareness when exhaustion takes hold, who will grant that state here except the Lord who shares his form with the Mother, O heart?
commentary: The world can hand out endless gifts, like wealth, land and comfort. It cannot give inner peace. When physical or mental exhaustion sets in, only the divine presence keeps the soul's awareness steady and joyful.

translit: paṇceyta coṉmaṅkai pākāveṇ pāṟkaṭal paḷḷikoṇṭōṉ tiṇceyta cakkaraṅ koḷvāṉ aruccaṉai ceytiṭṭanāḷ viṇceyta niṉṉaruṭ cēvaṭi mēṟpaṭa vēṇṭiyavaṉ kaṇceyta naṟṟavam yātō karuttil kaṇipparitē.
translation: O Lord who shares your form with the Goddess whose words are like music! The one who rests on the white milky ocean worshipped you to obtain the mighty discus. On that day, he desired to place his own eye upon your divine, gracious red feet. What great penance did that eye perform? It is impossible to measure in thought.
commentary: An ancient story tells how Vishnu, the preserving deity, worshipped the Lord to obtain the discus and offered his own eye as a lotus flower. That eye earned the rare privilege of touching the divine feet. Its spiritual merit must be beyond anything Vallalar can measure.

translit: māppiṭṭu nērntuṇṭu vantiyai vāḻvitta vaḷḷaluṉveṇ kāppiṭṭu mēṟpala pāppiṭṭa mēṉiyaik kaṇṭutoḻak kūppiṭṭu nāṉiṟka vantilai nātaṉaik kūṭa-illāḷ pūppiṭṭa kālattil kūppiṭṭa pōtiṉum pōvatuṇṭē.
translation: O generous Lord who gladly ate the sweet flour offering and blessed the old woman Vandi! I stand here calling out to see and worship your form adorned with white ash and many snakes, but you have not come. A husband will surely go to his wife when she calls him, even during her time of monthly seclusion.
commentary: In a famous story the divine took the form of a laborer to help a poor old woman named Vandi, carrying earth in exchange for sweet flour. Vallalar calls out, and the Lord has not come. A loving husband answers his wife's call even during her traditional time of impurity. God is bound by deeper love than that, and must surely answer an earnest cry for grace, whatever the soul's perceived impurities.

translit: eṉmēṟ piḻaiyilai yāṉeṉcey kēṉeṉ iṭattirunteṉ coṉmēṟ koḷāteṉai iṉmēl turumpeṉac cuṟṟuneñcat tiṉmēṟ piḻaiyatu puṉmēṟ paṉiyeṉac ceytoḻikka niṉmēṟ paramviṭai taṉmēṟkoṇ ṭaṉparmuṉ niṟpavaṉē.
translation: There is no fault in me. What can I do? The spinning heart stays within me, refuses to heed my words, and throws me about like a piece of dry straw. The fault lies entirely with this heart. The burden is yours to wipe away this fault like dew on a blade of grass, O Lord who mounts the bull and stands before your devotees!
commentary: The soul itself is pure and without fault. The real source of the struggle is the restless mind, spinning out of control and dragging a person along like dry straw in the wind. Vallalar asks the divine to take responsibility for this unruly mind and wipe away its faults as easily as the sun melts dew from grass.

translit: maiviṭṭi ṭāmaṇi kaṇṭāniṉ taṉṉai vaḻuttumeṉṉai neyviṭṭi ṭā-uṇṭi pōliṉpi lāṉmeyn neṟiyaṟiyāṉ poyviṭṭi ṭāṉvem pulaiviṭṭi ṭāṉmayal pōkamelām kaiviṭṭi ṭāṉeṉak kaiviṭṭi ṭēlvantu kāttaruḷē.
translation: O Lord whose throat bears the unfading dark stain! Do not abandon me, who praises you, by saying, "He is joyless like a meal served without ghee. He does not know the true path. He does not give up lies. He does not give up cruel flesh. He refuses to let go of delusive worldly pleasures." Please come and protect me with your grace.
commentary: Vallalar begs for protection despite a heavy burden of personal flaws, including falsehood, worldly attachment, and the cruel consumption of meat. He addresses God as the one who swallowed poison to save the universe and still bears its dark stain on his throat. A Lord with that much compassion can surely extend grace to a struggling soul without turning away.

translit: nallamu tamcivai tāṉtarak koṇṭuniṉ naṟcevikkuc collamu tantanta eṅkaḷ pirāṉvaḷañ cūḻmayilai illamu tantikaḻ peṇṇāka eṉpai eḻuppiyanāḷ cillamu tampeṟṟa tēvarai vāṉañ cirittataṉṟē.
translation: Our lord received the good nectar given by Sivai and gave the nectar of words to your good ears. On the day he resurrected bones into a radiant woman of the home in prosperous Mylapore, the heavens laughed at the devas who had obtained only a meager nectar.
commentary: The child-saint Sambandar was fed the milk of divine wisdom by the Goddess and poured it out as sweet hymns for all to hear. Through his devotion he turned cremated bones back into a living young woman. The heavenly beings (devas) churned the cosmic ocean for the nectar of immortality, yet Vallalar says they received the lesser prize, because true divine grace holds absolute power over life and death.

translit: coṟṟuṇaivētiyaṉ eṉṉumpatikac curutiyainiṉ poṟṟuṇai vārkaḻaṟ kēṟṟiyap poṉṉaṭip pōtiṉaiyē naṟṟuṇai yākkarai ēṟiya puṇṇiya nāvaracaik kaṟṟuṇai yātintak kaṟṟuṇai yāmeṉ kaṭaineñcamē.
translation: The holy king of speech offered the sacred hymn beginning with "Sotrunai Vedhiyan" to your long golden feet. Making those lotus-like golden feet his true companion, he reached the shore. My lowly heart remains a stone pillar and does not learn from him.
commentary: The "holy king of speech" is the saint Appar. His enemies tied him to a heavy stone and threw him into the sea. He sang a famous hymn and held fast to God's feet in his heart, and the stone floated him safely to shore. Vallalar laments that his own mind stays stubborn as a stone pillar, failing to learn from the saint's pure faith.

translit: caṭaiyava nīmuṉ taṭuttāṇṭa nampikkuc caṟṟeṉiṉum kaṭaiyava ṉēṉceyuṅ kaimmā ṟaṟintilaṉ kālvarunti naṭaiyuṟa niṉṉaip paravaitaṉ pāṅkar naṭatti-aṉpar iṭaivarum uṉṟaṉ irakkattait tāṉveḷi yiṭṭataṟkē.
translation: O Lord with matted hair, I am a lowly person. I do not know any way to repay the trusted devotee whom you previously intervened and claimed. He made you walk until your feet ached to the side of Paravai. By doing so, he revealed the compassion you show to your devotees.
commentary: The saint Sundarar once asked God to act as a messenger of love to his wife, Paravai. God agreed and walked the night streets until his feet ached. Vallalar marvels that the Lord will serve his devotees this far, and knows no way to repay Sundarar, whose bold request showed the world the staggering, intimate compassion God has for those who love him.

translit: tiruvāta vūrem perumāṉ poruṭṭaṉṟu teṉṉaṉmuṉṉē veruvāta vaitikap pāypari mēṟkoṇṭu mēviniṉṟa oruvāta kōlat toruvā-ak kōlattai uḷkuḷirntē karuvāta nīṅkiṭak kāṭṭukaṇ ṭāyeṉ kaṉaviṉilē.
translation: For the sake of our lord of Thiruvadavur, you mounted a fearless leaping Vedic horse before the southern king on that day and stood there in a matchless form. O peerless one, show that form in my dreams so my heart cools and the afflictions of birth depart.
commentary: To save the saint Manikkavasagar from a furious king, God turned a pack of wild jackals into majestic horses. He rode into the royal court at their head in a matchless form. Vallalar asks to see that same form in a dream, so the vision might cool his weary heart and break the cycle of worldly affliction.

translit: cīrtaru nāvuk karaiyaraip pōlic ciṟiyaṉumōr kārtaru māyaic camaṇāṉ maṉakkaruṅ kalliṟkaṭṭip pārtaru pāvak kaṭaliṭai vīḻttiṭap paṭṭuḻaṉṟē ērtarum ainteḻut tōtukiṉ ṟēṉkarai ēṟṟaracē.
translation: Like the excellent king of speech, I am a lowly person tied to the black stone of the mind by dark illusion. Cast into the earthly ocean of sins, I struggle. I chant the beautiful five letters. Lift me to the shore, O King.
commentary: Vallalar takes Appar's rescue from the sea and makes it his own spiritual struggle. He feels tied to the heavy black stone of his own mind, drowning in an ocean of worldly illusion and past wrongs. He chants the sacred five letters of Siva's name (Na-Ma-Si-Va-Ya) and asks God to pull him out of the dark water onto the shore.

tamil: நீக்கமும் நின்மல நெஞ்சமும் சாந்த நிறைவும் அருள்
translit: tūkkamum cōmpalum tukkamum vāḻkkaiyait toṭṭuvarum ēkkamum nōyum iṭaiyūṟum maṟṟai iṭarumviṭṭa nīkkamum niṉmala neñcamum cānta niṟaivum aruḷ ākkamum niṉpatat taṉpum taruka aruṭcivamē.
translation: O Sivam of Grace, grant me freedom from sleep, lethargy, sorrow, the anxiety that clings to life, disease, obstacles, and all other miseries. Grant me a pure heart, perfect peace, the wealth of grace, and love for your feet.
commentary: Sleep and sluggishness head Vallalar's list, ahead of sorrow, worry and sickness. These are the ordinary weights of a human life, and he asks Sivam of Grace to lift them. In their place he wants a heart wiped clean, settled peace, and love for the Lord's feet.

translit: poyvanta vāyum pulaivanta ceykaiyum puṉmaiyellām kaivanta neñcamum kaṇṭēṉ iṉinaṟ kaṉivuṭaṉyāṉ meyvanta vāyum vitivanta ceykaiyum vīṟaṉpiṉāl taivanta neñcamum kāṇpateṉ ṟōceñ caṭaikkaṉiyē.
translation: I have seen a mouth full of lies, actions full of baseness, and a heart mastered by all forms of meanness. O sweet fruit with red matted hair, when will I tenderly see a mouth that speaks the truth, actions governed by righteousness, and a heart softened by immense love?
commentary: He looks at himself honestly first. A lying mouth, base deeds, a heart ruled by meanness: he has seen all of it. What he longs for is the reverse, with true speech, upright action and a heart softened by love. He calls the Lord a sweet fruit with the red matted hair of an ascetic, and asks when that day will come.

translit: kaṅkaikoṇ ṭāymalar vēṇiyi lē-aruṭ kaṇṇimalai maṅkaikoṇ ṭāyiṭap pākatti lē-aiya maṟṟumoru naṅkaikoṇ ṭāleṅku koṇṭaruḷ vāyeṉṟu naṇṇumaṉpar caṅkaikoṇ ṭālataṟ keṉcollu vāymukkaṭ caṅkaraṉē.
translation: O three-eyed Sankara, you hold the river Ganges in your flower-adorned matted hair. You hold the mountain maiden with eyes of grace on your left side. O Lord, if devotees draw near and doubtfully ask, 'If you take another woman, where will you graciously place her?', what will you say to them?
commentary: Sankara is a name for Siva. In the old stories he carries the river goddess Ganga in his matted hair and shares half his body with his wife, the mountain goddess. So the devotees tease him. With his head and his side both taken, where would another woman go? Only a close friend could joke like that, and that easy intimacy with the divine is the point.

translit: vāṭkoṇṭa kaṇṇiyar māyā vikāra valaipiḻaittuṉ tāṭkoṇṭa nīḻalil cārntiṭu māṟeṉ ṟaṉakkaruḷvāy kīṭkoṇṭa kōvaṇap pēraḻa kā-eṉaik kētamaṟa āṭkoṇṭa nī-iṉṟu vāḷā iruppa taḻakallavē.
translation: Grant me the grace to escape the net of illusory passions cast by women with sword-like eyes and to take refuge in the shade of your feet. O great beauty wearing a torn loincloth, you who claimed me and ended my sorrow, it is not fitting for you to remain silent today.
commentary: Worldly desire works like a net, and Vallalar asks for the grace to slip out of it and rest in the shade of the Lord's feet. He calls God a great beauty in a torn loincloth, the supreme ascetic. That Lord has already claimed him and ended his sorrow, so staying silent now does not suit him.

translit: vīṭṭut talaivaniṉ tāḷvaṇaṅ kārtam viritalaicum māṭṭut talaipaṭṭi māṭṭut talaipuṉ varākattalai āṭṭut talaiveṟi nāyttalai pāmpiṉ aṭuntalaikaṟ pūṭṭut talaivem pulaittalai nāṟṟap puḻuttalaiyē.
translation: O Lord of liberation, the broad heads of those who do not bow to your feet are mere load-bearing heads. They are heads of stray cattle, heads of lowly boars, heads of goats, heads of mad dogs, deadly heads of snakes, heads locked like stone, cruel and base heads, and stinking worm-infested heads.
commentary: A head that will not bow to the Lord of liberation, Vallalar says, is no human head at all. He calls it a block for carrying loads, then runs through the beasts: stray cattle, boars, goats, mad dogs, snakes, stinking worms. Without reverence the body is only decaying animal matter, and the life is wasted.

translit: teṇṇīr muṭiyaṉaik kāṇārtaṅ kaṇiruḷ cērkuruṭṭuk kaṇṇīr corintakaṇ kācakkaṇ puṉmulaik kaṇnakakkaṇ puṇṇīr oḻukuṅ koṭuṅkaṇ poṟāmaikkaṇ puṉkaṇvaṉkaṇ maṇṇīrmai yuṟṟakaṇ māmaṇi nīttakaṇ mālaikkaṇṇē.
translation: The eyes of those who do not look upon the Lord who wears clear waters on His head are blind eyes steeped in darkness. They are eyes pouring with tears, eyes clouded by cataracts, the eye of a base breast, the eye of a fingernail, harsh eyes dripping with pus from a wound, eyes of jealousy, miserable eyes, cruel eyes, eyes holding the nature of dirt, eyes devoid of their precious pupils, and night-blind eyes.
commentary: Eyes failing to look toward the Divine are functionally blind. Vallalar compares them to diseased wounds or useless marks on the body. He teaches that physical sight means nothing without spiritual vision.

translit: kaṇṇuta lāṉpukaḻ kēḷār cevipoyk katai-oliyum aṇṇuṟa mātaru maintaruṅ kūṭi aḻumoliyum tuṇṇeṉun tīccol oliyumav vantakaṉ tūtarkaṇmot tuṇṇuṟa vāveṉ ṟurappoli yumpukum ūṉceviyē.
translation: The ears of those who do not listen to the glory of the Lord with an eye on His forehead are mere ears of flesh. Into them enter the sounds of false tales, the wailing of closely gathered women and children, the sounds of terrifying harsh words, and the loud roaring of the messengers of Death shouting to come and suffer their beatings.
commentary: Ears that will not hear the glory of the Lord with the eye on his forehead become lumps of flesh. What enters them instead is empty gossip, the wailing of family, harsh words, and at last the shouting of Death's messengers.

translit: maṇikoṇṭa kaṇṭaṉai vāḻttārtam vāytteru maṇṇuṇṭavāy piṇikoṇṭa vāyviṭap piccuṇṭa vāyvarum pēccaṟṟavāy tuṇikoṇṭa vāyaṉaṟ cūṭuṇṭa vāymalañ cōrntiḻivāy kuṇikoṇṭa uppilik kūḻuṇṭa vāyeṉak kūṟupavē.
translation: The mouths of those who do not praise the Lord with the jewel-like throat are called mouths that eat the dirt of the streets. They are diseased mouths, mouths that consume poison, mouths bereft of speech, mouths stuffed with cloth, mouths burnt by the heat of fire, mouths dripping with foul waste, and mouths that drink tasteless unsalted gruel.
commentary: A mouth that will not praise the Lord with the jewel-like throat is wasted, and Vallalar spares it nothing. He has it eating street dirt, swallowing poison, dripping with filth. Speech without devotion only drags a person down.

translit: cakamilai yē-eṉ ṟuṭaiyāṉai eṇṇalar taṅkaḷneñcam cukamilai yē-uṇac cōṟilai yēkaṭṭat tūcilaiyē akamilai yēporu ḷāvilai yēvaḷḷa lārilaiyē ikamilai yē-oṉṟum iṅkilai yē-eṉ ṟiraṅkuneñcē.
translation: The hearts of those who do not meditate on the Lord our Master are hearts that constantly lament. They cry out complaining there is no comfort, there is no rice to eat, there is no cloth to wear, there is no house, there is no wealth, there are no generous patrons, there is no life in this world, and there is nothing at all here.
commentary: A heart that never thinks of the Master has no rest. It weeps all day over rice, cloth, a house, money and patrons, until it says there is nothing here at all. Fulfillment was waiting in grace, and it never looked there.

translit: poṅkarum pērmulai maṅkaik kiṭantanta puttamutē ceṅkarum pēnaṟun tēṉē maturac ceḻuṅkaṉiyē tiṅkaḷuṅ kaṅkaiyuñ cērntoḷir vēṇic civakkoḻuntē eṅkaḷai āṭkoṇṭum eṉṉē tuyaril iruttuvatē.
translation: O fresh ambrosia who gave half of Your form to the Goddess with great swelling breasts! O red sugarcane! O fragrant honey! O sweet and luscious fruit! O tender flame of Siva whose shining matted hair bears the moon and the river Ganga! Having taken us as Your own, why do You keep us in sorrow?
commentary: Even a soul that grace has taken in can still feel the sting of sorrow. Vallalar heaps sweet names on the Lord: ambrosia, red sugarcane, honey, ripe fruit, the tender flame of Siva who gave half his form to the Goddess. Then he asks him plainly why the sorrow stays.

translit: villaippoṉ ṉākkaraṅ koṇṭōyvaṉtoṇṭar virumpuṟacceṅ kallaippoṉ ṉākkik koṭuttōyniṉ pātaṅ karuttilvaiyār pullaippoṉ ṉākkoḷum pullarkaḷ pāṟceṉṟu poṉṉaḷikka vallaippoṉ ṉārpuya eṉpār iḵteṉcol vāṇarkaḷē.
translation: You hold the golden mountain as a bow in your hand. You turned red bricks into gold and gave them to Vanthondar who desired it. Those who do not keep your feet in their hearts go to petty people who consider grass as gold, and they praise them saying, "You have the power to give gold, you have shoulders covered in gold." What kind of words are these, O scholars?
commentary: People flatter petty rich men for money and forget that God is the true source of all wealth. Vallalar recalls Vanthondar, the saint for whom the Lord turned ordinary bricks into gold. He puts it to the scholars. Why praise misers who take grass for gold, when the Lord provides for every need?

translit: kūttuṭai yāyeṉ ṉuṭaiyāymut tēvarum kūṟukiṉṟa ēttuṭai yāyaṉpar ēttuṭai yāyeṉṟaṉ eṇmaimoḻic cāttuṭai yāyniṉ taṉakkē parameṉait tāṅkutaṟkōr vēttuṭai yārmaṟ ṟilai-aruḷ īteṉṟaṉ viṇṇappamē.
translation: O Lord of the dance! You are my master. You receive the praises of the three chief gods. You receive the praises of your devotees. You wear the garland of my simple words. The responsibility to support me is yours alone. There is no other king to sustain me. Grant your grace. This is my plea.
commentary: Surrender here means trusting the Lord of the dance as the only king who can sustain you. The three chief gods praise him, yet he wears Vallalar's plain, unpolished words like a garland. So Vallalar sets the whole burden of his care on that grace.

translit: veppilai yē-eṉum taṇviḷak kēmukkaṇ vittakaniṉ oppilai yē-eṉum cīrpuka lārpuṟkai uṇṇutaṟkōr uppilai yēporu ḷoṉṟilai yē-eṉ ṟuḻalpavarmēl tappilai yē-avar puṉtalai ēṭṭil tavamilaiyē.
translation: O cool lamp that yields no heat! O three-eyed master! Those who do not praise your peerless glory wander about lamenting, "There is no salt to eat with our gruel, there is no wealth at all." The fault is not theirs. There is simply no merit written on their petty heads.
commentary: The cool lamp that gives no heat is Vallalar's name for the Lord. Those who never praise him wander about complaining there is no salt for their gruel and no money at all. He says the fault is not theirs. No merit was written on their heads, so they are left obsessing over survival instead of turning to that cooling light of grace.

translit: eṉaippeṟṟa tāyiṉum aṉpuṭai yāyeṉak kiṉpanalkum uṉaippeṟṟa uḷḷat tavarmalarc cēvaṭik kōṅkumaṉpu taṉaippeṟṟa naṉmaṉam tāmpeṟṟa mēlavar cārpaippeṟṟāl viṉaippeṟṟa vāḻviṉ maṉaippeṟṟam pōla melivatiṉṟē.
translation: You show more love to me than the mother who bore me. You grant me joy. The great ones possess good minds overflowing with love for the blooming red feet of those who hold you in their hearts. If one attains the company of such great ones, one will never languish in this karma-bound life like a domestic beast of burden.
commentary: The Lord loves Vallalar more than the mother who bore him, yet the secret he points to here is the company we keep. He honors the great ones whose good minds overflow with love for the feet of those who carry God in their hearts. Spend your days with people like that and this karma-bound life will never wear you down like a beast of burden.

translit: niṟaimati yāḷar pukaḻvōy caṭaiyuṭai nīṇmuṭimēl kuṟaimati tāṉoṉṟu koṇṭaṉai yē-ak kuṟippeṉavē poṟaimati yēṉṟaṉ kuṟaimati taṉṉaiyum poṉṉaṭikkīḻ uṟaimati yākkoṇ ṭaruḷvāy ulakam uvappuṟavē.
translation: O Lord praised by those of perfect wisdom! You wear the crescent moon upon your tall crown of matted hair. Taking that as a sign, graciously accept my own flawed mind and make it abide beneath your golden feet so the world may rejoice.
commentary: Traditional imagery puts the crescent moon in Siva's matted hair, an incomplete, waning shape given the place of highest honor. Vallalar takes that as his argument. Let the Lord take his flawed and limited mind too, and give it a lasting, peaceful home beneath the golden feet, so the world may rejoice.

translit: tuṭivaitta ceṅkai aracēnal lūrilniṉ tūmalarppoṉ aṭivaitta pōteṅkaḷ appartam ceṉṉi yatukuḷirntep paṭivaitta tō-iṉpa miyāṉeṇun tōṟumip pāvikkumāl kuṭivaitta puṉtalai oṉṟō maṉamum kuḷirkiṉṟatē.
translation: O King whose red hand holds the small drum! When you placed your pure, flower-like golden feet in Nallur, the head of our Appar grew delightfully cool. What kind of bliss did you bestow on him? Whenever I think of this, my base head harboring delusion grows cool. My mind too becomes delightfully cool, even for a sinner like me.
commentary: At Nallur the Lord placed his feet on the head of Appar, the revered seventh-century Tamil saint, and that head grew cool with bliss. Vallalar only has to remember it. His own muddled head goes cool, and his heavy heart with it. The memory of that mercy works on him like mercy itself.

translit: orumuṭi mēlpiṟai vaittōy ari-ayaṉ oṇmaṟaitam perumuṭi mēluṟa vēṇṭa varātuṉaip pittaṉeṉṟa marumuṭi yūraṉ muṭimēl maṟuppavum vantatavar tirumuṭi mēleṉṉa ācaikaṇ ṭāyniṉ tiruvaṭikkē.
translation: O Lord who placed the crescent moon on your matchless crown! Vishnu, Brahma, and the great crowns of the bright Vedas begged your feet to rest upon them, but they refused to go. Yet they went and rested on the head of Arooran who called you a madman and refused them. What a great desire your sacred feet have for his sacred head!
commentary: God gives his grace to raw, intimate devotion rather than formal religious status. Vallalar contrasts the great creator and preserver gods, Brahma and Vishnu, along with the ancient scriptures known as the Vedas, who all begged for the touch of God's feet and were denied. Yet God rushed to bless the saint Arooran, who angrily called the divine a madman and tried to reject him. Divine love ignores polite reverence and chases after the devotee who treats God as a familiar friend.

translit: vēlkoṇṭa kaiyumun nūlkoṇṭa mārpamum meṉmalarppoṟ kālkoṇṭa oṇkaḻaṟ kāṭciyum paṉṉiru kaṇṇumviṭai mēlkoṇṭa ceñcuṭar mēṉiyum caṇmuka vīṟuṅkaṇṭu mālkoṇṭa neñcam makiḻvaten nāḷeṉkaṇ māmaṇiyē.
translation: O great gem of my eyes! When will my infatuated heart rejoice at seeing your spear-bearing hand, your chest wearing the sacred thread, the sight of bright anklets on your soft flower-like golden feet, your twelve eyes, your red-flame body upon your mount, and the majesty of your six faces?
commentary: Here is Murugan as tradition pictures him: six faces, twelve eyes, the spear in his hand, the sacred thread across his chest, the anklets on his feet, the body blazing red. Vallalar goes over each feature slowly because he is hungry to see them face to face. Only that joyful encounter will satisfy his infatuated heart.

translit: viṇpūtta kaṅkaiyum miṉpūtta vēṇiyum meṉmukamum kaṇpūtta neṟṟiyum peṇpūtta pākamum kārmiṭaṟum taṇpūtta pātamum poṉpūtta mēṉiyum cārntukaṇṭē maṇpūtta vāḻkkaiyai viṇpūtta pūviṉ matippateṉṟē.
translation: Approaching and seeing the Ganges born of the sky, your matted hair shining with lightning, your gentle face, your forehead blossoming with an eye, your side blossoming with the Goddess, your dark throat, your cool feet, and your golden-hued body, when will I regard this earthly life as an illusory flower blooming in the sky?
commentary: Siva's traditional form fills this verse, with the Ganges in his matted hair, the third eye on his forehead, the dark throat, and the Goddess sharing his body. Vallalar hopes that once he truly sees all this, his whole outlook will change. Earthly life, with its daily struggles, would then look as weightless and unreal as a flower blooming in the empty sky.

translit: taṇmati yō-ataṉ taṇṇamu tō-eṉac cārntiruṇīt tuṇmati yōrkkiṉ putavuniṉ pēraruḷ uṟṟiṭavē eṇmati yōṭiccai eytā talaiyumeṉ ēḻaimati peṇmati yō-aṉṟip pēymati yō-eṉṉa pēcuvatē.
translation: Your great grace dispels darkness and grants bliss to those of inner wisdom, making them wonder if it is the cool moon or its cool nectar. My poor mind wanders without the thought or desire to attain your grace. What can I say of this mind? Is it a woman's mind, or the mind of a demon?
commentary: To those with inner wisdom, grace comes like the cool moon or its nectar, and their darkness lifts. Vallalar watches his own mind drift, with no real drive to reach that light, and the self-reproach is bitter. He reaches for traditional poetic comparisons to name it. Is his mind merely weak and fickle, or possessed by a demon?

translit: piṭṭukkum vantumuṉ maṇcuman tāyeṉpar pittaṉeṉṟa tiṭṭukkum cīraruḷ ceytaḷit tāyeṉpar tīviṟakuk kaṭṭukkum poṉmuṭi kāṭṭiniṉ ṟāyeṉpar kaṇṭiṭa-eṉ maṭṭukkum vañcakat teyvameṉ kōmukkaṇ māṇikkamē.
translation: They say you once came for steamed rice flour and carried earth. They say you bestowed your supreme grace even for the scolding that called you a madman. They say you revealed your golden crown even for a bundle of firewood. But when it comes to me, shall I call you a deceitful deity, O three-eyed ruby?
commentary: Three old stories of easy mercy stand behind this verse. The Lord carried earth for a poor woman in return for her steamed rice cakes, blessed a saint who scolded him as a madman, and revealed his golden crown to a humble firewood seller. Set beside these, Vallalar's own wait feels long. Half playful, he asks whether this God is deceiving him.

translit: maiyiṭṭa kaṇṇiyar poyyiṭṭa vāḻviṉ matimayaṅkik kaiyiṭṭa nāṉumuṉ meyyiṭṭa cīraruḷ kāṇkuvaṉō paiyiṭṭa pāmpaṇi yaiyiṭṭa mēṉiyum pattaruḷḷa moyyiṭṭa kāluñcev vaiyiṭṭa vēluṅkoḷ muṉṉavaṉē.
translation: Will I, whose mind is deluded by the false life of women with kohl-rimmed eyes, ever see your true and supreme grace? O primal Lord, your body is adorned with a hooded snake and alms. Your feet reside in the hearts of devotees, and you hold a perfect spear.
commentary: A mind clouded by infatuation and the false life of the world struggles to see grace at all. Against that state Vallalar sets the primal Lord, who wears a hooded snake, takes alms, and holds a perfect spear, with his feet resting in the hearts of true devotees. That reality stands completely apart from everyday illusions.

translit: tavamē puriyum paruvami lēṉpoyc cakanaṭaikkaṇ avamē puriyum aṟivili yēṉuk karuḷumuṇṭō uvamēya meṉṉappa ṭāteṅku māki oḷiroḷiyām civamēmuk kaṇṇuṭait tēvēniṉ cittan terintilaṉē.
translation: I lack the maturity to perform penance. Is there any grace for this ignorant one who does useless deeds in the false ways of the world? O Sivam, the incomparable radiant light that has become everything everywhere. O three-eyed God, I do not understand your will.
commentary: Vallalar admits he lacks the maturity for penance and spends himself on the hollow habits of worldly life. Still he calls straight to Sivam, the incomparable radiant light that has become everything everywhere. From that admitted ignorance he keeps looking toward the light. He accepts that he cannot understand its will.

translit: maṭṭuṇṭa koṉṟaic caṭaiyara cē-aṉṟu vantiyiṭṭa piṭṭuṇṭa piccaip peruntakai yēkoṭum peṇmayalāl kaṭṭuṇṭa nāṉcukap paṭṭuṇṭu vāḻvaṉik kaṉmaṉamām tiṭṭuṇṭa pēyttalai veṭṭuṇṭa nāḷileṉ tīmaiyaṟṟē.
translation: O King with matted hair adorned with honeyed konrai flowers. O great mendicant who ate the steamed rice flour offered by Vandi on that day. Bound by cruel infatuation with women, I will live in true happiness on the day my evils are eradicated, when the demonic head of this stony, stubborn mind is severed.
commentary: All this misery flows from one source, the stubborn, stony mind. Vallalar calls it a demonic head, and it keeps him bound to cruel infatuation. Happiness comes on the day that head is severed and his evils go with it. Until then he stays trapped in the very illusions he longs to escape.

translit: āṭṭukkuk kāleṭut tāyniṉaip pāṭalar āṅkiyaṟṟum pāṭṭukkup pēreṉkol paṇṇeṉkol nīṭṭiyap pāṭṭeḻutum ēṭṭukku maiyeṉkol cēṟṟil uṟaṅka iṟaṅkuṅkaṭā māṭṭukku vīṭeṉkol pañcaṇai eṉkol matittiṭiṉē.
translation: You lifted your foot for the cosmic dance. As for those who do not sing of you, what is the name of the song they compose? What is its melody? What is the ink for the palm leaf on which they write such a lengthy song? When one considers this, what use is a house or a soft cotton mattress to a buffalo that descends into the mud to sleep?
commentary: Fine poetry about anything other than the divine is a waste of ink. Vallalar asks what such a song could even be called, and what its melody would be. Offer a water buffalo a house and a soft cotton mattress and it will still go down into the mud to sleep. A mind with no spiritual longing spends its talents the same way, on the dirt of worldly matters, and misses the cosmic dance of the Lord entirely.

translit: oppaṟṟa mukkaṭ cuṭarēniṉ cīrtti uṟātaveṟum tuppaṟṟa pāṭṭil cuvaiyuḷa tō-ataic cūḻntukaṟṟuc ceppaṟṟa vāykkut tiruvuḷa tōciṟi tēṉumuṇṭēl uppaṟṟa puṉkaṟi uṇṭōrtan nāvuk kuvappuḷatē.
translation: O incomparable three-eyed flame! Is there any flavor in an empty, useless song that does not carry your glory? Is there any true wealth for the unrefined mouth that thoroughly studies and recites it? If there is even the slightest bit of sweetness in it, then those who eat a meager dish cooked without salt would find pleasure on their tongues.
commentary: A song that does not carry the Lord's glory has no flavor, and the mouth that studies and recites it gains no real wealth. If such a song has any sweetness at all, Vallalar says, then a meager dish cooked without salt must please the tongue too. The words may sound pleasant, yet they leave the soul unnourished.

translit: cēlvaruṅ kaṇṇi iṭattōyniṉ cīrttiyaic cērttiyanta nālvarum ceytamiḻ kēṭṭup puṟattil naṭakkaccaṟṟē kālvarum āyiṉum iṉpuru vākik kaṉimaṉamap pālvaru mō-ataṉ pāṟpeṇ kaḷaiviṭṭup pārkkiṉumē.
translation: O Lord who keeps the goddess with fish-like eyes on your left side! Upon hearing the Tamil verses composed by those four saints praising your glory, even if my feet manage to take a step outside, will my ripened mind, transformed into bliss, go in that worldly direction? It will not, even if I abandon worldly women and look toward it.
commentary: The four great Saiva saints (nālvar) sang the Lord's glory in Tamil, and hearing their hymns ripens the mind into pure bliss. The feet may still wander a step outside into ordinary life. The mind will not follow, even if Vallalar leaves worldly women behind and turns to look. That sweetness simply overpowers every lesser desire.

translit: kārmuka mākappoṟ kalvaḷait tōyik kaṭaiyavaṉēṉ cōrmuka mākaniṉ cīrmukam pārttut tuvaḷukiṉṟēṉ pōrmuka mākaniṉ ṟōraiyum kāttaniṉ poṉṉaruḷip pārmuka māka-eṉ ōrmukam pārkkap parintilatē.
translation: O Lord who bent the golden mountain into a bow! I, the lowest of the low, look at your glorious face with a weary countenance and languish. Your golden grace, which protected even those standing on the battlefront, has not shown compassion to look at my solitary face on this earth.
commentary: This is the Lord who bent the golden mountain into a bow, whose grace protected even those standing on the battlefront. Vallalar, calling himself the lowest of the low, gazes at that glorious face with weariness, waiting for a single glance of compassion. He cannot understand why such boundless mercy has not yet looked at his one face on this earth.

translit: vāṉvaḷart tāyinta maṇvaḷart tāyeṅkum maṉṉuyirkaḷ tāṉvaḷart tāyniṉ takai-aṟi yā-eṉ ṟaṉai-aracē ēṉvaḷart tāykoṭum pāmpaiyel lāntaḷ ḷilaivaḷarttāy māṉvaḷart tāykarat tārniṉaip pōla vaḷarppavarē.
translation: You nurtured the sky. You nurtured this earth. You nurtured the enduring souls everywhere. O King, why did you nurture me when I do not comprehend your greatness? You nurtured the deadly snake without rejecting it. You nurtured the deer. O Lord who holds them in your hands, who else nurtures exactly like you?
commentary: God cares for all living beings without exception, sustaining the vast sky, the earth, and every soul. The divine holds both the gentle deer and the deadly snake, providing for them equally. Seeing this limitless compassion, Vallalar marvels that God continues to nurture him even when he feels blind to such greatness. This universal care proves that divine love does not depend on our personal worthiness.

translit: aṟkaṇṭam ōṅkum aracēniṉ ṟaṉaṭi yārmaturac coṟkaṇṭa pōtumeṉ puṟkaṇṭa neñcam tuṇintunillā tiṟkaṇṭa meyttavar pōlōṭu kiṉṟa teṟintatutīṅ kaṟkaṇ ṭeṉiṉumak kaṟkaṇṭa kākkainiṟ kāteṉparē.
translation: O King who stands eminent with a dark throat! Even when hearing the sweet words of your devotees, my petty mind does not stand resolute. It runs away like true ascetics fleeing the sight of domestic household life. They say a crow will not wait even if you throw sweet rock candy at it because it mistakes the candy for a thrown stone.
commentary: Even the sweet words of the Lord's devotees cannot hold Vallalar's petty mind still. It runs off like a true ascetic fleeing the sight of household life. Throw a piece of rock candy to a crow and it flies away in fear, taking the sweet for a thrown stone. The anxious heart does the same when the sweetness of divine teaching is offered to it freely.

translit: collukiṉ ṟōrkkamu tampōl cuvaitarum tolpukaḻōy vellukiṉ ṟōriṉṟic cummā alaiyumeṉ vēṭaneñcam pullukiṉ ṟōrtamaik kaṇṭāleṉ ṉāṅkol pukalveṟumvāy mellukiṉ ṟōrkkoru nellaval vāykkil viṭuvaraṉṟē.
translation: O Lord of ancient glory, you offer sweetness like nectar to those who chant your praise. My hypocritical heart wanders idly with no one to subdue it. Tell me what will happen if it sees those who embrace worldly attachments. If people chewing on an empty mouth get a handful of flattened rice, will they ever let it go?
commentary: The mind is restless by nature. Vallalar pictures it as a starving man chewing on an empty mouth who suddenly gets a handful of flattened rice. Once it tastes worldly pleasure, it grabs hold and will not let go.

translit: cīriṭu vārporuṭ celvarkka lāmalit tīṉarkaṭkiṅ kāriṭu vārpiccai āyiṉum piccaṉ acaṭaṉeṉṟē pēriṭu vārvampup pēcciṭu vārintap peṟṟikaṇṭum pōriṭu vārniṉaip pōṟṟāreṉ ṉēmukkaṭ puṇṇiyaṉē.
translation: People here offer wealth only to the rich who already possess material goods. Who will give alms to these destitute people? They simply brand a poor person a madman and a fool, and they spread idle gossip. Even after seeing this worldly nature, people fight among themselves, and they do not praise you. What is this, O virtuous three-eyed Lord?
commentary: The rich get the gifts, and the destitute get mocked as fools. Vallalar sees people watch this cruelty, know how empty it is, and still fight each other for status instead of turning to God.

translit: cēlukku nērviḻi maṅkaipaṅ kā-eṉ ciṟumatitāṉ mēlukku neñcaiyuṭ kāppatu pōlniṉṟu vevviṭaya mālukku vāṅki vaḻaṅkavun tāṉcam matittatukāṇ pālukkuṅ kāvalvem pūṉaikkun tōḻaṉeṉ pārituvē.
translation: O Lord who shares your form with the lady whose eyes resemble carp. My petty mind outwardly pretends to guard my heart, but it has secretly agreed to hand it over to the fierce delusion of sensory pleasures. This is exactly what they mean when they speak of guarding the milk while befriending the hungry cat.
commentary: Vallalar catches his own mind playing a double game. It stands at the gate as if guarding the heart, while it has already agreed to hand that heart over to sensory desire. He reaches for a common proverb to name the betrayal: guarding the milk while befriending the hungry cat.

translit: iṇaiyētum iṉṟiya tēvē kaṉaliṉaṉ inteṉumuk kaṇaiyē koḷumceṅ karumpē piṟavik kaṭalkaṭattum puṇaiyē tiruvaruṭ pūraṇa mēmeyp pulamaḷikkum tuṇaiyē-eṉ tuṉpan tuṭaittāṇṭu koḷḷat tuṇintaruḷē.
translation: O God without equal. O sweet red sugarcane who possesses the three eyes of fire, the sun, and the moon. O raft that carries us across the ocean of birth. O perfection of divine grace. O companion who grants true knowledge. Kindly resolve to wipe away my sorrow and take me as your own.
commentary: God is the one raft across the endless sea of birth and death. Vallalar asks that raft to wipe away his sorrow, grant him true knowledge, and claim him completely.

translit: nilaikāṭṭi āṇṭaniṉ tāṭkaṉpi lātaṉpil nīṇṭavaṉpōl pulaikāṭ ṭiyamaṉat tēṉkoṇṭa vēṭam puṉai-iṭaimēl kalaikāṭṭik kaṭṭu mayirttalai kāṭṭippuṉ kantaicuṟṟi mulaikāṭṭi āṇmakaṉ peṇvēṭam kāṭṭu muṟaimaiyaṉṟē.
translation: You showed me the true state and ruled over me. I have no true love for your feet, yet I act like someone with immense devotion, though my mind is filled with baseness. The disguise I wear is exactly like a man dressing up as a woman, donning a garment around his waist, tying up his hair, and stuffing rags to simulate breasts.
commentary: Pretended devotion fools no one, least of all God. Vallalar owns up to acting the devotee with no real love inside, and he paints the picture bluntly. He is like a man stuffing rags under his clothes to pass as a woman. That is how foolish an empty spiritual disguise looks.

translit: viṭanākap pūṇaṇi mēlōyeṉ neñcam viritalviṭṭeṉ uṭaṉāka meyaṉpu ḷūṟṟāka niṉṉaru ḷuṟṟiṭutaṟ kiṭaṉāka meynneṟik kīṭākac ceykuva tiṅkuṉakkē kaṭaṉāka niṟpatu kaṇṭēṉpiṉ tuṉpoṉṟuṅ kaṇṭilaṉē.
translation: O Supreme Lord adorned with a venomous snake as an ornament! I realized it is your duty here to stop my heart from scattering, to unite it with me, to make true love well up as a spring inside, to make it a fit receptacle for your Grace, and to align it with the true path. After realizing this, I saw no suffering at all.
commentary: Vallalar lays the whole burden of his progress at God's feet. Only God can gather his scattered mind and fill it with love. Once he sees that, his anxiety goes, and he finds no suffering left.

translit: nayappaṭum ōrniṉ aruḷeṉak kiṉṟeṉil nāymaṉameṉ vayappaṭu mōtuyar maṇpaṭu mōnalla vāḻvai-eṉṉāl ceyappaṭu mōkuṇam cīrppaṭu mōpavam cēraccaṟṟum payappaṭu mōmalam pāḻpaṭu mō-em pacupatiyē.
translation: O our Lord of souls! If I do not receive your delightful Grace today, will my dog-like mind come under my control? Will my sorrow be buried in the earth? Can I lead a good life? Will my character be set right? Will my mind fear even slightly to accumulate worldly bonds? Will my impurities be destroyed?
commentary: Effort alone will not tame this dog-like mind or scrub out deep-seated flaws. Every question in the verse comes back to Grace. Without it, sorrow stays unburied, the impurities stay, and the mind keeps running wild, helplessly bound to the world.

translit: cōpaṅkaṇ ṭārkkaruḷ ceyvōy matikkaṉṟic cūḻntiṭuven tīpaṅkaṇ ṭālum iruḷpōmiv vēḻai tiyaṅkumpari tāpaṅkaṇ ṭāyaruḷ ceyyāteṉ kuṟṟan taṉaikkuṟittuk kōpaṅkaṇ ṭālunaṉ ṟaiyā-eṉ tuṉpak kotippaṟumē.
translation: O Lord who grants Grace to those who experience sorrow! Darkness departs when a hot lamp glows nearby, apart from the light of the moon. You saw the pitiable suffering of this poor bewildered soul. If you do not grant Grace, it would still be good if you show anger upon noting my faults, O Lord. The boiling heat of my sorrow would then be severed.
commentary: Vallalar would rather be scolded than ignored. Let God notice his faults and flare up in anger, he says, and even that wrath would work like a lamp in the dark, burning away his sorrow.

translit: ellā muṭaiya iṟaiyava ṉēniṉai ēttukiṉṟa nallār tamakkoru nāḷēṉum pūcai nayantiyaṟṟic collāl avarpukaḻ collātiv vaṇṇam tuyarvataṟkeṉ kallāmai oṉṟumaṟ ṟillāmai oṉṟiru kāraṇamē.
translation: O God who possesses everything! I have not joyfully performed worship for even a single day for the good devotees who praise you. I have not spoken their praises with words. There are two reasons for my suffering in this manner: one is my ignorance, and the other is my poverty.
commentary: Caring for God's devotees is real spiritual practice, and Vallalar counts his neglect of it as the cause of his suffering. He never once worshipped them or spoke their praise. He names two reasons he fell short: he lacked spiritual knowledge, and he lacked wealth.

translit: piṟaiyāṟu koṇṭacev vēṇip pirāṉpatap pēṟaṭaivāṉ maṟaiyāṟu kāṭṭuniṉ taṇṇaru ḷēyaṉṟi māyai-eṉṉum niṟaiyāṟu cūḻun turumpāyc cuḻalumeṉ neñciṉuḷḷa kuṟaiyāṟu taṟkiṭam vēṟillai kāṇik kuvalaiyattē.
translation: To attain the supreme state at the feet of the Lord whose reddish matted hair bears the crescent moon and the river, there is nothing but your cool Grace which reveals the path of the Vedas. There is no other refuge in this world to soothe the deficiencies in my heart, which spins like a speck of dust caught in the flooding river of illusion.
commentary: Picture a speck of dust spinning in a river in flood. That is the mind caught in illusion. Vallalar finds no refuge for it except the cool Grace that shows the path and leads the soul to the supreme state.

translit: mālaṟi yātavaṉ aṉṟē-at teyva varataṉuniṉ kālaṟi yātavaṉ eṉṟālak kālai-ek kālai-emaip pōlaṟi yātavar kāṇpārmuṟ kaṇṭameyp puṇṇiyartam pālaṟi yātavaṉ nāṉitu kēṭṭuṇar pālaṉaṉṟē.
translation: Vishnu did not know you. If even the divine bestower Brahma did not know your feet, how will ignorant ones like us ever see those feet? I have not learned from the truly meritorious ones who saw them before. I am a mere child seeking to listen and realize this.
commentary: Even Vishnu and Brahma could not find the Lord's feet. Faced with a reality that large, Vallalar takes the only honest stance, total humility. He calls himself a child who never learned from the sages who saw those feet, yet who still longs to see what the gods themselves could not.

translit: oṉṟē-eṉ āruyirk kōruṟa vē-eṉak kōramutē naṉṟēmuk kaṇṇuṭai nāyaka mēmikka nallakuṇak kuṉṟē niṟai-aruṭ kōvē eṉatu kulateyvamē maṉṟē oḷirmuḻu māṇikka mē-eṉai vāḻvikkavē.
translation: O One. O sole relation to my precious life. O unique nectar to me. O goodness. O three-eyed Lord. O mountain of exceptionally good qualities. O King of perfect grace. O my family deity. O flawless ruby shining in the hall to make me flourish.
commentary: Look at the names Vallalar uses: sole relation, family deity, flawless ruby shining in the hall. These are words for someone close, someone kin. He addresses the three-eyed Lord of the cosmic dancing hall as the one true companion of his life.

translit: tāḻvētum iṉṟiya kōvē eṉakkut taṉittaperu vāḻvē nutaṟkaṇ maṇiyē-eṉ uḷḷa maṇiviḷakkē ēḻvēlai eṉṉiṉum pōtā iṭumpai iṭuṅkuṭumpap pāḻvē taṉaippaṭa māṭṭēṉ eṉakkuṉ patamaruḷē.
translation: O King without any flaw. O my unique great life. O jewel with an eye on the forehead. O radiant lamp within my heart. Even the seven oceans are not enough to measure the afflictions of this worldly family life. I cannot endure its ruinous agony. Bestow your feet upon me.
commentary: The seven oceans together could not hold the afflictions of worldly family life. Worn down by that ruinous agony, Vallalar turns inward to the Lord he calls a radiant lamp within his heart, and asks for His feet.

translit: vaṇṭukoṇ ṭārnaṟuṅ koṉṟaiyi ṉāṉṟaṉ malaraṭikkut toṇṭukoṇ ṭārtañ cukattukkum vāḻkkaic cuḻaliṟṟaḷḷum peṇṭukoṇ ṭārtam tuyarukkum oppiṉṟu pēcileṉṟē kaṇṭukoṇ ṭāyiṉi neñcēniṉ uḷḷak karuttetuvē.
translation: There is no comparison between the bliss of those who serve the flower-feet of the Lord wearing the fragrant laburnum garland swarming with bees, and the sorrow of those who take wives and plunge into the whirlpool of worldly life. You have realized this. O heart, what is your intention now?
commentary: Set the two lives side by side. Those who serve the Lord's flower-feet live in bliss, while those who marry and plunge into domestic life are pulled into a whirlpool of sorrow. Vallalar tells his heart it has already seen this, and now it must choose.

translit: malaṅkaviḻn tārmaṉam vāṉkaviḻn tālumav vāṉpuṟamām calaṅkaviḻn tālum caliyāteṉ puṉmaṉan tāṉkaṭalil kalaṅkaviḻn tārmaṉam pōlē calippatu kāṇkuṭumpa vilaṅkaviḻn tālaṉṟi nillāteṉ ceyval viṭaiyavaṉē.
translation: The minds of those who have overthrown their impurities will not waver even if the sky falls or the cosmic waters surrounding the sky overflow. See how my petty mind trembles like the minds of those whose ship has capsized in the ocean. It will not grow steady unless the shackles of family life are broken. What shall I do, O rider of the bull?
commentary: Those who have overthrown their impurities stay steady even if the sky falls or the cosmic waters flood. Vallalar's own mind shakes like that of someone whose ship has capsized. He names the cause plainly: family ties are shackles, and until they break, the mind will not settle.

translit: maikoṭut tārneṭuṅ kaṇmalai māṉukku vāyntorupāl meykoṭut tāytavar viṭṭavem māṉukku mēvuṟa-ōr kaikoṭut tāymayal kaṇṇiyil vīḻntuṭ kalaṅkuṟumeṉ koykoṭut tāḻmaṉa māṉukkuk kālaik koṭuttaruḷē.
translation: You gave one half of your body to the mountain deer whose long eyes are painted with collyrium. You gave one hand to hold the fierce deer sent by the ascetics. My mind is a deer that has fallen into the snare of delusion and suffers in deep turmoil. Please grant your holy feet to save this deer of my mind.
commentary: Three deer run through this verse. Siva gave half his body to the goddess Parvati (called a mountain deer), and in one hand he holds the wild deer the ascetics sent against him. The third is Vallalar's own mind, caught in the snare of worldly delusion. For that one he begs the Lord's holy feet as a sanctuary.

translit: uṭampār uṟumayirk kālpuḻai tōṟaṉal ūṭṭiveyya viṭampāc ciya-irup pūcikaḷ pāycciṉum metteṉṉumit taṭampār ciṟunaṭait tuṉpañcey vētaṉait tāṅkariteṉ kaṭampānaṟ paṉṉiru kaṇṇā iṉi-eṉaik kāttaruḷē.
translation: Feeding fire into every hair follicle of this body and piercing them with iron needles dipped in fierce poison would feel gentle. The agonizing misery caused by the petty ways of this vast world is unbearable. O my Kadamba Lord with twelve beautiful eyes, please protect me now.
commentary: Fire fed into every pore, needles dipped in poison. Vallalar says even these would feel gentle beside the misery the world's petty ways inflict. Out of that agony he cries to Lord Murugan (addressed here as the twelve-eyed Lord of Kadamba flowers) to protect him now.

translit: maṇṇālum maṇṇuṟṟa vāḻkkaiyi ṉālumav vāḻkkaikkuṟṟa peṇṇālum nontuvan tārai elāmaruṭ pēṟeṉumuk kaṇṇālum pārttaintu kaiyālum īyum kaṇapatiniṉ paṇṇālum māmaṟai mēṟṟāḷai eṉṉuṭ patittaruḷē.
translation: O Vinayakar. You look with your three eyes of supreme grace upon all who come to you suffering from attachments to land, worldly life, and women bound to that life. You grant them boons with your five hands. Please plant your holy feet within my heart, feet that are celebrated by music and the great Vedas.
commentary: Lord Vinayakar (Vinayakar) is traditionally shown with three eyes and five hands, and Vallalar puts them all to work. The eyes pour supreme grace on everyone worn down by attachment to property, worldly life and family, and the hands give freely. For himself he asks one thing. Let those holy feet be planted firmly in his heart.

translit: vāṉāḷa mālayaṉ vāḻvāḷa aṉṟi-im maṇmuḻutum tāṉāḷa niṉpatam tāḻpavar tāḻka-oṇ caṅkaiyaṅkai māṉāḷa meyyiṭan tantōytuṉ paṟṟa maṉamatoṉṟē nāṉāḷa eṇṇiniṉ tāḷēttu kiṉṟaṉaṉ nalkukavē.
translation: Let those who bow at your feet do so to rule the heavens, to attain the glorious lives of Vishnu and Brahma, or to rule this entire earth alone. O Lord who gave half your body to the deer-like goddess wearing bright conch bangles on her lovely hands. I praise your feet with the sole intention of mastering a sorrowless mind. Please grant this to me.
commentary: Let others bow for heaven, for the lives of Vishnu and Brahma, or to rule the whole earth. Vallalar wants none of it. He praises the Lord's feet for one thing only, a mind completely free of sorrow.

translit: īṭaṟi yātamuk kaṇṇāniṉ aṉpar iyalpiṉai-in nāṭaṟi yātuṉ aruḷaṉṟi ūṇcuvai nāvaiyaṉṟi mēṭaṟi yātunaṟ pāṭṭaikkaṟ ṟōraṉṟi mēṟcumanta ēṭaṟi yātavai yēṉaṟi yā-eṉ ṟikaḻvaraṉṟē.
translation: O incomparable three-eyed Lord. This world does not understand the nature of your devotees without your grace. Only the tongue knows the taste of food, not the vessel holding it. Only the learned appreciate a good song, not the palm-leaf manuscript that carries the words. Yet the ignorant mock your devotees, asking why they lack worldly knowledge.
commentary: Worldly people mock devotees for lacking practical knowledge. Vallalar answers that divine love is understood only through grace. The tongue knows the sweetness of food and the learned listener knows a good song, while the vessel and the palm-leaf manuscript hold the treasure and know nothing of it.

translit: cūṭuṇṭa pūñaikkuc cōṟuṇṭa vāypiṉ tuṭippataṉṟi ūṭuṇṭa pāliṭṭa ūṇkaṇṭa tēṉum uṇattuṇiyā tīṭuṇṭa eṉmaṉam antō tuyaril iṭiyuṇṭumiv vīṭuṇṭa vāḻkkaiyil vīḻuṇṭa tālem viṭaiyavaṉē.
translation: O our Lord mounted on the bull! A scalded cat's mouth might twitch for rice, but it dares not eat even when it sees food soaked in milk. Alas, my afflicted mind, though battered by sorrow, has still fallen back into this domestic worldly life.
commentary: A scalded cat will not touch food even when it is soaked in milk. The human mind is less wise than that cat. Battered again and again by the sorrows of worldly attachment, it keeps falling back into the very domestic life that hurts it.

translit: karaṅkāṭṭi maiyiṭṭa kaṇkāṭṭi eṉperuṅ kaṉmaneñcak kuraṅkāṭṭic cēymaiyil niṟkiṉṟa mātaraik koṇṭukallār uraṅkāṭṭik kōloṉ ṟuṭaṉīṭṭik kāṭṭi urappi-oru maraṅkāṭ ṭiyakuraṅ kāṭṭukiṉ ṟōreṉ maṇikaṇṭaṉē.
translation: O Lord with the sapphire neck. The ignorant use distant women who flash their hands and kohl-lined eyes to make the monkey of my karmic heart dance. They show their strength, hold out a stick, shout, and make this monkey on the tree dance.
commentary: The restless human mind is compared to a captive monkey forced to dance. Worldly temptations act like a trainer with a stick, agitating the heart and keeping it trapped in endless, involuntary reactions.

translit: kaḷaṅkaṉi pōlmaṇi kaṇṭāniṉ poṟkaḻal kāṇaṟkeṉciṟ ṟuḷaṅkaṉi yātuniṉ cīrkēṭ kiṉumaṉ puṟa-urukā vaḷaṅkaṉi kāmañ ciṟavāmal ciṟṟil vakuttuḻalum iḷaṅkaṉi pōlniṉṟa teṉceyku vēṉem iṟaiyavaṉē.
translation: O Lord with a neck dark as the kala fruit. O our Lord. My petty heart does not ripen to seek your golden feet. Even when hearing your glories, it does not melt with love. Without maturing into fruitful devotion, it remains like a young child who wanders about building playhouses in the sand. What shall I do?
commentary: The heart here is unripe fruit. Hearing the Lord's glories should melt it, yet it stays hard and spends itself on trivial things, like a child absorbed in building playhouses out of sand.

translit: māmatti ṉālcuḻal veṇtayir pōṉṟu maṭantaiyartam kāmatti ṉālcuḻal eṉṟaṉneñ cō-uṉṟaṉ kālai-aṉpām tāmatti ṉāltaḷai yiṭṭaneñ cō-it takai-iraṇṭiṉ nāmattiṉāl pittaṉ eṉpōy niṉakketu nallaneñcē.
translation: O Lord known as a madman. Is my heart the one that spins from lust for women like white curd spun by a great churning rod, or is it the heart bound to your feet by the garland of love? Of these two, which heart is good for you?
commentary: Two hearts are set side by side. One spins with desire the way curd spins under the churning rod. The other is tied to the Lord's feet with a garland of love. Vallalar puts the question straight to the Lord called a madman: which of these is truly acceptable to you?

translit: ēṟṟiliṭ ṭārkoṭi koṇṭōy viḷakkiṉai ēṟṟaperuṅ kāṟṟiliṭ ṭālum iṭalāmnel māvaik kalittiṭunīr āṟṟiliṭ ṭālum peṟalāmuṭ kālai aṭuṅkuṭumpac cēṟṟiliṭ ṭālpiṉ paritām evarkkum tiruppuvatē.
translation: O Lord holding the banner of the bull. One might light a lamp and place it in a fierce wind. One might drop rice flour into a rushing river and still recover it. But if one places their inner foot into the destructive mud of domestic life, it is impossible for anyone to ever pull it back.
commentary: A lamp in a gale might be kept burning. Flour dropped in a rushing river might be recovered. Put your foot into the mud of domestic life, though, and no one can ever pull it back out.

translit: tērōṅku kāḻikkaṇ meyññāṉappāluṇṭa cemmaṇiyaic cīrōṅku muttuc civikaiyiṉ mēlvaitta tēva-uṉṟaṉ pērōṅkum ainteḻut taṉṟō paṭaippaip piramaṉukkum ērōṅku kāppait tiruneṭu mālukkum īntatuvē.
translation: O God, you placed the perfect gem who drank the milk of true wisdom in Kazhi, a city of towering chariots, upon a glorious pearl palanquin. It is your exalted five-lettered name that granted the work of creation to Brahma and the work of beautiful protection to the tall and holy Vishnu.
commentary: The "perfect gem" is the child saint Sambandar of Kazhi, who tradition says was fed the milk of divine wisdom by the Goddess and later granted a pearl palanquin by the Divine. Vallalar names the five-lettered mantra (Na-Ma-Si-Va-Ya) as the true source behind all cosmic functions. It gave Brahma the power to create and Vishnu the power to protect.

translit: vētaṉai yāmatu cūtaṉai yā-eṉṟu vētaṉaiyāl pōtaṉai yāniṉ ṟuṉaikkūvu mēḻaiyaip pōtaṉaikēḷ vātaṉai yātiṅku vātaṉai yāveṉṟuṉ vāymalarac cōtaṉai yāyiṉuñ cōtaṉai yāciṟ cukapporuḷē.
translation: O substance of supreme bliss. Listen to the cry of this poor one who stands bewildered and calls out to you in agony, asking who brings affliction and who brings deceit. Even if it is only a test, let your blossoming mouth speak and say, "What is this torment? Come here."
commentary: Bewildered by suffering, Vallalar wants just one word of comfort from the Lord's own mouth. "What is this torment? Come here" would be enough, even if the whole ordeal is only a test.

translit: iṉpaṟṟa icciṟu vāḻkkaiyi lēveyi lēṟavempum eṉpaṟṟa puṉpuḻup pōltaḷar ēḻai eṉiṉumivaṉ aṉpaṟṟa pāvi-eṉ ṟantō eṉaiviṭil aiyavaiyat teṉpaṟṟa tākamaṟ ṟillaikaṇ ṭāyeṉai ēṉṟukoḷḷē.
translation: In this joyless petty life, I languish as a frail wretch, like a boneless miserable worm scorching in the rising heat of the sun. Even so, O Lord, if you abandon me and call me a loveless sinner, I have no other attachment in this world. Please accept me.
commentary: A boneless worm drying in the hot sun is how helpless Vallalar feels in this joyless life. He strips away all pride and admits he may be a loveless sinner. Still he pleads for grace, because he has surrendered entirely and has nowhere else to turn.

translit: kaḷaṅkoṇṭa ōrmaṇik kāṭciyum muccuṭark kaṇaruḷum vaḷaṅkoṇṭa teyvat tirumuka māṭciyum vāyntapari maḷaṅkoṇṭa koṉṟaic caṭaiyumpoṟ cēvaṭi māṇpumoṉṟa uḷaṅkoṇṭa puṇṇiyar aṉṟō-eṉ taṉṉai uṭaiyavarē.
translation: The meritorious ones who hold in their hearts the united vision of the unparalleled gem with the dark throat, the grace of the three luminous eyes, the majesty of the divine holy face, the fragrant matted hair adorned with konrai flowers, and the glory of the golden feet are indeed my true masters.
commentary: Here is the traditional form of Siva, with the poisoned dark throat, the three luminous eyes, the holy face, the matted hair fragrant with konrai flowers and the golden feet. Whoever holds this whole image in the heart is, for Vallalar, a master worth serving. He claims such people as his own guides.

translit: kāvikku nērmaṇi kaṇṭāvaṇ ṭārkuḻal kaṟparuḷum tēvikku vāmaṅ koṭuttōyniṉ māmalarc cēvaṭippāl cēvikkum cēvakañ ceyvōrai āyiṉuñ cēvikka-ip pāvikku vāykkileṉ āvikku nīṇṭa payaṉatuvē.
translation: O Lord with a gem-like throat matching the dark lily. O Lord who gave your left half to the Goddess who grants chastity, whose hair hums with bees. If this sinner is blessed to serve at least those who offer service and worship at your great blossoming rosy feet, that will be the lasting reward for my soul.
commentary: The Lord appears sharing half his body with the Goddess, the perfect union of masculine and feminine divine principles. Vallalar asks for very little. Let him serve even those who serve at the Lord's feet, and his soul will have its lasting reward. Service to God's servants is, for him, the highest possible calling for the soul.

translit: koṅkiṭṭa koṉṟaic caṭaiyumniṉ ṉōrpacuṅ kōmaḷappeṇ paṅkiṭṭa veṇtiru nīṟṟoḷi mēṉiyum pārttiṭilpiṉ iṅkiṭṭa māyaiyai eṅkiṭṭa vā-eṉ ṟicaippiṉumpōyc caṅkiṭṭa ōcaiyil poṅkiṭṭa vāykoṭu tāṇṭiṭumē.
translation: If one beholds your matted hair adorned with fragrant konrai flowers and your radiant body, smeared with white holy ash and sharing half with the tender green lady, then even if one calls out to the illusion stationed here saying, "Where are you, come," it will flee. It will leap away, its mouth bubbling over like the resounding roar of a blown conch.
commentary: A true vision of the divine completely shatters worldly illusion. Vallalar says that once a person beholds the radiant form of God, the deceptive pull of the material world loses all its power. Even if you were to invite that illusion back, it would flee in terror, roaring like a blown conch shell as it escapes.

translit: vemperu māṉukkuk kaikoṭut tāṇṭa mikuṅkaruṇai emperu māṉukku viṇṇappam tēvar iḷampiṭiyār tamperu māṉukkum cārmalai māṉukkum cāṟṟumaiṅkaic cemperu māṉukkum entāykkum nāṉpaṇi ceyyacceyyē.
translation: This is a petition to our Lord of immense grace, who extended a helping hand and saved the fierce lord. Grant that I may render service to the lord of the young celestial elephant-lady, to the deer of the mountain, to the celebrated red lord of five hands, and to my mother.
commentary: A prayer to serve the whole sacred family of the Saiva tradition: the supreme Lord, the mother goddess, and their sons Murugan and Vinayakar. Vallalar reaches for poetic names. The goddess is the deer of the mountain, and Vinayakar is the red lord of five hands.

translit: cāṟṟava ṉēkanaṉ ṉāvuḷḷa tāyiṉum cāṟṟaritām vīṟṟava ṉēveḷḷi veṟpava ṉē-aruḷ mēviyaveṇ nīṟṟava ṉēniṉ ṉaruḷtara vēṇṭum neṭumuṭiveḷ ēṟṟava ṉēpali ēṟṟavaṉē aṉpark kēṟṟavaṉē.
translation: Even if one possessed countless good tongues to speak, you would remain impossible to describe. O supreme one, O lord of the silver mountain, O lord of the white ash imbued with grace! You must grant your grace. O lord riding the tall-crowned white bull, O receiver of alms, O lord perfectly suited to your devotees!
commentary: Language cannot hold God. Give a person countless tongues and the Lord would still be beyond telling. So Vallalar calls him by the old images of the ascetic Siva, the silver mountain, the white ash, the bull, the alms he receives, and asks for the one thing that matters, his grace.

translit: patiyē caraṇam paramē caraṇam paramparamām titiyē caraṇam civamē caraṇam civamuṇarntōr katiyē caraṇameṉ kaṇṇē caraṇammuk kaṭkaruṇā nitiyē caraṇam caraṇameṉ pālmeyn nilaiyaruḷē.
translation: O Supreme Lord, I surrender. O Supreme Reality, I surrender. O state of the absolute supreme, I surrender. O Sivam, I surrender. O refuge of those who have realized Sivam, I surrender. O my eye, I surrender. O three-eyed treasure of grace, I surrender. I surrender. Bestow the true state upon me.
commentary: Surrender, Vallalar says, is the only way to the final truth. In a rhythmic chant he yields himself again and again to the supreme reality he calls Sivam. Then he asks this treasure of grace for the true, lasting state.

translit: eṉṉuṟa vē-eṉ kuruvē-eṉ uḷḷat teḻumiṉpamē eṉṉuyi rē-eṉṟaṉ aṉpē nilaipeṟṟa eṉcelvamē eṉṉaṟi vē-eṉṟaṉ vāḻvē-eṉ vāḻvuk kiṭumutalē eṉṉara cē-eṉ kulateyva mē-eṉai ēṉṟukoḷḷē.
translation: O my relation, O my Guru, O bliss rising in my heart! O my life, O my love, O my enduring wealth! O my knowledge, O my life, O the root capital of my life! O my king, O my family deity, please accept me.
commentary: Every name a person could need, Vallalar gives to God: relative, teacher, bliss, wealth, the breath of his life, his king, his family deity. He calls the Lord the root capital of his life, the stock his whole existence runs on. Then he asks only to be accepted.

translit: kāṉpōl iruṇṭa-iv vañcaka vāḻkkaiyil kaṉṉeñcamē māṉpōl kutittukkoṇ ṭōṭēl amuta mativiḷaṅkum vāṉpōl kuḷirnta civāṉanta vāḻkkaiyiṉ vāḻvuṟaccen tēṉpōl iṉikkum civāya nama-eṉac cintaiceyyē.
translation: O stony heart, do not leap and run like a deer in this deceitful life that is dark as a forest. To attain a life of divine bliss that is cool like the sky where the ambrosial moon shines, meditate on "Sivaya Nama" which is sweet as red honey.
commentary: Vallalar talks to his own stony heart. Stop leaping about like a startled deer in the dark forest of this deceitful life, he tells it. The remedy is to meditate on the mantra Sivaya Nama (a salutation to Siva), sweet as red honey. It brings a calm as cool as a moonlit sky.

translit: vētaṉeṉ kōtaṟa vēṇṭumeṉ kō-eṉa viṇṇappañcey pātaṉeṉ kōkaṭaṟ paḷḷikoṇ ṭāṉtoḻum paṇpaṉeṉkō nātaṉeṉ kōpara nātaṉeṉ kō-eṅkaḷ nampikkunal tūtaṉeṉ kō-avaṉ tōḻaṉeṉ kōniṉait tūymaṇiyē.
translation: O pure gem, shall I call you the one whose feet Brahma begs to clear his faults? Shall I call you the noble one worshipped by Vishnu who slumbers on the ocean? Shall I call you the Lord? Shall I call you the Supreme Lord? Shall I call you the good messenger for our beloved Sundarar? Shall I call you his friend?
commentary: Vallalar cannot settle on a name for God. Brahma (the creator god) and Vishnu (the preserver god) worship him, and he is Lord and Supreme Lord. Yet the same being carried messages for the great Tamil poet-saint Sundarar and walked beside him as a friend. God is that vast and that close at once.

translit: iyaṅkā maṉamum kayaṅkā nilaiyum ikaparattē mayaṅkā aṟivum tiyaṅkā neṟiyum makiḻntaruḷvāy vayaṅkā nilattiṉ muyaṅkā uyartavar vāḻttukiṉṟa puyaṅkā tutittaṟ kuyaṅkā tavaruṭ pukuntavaṉē.
translation: O Lord adorned with a serpent, you are praised by exalted ascetics who do not entangle themselves in this transient world. You enter the hearts of those who never tire of praising you. Joyfully grant me an unwavering mind, an undegraded state, a wisdom free from delusion in this world and the next, and an unfaltering path.
commentary: Steadiness is what Vallalar asks for: a mind that does not wander, wisdom free of confusion in this life and the next, a path that never falters, an inner state that never slips. Worldly distractions entangle a mind that lacks it. He notes that the Lord enters the hearts of those who never tire of praising him.

translit: civacaṅka rāciva yōkā civakatic cīraḷikkum civacampu vēciva lōkā civānantac celvanalkum civacunta rāciva pōkā civākamac cenneṟicol civapuṅka vāciva ñāṉikaḷ vāḻttum civakuruvē.
translation: O Siva Sankara. O Siva Yoga. O Siva Sambhu who grants the excellence of the divine state. O Lord of Sivaloka. O Siva Sundara who bestows the wealth of divine bliss. O Siva Bhoga. O supreme Siva who speaks the righteous path of the Sivagamas. O Siva Guru praised by the sages of divine wisdom.
commentary: A stream of sacred names, each one beginning with Siva. Vallalar honors him as Lord of Sivaloka (the divine world) and as the one who speaks the path of the Sivagamas (ancient scriptures guiding spiritual practice). Calling him the Siva Guru says that true wisdom and lasting joy come to us as gifts of grace.

translit: matitattu vānta aruṭciva mēciṉ mayacivamē tuticit telāmvalla meycciva mēciṟ cukacivamē katinitta cuttac civamē viḷaṅkumuk kaṭcivamē paticacci tānanta ciṟciva mē-em paracivamē.
translation: O Siva of grace at the pinnacle of intellectual principles. O Siva of pure consciousness. O true Siva capable of all praised mystical powers. O Siva of conscious bliss. O eternal and pure Siva who is our ultimate refuge. O shining three-eyed Siva. O Lord who is the conscious Siva of existence, knowledge, and bliss. O our Supreme Siva.
commentary: God here is existence, knowledge and bliss together, a pure consciousness above every concept the intellect can build. Vallalar names him the source of all mystical powers. That eternal, shining presence is his refuge and the true home of the soul.

translit: kaṭumpula vēṭarkaḷ ōraivar intiyak kaḷvaraivar koṭuṅkara ṇattuṭṭar nālvarkaḷ vaṉmalak kōḷaraivar aṭumpaṭai kōṭikoṇ ṭuṟṟārmaṟ ṟēḻaiyaṉ yāṉoruvaṉ iṭumpaṭai yātumi lēṉvelva teṅṅaṉ iṟaiyavaṉē.
translation: Five fierce hunters of the senses, five thieves of the organs, four scoundrels of the inner faculties, and five tyrants of strong impurity have arrived with a murderous army of millions. I am a single poor soul. I have no weapons to fight them. How can I conquer them, O Lord?
commentary: Vallalar counts his enemies like a general counting an army: five hunters of the senses, five thieves of the organs, four scoundrels of the inner faculties, five tyrants of impurity, millions more behind them. He stands alone and unarmed. Without God's direct help he cannot win.

translit: iṭaikkoṭi vāmat tiṟaivāmeyñ ñāṉikaṭ kiṉpanalkum viṭaikkoṭi ēntum valattāyniṉ nāmam viyanturaiyār kaṭaikkoṭi pōlak kataṟukiṉ ṟārpoyk kataiyavartām puṭaikkoṭi yālaṉṟip pullāl eyilaip puṉaipavarē.
translation: O Lord with the creeper-waisted Goddess on your left. You hold the bull banner on your right and grant bliss to true sages. Those who follow false tales and do not praise your name will wail endlessly. They are like fools who build a fortress out of weak grass instead of strong vines.
commentary: The Lord appears in his traditional form, the Goddess on his left and the bull banner in his right hand. True sages find joy, while those who follow invented religious tales find only misery. Relying on these false stories is like building a fortress out of weak grass, since it offers no real protection when life gets hard.

translit: urumatti lēpaṭṭa puṉpuḻup pōliv ulakanaṭaik karumatti lēpaṭṭa eṉmaṉan tāṉniṉ kaḻalaṭaiyum tarumatti lēpaṭṭa tiṉṟē-eṉ ṟeṇṇun taṉaiyumantō marumatti lēpaṭṭa vāḷiyaip pōṉṟu varuttuvatē.
translation: Like a lowly worm caught in the scorching sun, my mind is trapped in the actions of worldly life. When I wonder if my mind has attained the merit of reaching your feet today, alas, that very thought torments me like an arrow piercing my vital chest.
commentary: Worldly life is a scorching sun, and the mind caught in its daily tasks dries up like a worm in the heat. Even the hope of reaching the Lord's feet hurts. The longing strikes Vallalar's chest like an arrow, because it reminds him how far he still is from grace.

translit: eṉṉiṟai vā-imai yōriṟai vāmaṟai yiṉmuṭipiṉ muṉṉiṟai vāmalai miṉṉiṟai vāmalar muṇṭakattōṉ taṉṉiṟai vātitit tāṉiṟai vāmeyt tapōtaṉaruḷ maṉṉiṟai vā-iṅku vā-eṉ ṟeṉakkunal vāḻvaruḷē.
translation: O my Lord. O Lord of the celestials. O Lord standing at the pinnacle of the Vedas. O Lord of the Goddess who shines like mountain lightning. O Lord of Brahma on the lotus flower. O Lord of Vishnu the sustainer. O Lord abiding in the grace of true ascetics. Call out to me saying "Come here" and grant me a good life.
commentary: The ultimate Lord stands far above all traditional deities, scriptures, and heavenly beings. Figures like Brahma the creator and Vishnu the sustainer are mentioned only to show that the one true God rules over them all. After all those titles, Vallalar wants one thing: to hear that voice say "Come here" and to be given a life of true goodness.

translit: pōṟṟi-eṉ āvit tuṇaiyē-eṉ aṉpil pukuñcivamē pōṟṟi-eṉ vāḻviṉ payaṉē-eṉ iṉpap putunaṟavē pōṟṟi-eṉ kaṇṇuṇ maṇiyē-eṉ uḷḷam puṉai-aṇiyē pōṟṟi-eṉ ōrperun tēvē karuṇai purintaruḷē.
translation: Praise to you, companion of my soul. Praise to you, Sivam entering my love. Praise to you, the fruit of my life. Praise to you, the fresh honey of my bliss. Praise to you, the pupil of my eye. Praise to you, the adornment worn by my heart. Praise to you, my one great God. Bestow your grace upon me.
commentary: Pure love poured out. Sivam is as close as can be, companion of the soul, pupil of the eye, fresh honey of Vallalar's own joy, the ornament his heart wears.

translit: kañcatti lērmuka mañcatti lērnaṭaik kaṉṉiyarkaṇ nañcatti lē-avar vañcatti lēpaṭṭu nāṇuṟumpuṉ neñcatti lē-ataṉ tañcatti lēmuk kaṇitta-eṉpōl pañcatti lēpira pañcatti lē-uḻap pārevarē.
translation: Who suffers in this famine, in this worldly life, like me? I am caught in the poison of the eyes of maidens with lotus-like faces and beautiful gaits. I am caught in their deceit, taking refuge in a base and shameful heart, completely ruined.
commentary: The image is a classic one in Tamil poetry: a man ruined by his pull toward beautiful women. Vallalar uses it to speak of being dragged about by physical desire. He calls this ordinary worldly life a famine, because it leaves the soul starving and ashamed, far from the nourishment of grace.

translit: nāṉmukat tōṉum tiruneṭu mālumeyñ ñāṉameṉṉum vāṉmukak kaṇkoṇṭu kāṇāmal tamuru māṟiyumniṉ tēṉmukak koṉṟai muṭiyumcen tāmaraic cēvaṭiyum ūṉmukak kaṇkoṇṭu tēṭiniṉ ṟārcaṟ ṟuṇarvilarē.
translation: The four-faced Brahma and the great Lord Vishnu failed to see you with the heavenly eye of true wisdom. Changing their forms, they stood searching for your crown adorned with honey-laden konrai flowers and your red lotus-like feet using their physical eyes of flesh. They have no understanding at all.
commentary: In the old story, Brahma and Vishnu set out to find the crown and feet of the supreme Lord, and both failed. Vallalar says why. They changed their forms and searched with eyes of flesh, when the divine light is seen only with the inner eye of real wisdom.

translit: iruvark kaṟiyap paṭāteḻun tōṅkiniṉ ṟēttukiṉṟōr karuvarkka nīkkum karuṇaiveṟ pē-eṉ kavalaiyai-iṅ koruvarkku nāṉcola māṭṭēṉ avareṉ ṉuṭaiyavarō veruvaṟka eṉṟeṉai āṇṭaruḷ īteṉṟaṉ viṇṇappamē.
translation: O mountain of compassion who rose high, unperceived by the two, and who removes the cycle of birth for those who praise you! I will not tell my sorrow to anyone here. Are they my people? Rule me, saying "do not fear." This is my petition.
commentary: Still thinking of the two gods who could not measure the light, Vallalar turns to God as a mountain of compassion. He will not carry his sorrow to people here, who cannot truly help him. His petition goes straight to the Lord, and he asks for one thing only: to hear the words that end his fear.

translit: oṇṇutal ēḻai maṭavārtam vāḻkkaiyiṉ uṟṟiṭiṉum paṇṇuta lērmaṟai āyirañ cūḻuniṉ pātattaiyāṉ eṇṇuta lētoḻi lākaccey vitteṉṉai ēṉṟukoḷvāy kaṇṇuta lēkaru ṇaikkaṭa lē-eṉ karuttituvē.
translation: Even if I am caught in the worldly life with bright-foreheaded women, make my sole duty the contemplation of your feet surrounded by thousands of beautiful, musical Vedas, and accept me. O Lord with an eye on your forehead! O ocean of compassion! This is my intention.
commentary: The grace Vallalar asks for is specific. His outward life may stay tied to a household and its duties. Inside, he wants the ocean of compassion to make the constant thought of the Lord's feet his only real work.

translit: taḷaikkiṉṟa māyak kuṭumpap peruntuyar tāṅki-antō iḷaikkiṉṟa ēḻaik kiraṅkukaṇ ṭāyciṟi tē-iṟaku muḷaikkiṉṟa pōtaṟup pārpōlniṉ ṉāma moḻintiṭuṅkāl vaḷaikkiṉṟa māyaikkiṅ kāṟṟēṉmuk kaṇṇuṭai māmaṇiyē.
translation: Bearing the great sorrow of the illusory family life that binds me, alas, I grow weary. Have pity on this poor one. Like those who cut off wings just as they begin to sprout, illusion surrounds and subdues me when I speak your name. I cannot bear it here, O great gem with three eyes!
commentary: Worldly illusion (maya) gets a painful image. The moment Vallalar tries to lift himself by speaking the divine name, the pressures of family life pull him back down, like someone clipping a young bird's wings just as they begin to sprout. He begs the Lord to take pity on his weariness.

translit: mañcaṭai vāṉa niṟattōṉ ayaṉmutal vāṉavarkkā nañcaṭai yāḷa miṭumiṭaṟ ṟōykaṅkai naṇṇukiṉṟa ceñcaṭai yāyniṉ tiruppeya rākac ciṟanta-eḻut tañcaṭai yārkaṇkaḷ pañcaṭai yāmuṉ ṉaṟivilarē.
translation: You bear the mark of poison on your throat for the sake of the cloud-hued Vishnu, Brahma, and the celestials. You wear the Ganges in your red matted hair. Those who fail to take refuge in the five great letters of your holy name lack wisdom, even before cotton plugs their eyes in death.
commentary: The five great letters are Na-Ma-Shi-Va-Ya, the sacred mantra of Siva. Vallalar recalls how Siva swallowed a deadly poison to save the other gods, proof of his compassion. Whoever fails to take refuge in this name stays spiritually ignorant right up to death, when cotton is traditionally placed over the eyes of the dead.

translit: ilaṅkā purattaṉ irākkatar maṉṉaṉ irāvaṇaṉmuṉ malaṅkāniṉ veḷḷi malaikkī ḻiruntu varuntaniṉcīr kalaṅkāmal pāṭiṭak kēṭṭē iraṅkik karuṇaiceyta nalaṅkāṇiṉ taṉmai-iṉ ṟeṉṉaḷa viyāṇṭaiyiṉ naṇṇiyatē.
translation: Ravana, the lord of Lanka and king of the Rakshasas, once suffered beneath your unshakeable silver mountain. Hearing him sing your glories without faltering, you took pity and showed him grace. Where has that beautiful nature of yours gone today when dealing with me?
commentary: The demon king Ravana, crushed beneath Mount Kailash, won Siva's mercy by singing his praises without faltering. Vallalar turns that old story into an intimate, desperate plea. If God showed such compassion to a trapped demon, where has that same grace gone today?

translit: uṭaiyeṉṟum pūṇeṉṟum ūṇeṉṟum nāṭi uḻaṉṟiṭumin naṭaiyeṉṟum cañcalañ cañcalaṅ kāṇiti ṉāṉciṟiyēṉ puṭaiyeṉṟu veyya luṟumpuḻup pōṉṟu puḻuṅkukiṉṟēṉ viṭaiyeṉṟu mālaṟaṅ koṇṭōyeṉ tuṉpam vilakkukavē.
translation: I wander about seeking clothes, ornaments, and food. This worldly life brings endless sorrow. I, a lowly one, swelter like a worm cast out into the scorching heat. You who made Vishnu your bull of dharma, please remove my suffering.
commentary: Chasing food and clothing keeps the mind in endless anxiety. Vallalar feels like a worm thrown out onto scorching ground. He turns to God, traditionally described as riding the steadfast bull of righteousness (dharma), the only refuge who can rescue the soul from the burning heat of ordinary life.

translit: aruḷara cē-aruṭ kuṉṟēmaṉ ṟāṭum aruḷiṟaiyē aruḷamu tē-aruṭ pēṟē niṟainta aruṭkaṭalē aruḷaṇi yē-aruṭ kaṇṇēviṇ ṇōṅkum aruḷoḷiyē aruḷaṟa mē-aruṭ paṇpēmuk kaṇkoḷ aruṭcivamē.
translation: King of grace! Mountain of grace! Lord of grace dancing in the hall! Ambrosia of grace! Boon of grace! Brimming ocean of grace! Jewel of grace! Eye of grace! Light of grace rising to the heavens! Dharma of grace! Virtue of grace! Three-eyed Siva of grace!
commentary: Each name piles grace (arul) upon grace. For Vallalar, God is nothing like a distant ruler or harsh judge. He is compassion itself, the mountain and the ocean of it, its light and its treasure.

translit: nilaiyaṟi yāta kuṭumpat tuyareṉṉum nīttattilē talaiyaṟi yātu viḻuntēṉai āṇṭaruḷ tāṉaḷippāy alaiyaṟi yāta kaṭalēmuk kaṇkoṇṭa āramutē vilaiyaṟi yāta maṇiyē viṭēliteṉ viṇṇappamē.
translation: I fell headlong into the bottomless flood of family sorrow. You must rule me and bestow your grace. Waveless ocean! Rare three-eyed ambrosia! Gem of inestimable price! Do not forsake me. This is my plea.
commentary: Family attachment pulls the mind down like a turbulent, bottomless flood. Against that chaos stands God, a waveless ocean, perfectly still. Vallalar's plea is simple: lift me out of the drowning waters of sorrow and settle me safely in that quiet grace.

translit: meyyakat tēkaṇap pōtum viṭātu virumpukiṉṟōr kaiyakat tēniṉ ṟoḷirkaṉi yēnutaṟ kaṭkarumpē vaiyakat tēniṉai allāmal naṟṟuṇai maṟṟilai-ip poyyakat tēṉceyum tīṅkā yiramum poṟuttaruḷē.
translation: O fruit shining in the hands of those who truly love You without letting go even for a moment! O sugarcane with an eye on Your forehead! There is no good companion in this world other than You. Please forgive the thousand wrongs committed by me, a person with a false heart.
commentary: God is the only true companion in this world, and Vallalar asks him to forgive his many wrongs. He calls on Siva with the third eye on his forehead, sweet as fruit and sugarcane to those who hold on to him with constant love.

translit: mulaikkalaṅ kāra miṭumaṭa vārmayal mūṭi-avar talaikkalaṅ kāra malarcūṭu vārniṉ ṟaṉaivaḻuttār ilaikkalaṅ kārav viyamaṉvan tāleṉ icaipparveḷḷi malaikkalaṅ kāra maṇiyēmuk kaṇkoṇṭa māmaruntē.
translation: Overcome by infatuation for women wearing ornaments on their breasts, people adorn those women's hair with decorative flowers and do not praise You. When the fearful Yama arrives bringing death, what will they say? O jewel adorning the silver mountain! O great medicine with three eyes!
commentary: People spend their lives chasing physical desire and never praise the Lord. When Yama (the god of death) arrives, none of those infatuations will protect them. Vallalar calls out to God as the great medicine for this fatal ignorance.

translit: purikiṉṟa vīṭṭakam pōntaṭi paṭṭup puṟaṅkaṭaiyil tirikiṉṟa nāykkum cirippāmeṉ pāvic ciṟupiḻaippaic corikiṉṟa puṇṇil kaṉaliṭal pōleṇun tōṟuneñcam erikiṉṟa teṉceyku vēṉpiṟai vārcaṭai eṉṉamutē.
translation: My sinful, petty existence is laughable even to a dog that gets beaten after entering a house and wanders in the backyard. Every time I think of it, my heart burns like fire placed on an oozing wound. What shall I do? O my ambrosia with long matted hair wearing the crescent moon!
