commentary: Vallalar's remorse over his petty, worldly life is so sharp that he says even a beaten stray dog would laugh at him. Every thought of his failings burns like fire on an open wound. He cries for help to Siva, with his matted hair and crescent moon.

translit: maṉakkēta māṟṟu maruntē potu-oḷir māṇikkamē kaṉakkē tuṟa-eṉ karuttaṟi yāmal kaḻaṟukiṉṟa taṉakkēḷar pāṟceṉ ṟaṭiyēṉ itayam taḷarvatellām niṉakkē terinta teṉakkē aruḷa niṉaintaruḷē.
translation: O medicine that removes the mind's sorrow! O ruby shining in the common hall! You alone know how my heart falters when I go to relatives who speak without understanding my intentions, causing me heavy sorrow. Please decide to grant me Your grace.
commentary: Going to relatives for comfort brings only misunderstanding and grief. God alone is the medicine that heals the mind's sorrow. Vallalar asks for grace to rescue him from the exhaustion of these hollow social ties.

translit: mōkaṅ kalanta maṉattēṉ tuyaraṅkaḷ muṟṟumaṟṟut tēkaṅ kalanta pavantīrkkum niṉpatam cintikkumnāḷ pōkaṅ kalanta tirunāḷ malaiyaṟ putappacuntēṉ pākaṅ kalantacem pālē nutaṟkaṭ parañcuṭarē.
translation: The day I meditate on Your feet, which cut away all my sorrows and end the cycle of birth tied to this body, is a holy day of true joy for me, a person whose mind is mixed with delusion. O wonderful fresh honey from the mountain! O pure milk mixed with sweet syrup! O supreme light with an eye on Your forehead!
commentary: Joy arrives on the day the mind rests wholly on the Lord's feet. That meditation cuts through delusion and breaks the cycle of rebirth. Vallalar finds this supreme light as pure and sweet as fresh mountain honey mixed with milk.

translit: kōloṉṟu kaṇṭa iṟaimakaṉ vāḻviṉum kōṭipaṅku mēloṉṟu kaṇṭaṉam neñcē-eṉ collai virumpiṉiyañ cēloṉṟu kaṇṭa maṇiyāṉ varaippacun tēṉkalanta pāloṉṟu kaṇṭakaṇ koṇṭuyar vāḻvu palittatuvē.
translation: O mind, we have found a state ten million times greater than the life of a monarch wielding an unrivaled scepter. Desire my words and fear no more. Our exalted life has found fulfillment, seeing with eyes that behold the supreme Lord who is like fresh mountain honey mixed with milk.
commentary: Vallalar tells his mind it has found a state ten million times richer than a king's life under his scepter. Seeing the supreme Lord tastes like fresh mountain honey mixed with milk. Once that is tasted, fear has nowhere left to stand, and all he asks is that the mind want his words.

translit: pulaiyaḷa vō-eṉum neñcaka ṉēṉtuyarp pōkameṭṭu malaiyaḷa vō-inta maṇṇaḷa vōvanta vāṉaḷavō alaiyaḷa vōvaṉṟu maṉṟuṇiṉ ṟōṅkum arumaruntē ilaiyaḷa vō-eṉun tēvē aṟintum iraṅkilaiyē.
translation: My heart is steeped in baseness. Is the harvest of my sorrow the size of the eight great mountains? Is it the size of this earth? Is it the size of the vast sky? Is it the size of the rolling oceans? O rare medicine towering in the hall! O God sharing your form with the Goddess of the slender leaf-like waist! Even knowing the boundless measure of my grief, You show no pity.
commentary: The sorrow of carrying worldly flaws feels vast and overwhelming. Vallalar asks if his grief is as large as the earth, the sky, the oceans, or the great mountains. He calls out to God, appearing here as the rare healing medicine in the hall of grace, pleading for relief from this boundless pain.

translit: kalleṉṟu valleṉṟu miṉṉār puḷakak kaṉataṉattaic colleṉṟu collumuṉ colluman tōniṉ tuṇaiyaṭikkaṇ nilleṉṟu palla nikaḻttiṉum eṉmaṉam niṟpataṉṟē alleṉṟu velkaḷaṅ koṇṭōyeṉ ceyva taṟintilaṉē.
translation: Before anyone even asks it to speak, my mind speaks of the heavy, thrilling breasts of radiant women, calling them hard as stone. Alas! Even if I offer many reasons and tell my mind to rest at Your twin feet, it refuses to stay. O Lord who conquered the darkness on the battlefield! I do not know what to do.
commentary: An honest confession. Before anything prompts it, Vallalar's mind runs off to admire the beauty of women. He reasons with it and tells it to rest at the Lord's feet, and it will not stay. Calling on the Lord who conquered darkness on the battlefield, he admits he does not know what to do.

translit: kaḷḷā ṭiyakoṉṟaic ceñcaṭai yōynaṟ kaṉakamaṉṟiṉ uḷḷā ṭiyamalarc cēvaṭi yōyiv vulakiyaṟkaṇ eḷḷā ṭiyacek kiṭaippaṭal pōltuṉ piṭai-iḷaittut taḷḷā ṭiyanaṭai koṇṭēṟku naṉṉaṭai tantaruḷē.
translation: O Lord with red matted hair wearing konrai flowers dripping with nectar! O Lord whose red lotus feet dance within the beautiful golden hall! Like sesame seeds crushed in an oil press, I have grown weary amidst the sorrows of worldly life, staggering with faltering steps. Gracefully grant me a steady path.
commentary: Worldly sorrow crushes Vallalar the way an oil press crushes sesame seeds, until he is worn out and staggering. He turns to the Lord who dances in the golden hall, red matted hair hung with nectar-dripping koṉṟai (Indian laburnum) flowers. He asks that his faltering steps be made firm and steady.

translit: marukkā malarkkuḻal miṉṉār mayalcaṇṭa mārutattāl irukkā tuḻalumeṉ ēḻaineñ cē-iv viṭumpaiyilē cerukkā turukic civāya nama-eṉat tērntaṉpiṉāl orukkāl uraikkil perukkākum nalliṉpam ōṅkiṭumē.
translation: O my poor mind! Tossed by the fierce hurricane of infatuation for radiant women wearing fragrant flowers in their hair, you wander restlessly. Do not be arrogant in this suffering. Melt in devotion. If you understand the truth and utter the sacred syllables "Sivaya Nama" with love even once, supreme bliss will multiply and soar.
commentary: Infatuation blows through the mind like a hurricane and leaves it restless and worn out. Vallalar's cure is simple. Drop the pride and melt in devotion. Say Sivaya Nama (a traditional mantra offering reverence to the divine) with real love even once, and bliss will multiply.

translit: matikkaṇṇi vēṇip peruntakai yēniṉ malaraṭikkut tutikkaṇṇi cūṭṭumeyt toṇṭaril cērntuniṉ tūya-oṟṟip patikkaṇṇi niṉṉaip paṇintētti uḷḷam paravacamāk katikkaṇṇi vāḻum paṭi-aru ḷāyeṉ karuttituvē.
translation: O great Lord wearing the crescent moon on your matted hair, this is my single desire. Grant me the grace to join the true devotees who adorn your flower-like feet with garlands of praise. Let me reach your pure city of Otri, bow and praise you with an enraptured heart, and live focused entirely on the supreme state.
commentary: Vallalar asks for one blessing, the company of true devotees who garland the Lord's feet with praise. Among them he wants to live in the sacred town of Otri (Tiruvottiyur), bowing and praising God with an enraptured heart. There his mind could stay fixed on the highest state.

translit: iraiyēṟṟu tuṉpak kuṭumpa vikāra iruṭkaṭalil puraiyēṟṟu neñcam pularntuniṉ ṟēṉaip poruṭpaṭuttik karaiyēṟṟa vēṇṭumeṉ kaṇṇē pavattaik kaṭimaruntē tiraiyēṟṟu ceñcaṭait tēvē amarar cikāmaṇiyē.
translation: O my eye! O potent medicine that cures the disease of worldly existence! O God with red matted hair bearing the river waves! O crown jewel of the immortals! I stand with a withered and flawed heart in the dark ocean of sorrowful domestic afflictions, merely seeking sustenance. You must deem me worthy and lift me to the shore.
commentary: Family burdens and the daily struggle just to eat make a dark ocean, and Vallalar stands in it with a withered heart. He calls God his eye, the crown jewel of the immortals, the medicine for the disease of worldly existence. Deem me worthy, he says, and lift me onto the shore.

translit: cīrkoṇṭa oṟṟip patiyuṭai yāṉiṭam cērntamaṇi vārkoṇṭa koṅkai vaṭivām pikaitaṉ malaraṭikkut tārkoṇṭa centamiḻp pāmālai cāttat tamiyaṉukkē ērkoṇṭa nallaruḷ īyum kuṇālaya ērampaṉē.
translation: O Heramba, ocean of virtues. Bestow your beautiful grace upon this lonely one so I may offer a garland of classical Tamil verses at the lotus feet of Vadivambigai. She is the jewel with firmly bound breasts who joined the left side of the Lord of the excellent city of Otri.
commentary: Heramba is the elephant-headed deity of beginnings, so Vallalar goes to him first and asks for the grace to compose a perfect Tamil poem. He means to lay these verses like a real garland at the feet of Vadivambigai, the Goddess of Beauty. She shares the left side of Siva, a picture of the divine as both male and female.

translit: kaṭalamu tēceṅ karumpē aruṭkaṟpa kakkaṉiyē uṭaluyi rē-uyirk kuḷuṇar vē-uṇar vuḷoḷiyē aṭalviṭai yāroṟṟi yāriṭaṅ koṇṭa arumaruntē maṭalaviḻ ñāṉa malarē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O nectar of the ocean. O red sugarcane. O fruit of the wish-granting tree of grace. O body and life. O awareness within life. O light within awareness. O rare medicine sharing the left side of the Lord of Otri who rides the mighty bull. O blooming flower of wisdom. O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Watch how the verse moves inward. She is the body, then the life force within the body, then the awareness within life, and last the light shining within that awareness. Vallalar places the divine mother at the very core of human existence, close enough to be the medicine that heals the soul.

translit: aṇiyē aṇipeṟum oṟṟit tiyākartam aṉpuṟucaṟ kuṇiyē-em vāḻkkaik kulateyva mēmalaik kōṉtavamē paṇiyēṉ piḻaipoṟut tāṭkoṇṭa teyvap patikoḷcintā maṇiyē-eṉ kaṇṇuṇ maṇiyē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O exquisite jewel. O loving and virtuous one of Thyagar in beautiful Otri. O family deity of our life. O penance of the king of mountains. O divine wish-fulfilling gem who forgave the faults of this unbowing servant and claimed me. O pupil of my eye. O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: She forgives and claims even the one who refuses to bow. Vallalar calls her his family deity and the pupil of his own eye, which is about as personal as devotion gets. "Penance of the mountain king" points to the traditional story of the Goddess born as the daughter of the Himalayas.

translit: māṉēr viḻimalai māṉē-em māṉiṭam vāḻmayilē kāṉēr aḷakap pacuṅkuyi lē-aruṭ kaṭkarumpē tēṉē tiruvoṟṟi mānakar vāḻum civacattiyē vāṉē karuṇai vaṭivē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O mountain daughter with deer-like eyes. O peacock living with our Lord. O green cuckoo with dense dark hair. O sweet sugarcane of grace. O honey. O Siva-Sakti residing in the great city of Otriyur. O vast sky. O embodiment of compassion. O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Deer, peacock, singing cuckoo. Vallalar finds her in the living beauty of nature, and in the vast open sky as well. Above all she is Siva-Sakti, the active energy of God, and compassion itself given a form.

translit: poruḷē aṭiyar pukaliṭa mē-oṟṟip pūraṇaṉtaṇ aruḷē-em āruyirk kāntuṇai yēviṇ ṇavarpukaḻum teruḷēmeyñ ñāṉat teḷivē maṟaimuṭic cemporuḷē maruḷēta nīkkum oḷiyē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O supreme reality. O refuge for devotees. O cool grace of the perfect Lord of Otri. O ultimate companion to our precious life. O clarity praised by the celestials. O clarity of true wisdom. O perfect truth at the crown of the Vedas. O light that dispels the darkness of delusion. O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Human confusion is a darkness, and her grace is the light that drives it away. She is the truth found at the very peak of the Vedas, the ancient scriptures. To the devotee she is cool and comforting, the most reliable companion in life.

translit: tirumālum nāṉmukat tēvumuṉ ṉāḷmikat tēṭimaṉat tarumā luḻakka aṉaluru vāki amarntaruḷum perumāṉem māṉoṟṟip pemmāṉkaim māṉkoḷum pittaṉmalai marumāṉ iṭaṅkoḷpeṇ māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: In ancient times, Vishnu and the four-faced god Brahma searched endlessly and suffered delusion in their minds. The great Lord then graciously appeared in the form of fire. He is our Lord, the Lord of Otriyur, the madman who holds a deer in his hand, and the son-in-law of the mountain king. O female deer occupying his left side, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Vishnu and Brahma once tried in vain to find the limits of the supreme Lord, and he appeared as an endless pillar of fire to humble their pride. That infinite, fiery Lord is the one in Otriyur, and the Goddess rests gracefully on his left side. Vallalar has some fun with the picture. He is a wild figure holding a deer, and she shines beside him like a gentle female deer.

translit: uṉṉēr aruḷteyvam kāṇēṉ maṉattum uraikkappaṭāp poṉṉē-ap poṉṉaṟ puta-oḷi yēmalarp poṉvaṇaṅkum aṉṉē emāruyirk kōruyi rē-oṟṟi yampativāḻ maṉṉē riṭamvaḷar miṉṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: I see no deity of grace equal to you. O gold that even the mind cannot describe. O wondrous light of that gold. O mother worshipped by Lakshmi seated on the lotus. O singular life within our precious life. O lightning shining on the left side of the King who resides in the beautiful city of Otriyur. O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Her golden light of grace is beyond anything the mind can imagine. Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth who sits on a lotus, bows to her in worship. And still she is intimately close, the very life breathing within our own life, living beside the Lord in Otriyur.

translit: kaṇṇē-ak kaṇṇiṉ maṇiyē maṇiyil kalantoḷicey viṇṇē viyaṉoṟṟi yūraṇṇal vāmattil vīṟṟirukkum peṇṇē malaipeṟum peṇmaṇi yēteyvap peṇṇamutē maṇnēyam nīttavar vāḻvē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O eye, O pupil of that eye. O space that blends with the pupil and radiates light. O lady seated on the left side of the Lord of vast Otriyur. O gem of a woman born to the mountain king. O divine feminine nectar. O life of those who have abandoned attachment to the earth. O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: She is the light within the pupil of the eye, what gives the soul its vision and awareness. Born to the mountain king as divine nectar, she sits beside the Lord of Otriyur. Those who have given up clinging to worldly things find in her their whole life and sustenance.

translit: malaiyāṉ tavañceytu peṟṟamut tē-oṟṟi vāḻkaṉakac cilaiyāṉ maṇakka maṇakkuntey vīkat tirumalarē alaiyāṉ malikaṭal paḷḷikoṇ ṭāṉtoḻum āramutē valaiyāṉ arumai makaḷē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O pearl obtained through the penance of the mountain king. O divine sacred flower that radiates fragrance when embraced by the Lord of Otriyur who wields the golden mountain as his bow. O rare nectar worshipped by Vishnu who slumbers upon the wavy ocean. O precious daughter of the fisherman. O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Two images open the verse: a pearl earned through the mountain king's penance, and a sacred flower whose fragrance blooms when the Lord embraces it. Vishnu, who sleeps on the cosmic ocean, worships her. She is also hailed as the precious daughter of a fisherman. Traditional stories tell of the divine mother taking birth in a humble fishing village, and the title shows her loving closeness to ordinary people.

translit: kāmam paṭarneñ cuṭaiyōr kaṉaviṉum kāṇappaṭāc cēmam paṭarcelvap poṉṉē maturac ceḻuṅkaṉiyē tāmam paṭaroṟṟi yūrvāḻ pavaḷat taṉimalaiyiṉ vāmam paṭarpaiṅ koṭiyē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O golden treasure of protective wealth, unseen even in the dreams of those whose hearts are filled with lust. O rich and sweet fruit. O green creeper spreading across the left side of the unique coral mountain who resides in garland-filled Otriyur. O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Hearts clouded by lust and selfish desire never see her, not even in dreams. To the pure-hearted she is a sweet fruit and a protective golden treasure. Vallalar pictures her as a green vine winding gently around a unique coral mountain, which stands for the Lord of garlanded Otriyur.

tamil: நாடாத ஆனந்த நட்பேமெய் யன்பர் நயக்கும் இன்பே
translit: kōṭā aruṭkuṇak kuṉṟē civattil kuṟippilarai nāṭāta āṉanta naṭpēmey yaṉpar nayakkum iṉpē pīṭār tiruvoṟṟip pemmāṉ iṭañcey peruntavamē vāṭā maṇimalark kompē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O mountain of unwavering qualities of grace! O blissful friendship that avoids those who lack focus on the Divine! O delight cherished by true devotees! O great penance claiming the left side of the Lord of glorious Otriyur! O branch of unfading gem-like flowers! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: She is divine grace in its perfect form. True devotees find her a joyful companion, while she keeps her distance from minds that wander away from God. By claiming Siva's left side, she shows that the divine and its grace are permanently united.

translit: nālē eṉumaṟai antaṅkaḷ iṉṉamum nāṭiyeṉaip pōlē varunta veḷi-oḷi yāyoṟṟip puṇṇiyartam pālē irunta niṉaittaṅkai yākap pakarappeṟṟa mālē tavattil periyōṉ vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: The crown of the four Vedas still seeks you and suffers like me. Yet you reside as the radiant space of light by the side of the holy Lord of Otriyur. Vishnu, who earned the right to be called your brother, is truly great in his penance. O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: The deepest wisdom of the Vedas still struggles to grasp her, suffering just as Vallalar does. Yet beside the Lord of Otriyur she reveals herself openly, as pure light. So high is she that Vishnu, the great preserver, is raised simply by being known as her brother.

translit: kaṅkaikoṇ ṭōṉoṟṟi yūraṇṇal vāmam kalantaruḷcey naṅkai-el lā-ula kuntanta niṉṉai-an nāraṇaṟkut taṅkai-eṉ kō-aṉṟit tāyareṉ kōcol taḻaikkumalai maṅkaiyaṅ kōmaḷa māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O Lady who grants grace, uniting with the left side of the Lord of Otriyur who bears the Ganges! You gave birth to all the worlds. Shall I call you the younger sister of that Narayana, or shall I call you his mother? O mountain maiden whose praises flourish! O beautiful tender deer! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Tradition calls the goddess the younger sister of Narayana (Vishnu), and Vallalar playfully questions the title. She gave birth to the entire universe, so she is really the mother of all the gods, Vishnu included.

translit: cōlaiyiṭ ṭārvayal ūroṟṟi vaittuttaṉ toṇṭaraṉpiṉ vēlaiyiṭ ṭālceyum pittaṉai meyyiṭai mēvukarit tōlaiyiṭ ṭāṭum toḻiluṭai yōṉait tuṇintumuṉṉāḷ mālaiyiṭ ṭāyiḵteṉṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: He pledged away the fertile towns surrounded by groves. He acts like a madman, performing menial chores when commanded by the love of his devotees. He has the habit of dancing draped in an elephant's skin. You boldly garlanded him long ago. What is the meaning of this? O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: An old form of devotional teasing. Vallalar asks why a perfect goddess would marry Siva, who dances in a wild elephant skin and acts like a madman to serve his devotees. Underneath, the meaning is plain. Siva is completely conquered by the love of his followers, and she loves him for exactly that boundless compassion.

translit: taṉaiyāḷ pavariṉṟi niṟkum paramaṉ taṉi-aruḷāy viṉaiyāḷ uyirmala nīkkimey vīṭṭiṉ viṭuttiṭunī eṉaiyāḷ aruḷoṟṟi yūrvā ḻavaṉṟaṉ ṉiṭattumoru maṉaiyāḷ eṉaniṉṟa teṉṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: You are the peerless grace of the Supreme Lord who has no master to rule over him. You remove the impurities of souls bound by karma and grant them true liberation. What is the meaning of this, that you stand as a humble wife beside the Lord who rules me and lives in gracious Otriyur? O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: She is the liberating grace of God, with the power to wash away karma (the binding force of past actions) and set the soul free. Yet she appears quietly, as a devoted wife at the Lord's side. Vallalar marvels that so infinite a force would willingly take that ordinary form.

translit: piṉṉīṉṟa piḷḷaiyiṉ mēlārvam tāykkeṉap pēcuvarnī muṉṉīṉṟa piḷḷaiyiṉ mēlācai yuḷḷavā moyyacurar koṉṉīṉṟa pōrkkiḷam piḷḷaiyai ēvak koṭuttateṉṉē maṉṉīṉṟa oṟṟi mayilē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: People say a mother's affection is greatest for her younger child. However, your love is truly for your firstborn child. Why else did you send your young child into fierce battle against the swarming asuras? O Peafowl of Otriyur! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Vallalar teases the Goddess about her two divine sons, Vinayakar the elder and Murugan the younger. The proverb says a mother favors her youngest. Yet she kept her firstborn safe and sent the younger one off to fight the asuras (demonic beings). So, he suggests, she must secretly love the elder more.

translit: paiyāḷum alkul curarmaṭa vārkaḷ palaruḷumic ceyyāḷum veṇṇiṟa meyyāḷum ettavam ceytaṉarō kaiyāḷum niṉṉaṭik kuṟṟēval ceyyak kaṭaikkaṇittāy maiyāḷum kaṇṇoṟṟi vāḻvē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: Among the many celestial women with lovely hips, what penance did the red-hued goddess and the white-hued goddess perform? You have cast a favorable glance upon them, allowing their hands to perform humble service at your feet. O life of Otriyur with collyrium-dark eyes! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: The red goddess is Lakshmi, who governs wealth, and the white goddess is Saraswati, who governs learning. Of all the women in the heavens, these two hold the highest honor, serving at the feet of the Supreme Goddess. Vallalar wonders aloud what great spiritual disciplines they must have practiced to earn so rare a privilege.

translit: ilaiyāṟṟu nīmalark kālāl paṇikkuṅkuṟ ṟēvalelām talaiyāl ceyumpeṇkaḷ pallōril pūmakaḷ taṉṉaittaḷḷāy nilaiyāl periyaniṉ toṇṭartam pakka nilāmaiyiṉāṉ malaiyāṟ karuḷoṟṟi vāḻvē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: You give commands with your flower-like feet. Among the many women who bow their heads to perform these humble chores, you do not turn away the Goddess of the Lotus. Is it because she never stays permanently beside your truly great devotees? O life of Otriyur who bestows grace on the mountain! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: The Goddess of the Lotus is Lakshmi, the giver of wealth. Indian poetry knows wealth as fickle, rarely staying long with anyone. Vallalar jokes that the Supreme Goddess keeps Lakshmi busy with chores precisely because wealth refuses to stay for good in the homes of true spiritual seekers.

translit: kalaimaka ḷōniṉ paṇiyai-aṉ pōṭum kaṭaippiṭittāḷ alaimaka ḷō-aṉ poṭupiṭit tāḷeṟ kaṟaitikaṇṭāy talaimaka ḷē-aruṭ ṭāyēcev vāykkarun tāḻkuḻaṟpoṉ malaimaka ḷē-oṟṟi vāḻvē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: Did the Goddess of Learning take up your service with love? Or did the Goddess of the Ocean take it up with love? Tell me. O Supreme Lady! O Mother of Grace! O Daughter of the golden mountain with red lips and dark flowing hair! O life of Otriyur! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: The playful comparison goes on. Vallalar puts a direct question to the Goddess about her two famous servants. He wants to know whether the goddess of learning or the goddess of wealth does her daily duties with deeper devotion.

translit: poṉṉōṭu vāṇi-eṉ pōriru vōrum poruṇaṟkalvi taṉṉō ṭaruḷun tiṟaniṉkuṟ ṟēvalait tāṅkiniṉṟa piṉṉō alatataṉ muṉṉō teḷintiṭap pēcukanī maṉṉō ṭeḻiloṟṟi yūrvāḻ vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: The two goddesses known as Lakshmi and Saraswati bestow the gifts of wealth and fine education. Did they gain the power to grant these gifts after they took up humble service to you, or before? Speak and clarify this for me. O Vadivudai Manikkam residing in exquisite Otriyur!
commentary: Lakshmi and Saraswati are worshipped everywhere for granting riches and knowledge. Vallalar asks the Goddess where that power really came from. Did they have it on their own, or did they gain the power to bless people only after surrendering to her humble service? The implication is plain. All divine power flows directly from the Supreme Goddess.

translit: kāmaṭ ṭalartiru voṟṟiniṉ ṉāyakaṉ kantaicuṟṟi yēmaṭ ṭaraiyoṭu niṟpatu kaṇṭum iraṅkalarpōl nīmaṭṭu mēpaṭ ṭuṭukkiṉ ṟaṉai-uṉṟaṉ nēyameṉṉō māmaṭ ṭalarkuḻal māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: In sacred Otriyur where fragrant flowers bloom, your Lord stands with mere rags wrapped around his waist. Seeing this, you alone wear fine silk like those devoid of compassion. What kind of love is yours? O deer-like goddess whose hair is adorned with heavily scented flowers, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Her husband, Lord Siva, wears only an ascetic's rags while she dresses in fine silk, and Vallalar playfully questions her compassion for it. The gentle teasing brings out how differently the divine pair appear.

translit: vīṟṟārniṉ ṟaṉmaṇat tammiyiṉ mēlciṟu mellaṉiccam āṟṟāniṉ ciṟṟaṭip pōtiṉait tūkkivait tāreṉiṉmāl ēṟṟār tiruvoṟṟi yūrār kaḷakkaṟup pēṟṟavarē māṟṟā iyalkoṇ mayilē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: If your tiny flower-like feet, which cannot endure even soft anicha flowers, were lifted and placed upon the grinding stone during your wedding, it was truly the Lord of sacred Otriyur who mounts the great bull and bears a dark stain on his throat who did so. O peacock of steadfast nature, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: In traditional Hindu weddings, the groom places the bride's foot on a granite grinding stone as a sign of a firm and lasting marriage. Vallalar marvels at that moment in her wedding. Feet too soft even for anicha flowers met heavy stone, guided by the fierce Lord himself.

translit: poruppuṟu nīliyeṉ pārniṉṉai meyatu pōlumoṟṟi viruppuṟu nāyakaṉ pāmpā paraṇamum veṇtalaiyum neruppuṟu kaiyum kaṉalmēṉi yumkaṇṭu neñcamañcāy maruppuṟu koṅkai mayilē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: People call you the dark goddess of the mountains. That appears to be true. Seeing the beloved Lord of Otriyur with his serpent ornaments, white skull, hand holding fire, and fiery form, your heart feels no fear. O peacock with beautiful breasts, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: To others Siva looks terrifying, with his serpents, his skull and the raw fire in his hand. Vallalar suggests the Goddess must truly be the fierce mountain warrior she is named after. Only so fearless a heart could stand beside him undisturbed.

translit: aṉampoṟut tāṉpukaḻ oṟṟiniṉ nāyakaṉ aṅkumiḻit taṉampoṟut tāḷoru māṟṟāḷait taṉmuṭi taṉṉilvaittē tiṉampoṟut tāṉatu kaṇṭum ciṉamiṉṟic cērntaniṉpōl maṉampoṟut tārevar kaṇṭāy vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: Brahma, who is carried by a swan, praises sacred Otriyur. Your Lord placed upon his head a rival woman with beautiful breasts and bears her every day. Seeing this, you still embrace him without a trace of anger. Who else has a heart as tolerant as yours? O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: In Hindu stories, Lord Siva catches the river goddess Ganga in the locks of his hair to break her fall to earth. Vallalar praises the Goddess's endless patience. She accepts this rival woman on her husband's head without a trace of jealousy.

translit: oruru vāyoṟṟi yūramarn tārniṉ ṉuṭaiyavarpeṇ cīruru vākuniṉ māṟṟāḷai nīteḷi yāttiṟattil nīruru vākkic cumantār ataṉai niṉaintilaiyē vāruru vārkoṅkai naṅkāy vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: Your Lord dwells in sacred Otriyur in a singular form. Without you realizing it, he transformed your rival of beautiful feminine form into water and carried her upon himself. You do not even consider this. O lady with beautiful breasts, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Ganga again. Vallalar suggests Siva cleverly turned this rival wife into water just to hide her. With mock sympathy he wonders how the Goddess can stay so happily unaware of her husband's trick.

translit: cārntēniṉ pāloṟṟi yūrvāḻum nāyakar tāmakiḻvu kūrntē kulāvumak koḷkaiyaik kāṇil kotippaḷeṉṟu tērntē-ak kaṅkaiyaic ceñcaṭai mēlciṟai ceytaṉaroṇ vārntē kuḻaikoḷ viḻiyāy vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: The Lord who dwells in Otriyur approaches you and happily revels with you. Knowing that Ganga would seethe with jealousy if she saw this, He imprisoned her upon His red matted hair. O Goddess whose bright, elongated eyes reach your ear ornaments, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Now the joke turns the other way, toward the Lord's supreme love for the Goddess. The river Ganga (Ganges) is also seen as a consort of Siva, and Vallalar imagines Siva keeps her locked up in his matted hair so she cannot see his devotion to Vadivudai Manikkam and grow jealous. The lighthearted idea shows the Goddess's unmatched beauty and her place in the Lord's heart.

translit: nīyē eṉatu piḻaikuṟip pāyeṉil niṉṉaṭimaip pēyēṉ ceyumvaṇṇam evvaṇṇa mō-eṉaip peṟṟaḷikkum tāyē karuṇait taṭaṅkaṭa lē-oṟṟic cārkumuta vāyēr cavuntaramāṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: If you yourself take note of my faults, what can this demonic slave of yours do? O mother who bore and protects me, O vast ocean of compassion, O beautiful doe-like Goddess of Otriyur whose lovely mouth resembles a red water lily, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Vallalar throws himself entirely on the Goddess's mercy. He calls himself a demonic slave out of a deep sense of unworthiness, asking where he could turn if his own divine mother judged him strictly. Calling her a vast ocean of compassion, he reminds her that a mother forgives and protects her child, whatever the child's flaws.

translit: muppōtum aṉparkaḷ vāḻttoṟṟi yūrem mutalvarmakiḻ oppō tarumalaip peṇṇamu tē-eṉṟu vantuniṉai eppōtum cintit tiṭarnīṅki vāḻa eṉakkaruḷvāy maippō taṉaiyakaṇ māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: Grant me the grace to come and constantly think of you, saying, "O nectar-like daughter of the incomparable mountain, who delights our primal Lord of Otriyur praised by devotees in all three parts of the day." Grant this so that I may live free of sorrow. O doe with collyrium-dark eyes, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: What Vallalar asks for is continuous remembrance. For him, freedom from sorrow comes from keeping the mind fixed on her grace, whatever his outward circumstances. He calls her daughter of the mountain, echoing the tradition that the Goddess Parvati is the daughter of the Himalayas. The blessing he seeks is simply never to forget her.

translit: mītalat tōrkaḷuḷ yārvaṇaṅ kātavar mēvunaṭup pūtalat tōrkaḷuḷ yārpuka ḻātavar pōṟṟinitam pātalat tōrkaḷuḷ yārpaṇi yātavar paṟṟiniṉṟāḷ mātalat tōṅkoṟṟi vāḻvē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: Who among the beings of the upper worlds does not bow to you? Who among the beings of this middle earth does not praise you? Who among the beings of the netherworld does not daily worship and cling to your feet? O life of great Otriyur rising high on the earth, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Her authority and grace reach across the whole cosmos. Vallalar names the three traditional worlds: the upper worlds of the gods, the middle earth of humans, and the netherworlds below. By asking who in any of them fails to worship her, he declares her power absolute and recognized by every being everywhere.

translit: cēykkuṟṟam tāypoṟut tēṭā varukeṉac ceppuvaḷin nāykkuṟṟam nīpoṟut tāḷutal vēṇṭum naviṉmatiyiṉ tēykkuṟṟa māṟṟum tiruvoṟṟi nātartan tēvi-aṉpar vāykkuṟṟam nīkkum mayilē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: A mother bears the faults of her child and calls out, "Dear child, come here." You must bear the faults of this dog and rule me. O consort of the Lord of Otriyur who removes the waning flaw of the praised moon, O peacock who removes the flaws in the speech of devotees, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: A mother calls her child close despite its mistakes, and Vallalar leans on that love. He calls himself a dog to show his humility and asks the Goddess to overlook his flaws. Her husband, Siva, saved the moon from fading away completely. In the same way, Vallalar trusts she will remove the flaws in her devotees' speech and make them whole.

translit: ceṅkama lācaṉaṉ tēvipoṉ nāṇum tirumutalōr caṅkama tāmiṭaṟ ṟōṅkupoṉ nāṇum talaikuṉittut tuṅkamu ṟātuḷam nāṇat tiruvoṟṟit tōṉṟalpuṉai maṅkala nāṇuṭai yāḷē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O Vadivudai Manikkam! You wear the auspicious marriage thread tied by the Lord of sacred Otri. Seeing it, the golden thread of Brahma's consort and the golden thread on the neck of Vishnu's consort bow their heads, lose their pride, and feel ashamed in their hearts.
commentary: Her marriage thread stands for her supreme union with the Lord of sacred Otri. Beside it, the threads worn by the consorts of Brahma the creator and Vishnu the preserver lose their shine.

translit: cēṭā riyaṉmaṇam vīcac ceyaṉmaṇam cērntupoṅka ēṭār poḻiloṟṟi yūraṇṇal neñcam iruntuvakka vīṭā iruḷum mukilumpiṉ ṉiṭṭu veruvavaitta vāṭā malarkkuḻa lāḷē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O Vadivudai Manikkam! Your dark hair makes the unyielding darkness and the clouds retreat in fear. Adorned with unfading flowers, it spreads a rare fragrance and swells with sweet scents, delighting the heart of the Lord of Otriyur, a town surrounded by petal-filled groves.
commentary: Her beauty overpowers nature itself. Next to her dark hair, real clouds and real darkness look timid, and its unfading fragrance fills the Lord with joy.

translit: puranōkki ṉālpoṭi tēkkiya oṟṟip puṉitarkaḷak karanōkkinallamu tākkiniṟ pōṟṟuṅ karuttiṉarā taranōkki uḷḷiruḷ nīkkimeyñ ñāṉat taṉiccukantāṉ varanōkki āḷviḻi māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: The pure Lord of Otri turned the cities to ash with a single glance. You looked at the dark poison in His throat and turned it into good nectar. O doe-eyed Vadivudai Manikkam! You look with love upon devotees who praise you in their minds, dispelling their inner darkness and bestowing the supreme bliss of true wisdom through your ruling gaze.
commentary: Two glances sit side by side. The Lord's fierce look once burned mighty cities to ash, while her gentle look turned the deadly poison in his throat into sweet nectar. That same loving gaze falls on her devotees, clearing away their inner darkness and granting true wisdom.

translit: uṉṉum tiruvoṟṟi yūruṭai yārneñ cuvappa-eḻil tuṉṉum uyirppayir ellān taḻaikkac cukakkaruṇai eṉṉum tiruvamu tōyāmal ūṟṟi ematuḷattiṉ maṉṉum kaṭaikkaṇ mayilē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O Vadivudai Manikkam, a beautiful peacock whose sidelong glance dwells in my heart! To delight the Lord of sacred Otriyur and to make the crops of all living beings flourish, you unceasingly pour the sacred nectar of blissful grace.
commentary: Think of grace as water poured on a field. The Goddess pours out her blissful compassion without pause, delighting the Lord, and under it every soul's spiritual life takes root and grows.

translit: veḷḷam kuḷirum caṭaimuṭi yōṉoṟṟi vittakaṉtaṉ uḷḷam kuḷiramey pūrippa āṉantam ūṟṟeṭuppat teḷḷam kuḷiriṉ amutē aḷikkumcev vāykkumuta vaḷḷam kuḷirmutta māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O Vadivudai Manikkam, a cool pearl-like doe! To cool the heart of the wise Lord of Otri who bears the cold river on His matted hair, to thrill His body, and to make His bliss well up, you offer Him the clear, cold, sweet nectar from the bowl of your red lotus mouth.
commentary: The Lord carries a cold river in his matted hair, yet it is her sweetness that truly refreshes him. Her devotion brings him complete joy and cools his very heart.

translit: mānanta mārvayal kāḻik kavuṇiyar māmaṇikkaṉ ṟānanta iṉṉamu tūṟṟum tirumulai āraṇaṅkē kānanta vōṅkum eḻiloṟṟi yāruṭ kaḷittiyalum vānan tarumiṭai māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O beautiful Goddess whose sacred breasts pour forth the sweet nectar of bliss to the great, jewel-like child of the Kauniyar clan in Sirkazhi surrounded by magnificent fertile fields. You rejoice in the heart of the Lord of beautiful Otriyur surrounded by fragrant groves. O deer with a waist as subtle as the sky, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Vallalar recalls the famous story of the child saint Gnanasambandar, born in Sirkazhi, whom the Goddess fed with divine milk. That milk gave the child spiritual wisdom at once. The same Goddess rejoices in the heart of the Lord of Otriyur, and her grace still brings immediate enlightenment.

translit: vāṉtēṭa nāṉku maṟaitēṭa māluṭaṉ vāricamē lāṉtēṭa maṟṟai aruntavar tēṭa-eṉ aṉpiṉmaiyāl yāṉtēṭa eṉṉuḷam cēroṟṟi yūrem irunitiyē māṉtēṭum vāṭkaṇ mayilē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: While the heavens search, while the four Vedas search, while Vishnu and lotus-seated Brahma search, while great ascetics search, and while I search because of my lack of love, You enter my heart. O our great treasure of Otriyur. O peacock with bright, sword-like eyes that rival a deer's, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: The greatest gods, the ancient scriptures and the strict ascetics all search for her, and effort does not find her. Vallalar searched too, because his love was incomplete. Still she chose, by pure grace, to enter his heart. The divine comes as a free gift and passes over those who try to grasp it by effort alone.

translit: muttēvar viṇṇaṉmutaltēvar cittar muṉivarmaṟṟai ettē varuniṉ aṭiniṉai vārniṉaik kiṉṟilartām cettē piṟakkum ciṟiyaraṉ ṟō-oṟṟit tēvarnaṟṟā mattēvar vāma mayilē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: The three primal gods, Indra and the celestial lords, the siddhas, the sages, and all other gods meditate on your feet. Are those who do not meditate on you not merely petty beings trapped in the cycle of death and birth? O peacock standing on the left side of the Lord of Otriyur who wears fine garlands, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Every celestial god and enlightened sage keeps the Goddess constantly in mind. Vallalar is blunt about the rest. Whoever fails to meditate on her stays trapped in the endless cycle of birth and death, and devotion is the key that breaks free of mortal suffering.

translit: tirunāḷ niṉaittoḻum naṉṉāḷ toḻāmal celuttiyanāḷ karunāḷ eṉamaṟai ellām pukalum karuttaṟintē orunā ḷiṉuniṉ ṟaṉaimaṟa vāraṉpar oṟṟiyilvāḻ marunāṇ malarkkuḻal māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: The good days are those spent thinking of and worshipping you. Your devotees understand the truth proclaimed by all the Vedas that days passed without worshipping you are dark days leading back to rebirth. Therefore they never forget you for even a single day. O deer residing in Otriyur with tresses adorned with fragrant fresh flowers, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Time has value only when it is spent in devotion. A day passed without thinking of the Goddess is a dark day, Vallalar says, one that pulls the soul back toward another physical birth. Her true devotees understand this, so they remember her every single day.

translit: vāṇāḷ aṭaivar vaṟumai yuṟārnaṉ maṉaimakkaḷpoṉ pūṇāḷ iṭampukaḻ pōtam peṟuvarpiṉ puṉmai-oṉṟum kāṇārniṉ nāmam karutukiṉ ṟōroṟṟik kaṇṇutalpāl māṇārvam uṟṟa mayilē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: Those who meditate on your name attain long life and never face poverty. They gain a good home, children, gold, ornaments, servants, lands, fame, and wisdom. They will never see any misery thereafter. O peacock who holds great love for the Lord of Otriyur who wears an eye on his forehead, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Vallalar promises fulfillment in both the physical world and the spiritual life. Wealth, family, health and fame come to those who keep her name in mind, along with true inner wisdom. Her grace removes all misery and provides abundantly for every human need.

translit: cīraṟi vāyttiru voṟṟip parama civattainiṉaip pōraṟi vāyav aṟivām veḷikkap puṟattuniṉṟāy yāraṟi vārniṉṉai nāyēṉaṟiva taḻakuṭaittē vāreṟi pūṇmulai māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: You become the knowledge of those who meditate on the supreme Siva of holy Otri as the glorious supreme intelligence. You stand beyond the expanse of that knowledge. Who can truly know You? It is a spectacle indeed for a lowly dog like me to claim to know You. O deer whose breasts are bound with jewels! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: She is the spiritual insight of those who meditate on Siva, and also the vast reality beyond that insight. Human logic cannot fully hold her. Vallalar calls himself a lowly dog and wonders how an ordinary mind could ever claim to grasp a presence so immense.

translit: pōṟṟiṭu vōrtam piḻai-ā yiramum poṟuttaruḷcey vīṟṟoḷir ñāṉa viḷakkē marakata meṉkarumpē ēṟṟoḷir oṟṟi yiṭattāriṭattil ilaṅkumuyar māṟṟoḷi rumpacum poṉṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: You forgive a thousand faults of those who praise You and bestow Your grace. O majestic shining lamp of wisdom! O tender emerald sugarcane! You shine on the left side of the radiant Lord of Otri. O pure gold shining with high purity! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: She does not demand perfection from those who come to her. A thousand flaws are wiped away the moment someone approaches with praise, and she gives her bright wisdom and sweet grace freely.

tamil: ஆசைஉள் ளார்அயன் மால்ஆதி தேவர்கள் யாரும்நின் தாள்
translit: ācai-uḷ ḷārayaṉ mālāti tēvarkaḷ yārumniṉ tāḷ pūcaiyuḷ ḷāreṉil eṅkē ulakarcey pūcaikoḷvār tēcaiyuḷ ḷāroṟṟi yūruṭai yāriṭañ cērmayilē mācaiyuḷḷārpukaḻ māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: Brahma, Vishnu, and all the primordial gods focus purely on worshipping Your feet with devotion. If they do this, how will they ever accept the worship offered by worldly people? O peacock who joins the left side of the radiant Lord of Otri! O deer praised even by mortals burdened with flaws! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Brahma (the creator) and Vishnu (the preserver) are entirely absorbed in worshipping the Goddess. If they are that busy seeking her grace, they cannot possibly attend to the prayers of ordinary people. So go straight to the supreme mother herself, the source every other god relies on.

translit: aṇṭārai veṉṟula kāṇṭumeyñ ñāṉam aṭaintuviṇṇil paṇṭārai cūḻmati pōlirup pōrkaḷniṉ pattarpatam kaṇṭāraik kaṇṭavar aṉṟō tiruvoṟṟik kaṇṇutalcēr vaṇṭārai vēlaṉṉa māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: Those who conquer their foes, rule the world, attain true wisdom, and live like the moon surrounded by beautiful stars in the sky are truly the ones who have seen the seers of the feet of Your devotees. O deer whose eyes are like darting bees and sharp spears, joining the Lord of holy Otri who bears an eye on His forehead! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Greatness comes from being near those who love the divine. The highest things a person can reach, whether earthly power or spiritual wisdom, follow from contact with the devotees of the Goddess. Even seeing someone who knows her true followers is enough to lift a life completely.

translit: aṭiyār toḻuniṉ aṭippoṭi tāṉcaṟ ṟaṇiyappeṟṟa muṭiyāl aṭikkup perumaipeṟ ṟāram mukuntaṉcantak kaṭiyār malarayaṉ muṉṉōrteṉ oṟṟik kaṭavuṭcempāl vaṭiyāk karuṇaik kaṭalē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: The beautiful Vishnu, Brahma on his fragrant lotus, and the other primordial gods attained their greatness simply because their crowns were adorned with a speck of dust from Your feet worshipped by devotees. O unfailing ocean of grace residing on the noble side of the Lord of southern Otri! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: The power of the traditional gods is borrowed. Brahma and Vishnu hold their high status only because a single speck of dust from her feet fell upon their heads. She is the true ocean of compassion, and all divine authority flows outward from her alone.

translit: ōvā tayaṉmuta lōrmuṭi kōṭi uṟaḻntupaṭil āvā aṉiccam poṟāmalarc ciṟṟaṭi āṟṟuṅkolō kāvāy imayappoṟ pāvāy aruḷoṟṟik kāmarvalli vāvā eṉumaṉpar vāḻvē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: If millions of heads of Brahma and other gods constantly bow at your feet, alas, will your small flower-like feet that cannot even bear the soft anicham flower withstand the weight? Protect me, O golden lady of the Himalayas. O beautiful vine of graceful Otri. O life of the devotees who call out to you saying, "Come, come." O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Her feet are softer than the anicham flower, so delicate they can barely bear its touch. Now picture the heavy, jeweled crowns of Brahma and countless other gods pressing against them without end. Vallalar holds two things side by side here, the devotion she commands and her great tenderness, and he fears for those small feet.

translit: iṭṭār maṟaikkum upaniṭa tattiṟkum iṉṉuñcaṟṟum eṭṭāniṉ poṉṉaṭip pōteḷi yēṉtalaik keṭṭuṅkolō kaṭṭār caṭaimuṭi oṟṟi-em māṉneñca kattamarnta maṭṭār kuḻaṉmaṭa māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: Will your golden flower-like feet, which remain out of reach even for the vast Vedas and Upanishads, ever reach the head of this simple one? You sit in the heart of our Lord of Otri who wears a crown of tied matted hair. O gentle deer with hair full of sweet honey, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: The Vedas and Upanishads, the highest and oldest scriptures, reach for these feet and always fall short. So how could they ever come to rest on the head of someone as small as Vallalar? His humility shows the way in. It is open devotion, which no amount of intellectual mastery can replace.

translit: veḷiyāy veḷikkuḷ veṟuveḷi yāycciva mēniṟainta oḷiyāy oḷikkuḷ oḷiyām parainiṉai oppavarār eḷiyārk keḷiyar tiruvoṟṟi yārmey iṉitupari maḷiyāniṉ ṟōṅku maruvē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: You are the space, the absolute void within the space, and the light completely filled with Sivam. You are the supreme light within the light. Who can equal you? You are the towering fragrance that sweetly perfumes the body of the Lord of Otriyur, who is accessible to the simple. O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Don't think of the Goddess as only a form. She is space, the bare void within space, the light glowing within all light. That infinite power is also the radiance and sweet fragrance of the divine presence, and she stays within reach of anyone with a simple, open heart.

translit: viṇaṅkāta laṉpartam aṉpiṟkum niṉpula vikkumaṉṟi vaṇaṅkā matimuṭi eṅkaḷ pirāṉoṟṟi vāṇaṉumniṉ kuṇaṅkā talittumeyk kūṟutan tāṉeṉak kūṟuvaruṉ maṇaṅkā talitta taṟiyār vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: Our Lord who dwells in Otri never bows his crescent-crowned head to anyone, except to the pure devotion of his devotees and to your feigned lover's anger. People say he loved your virtues and gave you half his body. They do not know that he actually desired your sweet fragrance, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: The Lord of Otriyur bows to no one. Only two things bend his head: the pure love of his devotees and the playful, feigned anger of the Goddess. Tradition says he gave her the left half of his body because he loved her shining virtues. Vallalar teases that story. What really drew her into his form, he says, was her sweet, divine fragrance.

translit: paṉṉumpal vēṟaṇṭam ellāmav aṇṭap parappiṉiṉṟu tuṉṉum carācaram yāvaiyum īṉṟatu cūḻntumuṉṉai iṉṉum iḷantai aḻiyāta kaṉṉikai eṉpateṉṉē maṉṉum cukānanta vāḻvē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: You gave birth to all the diverse universes we speak of. You birthed all the moving and unmoving things that throng the expanse of those universes, and you envelop them all. Yet they call you the virgin whose youth never fades. How can this be? O enduring life of blissful joy, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: A lovely paradox. She gave birth to every universe and to every moving and unmoving creature in them, and she holds all of it in her embrace. Yet the mother of all existence is still praised as a pure maiden whose youth never fades, untouched by time.

translit: ciṉaṅkaṭan tōruḷḷac centā maraiyil ceḻittumaṟṟai maṉaṅkaṭan tōtumav vākkum kaṭanta maṟai-aṉṉamē tiṉaṅkaṭan tōrpukaḻ oṟṟi-em māṉiṭam cēramutē vaṉaṅkaṭan tōṉpukaḻ māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: You flourish in the red lotus hearts of those who have conquered anger. You are the swan of the Vedas, transcending both the mind and the spoken word. You are the nectar that unites with our Lord of Otriyur, praised by those who have transcended time. You are the deer praised by the sage who crossed the forest, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: The Divine Mother makes her home in the peaceful hearts of people who have let go of anger. Neither the human mind nor the Vedas (ancient scriptures) can put her fully into words.

translit: vallārum vallavar allārum maṟṟai maṉitarmutal ellārum niṉceyal allā taṇuvum iyakkilarēl illāmai yāluḻal pullēṉcey kuṟṟaṅkaḷ ētukaṇṭāy mallār vayaloṟṟi nallāy vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: The capable, the incapable, and all other beings cannot move even an atom without your action. If this is so, what faults can you find in the deeds of this lowly one suffering in poverty? O good Mother of Otriyur surrounded by fertile fields, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Surrender to the divine will, taken all the way. If no living being can move a single atom without the Mother's energy, Vallalar asks, how can she hold his human mistakes against him?

translit: eḻutā eḻiluyirc cittira mē-iṉ icaippayaṉē toḻutāṭum aṉpartam uṭkaḷip pēciṟ cukakkaṭalē ceḻuvār malarppoḻil oṟṟi-em māṉtaṉ tiruttuṇaiyē vaḻuvā maṟaiyiṉ poruḷē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: You are the unpainted beautiful living portrait. You are the returning fruit of sweet music. You are the inner joy of devotees who worship and dance. You are the ocean of supreme bliss. You are the divine companion of our Lord of Otriyur with lush flower groves. You are the meaning of the flawless Vedas, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: No human hand painted this portrait, and it is alive. She is the inner bliss devotees feel when they lose themselves in worship. She is also the true meaning hidden within the ancient scriptures.

translit: teruṭpā luṟumaiṅkaic celvarkkum nalliḷañ cēykkumakiḻn taruṭpāl aḷikkum taṉattaṉa mē-em akaṅkalanta iruṭpāl akaṟṟum iruñcuṭa rē-oṟṟi entai-uḷḷam maruṭpāl payilu mayilē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: You joyfully offer the milk of grace from your breasts to the wealthy five-handed Lord of wisdom and to the good young child. You are the great flame that merges in our hearts to dispel darkness. You are the peacock enchanting the heart of my Father of Otriyur, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Vallalar pictures her grace as nourishing milk given to her divine children, the elephant-headed god Vinayakar and the young warrior god Murugan. For her human devotees she is the bright flame that clears all spiritual darkness from the heart.

translit: ayilēntum piḷḷainaṟ ṟāyē tiruvoṟṟi aiyarmalark kayilēntarumpeṟal muttē icaiyil kaṉintakural kuyilē kuyiṉmeṉ kuḻaṟpiṭi yēmalaik kōṉpayanta mayilē matimuka māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: You are the good mother of the child who wields the spear. You are the rare pearl held in the flower-like hands of the Lord of holy Otriyur. You are the cuckoo with a voice ripened in music. You are the graceful female elephant with soft hair dark as clouds. You are the peacock born to the king of the mountains. You are the deer with a moon-like face, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Vallalar reaches for the loveliest things in nature to praise her. She sings with a cuckoo's sweet voice and moves with a deer's gentle grace. The Lord cherishes her as a rare, priceless pearl.

translit: ceyyakam ōṅkum tiruvoṟṟi yūril civaperumāṉ meyyakam ōṅkunal aṉpēniṉ pālaṉpu mēvukiṉṟōr kaiyakam ōṅkum kaṉiyē taṉimeyk katineṟiyē vaiyakam ōṅku maruntē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: In Tiruvottiyur of flourishing fertile fields, you are the pure love welling up within the true form of Lord Siva. You are the fruit resting in the hands of those who cherish love for you. You are the peerless path to the true goal. You are the medicine that uplifts the earth. O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Vadivudai Manikkam is the very essence of love within Lord Siva. She is also close enough to touch, resting like a fruit in the hands of those who love her. And she is the medicine that heals the suffering of the world.

translit: tarumpēr aruḷoṟṟi yūruṭai yāṉiṭañ cārntapacuṅ karumpē iṉiyakaṟ kaṇṭē maturak kaṉinaṟavē irumpēy maṉattiṉar pālicai yāta iḷaṅkiḷiyē varumpēr oḷicceñ cuṭarē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: You abide on the left side of the Lord of Otriyur who grants great grace. You are fresh sugarcane. You are sweet rock candy. You are the nectar of sweet fruit. O young parrot who never yields to those with dark demonic minds! You are the vast light of the rising red flame. O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: In Hindu tradition the goddess shares a single form with Lord Siva, occupying his left side. To her devotees she is pure sweetness, like sugarcane and rock candy. Those who harbor dark and cruel thoughts can never reach her.

translit: cēlēr viḻiyaruḷ tēṉē aṭiyaruḷ tittikkumcem pālē maturaccem pākēcol vētap paṉuvalmuṭi mēlē viḷaṅkum viḷakkē aruḷoṟṟi vittakaṉār mālē koḷumeḻil māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O nectar of grace with beautiful carp-like eyes! O pure milk that tastes sweet within the hearts of devotees! O sweet flawless syrup! O lamp shining upon the summit of the spoken Vedic scriptures! O beautiful deer who ignites deep desire in the wise Lord of Otriyur radiating grace! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: She shines like a lamp at the very summit of the Vedas, the highest truth those scriptures describe. The same goddess is an intimate, sweet presence in her devotees' hearts. Vallalar draws on classic Tamil imagery, giving her eyes like carp fish and the form of a graceful deer.

tamil: எம்பால் அருள்வைத் தெழிலொற்றி யூர்கொண் டிருக்கும் இறைச்
translit: empāl aruḷvait teḻiloṟṟi yūrkoṇ ṭirukkum iṟaic cempāl kalantapain tēṉē katalic ceḻuṅkaṉiyē vempālai neñcaruḷ mēvā malarppata meṉkoṭiyē vampāl aṇimulai māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: Bestowing grace upon us, you dwell in beautiful Otriyur. You are the fresh honey mingled with the pure milk of the Lord. You are a rich plantain fruit. O tender vine whose lotus feet never step into cruel desert-like hearts! O deer with beautifully adorned breasts! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Her grace is a refreshing sweetness that mingles with the Lord's presence like honey in milk. Harshness is where it cannot survive. Those soft, lotus-like feet will never walk into a heart gone dry and barren as a desert.

translit: ēmamuyp pōremak keṉṟē iḷaikkil eṭukkavaitta cēmavaip pē-aṉpar tēṭumeyñ ñāṉat tiraviyamē tāmamaik kārmalark kūntal piṭimeṉ taṉinaṭaiyāy vāmanaṟ cīroṟṟi māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: You are the secure treasure kept aside for us to take when we grow weary and seek safety. You are the wealth of true wisdom sought by loving devotees. Your dark cloud-like hair is adorned with flower garlands and your soft matchless gait is like a female elephant. O deer of beautiful and glorious Otriyur! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Think of her as a reserve put aside for hard days. When people are worn out by the struggles of life, she is the safe treasure of true wisdom they can draw on. Vallalar also praises her beauty in the traditional way, likening her slow, majestic walk to a female elephant's.

tamil: முன்னே அருந்தவம் என்னே முயன்றனர் முன்னும் ஒற்றி
translit: maṉṉēr malaiyaṉ maṉaiyumnaṟ kāñcaṉa mālaiyumnī aṉṉē eṉattiru vāyāl aḻaikkappeṟ ṟāravartām muṉṉē aruntavam eṉṉē muyaṉṟaṉar muṉṉum oṟṟi vaṉṉēr iḷamulai miṉṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: The wife of the mountain king and the good Kanchanamalai received the blessing of being called "Mother" by your sacred lips. What rare austerities they must have performed in the past! O lightning-like goddess with firm young breasts in ancient Otriyur, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Vallalar marvels at the women who raised the Goddess in her earthly births. Mena, wife of the mountain king, and Kanchanamalai each heard the mother of the universe call them "Mother" in return. He can only wonder what austerities earned them a bond that close.

translit: kaṇamoṉṟi lēṉumeṉ uḷḷak kavalaik kaṭalkaṭantē kuṇamoṉṟi lēṉetu ceykēṉniṉ uḷḷak kuṟippaṟiyēṉ paṇamoṉṟu pāmpaṇi oṟṟi-em māṉiṭap pālilteyva maṇamoṉṟu paccaik koṭiyē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: I have not crossed the ocean of sorrow in my heart for even a single moment. I possess no good qualities. What will I do? I do not know your heart's intention. O green creeper united in divine marriage with our Lord of Otriyur who wears the hooded snake as an ornament, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Vallalar confesses despair and unworthiness. He has no virtue to lean on and cannot read her will, so he stands helpless and waits. Even so, he pictures her as a green creeper resting beside Lord Siva and looks to her for quiet guidance in the dark.

tamil: திருவே அருள்செந் திருவே முதற்பணி செய்யத் தந்த
translit: karuvē taṉaiyaṟa eṉṉeñ cakattil kaḷippoṭoṟṟik kuruvē eṉumniṉ kaṇavaṉum nīyum kulavumantat tiruvē aruḷcen tiruvē mutaṟpaṇi ceyyat tanta maruvē maruvu malarē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: To end the agony of birth, you and your husband, the guru of Otriyur, joyfully sport within my heart. O auspicious goddess, O perfect red wealth of grace, O fragrance, O fragrant flower who granted me the foremost service to perform, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Liberation happens inside the devotee's own heart. Vallalar says the Goddess and Lord Siva have made his heart their joyful playground, and their presence there breaks the endless cycle of birth and death. Living within him, she gives him the first and highest privilege: to serve the divine directly.

translit: eṇṇiya eṇṇaṅkaḷ ellām palikka eṉakkuṉaruḷ paṇṇiya uḷḷaṅkoḷ uḷḷum puṟampum parimaḷikkum puṇṇiya mallikaip pōtē eḻiloṟṟip pūraṇarpāl maṇṇiya paccai maṇiyē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: You bestowed your grace so that all my thoughts and intentions bear fruit. O sacred jasmine flower whose fragrance radiates inside and outside my heart! O flawless green gem beside the perfect Lord of beautiful Otriyur, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Grace is what brings good intentions to life. Vallalar calls the Goddess a sacred jasmine whose sweet scent fills his inner thoughts and his outer world alike. Bathed in that grace, his desires and actions bear good fruit on their own.

translit: tītucey tālumniṉ aṉparkaḷ tammuṉ cerukkiniṉṟu vātucey tālumniṉ tāḷmaṟan tālum matiyiliyēṉ ētucey tālum poṟuttaruḷ vāyoṟṟi yiṉṉiṭaippū mātucey tāḻkuḻal māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: Even if I commit evil deeds, even if I stand arrogant and argue before your devotees, even if I forget your sacred feet, I am a fool. Whatever I do, please bear with my faults and grant me your grace. O doe with long hanging tresses and a slender waist in Otriyur, O flower-like lady, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: A plea for forgiveness with no conditions attached. Vallalar admits he is fool enough to do wrong, to argue arrogantly with true devotees, even to forget her feet altogether. Knowing his flaws, he asks the Goddess to be a patient mother and overlook them.

translit: maruntiṉiṉ ṟāṉoṟṟi yūrvāḻum niṉṟaṉ makiḻnaṉmuṉṉum tiruntiniṉ ṟārpukaḻ niṉmuṉṉum nallaruḷ tēṉviḻaintē viruntiṉiṉ ṟēṉcaṟṟum uḷḷiraṅ kāta vitattaikkaṇṭu varuntiniṉ ṟēṉitu naṉṟō vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: I stood as a guest longing for the honey of good grace before your Lord who dwells in Otriyur as the supreme medicine and before you whom perfected beings praise. Seeing how your heart shows no pity at all, I stand in sorrow. Is this right, O Vadivudai Manikkam?
commentary: Vallalar asks how the divine Mother can watch a devotee stand in sorrow and show no pity. He approaches her and the Lord of Otriyur as a hopeful guest seeking the hospitality of their grace. When she remains silent, he questions whether this indifference is right.

translit: eṉpōl kuṇattil iḻintavar illai-ep pōtumeṅkum niṉpōl aruḷil ciṟantavar illai-in nīrmaiyiṉāl poṉpōlum niṉṉaruḷ aṉṉē eṉakkum puritikaṇṭāy maṉpōl uyaroṟṟi vāḻvē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: There is no one anywhere at any time as degraded in character as I am. There is no one as exalted in grace as you. By this very nature, O Mother, you must bestow your golden grace upon me. O life of exalted Otriyur that stands like a sovereign, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: A bold argument for her favor. No one is lower in character than Vallalar, he says, and no one higher in grace than she, so the two are a perfect match. Grace that boundless is meant for someone in exactly his need.

translit: tuṉpē mikumiv aṭiyēṉ maṉattilniṉ tuyya-aruḷ iṉpē mikuvaten nāḷō eḻiloṟṟi entai-uyirk kaṉpēmeyt toṇṭar aṟivē civaneṟik kaṉpilarpāl vaṉpēmeyp pōta vaṭivē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: When is the day that the joy of your pure grace will overflow in the mind of this devotee who is filled with sorrow? O beloved of the life of my Father in beautiful Otriyur. O wisdom of true devotees. O fierce one to those who lack love for the path of Siva. O form of true knowledge, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: The Goddess shows two faces, depending on the heart before her. To those who walk the path of Siva (the supreme divine reality) with love, she is wisdom and joy. Those who lack that love meet her fierce and unyielding. Vallalar longs for the day her grace washes his sorrow away.

translit: caṟṟē yeṉiṉumeṉ neñcat tuyaram taviravumniṉ poṟṟē malarppatam pōṟṟavum uḷḷam puritikaṇṭāy coṟṟēr aṟiñar pukaḻoṟṟi mēvum tuṇaivartañcem maṟṟēr puyattaṇai māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: You must grant me the mind to dispel my heart's sorrow even a little and to praise your golden lotus feet brimming with honey. O deer who embraces the noble shoulders of your Consort who dwells in Otriyur praised by scholars skilled in words, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Devotion needs a mind that can hold it. Vallalar asks the Goddess for enough clarity to set his sorrow aside and praise her properly. Even the ability to worship, he knows, comes as her gift.

translit: cantōṭa māppiṟar ellām irukkavum cañcalattāl antō orutami yēṉmaṭṭum vāṭal aruṭkaḻakō nantōṭa nīkkiya naṅkāy eṉattiru nāṉmukaṉmāl vantōtum oṟṟi mayilē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: While everyone else lives in happiness, alas, is it fitting to your grace that I alone wither in distress? O peacock of Otriyur praised by sacred four-faced Brahma and Vishnu who come and declare, "O Lady who removed our flaws," O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Even Brahma the creator and Vishnu the preserver rely on the Goddess to remove their flaws. So why, Vallalar asks, is he alone left to suffer while everyone else is happy through her? He appeals to her name as the supreme purifier and asks whether ignoring his distress befits her grace.

translit: aṭiyēṉ micai-ep piḻaiyirun tālum avaipoṟuttuc ceṭiyētam nīkkinaṟ cīraruḷ vāytikaḻ teyvamaṟaik koṭiyē marakatak kompē eḻiloṟṟik kōmaḷamē vaṭiyēr ayilviḻi māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: Whatever faults lie upon this servant, forgive them. Remove my afflictions and bestow your excellent grace, O radiant creeper of the divine Vedas, O emerald branch, O tender beauty of beautiful Otriyur, O doe with sharp and beautiful spear-like eyes, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Vallalar asks the Goddess to forgive every fault, clear his afflictions away and grant her grace. He calls her by images from nature: a creeper, an emerald branch, a gentle doe. The names themselves show how lovingly he leans on her.

translit: kaṇṇappaṉ ēttunaṟ kāḷatti yārmaṅ kalaṅkoḷoṟṟi naṇṇappar vēṇṭum nalamē parāṉanta naṉṉaṟavē eṇṇap paṭā-eḻil ōviya mē-emai ēṉṟukoṇṭa vaṇṇap pacumpoṉ vaṭivē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O goodness desired by the Lord of Kāḷatti praised by Kaṇṇappaṉ, the Lord who resides in auspicious Otriyur. O sweet honey of supreme bliss. O painting of unimaginable beauty. O form of shining pure gold who accepted us. O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: The hunter Kannappan is famous in Tamil tradition for offering his own eyes to God out of pure, overwhelming love. Vallalar invokes that devotion as he praises the Goddess at Otriyur. She is beauty beyond imagining and the honey of supreme bliss, a golden form of grace that gladly takes human souls as her own.

translit: kaṟpē vikaṟpam kaṭiyumoṉ ṟē-eṅkaḷ kaṇniṟainta poṟpēmeyt toṇṭartam puṇṇiya mē-aruṭ pōta-iṉpē coṟpēr aṟivuṭ cukapporu ḷēmeyc cuyañcuṭarē maṟpēr peṟumoṟṟi māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O pure virtue. O One who dispels delusion. O golden beauty filling our eyes. O merit of true devotees. O joy of graceful wisdom. O reality of bliss within great knowledge. O true self-luminous flame. O doe of highly renowned Otriyur. O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: The Goddess destroys delusion and reveals clear truth. Vallalar calls her a self-luminous flame of inner knowledge. She is the joy of true wisdom and the very merit that sincere devotees earn.

translit: mikavē tuyarkkaṭal vīḻntēṉai nīkai viṭutalaruḷ takavē eṉakkunaṟ ṟāyē akila carācaramum cukavēlai mūḻkat tiruvoṟṟi yūriṭan tuṉṉippeṟṟa makavē eṉappurak kiṉṟōy vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: I have fallen deeply into the ocean of sorrow. Is it fitting for your grace to abandon me? O my good mother. You reside in Otriyur and protect all moving and unmoving things in the universe as your own children, immersing them in the ocean of bliss. O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Vallalar cries out to her as a mother. How could she leave him in a sea of sorrow, when she protects everything in creation, living and non-living, as her own children? He asks for that same care, and to be drawn into her endless joy.

translit: vētaṅka ḷāyoṟṟi mēvum civattiṉ viḷaivaruḷāyp pūtaṅka ḷāyppoṟi yāyppula ṉākip pukalkaraṇa pētaṅka ḷāyuyir ākiya niṉṉai-ip pētai-eṉvāy vātaṅka ḷālaṟi vēṉō vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: You stand as the Vedas, as the resultant grace of Siva residing in Otriyur, as the elements, as the sensory organs, as the senses, as the diverse inner faculties, and as life itself. Will I, this ignorant one, ever know you through my verbal arguments? O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: The Goddess is the whole universe, physical and spiritual. She forms the sacred scriptures, the elements, the five senses, the inner mind and life itself. Since she is the living reality behind everything, Vallalar admits that empty words and clever debate will never grasp her.

translit: matiyē matimuka māṉē aṭiyar maṉattuvaitta nitiyē karuṇai niṟaivē cukānanta nīḷnilaiyē katiyē kativaḻi kāṭṭuṅkaṇ ṇē-oṟṟik kāvalarpāl vatiyēr iḷamaṭa māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O moon! O deer with a moon-like face! O treasure placed in the hearts of devotees! O fullness of compassion! O vast state of blissful joy! O refuge! O eye that reveals the path to refuge! O beautiful, tender, young deer dwelling with the protector of Otri! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: She is the treasure kept in the hearts of devotees, and she is also the eye that shows the path. So grace is both where we are going and the one who takes us there. Those who seek her as refuge find her as full, blissful joy.

translit: āṟāt tuyarat taḻuntukiṉ ṟēṉai-iṅ kañcaleṉṟē kūṟāk kuṟai-eṉ kuṟaiyē iṉiniṉ kuṟippaṟiyēṉ tēṟāc ciṟiyark karitām tiruvoṟṟit tēvarmakiḻ māṟāk karuṇai maḻaiyē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: I am sinking in unceasing sorrow. Is it my fault that you have not told me to fear not? I do not know your intention now. You are rare to the ignorant. You bring joy to the Lord of Thiru Otri. O unfailing rain of compassion! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Vallalar cannot make sense of it. She is called an unfailing rain of compassion, yet he sinks in endless sorrow and hears no word telling him not to fear. He wonders whether his own faults have kept her silent. Even in despair he names her truly, a joy to the Lord of Otri and a mystery to those who lack understanding.

translit: eṟṟē nilai-oṉṟum illā tuyaṅkum eṉakkaruḷac caṟṟēniṉ uḷḷam tirumpilai yāṉceyat takkateṉṉē coṟṟēṉ niṟaimaṟaik kompēmeyñ ñāṉac cuṭarkkoḻuntē maṟṟēr aṇiyoṟṟi vāḻvē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: Alas! I suffer without any firm standing. Your heart does not turn even a little to bestow grace on me. What is there for me to do? O branch of the perfect Vedas of honeyed words! O tender flame of true knowledge! O life of beautifully adorned Otri! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Without her grace he has no ground to stand on. He asks only that her heart turn toward him a little. Calling her the branch of the Vedas and the tender flame of true knowledge, he admits that certainty and footing come from her grace alone.

translit: cevvēlai veṉṟakaṇ miṉṉēniṉ cittam tirumpi-eṉak kevvēlai ceyeṉ ṟiṭiṉumav vēlai iyaṟṟuvalkāṇ tevvēlai vaṟṟaccey avvēlai yīṉṟoṟṟit tēvarneñcai vavvēla vārkuḻal māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O radiant lightning with eyes that conquer the red spear! If your heart turns to me and commands me to do any task, I will surely perform it. You gave birth to the one who wields the spear that dried up the hostile ocean. O deer with long tresses who steals the heart of the Lord of Otri! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Surrender means being ready for any work. Let her heart turn to him and give one command, Vallalar says, and he will do it. He recalls her power as mother of the warrior god whose spear dried up the hostile ocean.

translit: tāyē mikavum tayavuṭai yāḷeṉac cāṟṟuvaric cēyēṉ paṭuntuyar nīkka-eṉ ṉē-uḷam ceytilaiyē nāyēṉ piḻai-iṉi nāṭātu nallaruḷ nalkavaru vāyē-em oṟṟi mayilē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: They say a mother is the most compassionate. Why have you not made up your mind to remove the sorrow suffered by this child? Will you come to bestow your good grace, no longer counting the faults of this dog-like one? O our peacock of Otri! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Everyone says a mother is the most compassionate of all, and Vallalar holds the Goddess to it. He asks why she has not yet resolved to end her child's sorrow. Let her stop counting the faults of this dog-like one and give grace the way a mother gives, without conditions.

translit: nāṉē niṉaikkaṭi yēṉeṉ piḻaikaḷai nāṭiyanī tāṉē eṉaiviṭil antō iṉi-evar tāṅkukiṉṟōr tēṉēnal vētat teḷivē katikkuc celuneṟiyē vāṉēr poḻiloṟṟi māṉē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: I am your slave even in my thoughts. If you examine my faults and abandon me yourself, alas, who will support me now? O honey, O clarity of the good Vedas, O path leading to liberation, O deer of Ortriyur with its sky-reaching groves, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Vallalar throws himself wholly on the Mother's mercy. If she weighs his faults and lets him go, who else will hold him up? He calls her Vadivudai Manikkam, the presiding Goddess of the sacred town of Otriyur, and the clear truth of the Vedas, the ancient sacred scriptures.

translit: kallā riṭattileṉ illāmai collik kalaṅki-iṭar nallāṇmai uṇṭaruḷ vallāṇmai uṇṭeṉiṉ nalkuvaiyō vallār evarkaṭkum vallār tiruvoṟṟi vāṇaroṭu mallār poḻiloṟṟi vāḻvē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: I speak of my poverty to the unlearned and suffer in confusion. If you possess good strength and the powerful strength of grace, will you not grant it to me? You reside with the Lord of Thiru Ortriyur who is the strongest among the strong. O life of Ortriyur with its dense groves, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Telling his poverty to the unlearned has only left him confused and hurting. So he turns to her supreme strength of grace, since she lives beside the Lord of Otriyur, strongest of the strong. Relief from suffering comes from divine strength, never from human wealth.

translit: cuntara vāṇmukat tōkāy maṟaikaḷ columpaiṅkiḷḷāy kantara vārkuḻaṟ pūvāy karuṇaik kaṭaikkaṇnaṅkāy antara nēriṭaip pāvāy aruḷoṟṟi aṇṇalmakiḻ mantara nērkoṅkai maṅkāy vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O peafowl with a beautiful radiant face, O green parrot speaking the Vedas, O flower with long fragrant tresses, O lady with merciful sidelong glances, O maiden with a waist as subtle as the sky, O woman with breasts like Mount Mandara who delights the gracious Lord of Ortriyur, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Peacock, speaking parrot, fragrant flower. Vallalar praises the Mother in the classic images of Tamil poetry. Her form delights the Lord of Otriyur, and her merciful sidelong glance protects every living being.

translit: pattartam uḷḷat tirukkōyil mēvum paramparaiyē cuttameyñ ñāṉa oḷippiḻam pēciṟ cukānantamē nittaniṉ cīrcola eṟkaruḷ vāyoṟṟi niṉmalaruṉ mattartam vāma mayilē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O supreme Goddess dwelling in the holy temple of your devotees' hearts, O mass of pure and true wisdom's light, O bliss of supreme consciousness, grant me the grace to sing your glories every day. O beautiful peafowl on the left side of the flawless Lord of Ortriyur who is mad with love for you, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: She lives in the temple of the devotee's heart as the pure light of true wisdom, the bliss of supreme consciousness. Vallalar asks for nothing more than the grace to sing her glories every day.

translit: pūvāy malarkkuḻal pūvāymey aṉpar puṉaintatamiḻp pāvāy niṟaintapoṟ pāvāycen tēṉiṟ pakarmoḻiyāy kāvāy eṉa-ayaṉ kāvāy pavaṉum karutumalar māvāy eḻiloṟṟi vāḻvē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O Goddess residing in the lotus flower, O lady with blossom-adorned tresses, O embodiment of the Tamil verses composed by true devotees, O perfect golden maiden, O one whose words are as sweet as red honey! Brahma begs you to protect him, and Vishnu contemplates you. O beautiful life of Ortriyur, O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: She is the living essence of the Tamil songs her true devotees compose. Even Brahma, the creator god, begs her protection, and Vishnu, the preserver god, contemplates her. She is the beautiful life of holy Otriyur.

translit: tātā uṇavuṭai tātā eṉappullar tammiṭaippōy mātākam uṟṟavar vaṉneñcil niṉaṭi vaikuṅkolō kātār neṭuṅkaṭ karumpēnal oṟṟik karuttarnaṭa vātā riṭamvaḷar mātē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: Will your feet abide in the hard hearts of those consumed by immense greed, who go to base men pleading, "Give, give me food and clothing, O patron"? O sweet sugarcane with long eyes extending to your ears! O lady flourishing on the left side of the supreme Lord of good Otriyur who never departs! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Greed hardens the heart. People driven by it run to base men crying for food and clothing, and Vallalar asks whether her feet could ever rest in hearts like that. Against them he sets the Goddess, all sweetness, dwelling forever beside the Lord in Otriyur.

translit: kaḷantirum pā-ik kaṭaiyēṉai āḷak karuṇaikoṇṭuṉ uḷantirum pāmaikkeṉ ceykēṉ tuyarkkaṭa lūṭalaintēṉ kuḷantirum pāviḻik kōmā ṉoṭuntoṇṭar kūṭṭamuṟa vaḷantirum pā-oṟṟi vāḻvē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: What can I do when your heart does not turn with compassion to rule me, this lowly one who never turns away from deceit? I wander lost in the ocean of sorrow. O life of Otriyur of undiminishing fertility, where the gathering of devotees unites with the Lord who has a steadfast frontal eye! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: A life rooted in deceit leaves a person adrift in sorrow, cut off from compassion. Vallalar cries out that he cannot change his own nature unless the Goddess steps in. He looks to her, the life of the city, hoping her grace will claim him as it unites the gathering of true devotees with the Lord.

translit: āraṇam pūtta aruṭkō maḷakkoṭi antaripūn tōraṇam pūtta eḻiloṟṟi yūrmakiḻ cuntaricaṟ kāraṇam pūtta civaipārp patinaṅ kavuri-eṉṉum vāraṇam pūtta taṉattāy vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O tender creeper of grace blossoming from the Vedas! O Antari! O Sundari rejoicing in beautiful Otriyur adorned with flower garlands! O Sivai blossoming as the true cause of everything! O Parvati! O our Gauri! O mother with breasts swelling like elephants! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: She is the source of all existence, the living grace the Vedas (ancient sacred scriptures) describe. Vallalar calls her by traditional names like Sivai (the absolute divine feminine), Parvati and Gauri. Each shows another of her countless sides, the beautiful ruler of the world and the nurturing mother.

translit: tiruvalli ēttum apiṭēka valli-eñ ceṉṉiyiṭai varuvalli kaṟpaka valli-oṇ paccai maṇivalli-em karuvalli nīkkum karuṇām pakavalli kaṇkoḷoṟṟi maruvalli eṉṟu maṟaitēr vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: The Vedas comprehend you as the creeper of anointment praised by Goddess Lakshmi, the creeper who descends upon our heads, the wish-fulfilling creeper, the bright emerald creeper, the creeper with compassionate eyes who severs the strong root of our births, and the fragrant creeper of captivating Otriyur. O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Vallalar strings image after image of the creeper. Grace is a sacred, life-giving vine reaching through every level of existence to bless us. The scriptures know her as the wish-fulfilling creeper who comes down to cut the deep root of repeated births, and her compassionate eyes free the soul from the endless round of worldly suffering.

translit: uṭaiyeṉṉa oṇpulit tōluṭai yārkaṇ ṭuvakkumiḷa naṭaiyaṉṉa mēmalarp poṉmuta lāmpeṇkaḷ nāyakamē paṭaiyaṉṉa nīḷviḻi miṉṉēr iṭaippoṟ pacuṅkiḷiyē maṭaimaṉṉu nīroṟṟi vāḻvē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O swan with a youthful gait, whom the Lord wearing a bright tiger skin beholds with joy! O supreme mistress of all goddesses starting with golden Lakshmi on the lotus! O golden green parrot with long weapon-like eyes and a waist like lightning! O life of Otriyur where water flows steadily through the sluices! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Even Lakshmi, goddess of wealth, stands beneath her. Her beauty brings joy to Lord Siva, traditionally shown wearing a fierce tiger skin. She moves with a swan's grace, bright as a golden green parrot, and she is the lifeblood of fertile, well-watered Otriyur.

translit: kaṟpatum kēṭpatum ellāmniṉ aṟputak kañcamalarp poṟpatam kāṇum poruṭṭeṉa eṇṇuvar puṇṇiyarē coṟpata māyavaik kappuṟa māyniṉṟa tūyccuṭarē maṟpatam cēroṟṟi vāḻvē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: The blessed ones consider all that they learn and hear to be for the purpose of seeing your wondrous golden lotus feet. O pure flame who stands as the meaning of words and yet beyond them! O life of Otriyur filled with abundance! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Learning and listening have one real purpose, and that is to experience the divine directly. The Goddess is the true meaning behind every word, yet she stands far beyond anything language can hold.

translit: niṉṉāl eṉakkuḷa ellā nalaṉum niṉai-aṭainta eṉṉāl uṉakkuḷa teṉṉaikaṇ ṭāyemai īṉṟavaḷē muṉṉāl varukkaruḷ oṟṟi-em māṉkaṇ muḻumaṇiyē maṉṉāṉ maṟaiyiṉ muṭivē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: All the goodness I have comes from you. See what you gain from me who has taken refuge in you! O mother who bore us! O flawless gem in the eye of our Lord of Otriyur who grants grace to those who approach Him! O conclusion of the enduring four Vedas! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Vallalar receives every good thing from the Goddess, and she gains nothing at all from taking him in. The relationship runs entirely one way. He calls her the ultimate truth found at the very end of the Vedas (the ancient sacred scriptures).

tamil: நின்றேநின் சேவடிக் குற்றேவல் செய்ய நினைத்தனன் ஈ
translit: naṉṟē civaneṟi nāṭumeyt toṇṭarkku naṉmaiceytu niṉṟēniṉ cēvaṭik kuṟṟēval ceyya niṉaittaṉaṉ ī teṉṟē muṭikuva tiṉṟē muṭiyil iṉitukaṇṭāy maṉṟēr eḻiloṟṟi vāḻvē vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: I resolved to do good to the true devotees who seek the path of Siva, and to stand and perform humble service to your red feet. When will this be fulfilled? It would be sweet if it is fulfilled today. O life of beautiful Otriyur! O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Serving God means serving those who love God. Vallalar longs to spend his life doing good to true devotees and offering humble service to the Goddess. He wants it granted today. Some unknown day in the future will not do.

translit: attaṉai oṟṟik kiṟaivaṉai ampalat tāṭukiṉṟa muttaṉaic cērnta-oṇ muttē matiya mukavamutē ittaṉai eṉṟaḷa vēlāta kuṟṟam iḻaittiṭumim mattaṉai āḷal vaḻakkō vaṭivuṭai māṇikkamē.
translation: O bright pearl joined with the Father, the Lord of Otriyur, the liberated one who dances in the hall! O nectar with a moon-like face! I commit faults that cannot be measured. Is it just for you to rule over this madman? O Vadivudai Manikkam!
commentary: Devotion often brings a deep sense of unworthiness with it. Looking at his own endless faults, Vallalar wonders why a perfect, radiant Goddess would ever choose to rule a flawed and foolish man like him.
