translit: pataṅkū ṟoṟṟip patiyīrnīr pacuvi lēṟum paricatutāṉ vitaṅkū ṟaṟattiṉ vititāṉō vilakkō viḷampal vēṇṭumeṉṟē ṉitaṅkū ṟiṭunaṟ pacuṅ kaṉṟai nīyumēṟi yiṭukiṉṟā yitaṅkū ṟiṭuka veṉkiṉṟā ritutāṉ cēṭi yeṉṉēṭī.
translation: I asked, "O Lord of Otriyur praised by sacred hymns! Is your act of mounting a bull a rule of dharma or a violation? You must tell me." He replies, "You too are mounting a good, tender young calf. Tell me the goodness of this." What is this, my friend?
commentary: She asks whether riding a bull is proper conduct for the Lord. He turns the joke around and says she too is riding a young calf, a playful Tamil way of describing a young woman's youth and pride. Vallalar pictures the soul and God as lovers trading wit as equals.

tamil: யோக முடையார் புகழொற்றி யூரிற் பரம யோகியராந்
தாக முடையா ரிவர்தமக்குத் தண்ணீர் தரநின் றனையழைத்தேன்
போக முடையாய் புறத்தண்ணீர் புரிந்து விரும்பா மகத்தண்ணீ
ரீக மகிழ்வி னென்கின்றா ரிதுதான் சேடி யென்னேடீ.
translit: yōka muṭaiyār pukaḻoṟṟi yūriṟ parama yōkiyarān tāka muṭaiyā rivartamakkut taṇṇīr taraniṉ ṟaṉaiyaḻaittēṉ pōka muṭaiyāy puṟattaṇṇīr purintu virumpā makattaṇṇī rīka makiḻvi ṉeṉkiṉṟā ritutāṉ cēṭi yeṉṉēṭī.
translation: I called you to offer water to this thirsty supreme yogi of Otriyur, a city praised by great yogis. He says, "O girl of pleasure! I do not desire outer water. Give me the inner water with joy." What is this, my friend?
commentary: She offers water for his thirst, and the supreme yogi turns it down. He wants the inner water, the pure joy of the heart. Vallalar's God has no use for material offerings. What he longs for is the joyful love that flows from the soul.

tamil: வளநீ ரொற்றி வாணரிவர் வந்தார் நின்றார் மாதேநா
முளநீர்த் தாக மாற்றுறுநீ ருதவ வேண்டு மென்றார்நான்
குளநீ ரொன்றே யுளதென்றேன் கொள்ளே மிடைமேற் கொளுமிந்த
விளநீர் தருக வென்கின்றா ரிதுதான் சேடி யென்னேடீ.
translit: vaḷanī roṟṟi vāṇarivar vantār niṉṟār mātēnā muḷanīrt tāka māṟṟuṟunī rutava vēṇṭu meṉṟārnāṉ kuḷanī roṉṟē yuḷateṉṟēṉ koḷḷē miṭaimēṟ koḷuminta viḷanīr taruka veṉkiṉṟā ritutāṉ cēṭi yeṉṉēṭī.
translation: This resident of Otriyur, a city rich in water, came and stood here. He said, "O lady, you must give me water to quench my inner thirst." I said, "I only have pond water." He replies, "I will not take that. Give me these tender coconuts held above your waist." What is this, my friend?
commentary: Offered pond water, the Lord refuses it and asks for the tender coconuts above her waist, a traditional poetic figure for a woman's breasts. The teasing is romantic, and it carries a deeper meaning. God wants the soul's complete and intimate surrender. Standard lifeless offerings do not quench that thirst.

tamil: மெய்ந்நீ ரொற்றி வாணரிவர் வெம்மை யுளநீர் வேண்டுமென்றா
ரந்நீ ரிலைநீர் தண்ணீர்தா னருந்தி லாகா தோவென்றேன்
முந்நீர் தனையை யனையீரிம் முதுநீ ருண்டு தலைக்கேறிற்
றிந்நீர் காண்டி யென்கின்றா ரிதுதான் சேடி யென்னேடீ.
translit: meynnī roṟṟi vāṇarivar vemmai yuḷanīr vēṇṭumeṉṟā rannī rilainīr taṇṇīrtā ṉarunti lākā tōveṉṟēṉ munnīr taṉaiyai yaṉaiyīrim mutunī ruṇṭu talaikkēṟiṟ ṟinnīr kāṇṭi yeṉkiṉṟā ritutāṉ cēṭi yeṉṉēṭī.
translation: This resident of Otriyur of true nature said, "I want hot water." I said, "I do not have that water. Can you not drink cold water?" He replies, "O girl resembling the daughter of the ocean! I drank this ancient water and it went to my head. Look at this state." What is this, my friend?
commentary: He asks for hot water, and when she offers cold he has a witty excuse. He once drank ancient water and it went straight to his head, which points to the myth of the Ganges flowing through his matted hair. He calls her daughter of the ocean, a title for the goddess of prosperity. Vallalar folds these old myths into a warm domestic quarrel between the soul and God.

tamil: சீலஞ் சேர்ந்த வொற்றியுளீர் சிறிதாம் பஞ்ச காலத்துங்
கோலஞ் சார்ந்து பிச்சைகொளக் குறித்து வருவீ ரென்னென்றேன்
காலம் போகும் வார்த்தைநிற்குங் கண்டா யிதுசொற் கடனாமோ
வேலங் குழலா யென்கின்றா ரிதுதான் சேடி யென்னேடீ.
translit: cīlañ cērnta voṟṟiyuḷīr ciṟitām pañca kālattuṅ kōlañ cārntu piccaikoḷak kuṟittu varuvī reṉṉeṉṟēṉ kālam pōkum vārttainiṟkuṅ kaṇṭā yitucoṟ kaṭaṉāmō vēlaṅ kuḻalā yeṉkiṉṟā ritutāṉ cēṭi yeṉṉēṭī.
translation: I asked, "O Lord of virtuous Otriyur! Even during a time of scarcity, you come in this beautiful form seeking alms. Why?" He says, "O girl with cardamom-scented hair, time passes but words remain. Is it proper for you to speak like this?" What is this, my friend?
commentary: She scolds him playfully for coming to beg in his beautiful form during a time of scarcity. He answers with a proverb. Hard times pass, but harsh words are remembered forever.

tamil: ஊற்றார் சடையீ ரொற்றியுளீ ரூரூ ரிரக்கத் துணிவுற்றீர்
நீற்றால் விளங்குந் திருமேனி நேர்ந்திங் கிளைத்தீர் நீரென்றேன்
சோற்றா லிளைத்தே மன்றுமது சொல்லா லிளைத்தே மின்றினிநா
மேற்றா லிகழ்வே யென்கின்றா ரிதுதான் சேடி யென்னேடீ.
translit: ūṟṟār caṭaiyī roṟṟiyuḷī rūrū rirakkat tuṇivuṟṟīr nīṟṟāl viḷaṅkun tirumēṉi nērntiṅ kiḷaittīr nīreṉṟēṉ cōṟṟā liḷaittē maṉṟumatu collā liḷaittē miṉṟiṉinā mēṟṟā likaḻvē yeṉkiṉṟā ritutāṉ cēṭi yeṉṉēṭī.
translation: I said, "O Lord of Otriyur with the spring flowing in your matted hair! You have resolved to beg from town to town. Your holy body shining with sacred ash has grown thin." He says, "We did not grow thin from a lack of food. We have grown thin today from your words. Any further reply will only invite contempt." What is this, my friend?
commentary: She teases that his endless begging from town to town has left his ash-smeared body thin. He turns it back on her. Hunger did not do it, he says. Her sharp words did.

tamil: நீரை விழுங்குஞ் சடையுடையீ ருளது நுமக்கு நீரூருந்
தேரை விழுங்கும் பசுவென்றேன் செறிநின் கலைக்கு ளொன்றுளது
காரை விழுங்கு மெமதுபசுக் கன்றின் றேரை நீர்த்தேரை
யீர விழுங்கு மென்கின்றா ரிதுதான் சேடி யென்னேடீ.
translit: nīrai viḻuṅkuñ caṭaiyuṭaiyī ruḷatu numakku nīrūrun tērai viḻuṅkum pacuveṉṟēṉ ceṟiniṉ kalaikku ḷoṉṟuḷatu kārai viḻuṅku mematupacuk kaṉṟiṉ ṟērai nīrttērai yīra viḻuṅku meṉkiṉṟā ritutāṉ cēṭi yeṉṉēṭī.
translation: I said, "O Lord whose matted hair swallowed the river! You have a cow that swallows the toad crawling in the water." He says, "Concealed within your garment is one thing that swallows the dark cloud. Today our calf will cleave and swallow the water toad." What is this, my friend?
commentary: A playful exchange of riddles with divine symbols hidden inside. She teases the Lord with veiled words for the river and the snake he wears. He replies by cleverly comparing her dark hair to a rain cloud.

tamil: பொன்னேர் மணிமன் றுடையீர்நீர் புரிந்த தெதுவெம் புடையென்றே
னின்னே யுரைத்தற் கஞ்சுதுமென் றாரென் னென்றே னியம்புதுமேன்
மின்னே நினது நடைப்பகையா மிருகம் பறவை தமைக்குறிக்கு
மென்னே யுரைப்ப தென்கின்றா ரிதுதான் சேடி யென்னேடீ.
translit: poṉṉēr maṇimaṉ ṟuṭaiyīrnīr purinta tetuvem puṭaiyeṉṟē ṉiṉṉē yuraittaṟ kañcutumeṉ ṟāreṉ ṉeṉṟē ṉiyamputumēṉ miṉṉē niṉatu naṭaippakaiyā mirukam paṟavai tamaikkuṟikku meṉṉē yuraippa teṉkiṉṟā ritutāṉ cēṭi yeṉṉēṭī.
translation: I asked, "O Lord of the golden hall of gems! What have you done to us?" He replied, "We are afraid to say it now." I asked, "Why?" He says, "O girl like lightning, if we speak, the words will denote the beast and the bird that rival your gait. Why should we speak of it?" What is this, my friend?
commentary: Classical Tamil poetry often compares a beautiful woman's walk to the graceful movement of an elephant or a swan. Asked what he has done, the Lord dodges the question, saying his words would only call up the very creatures that rival her gait.

tamil: அடையார் புரஞ்செற் றம்பலத்தே யாடு மழகீ ரெண்பதிற்றுக்
கடையா முடலின் றலைகொண்டீர் கரமொன் றினிலற் புதமென்றே
னுடையாத் தலைமேற் றலையாக வுன்கை யீரைஞ் ஞாறுகொண்ட
திடையா வளைக்கே யென்கின்றா ரிதுதான் சேடி யென்னேடீ.
translit: aṭaiyār purañceṟ ṟampalattē yāṭu maḻakī reṇpatiṟṟuk kaṭaiyā muṭaliṉ ṟalaikoṇṭīr karamoṉ ṟiṉilaṟ putameṉṟē ṉuṭaiyāt talaimēṟ ṟalaiyāka vuṉkai yīraiñ ñāṟukoṇṭa tiṭaiyā vaḷaikkē yeṉkiṉṟā ritutāṉ cēṭi yeṉṉēṭī.
translation: I said, "O beautiful Lord who destroyed the enemies' cities and dances in the Hall! In one hand you hold the head of a body that comes at the end of eight tens. This is a wonder." He says, "For the sake of your unbroken bangles, your hand has taken a thousand heads upon an unbreaking head." What is this, my friend?
commentary: She marvels at the skull in his hand, from the old story of his plucking off one of the creator god's heads. He answers with another intricate riddle about a thousand heads, matching her word for word and turning it into praise of her beauty.

tamil: தேவர்க் கரிய வானந்தத் திருத்தாண் டவஞ்செய் பெருமானீர்
மேவக் குகுகு குகுகுவணி வேணி யுடையீ ராமென்றேன்
தாவக் குகுகு குகுகுகுகுத் தாமே யைந்து விளங்கவணி
யேவற் குணத்தா யென்கின்றா ரிதுதான் சேடி யென்னேடீ.
translit: tēvark kariya vāṉantat tiruttāṇ ṭavañcey perumāṉīr mēvak kukuku kukukuvaṇi vēṇi yuṭaiyī rāmeṉṟēṉ tāvak kukuku kukukukukut tāmē yaintu viḷaṅkavaṇi yēvaṟ kuṇattā yeṉkiṉṟā ritutāṉ cēṭi yeṉṉēṭī.
translation: I said: O Lord who performs the sacred dance of bliss rare for the gods, You wear matted hair adorned with the sound kukuku kukuku. He replied: O woman of submissive nature, the five themselves shine making the sound kukuku kukukukuku. What is this, my friend?
commentary: She hears a rhythmic sound echoing in his matted hair and imitates it playfully, taking it for a charming ornament. He tells her it is the cosmic vibration of the five divine principles, such as the five sacred syllables, echoing through all creation. Speaking as a woman in love, the soul finds the whole universe vibrating within the divine presence.

tamil: கொன்றைச் சடையீர் கொடுங்கோளூர் குறித்தீர் வருதற் கஞ்சுவல்யா
னொன்றப் பெருங்கோ ளென்மீது முரைப்பா ருண்டென் றுணர்ந்தென்றேன்
நன்றப் படியேற் கோளிலியா நகரு முடையே நங்காய்நீ
யின்றச் சுறலென் னென்கின்றா ரிதுதான் சேடி யென்னேடீ.
translit: koṉṟaic caṭaiyīr koṭuṅkōḷūr kuṟittīr varutaṟ kañcuvalyā ṉoṉṟap peruṅkō ḷeṉmītu muraippā ruṇṭeṉ ṟuṇarnteṉṟēṉ naṉṟap paṭiyēṟ kōḷiliyā nakaru muṭaiyē naṅkāynī yiṉṟac cuṟaleṉ ṉeṉkiṉṟā ritutāṉ cēṭi yeṉṉēṭī.
translation: I said: O Lord with matted hair adorned with konrai flowers, You have chosen Kodungolur as Your destination, and I fear to come there knowing people will speak great slander against me. He replied: If that is so, O lady, I also possess the town of Kolili. Why do you fear today? What is this, my friend?
commentary: Both play on the names of real temple towns. She pretends to fear Kodungolur, whose name sounds like cruel slander or harsh planetary luck. He at once offers Kolili, a town whose name literally means free from malice or bad planets. Beneath the teasing lies a promise that whoever seeks God is protected from worldly gossip and cosmic misfortune.

tamil: புரியுஞ் சடையீ ரமர்ந்திடுமூர் புலியூ ரெனிலெம் போல்வார்க்கு
முரியும் புலித்தோ லுடையீர்போ லுறுதற் கியலு மோவென்றேன்
றிரியும் புலியூ ரன்றுநின் போற் றெரிவை யரைக்கண் டிடிற்பயந்தே
யிரியும் புலியூ ரென்கின்றா ரிதுதான் சேடி யென்னேடீ.
translit: puriyuñ caṭaiyī ramarntiṭumūr puliyū reṉilem pōlvārkku muriyum pulittō luṭaiyīrpō luṟutaṟ kiyalu mōveṉṟēṉ ṟiriyum puliyū raṉṟuniṉ pōṟ ṟerivai yaraikkaṇ ṭiṭiṟpayantē yiriyum puliyū reṉkiṉṟā ritutāṉ cēṭi yeṉṉēṭī.
translation: I said: O Lord with twisted matted hair, if the town where You abide is Puliyur, is it possible for women like us to dwell there just like You who wear a stripped tiger skin? He replied: That Puliyur is not a town of roaming tigers, but a town where tigers flee in fear if they see ladies like you. What is this, my friend?
commentary: Puliyur, the famous holy city, means Tiger Town. She jokes that he is safe wrapped in his tiger skin, while a delicate woman would be terrified to live there. He flirts back that her beauty is so striking real tigers would run from her. Light banter like this is a traditional poetic way to speak of the sweet, intimate closeness between the soul and God.

tamil: தெவ்வூர் பொடிக்குஞ் சிறுநகையித் தேவர் தமைநா னீரிருத்த
லெவ்வூ ரென்றே னகைத்தணங்கே யேழூர் நாலூ ரென்றார்பின்
னவ்வூர்த் தொகையி னிருத்தலரி தாமென் றேன்மற் றதிலொவ்வூ
ரிவ்வூ ரெடுத்தா யென்கின்றா ரிதுதான் சேடி யென்னேடீ.
translit: tevvūr poṭikkuñ ciṟunakaiyit tēvar tamainā ṉīrirutta levvū reṉṟē ṉakaittaṇaṅkē yēḻūr nālū reṉṟārpiṉ ṉavvūrt tokaiyi ṉiruttalari tāmeṉ ṟēṉmaṟ ṟatilovvū rivvū reṭuttā yeṉkiṉṟā ritutāṉ cēṭi yeṉṉēṭī.
translation: I asked this God, whose slight smile reduces enemy cities to ash: Which is the town where You reside? He smiled and answered: O beautiful lady, Elur and Nalur. I then said: It is difficult to reside in such a multitude of towns. He replied: From them, you have chosen one town as this town. What is this, my friend?
commentary: Elur and Nalur are real places whose names sound like numbers, Seven Town and Four Town. She takes him literally and complains that no one can settle in so many places at once. He warmly replies that from all these worlds and directions her loving heart has already chosen the one place where he will stay. So the presence that spans the universe makes its permanent home in the devotee's love.

tamil: மணங்கொ ளிதழிச் சடையீர்நீர் வாழும் பதியா தென்றேனின்
குணங்கொண் மொழிகேட் டோரளவு குறைந்த குயிலாம் பதியென்றா
ரணங்கின் மறையூ ராமென்றே னஃதன் றருளோத் தூரிஃது
மிணங்க வுடையே மென்கின்றா ரிதுதான் சேடி யென்னேடீ.
translit: maṇaṅko ḷitaḻic caṭaiyīrnīr vāḻum patiyā teṉṟēṉiṉ kuṇaṅkoṇ moḻikēṭ ṭōraḷavu kuṟainta kuyilām patiyeṉṟā raṇaṅkiṉ maṟaiyū rāmeṉṟē ṉaḵtaṉ ṟaruḷōt tūriḵtu miṇaṅka vuṭaiyē meṉkiṉṟā ritutāṉ cēṭi yeṉṉēṭī.
translation: I said: O Lord with matted hair adorned with fragrant konrai flowers, what is the town where You live? He said: Hearing your fine words, it is the town of the cuckoo reduced by one measure. I asked: Is it the town of the sacred Vedas? He replied: Not that, it is Arulothur, and we possess this in harmony too. What is this, my friend?
commentary: The Lord uses riddles based on bird names and words for scripture to reveal where He lives. The heroine guesses He lives in the town of the Vedas, meaning the ancient religious texts. He corrects her by naming Arulothur, a real temple town whose name means reciting grace. He is gently guiding her away from dry book learning to show that His true home is found in the living experience of divine grace.

tamil: ஆற்றுச் சடையா ரிவர்பலியென் றடைந்தார் நுமதூ ரியாதென்றேன்
சோற்றுத் துறையென் றார்நுமக்குச் சோற்றுக் கருப்பேன் சொலுமென்றேன்
றோற்றுத் திரிவே மன்றுநின்போற் சொல்லுங் கருப்பென் றுலகியம்ப
வேற்றுத் திரியே மென்கின்றா ரிதுதான் சேடி யென்னேடீ.
translit: āṟṟuc caṭaiyā rivarpaliyeṉ ṟaṭaintār numatū riyāteṉṟēṉ cōṟṟut tuṟaiyeṉ ṟārnumakkuc cōṟṟuk karuppēṉ columeṉṟēṉ ṟōṟṟut tirivē maṉṟuniṉpōṟ colluṅ karuppeṉ ṟulakiyampa vēṟṟut tiriyē meṉkiṉṟā ritutāṉ cēṭi yeṉṉēṭī.
translation: The Lord with the river in His matted hair came to me asking for alms. I asked, "What is your town?" He said, "Sotrutthurai." I asked, "Then tell me, why do you suffer a famine of food?" He replied, "We do not wander around defeated, nor do we wander in disguise, whereas the world speaks of a famine like the one you possess." What is this, my friend?
commentary: She teases the Lord for turning up at her door as a beggar. Sotrutthurai, the sacred town He names, means "the port of food," so she asks how a man from there comes to be starving. He turns the joke back on her. The famine the world talks about is her own, a woman wasting away from love-sickness.

tamil: ஓங்குஞ் சடையீர் நெல்வாயி லுடையே மென்றீ ருடையீரேற்
றாங்கும் புகழ்நும் மிடைச்சிறுமை சார்ந்த தெவனீர் சாற்றுமென்றே
னேங்கும் படிநும் மிடைச்சிறுமை யெய்திற் றலதீண் டெமக்கின்றா
லீங்குங் காண்டி ரென்கின்றா ரிதுதான் சேடி யென்னேடீ.
translit: ōṅkuñ caṭaiyīr nelvāyi luṭaiyē meṉṟī ruṭaiyīrēṟ ṟāṅkum pukaḻnum miṭaicciṟumai cārnta tevaṉīr cāṟṟumeṉṟē ṉēṅkum paṭinum miṭaicciṟumai yeytiṟ ṟalatīṇ ṭemakkiṉṟā līṅkuṅ kāṇṭi reṉkiṉṟā ritutāṉ cēṭi yeṉṉēṭī.
translation: I said, "O Lord with towering matted hair, You said You own the town of Nelvayil. If You own it, tell me why Your enduring fame is joined with such smallness in the middle?" He replied, "That smallness in the middle has reached your own waist, making you pine away. We have no such thing here. Look and see for yourself." What is this, my friend?
commentary: Another pun on the name of a sacred town. Nelvayil means "the gate of paddy," so she asks how someone with so much grain ended up so small in the middle, teasing Him about His poverty. He makes her words a compliment and a tease at once. That smallness in the middle is her own famously thin waist.

glossary.def: Agamas. The scriptures of temple worship and doctrine. Vallalar says their truth is known by grace, not by reading.
Ambalam. The hall or open stage where God dances. It is the hall at Chidambaram and, within, the space of consciousness where God is known.
Anavam. The root impurity of the ego, the "I-ness" that veils the soul. The first of the three impurities (malam).
The five syllables. The sacred mantra Na-Ma-Si-Va-Ya (Namasivaya). Vallalar calls it the ultimate refuge for the soul.
Appar. The revered Tamil saint also known as Thirunavukkarasar. Vallalar deeply admired his humble devotion and references the time his desperate song opened the locked doors at Maraikkadu.
Arjuna. The heroic prince of the Mahabharata. Vallalar refers to him to illustrate God's grace, recalling how Siva appeared as a hunter to test and bless him.

Hari. A name for Vishnu, the preserver deity. Vallalar references him to establish the absolute supremacy of Siva, whose pure grace remains beyond the comprehension of even the highest traditional gods.
Arunai. The holy city of Tiruvannamalai. Vallalar yearns to stand in the physical presence of God here to finally calm his restless heart.
ArutPerunJothi. The Vast Grace-Light. Vallalar's name for God, the one infinite Light of grace from which everything comes, open to every living being.
Ayan. A traditional name for Brahma, the creator deity. Vallalar invokes this name to emphasize that even the highest celestial beings must humbly worship the supreme divine light.
Sakkiyar, one of the Saiva saints, who worshipped God each day by throwing a stone at the Siva lingam. Vallalar recalls him to show that God accepts any offering made with a true heart.

Jains. Vallalar recalls the old stories of the Saiva saints and the Jain monks, and names the quarrelling Jains among those his heart turns away from. In his later songs he says that the Grace Light taught him from the beginning that caste, creed and religion are false.
Sambandar. The revered child saint of the Tamil devotional tradition, also called Gnanasambandar. Vallalar references him to illustrate how intimately God responds to a devotee.
Sankara. A name for Siva meaning the bringer of peace. Vallalar invokes this title to contrast God's peaceful protection with the terrifying nature of worldly conflict.
Sanmarkkam. The true path. Vallalar's name for the way of grace, compassion, and direct knowledge of God, open to every living being.
Saraswati. The goddess of speech, arts, and learning. Vallalar praises her as the source of all sacred sound and creative power.
Satguru. The true spiritual master. For Vallalar, God alone is the ultimate teacher who dwells within the soul and guides it toward enlightenment.
Sadasiva. The eternal and supreme form of Siva. Vallalar invokes this name to emphasize a divine nature that remains completely beyond the grasp of traditional deities.
Sakti. Divine energy. In traditional philosophy, this represents the active, creative power of the universe which Vallalar sees as an expression of supreme grace.
Chera. The saint-king Cheraman Perumal, who famously rode a horse to heaven. Vallalar uses his legendary journey to prove that steadfast devotion makes impossible spiritual goals attainable.
Chit Sabhai. The hall of wisdom or divine consciousness. Vallalar identifies this both as the sacred dancing space of the Lord at Chidambaram and the inner sanctum of the human heart.
Chitrambalam. The little hall or the innermost sanctum. Vallalar points to this as both the physical shrine in Thillai and the private space within the human heart where conscious bliss occurs.
Siruthondar. The Saiva saint who proved his devotion by cooking and offering his own son to God disguised as a devotee. Vallalar cites this to show the extreme lengths of pure devotion.
Chidambaram. The supreme space of pure consciousness and a major temple town. Vallalar identifies this as the ultimate spiritual arena where the divine performs the eternal dance of grace.
Siddhanta. The Saiva Siddhanta philosophy. Vallalar later taught that God transcends all such established philosophical systems.
Siddhar. Perfected beings or mystics who possess supernatural powers. Vallalar points out that even these highly advanced masters cannot fully comprehend the supreme nature of God.
Sivakama Valli. The goddess embodying the dynamic energy of divine grace. Vallalar invokes her to represent the profound joy that accompanies the supreme Lord's dance.
Sivakami. The goddess of divine grace and bliss, the consort of Nataraja. She represents the compassionate energy that accompanies the cosmic dance.
Sivam. The supreme divine reality. In Vallalar's poetry this represents the ultimate state of grace and truth, often equated directly with pure spiritual light.
Siva. The supreme Lord. Vallalar uses this name to address the ultimate reality that rules the universe and guides the soul toward supreme light.
Jothi. Light or flame. Vallalar identifies the ultimate divine reality as the supreme Jothi, a self-luminous presence that dispels the deep darkness of human delusion.
Sundarar. The eighth-century Tamil saint. Vallalar frequently references the traditional story where God appeared at Sundarar's wedding with a legal contract to claim him as a bonded servant.
Swayambhu. A self-manifested or uncreated being. Vallalar uses this term to describe the ultimate Divine that exists independently, providing an eternal refuge.
Ezhuthariyum Peruman. The Lord who knows the written destiny. A specific title for the presiding deity at the Otriyur temple, emphasizing that God sees past human ignorance.
Lakshmi. The goddess of wealth. Vallalar uses her to symbolize the supreme spiritual wealth granted to those who possess true devotion.
Indra. The king of the gods in traditional Hindu mythology. Vallalar completely rejects his heavenly paradise, insisting that receiving God's compassion is infinitely better.
Ravana. The mythical demon king. Vallalar refers to his story to show that even the most powerful and arrogant rulers are ultimately humbled by divine might.
Yama. The Hindu god of death and cosmic justice. Vallalar vividly describes his terrifying arrival to underscore the extreme urgency of spiritual awakening.
Jeevakarunyam. Active compassion for all living beings. For Vallalar, relieving the suffering of others is the primary requirement for experiencing true spiritual liberation.
Gajendra. The mythical elephant king whose foot was caught by a crocodile. Vallalar recalls how God rushed to his rescue, proving that sincere surrender always brings divine help.
Kailash. The sacred silver mountain abode of Lord Siva. Vallalar points out that pure chanting unlocks this supreme spiritual realm easily.
Kalahasti. An ancient temple town where the legendary hunter-saint Kannappar offered his eyes to God, representing the pinnacle of unlettered devotion.
Kama. The Hindu god of physical desire. Vallalar references the traditional story where the Lord burned this deity to ashes to show that divine focus burns away worldly lust.
Kanchi. A historic temple city in Tamil Nadu. Vallalar mentions it as one of the sacred earthly sites where the divine presence actively grants grace.
Ganges. The sacred river. Vallalar invokes the image of the Lord holding this river in his hair to symbolize the cooling grace that washes away the heat of worldly suffering.
Karma. The accumulated weight of past actions. Vallalar describes it as a force that turns the human heart into stone, which only divine grace can break.
Kannappar. A legendary hunter-saint who offered chewed meat and his own eyes to God. Vallalar invokes his story to prove that raw devotion matters far more than formal ritual purity.
Murder. Vallalar means the murder of any living being, not only of humans, and condemns it absolutely as a barrier to spiritual life.
Konrai. The golden shower flower. Vallalar frequently mentions this traditional floral garland of the Lord to invoke a familiar, approachable form of the divine.
Guru. Spiritual teacher. Vallalar identifies the supreme divine light as the ultimate guide who dispels human ignorance.
Malam. Filth or spiritual impurity. In Vallalar's poetry, this represents the accumulated ignorance and worldly attachments blocking the soul's path to divine light.

Manikkavasagar. A celebrated saint and poet in the Tamil tradition. Vallalar frequently recalls how God personally intervened to rescue this devotee to demonstrate divine readiness to save a beloved soul.
Maraikkadu. A sacred temple town. Vallalar references the legendary opening of its locked doors by the songs of Appar and Sambandar as proof of the power of sincere devotion.
Markandeyar. An ancient sage. Vallalar invokes the story of God saving this devoted youth from Yama to prove that divine grace can conquer mortality itself.
Madurai. An ancient temple city in southern India. Vallalar references this location as the famous earthly stage where God personally appeared to perform astonishing wonders.
Maya. Illusion or the deceptive nature of material existence. Vallalar identifies this as the force that traps human consciousness in physical desires and blinds it to the divine reality.
Meru. A massive mythical mountain. Vallalar refers to the story of God effortlessly bending this huge stone mountain into a bow to show that divine grace can conquer anything.
Murugan. The warrior-god, considered the son of Siva. Vallalar frequently addresses the supreme divine presence through this specific form in his early devotional phase.
Namasivaya. The sacred five-syllable mantra meaning adoration to Siva. Clinging to this name is the ultimate refuge for a soul completely devoid of merit.
Nandi. The sacred white bull. Vallalar invokes this traditional mount of Lord Siva to represent supreme divine majesty.
Nadam. The primordial sound. Vallalar teaches that the ultimate state of grace is found only when the soul transcends this subtle cosmic vibration.
Nataraja. The supreme dancing Lord of the cosmic hall. Vallalar views this form as the ultimate expression of divine grace and the true destination for the wandering soul.
Sacred ash worn on the body. Vallalar views this ash as a powerful spiritual shield that secures basic worldly needs and symbolizes the complete burning away of all earthly ignorance.
Om. The primordial sacred sound of the universe. Vallalar cries out this syllable as an intimate plea for relief from the poison of earthly sorrow.

Otriyur. The holy temple town by the sea at the northern edge of Chennai, also called Otri. Vallalar walked there to worship day after day in his early years. The word otri also means a pledge or mortgage, a pun the verses play on.
Pasupati. The Lord of all souls. Vallalar invokes this traditional title to describe God as the supreme caretaker and guide for all bound, struggling individuals.
Parvati. The goddess who serves as the consort of the supreme Lord. Vallalar envisions her as the cosmic witness to God's endless dance of existence.
Padambakkanathar. The Lord of Padampakkam, a local name for the deity at the Otriyur temple. Vallalar addresses God by this title to express an intimate and grounded devotion.
Brahma. The creator deity. Vallalar emphasizes that even major cosmic gods like him are unable to fully comprehend the supreme divine flame.
Baseness, moral impurity: living without truth, charity or love for other beings. Vallalar calls himself pulaiyēṉ, a base one; the word describes conduct, never birth.
Puliyur. An ancient name for the sacred town of Chidambaram. Vallalar reveres this town as the earthly location of the golden hall where the divine dances.
Pullirukkuvelur. A sacred temple town in Tamil Nadu renowned for its healing deity, Vaithiyanatha. Vallalar identifies the divine presence enshrined here as the ultimate spiritual medicine.
Rudraksha. Sacred prayer beads. Vallalar compares these beads to precious gems to show that true spiritual wealth replaces the need for worldly ornaments.
Tamil. The language. Vallalar views it as a refined, sacred medium through which God grants grace to sincere devotees.
Tattvas. The physical and mental building blocks of the universe. Vallalar teaches that supreme divine grace transcends every natural law and elemental category.
Thevaram. The foundational Tamil devotional hymns sung by saints like Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar. Vallalar deeply cherished these songs as pure expressions of grace.

Thillai. The sacred temple town of Chidambaram where Siva performs his cosmic dance. Vallalar views this location as a symbol of the ultimate spiritual space where the divine connects with the pure soul.
Thirumullaivayil. A sacred temple town near Chennai. Vallalar frequently visited its shrine and addressed the resident deity directly in his early devotional verses.
Thirunavukkarasar. The revered Tamil saint also known as Appar. Vallalar points to his life as proof that a sincere cry from the heart overpowers religious authority.
Thiruvasagam. The sacred collection of Tamil hymns composed by the saint Manikkavasagar, revered for their intense devotional outpouring.
Thiruvalithayam. A sacred site near Chennai, now called Padi. Vallalar sang intimate verses here, marveling at the contrast between the temple deity's supreme power and humble appearance.
Tiruvarur. A major temple town in Tamil Nadu dedicated to Siva. Vallalar addresses the deity of this shrine intimately as his father and absolute master.
Thyagar. The Great Giver, a famous title for the presiding deity at Otriyur. Vallalar playfully challenges this title by asking why a supposedly generous God refuses to speak a comforting word.

Turiya. The transcendent fourth state of consciousness beyond waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. Vallalar views this as the pure spiritual realm where the soul directly perceives and merges with the supreme Jothi.
Uma. The goddess, representing divine feminine energy. Vallalar invokes her alongside Siva to emphasize the maternal compassion that must always accompany divine power.
The Upanishads. Ancient philosophical scriptures. Vallalar points to the divine light as the ultimate truth shining at the very peak of these sacred texts.
Vaitheeswaran Koil. A famous temple of healing in Tamil Nadu. Vallalar identifies its presiding deity as the ultimate spiritual medicine for the soul.
Vallalar. The author of the Thiru Arutpa. This honorific name meaning "the supremely generous one" was given to Ramalinga Adigal by his followers.
Vadivudaimaanikkam. The Goddess at the Otriyur temple, also called Vadivudai or Vadivambigai. Vallalar praises her as the compassionate mother who continually showers grace on devotees.
Vadavur. The birthplace of the saint Manikkavasagar. Vallalar often uses this as a traditional name to affectionately address or refer to the saint.
The Vedas. The ancient spiritual scriptures. Vallalar teaches that the ultimate divine reality is so profound it escapes the understanding of even these foundational texts.
Vedanta. The philosophical culmination of the Vedas. Vallalar asserts that the supreme divine Light exists infinitely beyond the reach of Vedanta and all other philosophies.
Vinayakar. The elephant-headed Lord, commonly known as Vinayakar. Vallalar points to this form as a focal point for inward meditation to anchor the restless mind.
Bindu. The cosmic seed or point of spiritual light. Vallalar describes it as a subtle threshold that the soul must cross to reach true divine consciousness.

Vishnu. The preserver deity in Hindu tradition. Vallalar references him to establish the absolute supremacy of the ultimate Lord, whose pure grace remains beyond the comprehension of even the highest traditional gods.
